## Main Gate | Phenomenology & psychopathology
> Phenomenology & psychopathology. Source: NPMCN - Phenomenology & Psychopathology 2026.pdf. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Phenomenology and psychopathology
> - Descriptive phenomenology: the precise description and classification of the patient's subjective experience, as they experience it, without theorising about cause.
> - Karl Jaspers — "General Psychopathology" (1913) — father of psychopathology. Key method: empathic understanding (Verstehen) of the patient's experience; distinguished understanding (meaningful connections) from explaining (causal, Erklären).
> - Form vs content: the form (e.g. "this is a delusion", "this is a 3rd-person hallucination") carries diagnostic weight; the content (what it is about) reflects culture and life history.
> - The 4 Ds of abnormality: deviance (from norms), distress, dysfunction, danger.
> - Theories of psychopathology: humanistic (blocked self-actualisation), cognitive (biases), psychodynamic (unconscious conflict), biological (neurochemical/structural).
Q: The lecture defines phenomenology as a term that describes: = The type, value or quality of experiences that human beings have | The causes of mental illness | Brain anatomy | Drug effects | Only psychiatric symptoms
> 'It is a term that describes the type, value or quality of experiences that humans beings have.' It is not used only in psychiatry.
Q: Karl Jaspers described psychiatric symptoms comprehensively between: = 1910–1913 | 1845–1850 | 1893–1899 | 1938–1945 | 1960–1965
> 'Karl Jaspers is the father of psychopathology with his comprehensive methodological description of many psychiatric symptoms between 1910–1913.'
Q: Which is NOT one of the 4 Ds of psychopathology? = Delusion | Deviance | Distress | Dysfunction | Dangerous
> 'Deviance from norm; Distress in patient or others; Dysfunction limiting or disabling; Dangerous — can harm patient or others.'

### Disorders of perception — 1: sensory distortions (a real object, perceived differently)
> - Intensity: hyperaesthesia (louder, brighter — anxiety, migraine, hallucinogens, mania), hypoaesthesia (dulled — depression, delirium).
> - Quality: colour changes (xanthopsia — yellow vision in digoxin toxicity), changed taste.
> - Size/shape (dysmegalopsia): micropsia (smaller), macropsia (larger), distorted shape — temporal/parietal lobe lesions, epilepsy, migraine ("Alice in Wonderland" syndrome), eye disease.
> - Time: time seeming to stand still or speed up; telescoping of past events (TLE, dementia).
> - Derealisation — the world feels unreal, as if behind glass.
Q: A sensory distortion differs from a sensory deception because in distortion: = There is a real external object perceived in a distorted way | There is no external object | It is always a hallucination | It only occurs in schizophrenia | It is voluntary
> 'Sensory Distortions: there is a real external object, but which is perceived in a distorted way.'
Q: Seeing objects as smaller than they are is called: = Micropsia (Lilliputian) | Macropsia | Derealisation | Pareidolia | Hyperaesthesia
> 'Changes in spatial form (dysmegalopsia): smaller sizes / lilliputian / micropsia; macropsia — larger sizes.'
Q: Telescoping — distant events seeming quite recent — occurs in: = Temporal lobe epilepsy and dementias | Mania | OCD | Anxiety | Normal grief only
> 'Telescoping (distant events seem quite recent) e.g. temporal lobe epilepsy, dementias; receding as in schizophrenia.'

### Disorders of perception — 2: illusions (misperception of a real stimulus)
> - Completion illusion — inattention fills in gaps (misreading a word); corrected on attention.
> - Affect illusion — mood colours perception (a frightened person on a dark road sees a coat as a man) — fear, delirium.
> - Pareidolia — vivid images seen in vague stimuli (faces in clouds or fire); increase with attention rather than disappearing; occur in normal people, delirium, and Lewy body dementia.
> - Illusions alone are not diagnostic of psychosis.
Q: An illusion is produced when: = Stimuli from a perceived object combine with one's mental image to give a false perception | There is no stimulus at all | A memory is falsified | Thoughts are inserted | A person lies
> 'Stimuli from a perceived object are combined with one's mental image to produce a false perception or to misinterpret a situation, e.g. in anxiety or delirium.'

### Hallucinations — perception without an object
> - Definition (Esquirol): a perception without an external stimulus, experienced as real, in external objective space, through the normal senses, and not under voluntary control.
> - Pseudohallucination (Kandinsky; Jaspers): lacks the full quality of real perception — typically located in inner subjective space ("in my head", "in my mind's eye") and/or recognised as not real; seen in grief, dissociation, PTSD, personality disorder — not specific for psychosis.
> - Modality clues: auditory → schizophrenia, mood disorders; visual → organic (delirium, Lewy body, drugs, Charles Bonnet); tactile/formication → cocaine, alcohol withdrawal; olfactory/gustatory → temporal lobe epilepsy, depression (smells of rotting).
> - Special types:
> - Functional hallucination — triggered by a real stimulus in the same modality (hears voices only when the tap runs), both perceived at once.
> - Reflex hallucination — a stimulus in one modality produces a hallucination in another (synaesthesia-like).
> - Extracampine — outside the sensory field (sees someone behind him).
> - Hypnagogic (falling asleep) / hypnopompic (waking) — normal; common in narcolepsy.
> - Autoscopy — seeing oneself (heautoscopy, Doppelgänger).
> - Lilliputian — tiny people (alcohol withdrawal, anticholinergics).
Q: The lecture defines a hallucination as: = An involuntary perceptual experience without an object | A misinterpreted real stimulus | A false belief | A vivid memory | A voluntary image
> 'Hallucinations — this is an involuntary perceptual experience without an object; could be visual, tactile, auditory, somatic, gustatory.'
Q: According to the lecture, pseudohallucinations: = Do not necessarily indicate psychopathology | Always indicate schizophrenia | Are always visual | Only occur in delirium | Are the same as illusions
> 'Pseudo hallucinations — their presence does not necessarily indicate psychopathology, unlike true hallucinations, which could be indicative of serious mental illness.'
Q: A man hears voices only when the tap runs, hearing both. This is a: = Functional hallucination | Reflex hallucination | Extracampine hallucination | Pseudohallucination | Illusion
> Functional — same modality, both perceived. Reflex ＝ different modality.
Q: Which hallucination most suggests temporal lobe epilepsy? = Olfactory | Third-person auditory | Running commentary | Hypnagogic | Lilliputian
> Olfactory/gustatory — uncinate fits.

### Disorders of thought — stream (rate and flow)
> - Flight of ideas — rapid shifts of topic linked by chance associations, clang (rhymes) and puns, but each step is understandable — mania.
> - Pressure of speech — increased quantity and rate; hard to interrupt.
> - Retardation/inhibition of thought — slowed, impoverished — depression.
> - Circumstantiality — reaches the goal eventually, via unnecessary detail — obsessional personality, epilepsy, learning disability, anxiety.
> - Tangentiality — answers drift off and never return to the point.
> - Thought block — sudden total stop of the train of thought with a blank mind; patient may explain it as thought withdrawal — schizophrenia.
Q: Circumstantiality is described in the lecture as: = A convoluted path to the goal of thought | Sudden stop in thinking | Thoughts removed from the mind | Repetition of a word | Fusion of ideas
> 'Circumstantiality (convoluted path to goal of thought or idea)' — a disorder of the stream of thought.

### Disorders of thought — possession
> - Thought alienation (first-rank symptoms): insertion (thoughts put in by an outside agency), withdrawal (taken out), broadcasting (others can hear/know them). The patient believes the thoughts are not their own — schizophrenia.
> - Obsessions — recurrent, intrusive, ego-dystonic thoughts/images/impulses that the person recognises as their own (unlike insertion), finds senseless and resists; cause anxiety. Compulsions — repetitive acts done to reduce that anxiety.
> - Key distinction: obsession ＝ "my own unwanted thought"; thought insertion ＝ "someone else's thought in my head".
Q: The experience of thought alienation is: = Ego-dystonic and distressing | Ego-syntonic and pleasant | Voluntary | A normal experience | Only in OCD
> 'Thought Alienation — thoughts generated are believed to be foreign/strange and outside their control. The experience is ego-dystonic and distressing.'
Q: The belief that one's thoughts are shared with the environment is: = Thought broadcasting | Thought insertion | Thought withdrawal | Thought blocking | Flight of ideas
> 'Thought broadcasting – shared to their environment; insertion – imported into the person; withdrawal – removed from the mind.'
Q: Compulsions are described in the lecture as: = Repetitive actions emanating from obsessional thoughts | Intrusive thoughts | Inserted thoughts | Hallucinated commands | Delusions
> 'Compulsions — are the repetitive actions emanating from obsessional thoughts or being carried out due to the obsessional thinking.'

### Disorders of continuity
> - Perseveration — inappropriate persistence of a response after the stimulus has changed (repeats the previous answer to a new question) — organic brain disease (frontal lobe, dementia), also schizophrenia.
> - Verbigeration (verbal stereotypy) — senseless repetition of the same word or phrase regardless of context — chronic schizophrenia, catatonia, organic states.
> - Echolalia — repeating the examiner's words — catatonia, autism, dementia.
> - Logoclonia — repeating the last syllable of a word (Alzheimer's).
> - Palilalia — repeating one's own words with increasing speed (Parkinsonism).
Q: An idea that continues to persist even when no longer relevant is: = Perseveration | Verbal stereotypy | Obsession | Compulsion | Thought block
> 'Perseveration — idea continues to persist even when no longer relevant.' Verbal stereotypy ＝ same word regardless of situation.
Q: Repetition of the same word regardless of the situation is: = Verbal stereotypy | Perseveration | Echolalia | Neologism | Palilalia
> 'Verbal stereotypy — repetition of same word regardless of the situation.'

### Formal thought disorder — disturbed form of thinking (schizophrenia, organic states)
> - Schneider's terms: derailment (thought slides onto a subsidiary track), substitution (major thought replaced by a subsidiary one), omission (senseless gaps), fusion (heterogeneous ideas interwoven), drivelling (elements jumbled, the order lost); desultory thinking (grammatical but purposeless).
> - Cameron's terms: overinclusion (can't keep conceptual boundaries — irrelevant ideas included), asyndesis (lack of genuine causal links), metonyms, interpenetration of themes.
> - Goldstein: concrete thinking — inability to abstract (proverb "people in glass houses…" interpreted literally) — schizophrenia, organic brain damage, learning disability.
> - Bleuler: loosening of associations ("knight's move" thinking).
> - Severe forms: word salad (schizophasia), neologisms.
> - Also: condensation, displacement, misuse of symbols.
Q: Two ideas with a theme in common fused into one false concept is: = Condensation | Displacement | Fusion | Substitution | Omission
> 'Condensation — two ideas with a theme in common are fused into one false concept.' Fusion ＝ diverse, unrelated ideas woven together.
Q: Using the concrete aspects of a symbol simplistically instead of its symbolic meaning is: = Concretisation | Misuse of symbols | Overinclusion | Drivelling | Displacement
> 'Concretization — involves using the concrete aspects of the symbol in a simplistic way instead of their symbolic meaning (concrete thinking).'
Q: Including many concepts and themes irrelevant to the task at hand is: = Overinclusion | Derailment | Desultory thinking | Omission | Condensation
> 'Overinclusion — involving so many concepts, attitudes, themes that are irrelevant to the task/topic at hand.'
Q: Speech that is grammatically correct but lacking plan or purpose is: = Desultory thinking | Drivelling | Fusion | Word salad | Substitution
> 'Desultory thinking — idea is grammatically correct but lacking in plan or purpose.' Drivelling ＝ repeated attempts to weave a concept without achieving it.
Q: Current ideas irrelevantly replaced by previously discussed ideas is: = Substitution | Omission | Derailment | Displacement | Perseveration
> 'Substitution — current ideas are irrelevantly replaced with previously discussed ideas.'

### Delusions — content of thought
> - Definition (Jaspers' three criteria): a belief held with extraordinary conviction/subjective certainty, incorrigible by experience or counter-argument, and with impossible or false content; plus out of keeping with the person's cultural and educational background (vital in Nigeria — witchcraft beliefs may be shared culturally).
> - Primary (autochthonous) delusions — arise de novo, not understandable from other experiences — schizophrenia. Forms:
> - delusional mood (Wahnstimmung) — a sense that something sinister is going on, before the delusion crystallises;
> - delusional perception — normal percept → sudden delusional meaning (first-rank);
> - delusional memory; autochthonous delusion (sudden idea).
> - Secondary delusions — understandable from another experience (mood, hallucinations): guilt in depression, grandiosity in mania.
> - Systematised delusions — a logically connected network built on one false premise (delusional disorder).
> - Overvalued idea (Wernicke) — a reasonable but emotionally charged belief that dominates life (e.g. anorexia "I'm fat", hypochondriasis); not held with delusional incorrigibility.
Q: Erroneous thoughts that arise de novo within the patient are: = Primary delusions | Secondary delusions | Systematised delusions | Overvalued ideas | Obsessions
> 'Primary Delusions – erroneous thoughts that arise de-novo within patient. Secondary — arising from some other morbid experience.'
Q: Delusions in which daily life is logically built on a series of errors of thought are: = Systematised | Primary | Secondary | Nihilistic | Mood-congruent
> 'Systematized delusions — smaller units of life's daily operations is logically built on series of errors of thoughts into a way of living.'
Q: Which is not one of Jaspers' criteria for a delusion? = Shared by the person's cultural group | Extraordinary conviction | Not amenable to argument | False or impossible content | Subjective certainty
> A culturally shared belief is not a delusion.
Q: A woman with anorexia insists she is fat. This is best described as: = Overvalued idea | Primary delusion | Secondary delusion | Obsession | Hallucination
> Overvalued idea (Wernicke).

### Delusional themes
> - Persecutory (commonest overall), reference (TV talks about me), grandiose (mania), guilt, poverty, nihilistic (Cotard's — depression), hypochondriacal/somatic, jealousy (Othello syndrome — alcohol, highest homicide risk), erotomanic (de Clérambault's — usually a woman believing a higher-status man loves her), infestation (Ekbom's — delusional parasitosis), control/passivity (first-rank), religious, misidentification.
> - Mood-congruent themes (guilt, poverty, nihilism in depression; grandiosity in mania) point to a mood disorder with psychotic features.
Q: Which is NOT a delusional theme listed in the lecture? = Obsessional | Infidelity | Love | Poverty | Nihilistic
> Themes: persecution, infidelity, love, ill health, guilt, grandiose, poverty, nihilistic. Obsessions are not delusions.

### Delusional misidentification syndromes
> - Capgras (1923) — a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor (hypo-identification). Schizophrenia, dementia, right-hemisphere lesions.
> - Fregoli — a persecutor is disguising themselves as different strangers (hyper-identification).
> - Intermetamorphosis — people change into one another, physically and psychologically.
> - Syndrome of subjective doubles — a double of oneself exists and acts independently.
> - Reduplicative paramnesia (Pick) — a place has been duplicated (two identical hospitals).
> - All suggest possible organic (right-hemisphere/frontal) pathology — examine and image.
Q: Belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor is: = Capgras syndrome | Fregoli syndrome | Cotard syndrome | Couvade syndrome | Ekbom syndrome
> Capgras — impostor. Fregoli — a persecutor disguised as strangers.

### Disorders of speech
> - Mutism — no speech in a conscious person: catatonia/stupor, severe depression, conversion, elective (selective) mutism (children — speaks only in some settings), akinetic mutism (organic).
> - Vorbeireden (talking past the point) / approximate answers — the answer shows the question was understood but is wrong ("How many legs has a cow?" — "Five") — the hallmark of Ganser syndrome (prisoners awaiting trial; dissociative), also schizophrenia, organic states.
> - Neologisms — new words, or old words with a private meaning — schizophrenia, aphasia.
> - Word salad / schizophasia — incoherent jumble.
> - Aphasia — Broca's (expressive, non-fluent, comprehension intact) vs Wernicke's (receptive, fluent but meaningless, poor comprehension — can be mistaken for psychosis).
> - Stammering/stuttering, dysarthria (motor speech).
Q: Elective mutism is: = Refusal to speak to certain people or in certain places | Total loss of speech from a stroke | Speech in neologisms | Stammering | Mutism in catatonia
> 'Elective mutism is refusal to speak to certain people or in certain places. Hysterical mutism (aphonia) — refusal to speak as a way of coping with stress.'
Q: Giving the correct answer to an imaginary question similar to the one asked is: = Vorbeireden (talking past the point) | Neologism | Schizophasia | Aphasia | Echolalia
> 'Talking past the point (Vorbeireden) – person gives correct answer to an imaginary question similar to the one they were asked, e.g. in hysteria, schizophrenia, PTSD.'
Q: In schizophasia (word salad), the lecture notes the person: = Can still carry out coordinated actions that don't involve words | Cannot perform any coordinated action | Is always unconscious | Has normal speech | Has aphasia
> '…profoundly confusing despite that the person is able to carry out coordinated actions that does not involve the use of words.'

### Disorders of memory
> - Stages: registration (encoding) → retention (storage) → retrieval (recall/recognition).
> - Types: sensory; short-term/working (7 ± 2 items, seconds–minutes); long-term — explicit/declarative (episodic, semantic — hippocampus/medial temporal lobe) and implicit/procedural (skills — basal ganglia, cerebellum).
> - Retrograde amnesia — events before the insult. Anterograde amnesia — inability to lay down new memories after it (Korsakoff's, hippocampal damage).
> - Ribot's law — in organic amnesia, recent memories are lost first, remote ones preserved.
> - Psychogenic (dissociative) amnesia — loss of personal identity and autobiographical memory with preserved general knowledge; patchy, related to trauma — the opposite of organic amnesia.
> - Korsakoff's syndrome — anterograde amnesia + confabulation, intact immediate recall and intellect, due to thiamine deficiency (mammillary bodies, dorsomedial thalamus).
Q: Which type of memory lasts only seconds and handles intake of external stimuli? = Sensory memory | Long-term memory | Short-term memory | Procedural memory | Semantic memory
> 'Sensory memory — very brief (seconds), perceptual, and is for intake and processing of external stimuli.'
Q: The lecture's four steps of memory formation (the 4 Rs) are: = Registration, retention, retrieval, recall | Reading, recording, rehearsing, recall | Recognition, repetition, retention, reproduction | Registration, rehearsal, recognition, review | Retention, revision, recall, reflection
> 'The process of remembering or recall (RRRR) occurs in four steps: Registration, Retention, Retrieval, Recall.'
Q: Inability to recall events after the injury is: = Anterograde amnesia | Retrograde amnesia | Psychogenic amnesia | Screen memory | Confabulation
> 'Anterograde Amnesia — inability to recall events that happen after the injury (loss in memory encoding).' Retrograde ＝ events before the injury (loss of retrieval).
Q: Amnesia from defensive repression is called: = Katathymic amnesia | Organic amnesia | Anterograde amnesia | Transient global amnesia | Ribot's amnesia
> 'Psychogenic Amnesia — arises from severe psychic or physical trauma, malingering, dissociative states, defense repression (katathymic amnesia).'
Q: In the lecture, Korsakoff's syndrome is classified under organic amnesia from: = Subacute and chronic coarse brain disease | Acute brain disease only | Psychogenic causes | Depression | Anxiety
> Subacute: Korsakoff's psychosis in alcohol dependence, delirium, epilepsy, MS. Chronic coarse brain disease: Korsakoff's syndrome, tumours, dementias.
Q: Ribot's law states that in organic amnesia: = Recent memories are lost first | Remote memories are lost first | Procedural memory goes first | Identity goes first | All memory is lost equally
> Recent before remote. Loss of personal identity suggests dissociative amnesia.

### Memory distortions (paramnesias)
> - Confabulation — falsification of memory in clear consciousness, filling gaps with imagined, often plausible, contradictory material — Korsakoff's, frontal lesions.
> - Retrospective falsification — unconsciously distorting past memories to fit the present mood (depressed people recall failures).
> - False memory — vivid memory of events that never happened ("source amnesia").
> - Screen memory — a tolerable memory covering a painful one.
> - Pseudologia fantastica — fluent, plausible pathological lying, partly believed by the teller (antisocial/histrionic traits, factitious disorder).
> - Munchausen syndrome (Asher, 1951) — severe factitious disorder with hospital wandering and false histories; by proxy (Meadow, 1977) ＝ factitious disorder imposed on another (a carer induces illness in a child).
> - Déjà vu (false familiarity) / jamais vu (false unfamiliarity) — normal people, temporal lobe epilepsy aura.
> - Cryptomnesia — not recognising a memory as a memory (unintended plagiarism).
> - Hypermnesia: flashbulb memories, flashbacks (intrusive, re-lived — PTSD).
Q: Depressed people remembering past failures in exaggerated ways and forgetting successes is: = Retrospective falsification | False memory | Screen memory | Confabulation | Cryptomnesia
> 'Retrospective Falsification — depressed persons remember their past failures in exaggerated ways and forget their past successes. Hysterical persons do the opposite.'
Q: Recalling only part of a true memory because the whole is too painful is: = Screen memory | Confabulation | Déjà vu | False reconnaissance | Hypermnesia
> 'Screen Memory — only recalls part of the true memory because the entirety of the true memory is too painful to recall.'
Q: Confabulation is: = Filling in gaps in memory with imagined, untrue experiences | Pathological lying without brain disease | Forgetting one is remembering | A sense of familiarity | Approximate answers
> 'Confabulation — filling-in of gaps in memory by imagined and untrue experiences. Some of the statements made will be obviously contradictory.'
Q: Pseudologia fantastica occurs in people: = Without organic brain pathology, e.g. borderline or antisocial PD | With Korsakoff's syndrome | With dementia only | With epilepsy only | With delirium
> 'Pseudologia fantastica is frequent, fluent plausible lying… in those without organic brain pathology — borderline or antisocial personality disorder or hysterias.'
Q: Not remembering that one is remembering external information, which can lead to plagiarism, is: = Cryptomnesia | Déjà vu | Retrospective delusion | Screen memory | Flashback
> 'Cryptamnesia — the experience of not remembering that one is remembering an external information and believing the thoughts are arising de novo. It can lead to Plagiarism.'
Q: Patients who backdate their delusional experiences despite evidence of recent illness show: = Retrospective delusions | False memory | Confabulation | Déjà vu | Screen memory
> 'Retrospective delusions — found in some patients… who backdate their delusional experiences in spite of the clear evidence that the illness is of recent origin.'
Q: In Munchausen's syndrome by proxy: = A parent produces a factitious illness in their dependent, usually a child | The patient invents their own illness | A father has pregnancy symptoms | A person gives approximate answers | A twin imitates the other
> 'Munchausen by proxy is a form of this condition where a parent produces a factitious illness in their dependent, usually their child.'
Q: Sudden, unsolicited, brief, intrusive memories of a traumatic event are: = Flashbacks | Flashbulb memories | Déjà vu | Screen memories | Confabulations
> 'Flashbacks are sudden, unsolicited, brief, intrusive memories… of a previous personal traumatic event… e.g. PTSD.' Flashbulb memories ＝ vivid, detailed, emotional memories.
Q: Vivid, detailed, long-lasting memories tied to intense emotions are: = Flashbulb memories | Flashbacks | False memories | Screen memories | Pseudologia
> 'Flashbulb memories are those memories that are vivid, detailed and long-lasting, usually associated with intense emotions or events.'

### Disorders of emotion
> - Mood ＝ sustained; affect ＝ immediate, observed expression; feelings ＝ transient.
> - Blunted/flattened affect — reduced range and intensity (schizophrenia negative symptoms, depression, parkinsonism, antipsychotics).
> - Incongruous (inappropriate) affect — emotion out of keeping with thought content (laughing while describing a death) — schizophrenia.
> - Labile affect — rapid swings (organic brain disease, mania, borderline PD); emotional incontinence (pseudobulbar affect after stroke/MS).
> - Apathy — loss of feeling and motivation (frontal lesions, schizophrenia, chronic cannabis use).
> - La belle indifférence — inappropriate lack of concern about severe disability — conversion (dissociative neurological symptom) disorder; not specific (also seen in organic illness).
> - Alexithymia (Sifneos) — difficulty identifying and describing one's emotions — somatic symptom disorders.
> - Anhedonia — loss of pleasure (depression, schizophrenia).
Q: Which group is NOT listed in the lecture as showing apathy? = People with mania | Socially deprived persons | Cannabis users | Prisoners | People with schizophrenia
> 'Apathy… occurs in socially deprived persons, those with cannabis abuse, prisoners and those living with schizophrenia.' Mania shows elation and overactivity.
Q: A total lack of distress in reaction to severe or traumatic events happening to oneself is: = Belle indifférence (dissociation of affect) | Apathy | Blunted affect | Euphoria | Alexithymia
> 'Dissociation of Affect e.g. in belle indifférence, there is total lack of psychological distress in reaction to severe or traumatic incidents happening to the person personally.'
Q: Low mood or fear in response to a happy occasion is an example of: = Abnormal expression of emotion | Abnormal emotional reaction | Normal grief | Euthymia | Dissociation of affect
> 'Abnormal expressions of emotion — very different from the average normal reaction e.g. fear, anxiety, worry, low mood… in response to a happy occasion.' Abnormal reactions are understandable but excessive.

### Disorders of the experience of self
> - Jaspers' four formal characteristics of self-awareness:
> 1. activity — awareness of being the agent of one's actions (lost in passivity phenomena);
> 2. unity — being one person at a time (lost in dissociative identity, "possession");
> 3. identity/continuity — the same person over time (schizophrenic "I'm not who I was");
> 4. boundaries — distinction between self and the world (lost in thought broadcasting, transitivism).
> - Depersonalisation — feeling oneself is unreal, detached, like a robot; derealisation — the world seems unreal. Insight retained ("as if"). Seen in anxiety, depression, TLE, drugs, sleep deprivation, and depersonalisation-derealisation disorder.
> - Mentalisation — capacity to understand one's own and others' mental states (impaired in borderline PD; basis of MBT).
Q: A person with schizophrenia feeling they are not the same person as before the illness shows a disturbance of: = Continuity of self | Self-unity | Ego boundaries only | Consciousness | Memory
> 'Disturbance of the continuity of self — the individuals with schizophrenia may feel that they are not the same person that they were before the illness.'
Q: Feeling one is two persons, as in demoniac possession or multiple personality, is a disturbance of: = Self-unity | Continuity of self | Activity | Mentalisation | Orientation
> 'Disturbances in the awareness of self-unity — the person feels as if they are two persons e.g. delusions of demoniac possession, dissociative/conversion disorders, schizophrenia, multiple personality disorder.'
Q: Mentalisation is the ability to: = Correctly understand and interpret other people's mental states | Remember accurately | Solve mathematical problems | Hear voices | Control movements
> 'Mentalization — the ability of an individual to correctly understand and interpret the mental or psychological states of other people.'

### Disorders of consciousness
> - Clouding of consciousness — reduced clarity and awareness, drowsiness, poor attention and orientation — delirium hallmark.
> - Delirium — acute, fluctuating clouding with inattention, disorientation, illusions/hallucinations (especially visual), worse at night (sundowning).
> - Twilight state — restricted (narrowed) consciousness with preserved automatic behaviour, followed by amnesia — epilepsy (post-ictal), alcohol (pathological intoxication), dissociation.
> - Dream-like (oneiroid) state — vivid dream-like experiences with clouding.
> - Stupor — akinesis and mutism with relatively preserved consciousness (eyes often follow the examiner) — catatonia, depression, dissociative, organic.
> - Levels: alert → drowsy → stupor → coma (use GCS).
Q: General lowering of consciousness without hallucinations, illusions, delusions or restlessness is called: = Torpor | Twilight state | Stupor | Delirium | Coma
> 'Lowering of Consciousness — psychologically numbed… without hallucinations, illusions, delusions nor restlessness… Sometimes called turpor.'
Q: Reduced awareness limited to specific ideas and attitudes, as in twilight states, is: = Restriction of consciousness | Lowering of consciousness | Clouding | Stupor | Hypervigilance
> 'Restriction of consciousness — reduction in awareness is limited to some specific ideas and attitudes… e.g. twilight states.'
Q: Which statement about stupor and excitement is made in the lecture? = Though opposite, they often occur in the same psychiatric disorders | They never occur in the same illness | Stupor only occurs in depression | Excitement only occurs in delirium | Both require clouding
> 'Stupor and excitement, which although are opposed patterns of behaviour, often occur in the same psychiatric disorders.'
Q: Psychogenic stupor after wartime bombardment is described as being: = Paralysed with fear | Drunk with fear | Euphoric | Delirious | Psychotic
> 'The patient is, as it were, 'paralysed with fear' and is unable to retreat from danger.'

### Motor and behavioural disorders
> - Mannerism — an odd, stilted exaggeration of a normal, goal-directed movement (a peculiar salute instead of a handshake).
> - Stereotypy — a repetitive, non-goal-directed movement or posture (rocking) — schizophrenia, autism, intellectual disability.
> - Catatonic phenomena:
> - automatic obedience — follows every instruction regardless of consequence;
> - Mitgehen — moves the body in the direction of the slightest pressure ("anglepoise lamp");
> - Mitmachen — allows the body to be put in any position, then returns it;
> - waxy flexibility (flexibilitas cerea) — limbs held where placed, with plastic resistance;
> - negativism — motiveless resistance; Gegenhalten — opposing passive movement with equal force;
> - ambitendency — starts a movement then stops, as if torn;
> - echopraxia/echolalia, posturing, psychological pillow (head held off the bed).
> - Tics — sudden, repetitive, non-rhythmic, briefly suppressible.
> - Antipsychotic-induced: acute dystonia (hours–days), akathisia (days–weeks; inner restlessness), parkinsonism (weeks), tardive dyskinesia (months–years).
Q: In delusions of passivity, movements are experienced as: = Foreign or produced against one's will by an outside influence | Under full personal control | Absent | Painful | Voluntary but slow
> 'Alienation of motor acts e.g. in Delusions of passivity where the person experiences their movement as foreign or produced against their will by some foreign influence. Secondary delusions may then explain it (witchcraft, radioactive waves, TV, internet).'
Q: A manneristic posture is: = An odd exaggeration of a normal posture | A rigidly maintained maladaptive posture | Waxy flexibility | A tic | Opisthotonus
> 'A manneristic posture is an odd exaggeration of a normal posture. A stereotyped posture is a rigidly maintained maladaptive posture.'
Q: Excessive compliance with instructions regardless of consequences is: = Automatic obedience | Negativism | Perseveration | Ambitendency | Akathisia
> 'Excessive compliance to instructions… without due regard to the consequences — called automatic obedience; seen in echolalia, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, dementia, catatonia.'
Q: Which antipsychotic side effect is described as restlessness or inability to keep still? = Akathisia | Acute dystonia | Tardive dyskinesia | Parkinsonism | Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
> 'Akathisia (restlessness or inability to keep still), acute dystonia (sustained muscle spasm), tardive dyskinesia (repetitive purposeless movements of mouth, tongue, face).'
Q: Spiteful, childish behaviour such as pulling chairs away is described in: = Hebephrenic schizophrenia | Paranoid schizophrenia | Mania | Depression | Catatonia
> 'Hebephrenic schizophrenia behave spitefully childishly — may pull chairs away from other patients who are about to sit down.'

### Eponymous syndromes — the "define these" list
> - Briquet's syndrome — chronic multiple somatic complaints (old name for somatisation disorder).
> - Blocq's disease — astasia-abasia: inability to stand or walk normally despite normal leg function in bed (conversion).
> - Charles Bonnet syndrome — complex visual hallucinations in visually impaired, cognitively intact elderly, with insight.
> - Cotard's — nihilistic delusions (dead, rotting, no organs).
> - Couvade — the male partner experiences pregnancy symptoms (nausea, abdominal pain).
> - De Clérambault's — erotomania.
> - Diogenes syndrome — extreme self-neglect and hoarding in the elderly, often with frontal impairment.
> - Ekbom's — delusional parasitosis (also the name for restless legs syndrome — Willis-Ekbom).
> - Ganser syndrome — approximate answers (Vorbeireden), clouding, pseudohallucinations, conversion symptoms; prisoners.
> - Othello — morbid delusional jealousy.
> - Culture-bound syndromes — e.g. brain fag (West African students: head pain/heat, poor concentration from studying), koro (penis retracting — SE Asia), amok, dhat, susto. ICD-11/DSM-5 now speak of cultural concepts of distress.
Q: Blocq's disease refers to: = Astasia-abasia | Somatisation disorder | Erotomania | Self-neglect | Delusional parasitosis
> Blocq's disease — astasia-abasia (conversion). Briquet's ＝ somatisation; De Clérambault's ＝ erotomania; Diogenes ＝ self-neglect; Ekbom's ＝ parasitosis.
Q: Complex visual hallucinations with insight in a visually impaired elderly person suggest: = Charles Bonnet syndrome | Lewy body dementia | Schizophrenia | Delirium | Cotard's
> Charles Bonnet syndrome — visual impairment, intact cognition, insight preserved.
Q: Brain fag syndrome is classically described in: = West African students | South-East Asian men | Latin American women | Inuit hunters | Japanese workers
> West African (often Nigerian) students — head heat, poor concentration with study (Prince, 1960).

### Mixed questions: Phenomenology & psychopathology
> Questions from the lecture that are not tied to one summary point.
Q: Under which theory is psychopathology a failure of self-realisation due to stifling? = Humanistic | Cognitive | Psychodynamic | Organic | Behavioural
> 'Failure of self realization due to stifling (Humanistic theory); cognitive biases (Cognitive); unconscious conflict (Psychodynamic); biochemical and structural imbalances (Organic).'
Q: Unconscious conflict as the basis of psychopathology belongs to which theory? = Psychodynamic | Humanistic | Cognitive | Psychobiological | Social learning
> Psychodynamic theory — unconscious conflict.
Q: Thinking that attempts to solve a problem using de novo and received information is: = Rational or conceptual thinking | Undirected fantasy thinking | Imaginative thinking | Autistic thinking | Magical thinking
> 'Rational thinking or conceptual thinking, which attempts to solve a problem (de-novo and received).'
Q: Which is NOT one of the five types of thought disorder in the lecture? = Intensity | Stream | Content | Possession | Continuity
> Disorders of: stream, content, possession, continuity, form (formation) of thought.
Q: According to the lecture, cognitive impairment leads to loss of the ability to think and act: = Rationally, logically and appropriately within a context, culture or community | Creatively | Quickly only | Emotionally | Violently
> '…which may lead to loss in ability to think and act rationally, logically and appropriately within a given context, culture or in a community.'

> Say: Rapport. “Sometimes, when we go through stressful situations, we tend to respond in certain ways. I would like to ask about how you deal with stress.”

Which phase is this line from? - Suppression: “Do you make a conscious effort to push unwanted thoughts or feelings aside until later?” - Altruism: “Do you cope by focusing on the needs of others?” -… = Mature defences (SASH + anticipation) | Open | Neurotic defences | Immature defences | Close
> What to say: - Suppression: “Do you make a conscious effort to push unwanted thoughts or feelings aside until later?” - Altruism: “Do you cope by focusing on the needs of others?” - Anticipation: “When facing something difficult, do you imagine what it will be like and plan how to cope?” - Sublimation: unacceptable impulses turned into acceptable ones (an aggressive person becomes a boxer). - Humour: “Are you able to laugh at yourself?”

> Say: - Idealisation: exaggerating the good qualities of a person or situation to avoid disappointment. - Reaction formation: behaving in the opposite way to anxiety-provoking feelings. - Undoing: trying to cancel an unacceptable thought or act with the opposite behaviour. - Isolation of affect: “Do people say you don’t show emotions?”

> What to say: - Displacement: redirecting feelings to a less threatening target. - Denial: refusing to accept an unwanted reality. - Dissociation: feeling disconnected from thoughts, feelings or surroundings. - Devaluation: undervaluing self or others to manage inadequacy. - Projection: “Do you often feel people mistreat you?” - Passive aggression, splitting, somatisation, acting out.
