> Using jargon with the patient instead of plain examples.

### Bonus drill: Definitions & psychopathology
> Psychopathology is the language of psychiatry. Descriptive psychopathology (Karl Jaspers) separates FORM from CONTENT.
> - Form = the type of experience (a hallucination, a delusion, an obsession).
> - Content = what it is about (voices about witchcraft, a belief of being poisoned).
> Exams reward naming the form precisely. Sort every phenomenon into its family: perception (hallucination, illusion, pseudohallucination), thought content (delusion, overvalued idea, obsession), self-experience (depersonalisation, derealisation, passivity) and memory (confabulation).
Q: Delusion = A fixed, false belief held despite contrary evidence and out of keeping with the person's culture | A fixed, false belief held despite contrary evidence, even when shared by the person's culture :: Culturally shared beliefs are excluded; a delusion must be out of keeping with the person's culture | A false belief held with some doubt that yields to evidence :: A belief that yields to evidence is a mistake or an overvalued idea; delusions are held with full conviction | A fixed, false belief the person recognises as senseless and resists :: Recognising it as senseless and resisting it describes an obsession
> Jaspers' criteria: held with extraordinary conviction, not changed by counter-argument or experience, and false or impossible in content.
> - Culture matters: beliefs shared by the person's culture (for example witchcraft or spiritual attack in many Nigerian communities) are NOT delusions.
> - Primary (autochthonous) delusions arise suddenly with no explanation. Secondary delusions are understandable from another experience such as low mood or hallucinations.
> - Classify by content: persecutory, grandiose, nihilistic, jealous, erotomanic, somatic, of reference, of guilt.
Q: Hallucination = A perception without an external stimulus, with the full quality of a real perception | A perception without an external stimulus, located in inner subjective space :: Inner space and reduced vividness describe a pseudohallucination | A perception of a real external stimulus, distorted by mood or expectation :: A real stimulus distorted by mood is an (affect) illusion | A perception without an external stimulus that the person can summon and dismiss at will :: Voluntary control describes mental imagery; hallucinations are involuntary
> A true hallucination is vivid and substantial, located in external space, and not under voluntary control.
> - Describe it by modality: auditory (commonest in schizophrenia), visual (think organic causes and delirium), tactile, olfactory, gustatory, somatic.
> - Hypnagogic (falling asleep) and hypnopompic (waking up) hallucinations can be normal.
> - Third-person voices arguing or commenting are first-rank symptoms.
Q: Illusion = A misperception of a real external stimulus | A perception without any external stimulus, with full vividness :: No stimulus at all makes it a hallucination | A normal perception of a real stimulus given a sudden delusional meaning :: That is delusional perception; the perception itself is normal | A misperception of a real stimulus held afterwards with unshakeable conviction :: Once it is held with fixed conviction it has become a delusion
> Three types of illusion:
> - Completion illusions: the mind fills gaps, like reading a word with a missing letter.
> - Affect illusions: mood shapes perception, like a frightened person seeing a shadow as an attacker.
> - Pareidolia: vivid images seen in vague stimuli, like faces in clouds. It persists even with attention.
> Illusions increase with fatigue, fever, poor lighting and delirium.
Q: Pseudohallucination = A perception experienced in inner subjective space, lacking full vividness | A perception in external space with full vividness, recognised as unreal :: External space and full vividness make it a true hallucination, even with insight | A misperception of a real stimulus, located in inner space :: A misperception of a real stimulus is an illusion | A vivid mental image fully under voluntary control :: Voluntary control describes imagery; pseudohallucinations are involuntary
> The usual teaching (Kandinsky, Jaspers): it lacks the substantial quality of real perception and is located in inner subjective space ("in my head").
> - The person may recognise that it is not real.
> - Seen in grief, PTSD, dissociative states and personality disorders, as well as psychosis.
> - Definitions vary between textbooks. State the definition you are using.
Q: Overvalued idea = A plausible, emotionally charged belief that dominates life but is not delusional | A plausible belief that dominates life, held with full delusional conviction :: Full delusional conviction makes it a delusion | A plausible, emotionally charged idea that the person resists as senseless :: Resisting it as senseless marks an obsession; overvalued ideas are embraced | An implausible belief that dominates life but is not delusional :: Overvalued ideas are understandable and plausible, not implausible
> Described by Wernicke. The belief is understandable given the person's personality and history, but it dominates their life and actions.
> - Examples: body-shape beliefs in anorexia nervosa, non-delusional morbid jealousy, hypochondriacal preoccupation.
> - Unlike an obsession, it is NOT resisted: the person agrees with it (ego-syntonic).
Q: Obsession = A recurrent intrusive thought, recognised as one's own and usually resisted | A recurrent intrusive thought felt to be placed in the mind by an outside force :: Thoughts felt to come from outside are thought insertion, a first-rank symptom | A recurrent thought recognised as one's own that the person welcomes :: Obsessions are unwanted and distressing (ego-dystonic) | A recurrent intrusive image recognised as coming from outside the mind :: Obsessions are recognised as products of one's OWN mind
> The four features of an obsession: intrusive, recognised as a product of one's own mind, unwanted and distressing (ego-dystonic), and usually resisted.
> - Compulsions are repetitive acts or mental rituals done to reduce the anxiety.
> - ICD-11 OCD specifies insight: good or fair, poor, or absent. Poor insight does not make it psychosis.
Q: Delusional perception = A normal perception given a sudden delusional meaning | A false perception that is given a delusional meaning :: In delusional perception the perception itself is normal | A normal perception interpreted in line with an existing delusion :: That is delusional misinterpretation; delusional perception arises suddenly, not from an existing delusion | A normal perception that triggers a vivid, upsetting memory :: That is ordinary association, not a delusion
> A Schneiderian first-rank symptom with two stages: a real, normal perception, then a sudden delusional meaning with no logical link.
> - Example: "The traffic light turned red, and I knew I had been chosen to save Nigeria."
> - Often preceded by delusional mood: a sense that something strange and important is about to happen.
Q: Depersonalisation = Feeling that oneself is unreal or detached | Feeling that the surroundings are unreal or flat :: That is derealisation | A fixed belief that one does not exist :: With fixed conviction it is a nihilistic (Cotard) delusion; depersonalisation keeps insight | Feeling that one's actions are controlled by an outside force :: That is a passivity experience
> The person feels unreal, detached, or like an observer of themselves. They describe it "as if", and insight is kept.
> - Seen in anxiety, depression, exhaustion, temporal lobe epilepsy and depersonalisation-derealisation disorder.
> - If insight is lost ("I AM dead"), it becomes a nihilistic delusion.
Q: Derealisation = Feeling that the surroundings are unreal | Feeling that oneself is unreal or detached :: That is depersonalisation | A fixed belief that the world is no longer real :: With fixed conviction it is a nihilistic delusion; derealisation is 'as if', with insight | Seeing objects as smaller than they really are :: That is micropsia, a perceptual distortion
> The world feels flat, distant, dreamlike, or like a film set. It often occurs with depersonalisation, and insight is preserved.
Q: Confabulation = Filling memory gaps with false memories, without intent to deceive | Filling memory gaps with false memories, deliberately to deceive :: Confabulation has no intent to deceive; the patient believes it | Recalling a real memory with a new delusional meaning :: That is a delusional memory | Recalling false memories in an alert patient with intact memory :: Confabulation arises from memory impairment, as in Korsakoff syndrome
> "Honest lying." The classic setting is Korsakoff syndrome (thiamine deficiency, usually from alcohol); it is also seen with frontal lobe damage.
> - Provoked confabulation appears in response to questions. Spontaneous (fantastic) confabulation is rarer and suggests frontal involvement.
Q: Alexithymia = Difficulty identifying and describing one's own emotions | Difficulty reading written words :: That is alexia | Difficulty recognising emotions in other people's faces :: Alexithymia is about recognising and naming one's OWN emotions | Inability to experience pleasure :: That is anhedonia
> Term by Sifneos. Greek: a (without) + lexis (word) + thymos (emotion).
> - Linked to somatic symptom disorders, autism, PTSD and substance use. These people often report bodily sensations instead of feelings.
Q: Anhedonia = Loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities | Reduced outward expression of emotion :: Reduced expression is blunted or flattened affect, which the examiner observes | Lack of motivation to start activities :: That is avolition | Inability to put feelings into words :: That is alexithymia
> One of the two AFFECTIVE-cluster symptoms of an ICD-11 depressive episode (with depressed mood), so it can satisfy the core requirement on its own.
> - It is also a negative symptom of schizophrenia.
Q: Echolalia = Repeating another person's words | Repeating one's own words or phrases :: That is palilalia | Imitating another person's movements :: That is echopraxia | Repeating the last syllable of one's own words :: That is logoclonia
> Echo phenomena are echolalia (words) and echopraxia (movements).
> - Seen in catatonia, autism, Tourette syndrome and frontal lobe disease.
> - Do not confuse with palilalia (repeating your OWN words) or logoclonia (repeating the last syllable).
Q: Solastalgia = Distress caused by environmental change to one's home place | Anxiety about future climate change :: That is eco-anxiety, which looks ahead | Grief for ecosystems that have already been lost :: That is ecological grief | Homesickness after moving away from home :: That is nostalgia; solastalgia happens while you are still at home
> Coined by philosopher Glenn Albrecht (2005) from solace + nostalgia + algia (pain): the pain of losing the comfort of home while still living there.
> - Triggers: mining, drought, flooding, deforestation, desertification (relevant to northern Nigeria).
> - Related terms: eco-anxiety (future-focused worry) and ecological grief (mourning lost ecosystems).
Q: Insight = Awareness of being ill, of its cause, and of the need for treatment | Awareness of being ill, without needing to accept treatment :: Accepting the need for treatment is one of the three parts of insight | Agreement with every part of the doctor's view :: Insight is graded and multidimensional, not simple agreement | The ability to make sound decisions in daily life :: That is judgement
> Insight is graded, not all-or-nothing. David (1990) described three dimensions: recognising you have an illness, relabelling unusual experiences as part of it, and accepting treatment.
> Record it in the MSE in the patient's own words.
L: Piaget's stages of cognitive development = Sensorimotor | Preoperational | Concrete operational | Formal operational ~~ Latency :: That is a Freudian stage | Industry vs inferiority :: That is an Erikson stage | Phallic :: That is a Freudian stage
> - Sensorimotor (0-2 years): learns through senses and action; object permanence develops.
> - Preoperational (2-7): symbolic play; egocentrism and animism; cannot yet conserve.
> - Concrete operational (7-11): conservation and logical thinking about concrete things.
> - Formal operational (11+): abstract and hypothetical reasoning.
L: Freud's psychosexual stages = Oral | Anal | Phallic | Latency | Genital ~~ Sensorimotor :: That is Piaget's first stage | Concrete operational :: That is a Piaget stage | Trust vs mistrust :: That is Erikson's first stage
> Oral (0-1), anal (1-3), phallic (3-6, Oedipus complex), latency (6 to puberty), genital (puberty onwards).
> Fixation at a stage is said to shape personality. For example, anal traits are orderliness, obstinacy and parsimony.
L: Erikson's psychosocial stages = Trust vs mistrust | Autonomy vs shame and doubt | Initiative vs guilt | Industry vs inferiority | Identity vs role confusion | Intimacy vs isolation | Generativity vs stagnation | Integrity vs despair ~~ Oral :: That is a Freudian stage | Formal operational :: That is a Piaget stage | Hope vs fear :: Not one of Erikson's stages
> Eight stages across the whole lifespan. Each is a crisis that, if resolved, gives a virtue:
> - Infancy, trust: hope. Early childhood, autonomy: will. Preschool, initiative: purpose. School age, industry: competence.
> - Adolescence, identity: fidelity. Young adult, intimacy: love. Middle age, generativity: care. Old age, integrity: wisdom.

## Car Park | Psychiatric interview
> Psychiatric interview. Source: NPMCN - PSYCHIATRIC INTERVIEWING - A CLERKSHIP FORMAT.pdf. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Principles of the psychiatric interview
> - Setting: private, safe (you nearest the door, alarm), uninterrupted; introduce yourself, explain purpose and confidentiality and its limits.
> - Rapport and empathy: listen, reflect feelings, validate, avoid premature reassurance or judgement.
> - Questioning — the funnel: start with open questions ("Tell me what's been happening"), then focused, then closed to clarify specifics (duration, severity). Avoid leading and multiple questions.
> - Techniques: facilitation (nods, "go on"), clarification, summarising, signposting transitions ("I'd now like to ask about your family"), tolerating silence.
> - End: summarise, check understanding, invite questions, explain next steps.
> - Document start date/time, informants and their reliability.
Q: Which is listed among the goals of the lecture? = Synthesising informant, corroborative and documented histories with direct assessment | Prescribing clozapine | Performing ECT | Psychoanalysis | Writing court reports
> Goal 4: 'Use of collateral sources (significant others) and the importance of synthesizing informant and corroborative histories and documented histories with direct assessment.'
Q: The best way to begin exploring a presenting problem is with: = Open questions | Closed questions | Leading questions | Multiple questions | A rating scale
> Open → focused → closed: the funnel.

### The clerking structure (long-case backbone)
> 1. Biodata — name, age, sex, marital status, ethnicity/tribe, religion, education, occupation, address; source of referral; informants (relationship, length of acquaintance, reliability).
> 2. Presenting complaints — in the patient's own words, with duration, chronological order.
> 3. History of presenting complaint — onset (acute/insidious), precipitants, course, each symptom explored; negative findings; effect on function; treatment so far (orthodox, traditional, religious — in Nigeria ask about prayer houses, herbal treatment, chaining, scarification).
> 4. Past psychiatric history — each episode: year, diagnosis, treatment, response, recovery, follow-up, admissions, self-harm.
> 5. Past medical/surgical — epilepsy, head injury, hypertension, diabetes, sickle cell, HIV, surgeries.
> 6. Drug history — current medication, adherence, allergies.
> 7. Family history — genogram, mental illness, suicide, epilepsy, substance use in relatives; family dynamics.
> 8. Personal history (below), substance history, forensic history, premorbid personality.
> 9. Mental state examination, physical examination, investigations, formulation, diagnosis, management, prognosis.
Q: What should be documented at the very start (and end) of the clerking? = The starting date and time (and finishing time) | The patient's blood group | The fee paid | The ward number only | The consultant's phone number
> 'Starting Date and Time — document please' … and at the end, the Finishing Time.
Q: For a minor, the biodata should record who gave consent and: = Who gave assent | Who paid | Who referred | Who drove them | The school fees
> Biodata includes 'Consent given by' and 'Assent given by' — assent comes from the child.
Q: For each symptom in the history of presenting complaint, which is NOT something the lecture asks you to indicate? = The patient's blood pressure | Context of observed behaviour | Frequency | Distress to self and others | Effect on functioning
> 'Indicate the context of observed behaviors, frequency, distress to self and others, effect on functioning and general duration of each symptom.'
Q: Which area of functioning is NOT listed when assessing the effect of the current problem? = On blood sugar | Capacity for independent functioning | At school/at work | Within the family | On relationships with others
> Effects: (1) independent functioning, (2) school/work, (3) family, (4) relationships with others.
Q: For a past episode, the lecture asks where it was treated. Which options are listed? = Orthodox, herbal, religious, etc. | Only hospitals | Only abroad | Only private clinics | Only at home
> 'Where was it treated – orthodox, herbal, religious e.t.c.'
Q: Which treatments are explicitly listed as types that may have been given for a past episode? = None, drugs, herbs, floggings, tattoos, prayers | ECT and lithium only | Surgery only | Hypnosis | Acupuncture
> 'Type of treatment(s) given – none, drugs, herbs, floggings, tattoos, prayers e.t.c.'
Q: After treatment of a past episode, the lecture asks whether social and occupational functioning was: = Full or partial | Measured by IQ | Recorded by police | Assessed only by family | Irrelevant
> 'Social & occupational functioning after treatment — full or partial? Any RECOVERY at all? Full or partial?'
Q: Which past medical condition is specifically listed in the clerking format? = Sickle cell disease | Psoriasis | Glaucoma | Gout | Asthma only
> 'Hypertension, Diabetes, sickle cell disease, Recurrent Seizures/Convulsions, confusion/delirium, Fevers, Surgeries.'
Q: The past drug history should record medicines used, their duration and: = Their indication | Their price | Their manufacturer | Their colour | Who bought them
> 'List medicines used in the past, their duration and their indication.'
Q: In the sibling table, which is NOT recorded for each sibling? = Blood group | Mental state | Health status | Relationship with the patient | Current functioning
> Each sibling: name, gender, age, current status/functioning, mental state, health status, relationship with patient (cordial/poor).
Q: Which is listed among significant adverse life events in the family? = Deportation, relocation and financial downturn | Promotion | Graduation | Marriage only | Birth of twins
> 'Death(s), divorce, separations, disfigurement, stressors, rancor/fights, rivalry, deportation, immigration/relocation, change in schools, financial down-turn, chronic illness, severe trauma, robbery.'

### Personal (developmental) history — chronological
> - Pregnancy and birth: planned/wanted, antenatal care, maternal illness/infection (TORCHES), drugs/alcohol, gestation, place and mode of delivery, birth asphyxia, neonatal jaundice, birth weight.
> - Early development: milestones (motor, speech, social, toilet training), feeding, separation, temperament, play (solitary/parallel/interactive), childhood illnesses, febrile convulsions, neurotic traits (enuresis, nail-biting, night terrors).
> - Childhood adversity: separation, abuse, bereavement, family discord.
> - Education: schools attended, performance, peer relationships, bullying, truancy, conduct problems, highest qualification.
> - Occupation: jobs, reasons for leaving, performance, relationship with colleagues.
> - Psychosexual: puberty/menarche, orientation, relationships, sexual problems; marital history — polygamy, harmony, children.
> - Forensic: arrests, convictions, violence. Social circumstances: housing, finances, support.
Q: Which is part of the social history in the lecture? = Present living circumstances, toilet access and sleeping arrangements | Birth weight | Milestones | Serial 7s | Insight
> 'Present living circumstances – highbrow/ghetto, type of apartment, basic conveniences, easy toilet access, compound space to play… Home circumstances and sleeping arrangements.'
Q: In the social history, the lecture asks whether peers to play with are available: = At home and at school | Online | At church only | At the hospital | In other countries
> 'Peer play — peers to play with are available at home? … available in school?'
Q: Which maternal infections in pregnancy does the lecture ask about? = TORCHES | Malaria only | Influenza only | Cholera | None
> 'Incidents during pregnancy — placenta previa, threatened abortion, infections in the mother (TORCHES).'
Q: Which birth complication is specifically listed? = Birth asphyxia | Cleft palate | Club foot | Hernia | Cataract
> 'Birth complications – prolonged labor, small pelvis, large baby, birth asphyxia.'
Q: Which illness in the first month after birth is listed in the clerking format? = Jaundice | Measles | Chickenpox | Polio | Typhoid
> 'Illnesses occurring one month after Birth – Jaundice, infections, injuries, large head, others.'
Q: Which is the correct order of the play types listed in the lecture? = Lone, parallel, interactive | Interactive, parallel, lone | Parallel, lone, interactive | Lone, interactive, parallel | Interactive, lone, parallel
> 'Play type – 1. Lone play 2. Parallel play 3. Interactive play' — the developmental sequence.
Q: Infant temperament in the clerking format is rated as: = Easy, good enough or difficult | Happy or sad | Active or passive | Introvert or extrovert | Calm or anxious
> 'Temperament in infancy (easy, good enough, difficult).'
Q: For each level of schooling, which item is recorded? = Relationship with authority figures/teachers | Teachers' salaries | School fees | Uniform colour | Distance from home
> 'Relationship with authority figures/teachers – Good / Conflicts; withdrawal from or drop-out of school and reason(s) why.'
Q: Which is given as an example of an occupational hazard to record? = Commercial sex work or heavy-metal mining | Office work | Teaching | Farming only | Driving only
> 'Working in a lead company without shields, mining heavy metals, commercial sex worker etc.'
Q: Which is NOT listed under the forensic history? = Academic performance | Court cases/litigations | Deportations | Refugee status | Incarcerations
> Forensic: law-enforcement contact, court cases, deportation, political asylum, refugee status, incarcerations.
Q: The marital history in the lecture specifically asks about: = Marital harmony/discord, fidelity, extramarital affairs and polygamy | Wedding cost | Bride price only | In-laws' income | Number of guests
> 'Marital harmony/discord/fidelity or extramarital affairs /polygamy; sexual satisfaction in marriage.'

### Premorbid personality — what the person was like before the illness
> - Ask the patient and an informant: relationships (friends, family, intimate), leisure activities, predominant mood and its stability, character (shy, sociable, anxious, perfectionistic, suspicious, impulsive), attitudes (moral, religious standards), coping with stress, fantasy life, habits (alcohol, tobacco).
> - Purpose: separates illness change from enduring traits, shapes prognosis and treatment, and identifies personality disorder.
> - Pitfall: current mood distorts recall — rely on informants.
Q: Traits recorded in the clerking should preferably be: = Corroborated by an informant who has had long close contact with the patient | Self-reported only | Measured by MRI | Guessed by the doctor | Taken from social media
> 'Traits (preferably corroborated by an informant who has been in long close contact to the patient).'
Q: In the lecture's trait dimensions, compassion, politeness and trust in others describe: = Agreeableness | Extraversion | Conscientiousness | Neuroticism | Openness
> 'Agreeableness (compassion, politeness, trust in others).' Conscientiousness ＝ organisation, industriousness, reliability.
Q: The SWOT analysis in the clerking format refers to the patient's: = Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats | Symptoms, Withdrawal, Outcome, Treatment | Sleep, Weight, Orientation, Thought | Safety, Wellbeing, Occupation, Trauma | None of these
> 'SWOT Analysis — Strength(s), Weakness(es), Opportunities, Threats.'

### Substance use history
> - For each substance: age of first use, who introduced it, reasons, route, quantity and frequency, pattern (binge/daily), last use, cost and funding, attempts to stop, longest abstinence.
> - Dependence features (ICD-11): impaired control, increasing precedence over other activities, tolerance, withdrawal (and use to relieve it).
> - Complications: withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, psychosis, mood disorder, amnesic syndrome, sleep and sexual problems; medical (liver, HIV/hepatitis — injecting), legal, social, marital, occupational, financial.
> - Screening: CAGE (≥ 2 positive), AUDIT (≥ 8), ASSIST; calculate units of alcohol per week.
> - Stage of change (Prochaska & DiClemente) guides intervention.
Q: Which mode of drug use is listed in the lecture? = Chasing | Topical only | Rectal only | Eye drops | Nasal spray only
> 'Mode of use – smoking/chewing/inhalation/cooking/chasing/injecting etc.'
Q: Which is a drug-specific feature the lecture gives for cocaine? = Formication and dilated pupils | Pinpoint pupils | Red eyes and hunger | Forgetfulness | Slurred speech
> 'Features of the particular drug of abuse e.g. formication and dilated pupils for cocaine abuse, forgetfulness in alcohol abuse.'
Q: Craving is described in the lecture as: = Psychological dependence | Physical dependence | Tolerance | Withdrawal | Intoxication
> 'craving (psychological dependence); recurrent frequent use; abandons other social activities…'
Q: In the lecture's CAGE wording, the 'A' stands for: = Angry with self at use (annoyed) | Alcohol | Amnesia | Abstinence | Anxiety
> 'CAGE (Cut-down, Angry with self at use, Getting disapproval from others, Eye-opener).'
Q: Which is listed as a psychological complication of substance use? = Amnestic syndromes | Legal problems | Financial problems | Marital problems | Social problems
> Psychological: withdrawal (± seizures), delirium, psychosis, mood disorders, cognitive impairment – amnestic syndromes, sleep, sexual dysfunction, personality change. The others are 'other complications'.

### MSE 1 — appearance, behaviour, speech
> - Appearance: age-appropriateness, grooming, hygiene, clothing (appropriate to weather/occasion), self-neglect, scars (self-harm, injection sites), tattoos, weight.
> - Behaviour: eye contact, rapport, psychomotor activity (agitation, retardation), abnormal movements (tremor, tics, dyskinesia, EPSE), posture, catatonic signs, responding to unseen stimuli, attitude (cooperative, guarded, hostile, disinhibited).
> - Speech: rate, rhythm, volume, tone, quantity (poverty, pressure), latency, spontaneity, dysarthria, neologisms; record verbatim examples.
Q: Rocking and hand-flapping are recorded in the MSE under: = General behaviour — repetitive behaviours | Mood | Thought content | Cognition | Insight
> 'Repetitive behaviours (compulsions, rocking, hand flapping)' — under general behaviour.
Q: 'Lack of social responsiveness, avoids eye contact' is recorded under: = Interaction with interviewer, caregiver or environs | Appearance | Perception | Judgement | Physical examination
> Item 3: interaction — overly anxious, over-familiar, shy, dependent on caregiver, manipulative, lack of social responsiveness, avoids eye contact, resistant to instructions.

### MSE 2 — mood and affect
> - Mood (subjective): in the patient's words ("How have you been feeling in your spirits?"); rate 0–10.
> - Mood (objective) / affect: observed — euthymic, depressed, elated, irritable, anxious, perplexed.
> - Affect qualities: range (restricted, blunted, flat), reactivity, lability, congruence with content (incongruous in schizophrenia).
> - Biological symptoms: sleep (early-morning waking), appetite, weight, energy, libido, diurnal variation, concentration.
> - Always ask about suicidal ideation here — thoughts, plans, intent, means; and thoughts of harming others.
Q: In the MSE format, mood/affect is defined as the patient's: = External expression of his/her emotions | Internal feelings only | Thought content | Level of consciousness | Insight
> 'Mood/Affect (frequently observed mood) — patient's external expression of his/her emotions — normal, angry, irritable, anxious, elated, flat affect…'

### MSE 3 — thought and perception
> - Thought form: flow (flight of ideas, retardation), formal thought disorder (derailment, loosening, neologisms, word salad), circumstantiality, tangentiality, thought block, perseveration.
> - Thought content: delusions (type, conviction, systematisation, mood-congruence, how acted on), overvalued ideas, obsessions/compulsions, preoccupations, phobias, suicidal/homicidal ideas.
> - Thought possession: insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting.
> - Perception: hallucinations — modality, person (2nd/3rd), content (command?), location (inner/outer space), timing, response to them; illusions, depersonalisation/derealisation.
> - Command hallucinations to harm ＝ a risk item — ask whether they intend to obey.
Q: How does the lecture suggest hallucinations may show in a child who cannot describe them? = Hiding under tables, pointing at invisible things while crying, running from unseen objects | Higher IQ | Better sleep | Normal play | Increased appetite
> 'Seems disturbed by something… that other people cannot see or hear e.g. patient hides under tables, points at invisible things while crying, runs away from unseen objects.'
Q: Under thought processes, the lecture lists flow, form, content and: = Possession of thoughts | Speed of speech | Volume | Mood | Orientation
> 'Flow/stream of thought; Form of thoughts; Content of thoughts; Possession of thoughts.'

### MSE 4 — cognition (bedside)
> - Level of consciousness (alert, drowsy, clouded — GCS).
> - Orientation: time (lost first), place, person (lost last).
> - Attention/concentration: serial 7s from 100 (5 subtractions; the lecture: done in ~2 minutes, ≤ 1 error); serial 3s from 20 if 7s fail; months of the year / days of the week backwards; spell WORLD backwards; digit span (normal 7 ± 2 forward).
> - Memory: registration (repeat a name and address immediately), short-term recall (after 5 minutes), recent (events of the last 24–48 hours, recent news), remote (personal history, verified by informant).
> - General knowledge/intelligence: current affairs appropriate to education (current President, Governor).
> - Abstract thinking: proverbs, similarities (orange and banana) — concrete answers suggest schizophrenia, organic damage or low education.
> - Judgement: social situations ("what would you do if you found a stamped addressed envelope?").
> - Formal tools: MMSE, MoCA, ACE-III, AMTS.
Q: The lecture's standard for serial 7s is: = Start from 100, within 2 minutes, no more than one miss | Start from 50, 1 minute, no errors | Start from 20, 2 minutes | Start from 100, 5 minutes, three misses | Start from 70
> 'Serial 7 test (starts from 100, done in 2mins with not more than one miss).'
Q: If serial 7s fail, the lecture suggests serial 3s starting from: = 20 | 100 | 50 | 30 | 10
> 'Serial 3 test (start from 20, 2min time limit for execution with not more than 1 miss).'
Q: Short-term memory in the lecture refers to events within the last: = 24–48 hours | 5 minutes | 1 hour | 1 month | 1 year
> 'Short-term memory — events within last 24–48 hours.'
Q: Object permanence (looking for hidden items) appears at about: = 9–12 months | 1 month | 2–3 months | 4–6 months | 3 years
> 'Object permanence (looks for hidden items), good memory – 9–12mths.' Recognises mother's voice 2–3 months; familiar faces 4–6 months.
Q: According to the copying milestones in the lecture, a child copies a square at: = 5 years | 2 years | 3 years | 6 years | 7 years
> 'Copy designs: 2 years-circle, 3 years-cross, 5 years-square, 6 years-triangle, 7 years-diamond.'
Q: 'What would you do if fire broke out in the room?' tests: = Judgement | Insight | Attention | Memory | Orientation
> 'Judgement: ability to make the appropriate decisions and appropriately act on them in social situations.'

### Insight — not all-or-none
> - Lecture's six graded questions: (1) Has the patient noticed the symptoms others complain about? (2) Do they agree they are abnormal? (3) Do they attribute them to illness? (4) Do they appreciate the disability caused? (5) Do they believe treatment is needed? (6) Are they willing to accept treatment? — Yes to all ＝ full; some ＝ partial; none ＝ nil insight.
> - Anthony David (1990) — three dimensions: (1) recognition of illness, (2) ability to relabel unusual experiences as pathological, (3) acceptance of/adherence to treatment.
> - Insight predicts adherence and outcome; poor insight in schizophrenia partly reflects frontal (anosognosia-like) deficits, not just denial.
> - Distinguish insight from capacity (decision-specific: understand, retain, weigh, communicate).
Q: In the lecture's insight scale, a patient who answers 'No' to some of the six questions has: = Partial insight | Full insight | Nil insight | Psychotic insight | Normal insight
> 'Yes! to all 6 ＝ full insight; No! to some ＝ partial insight; No! to all ＝ nil insight.'
Q: Which is NOT one of the lecture's six insight questions? = Does the patient know the name of their drug? | Has the patient noticed the symptoms? | Does the patient agree they are abnormal? | Does the patient believe treatment is needed? | Is the patient willing to comply?
> The six: noticed symptoms, agrees abnormal, attributes to illness, appreciates disability, believes treatment needed, willing to comply.
Q: Anthony David's model of insight includes all EXCEPT: = IQ | Recognition of illness | Relabelling experiences as pathological | Acceptance of treatment | All are components
> David (1990): recognition, relabelling, treatment acceptance.

### Collateral (informant) history — essential, not optional
> - Fills gaps where the patient lacks insight, is psychotic, cognitively impaired, intoxicated, a child, or minimises (substance use, violence).
> - Gives premorbid personality, developmental history, onset and course, risk events, adherence, and family dynamics.
> - Sources: family, friends, GP/referrer, previous notes, police, school.
> - Consent and confidentiality: obtain the patient's consent where possible; you may receive information without breaching confidentiality, and may share without consent when there is serious risk.
> - Synthesise — note discrepancies between accounts and comment on each informant's reliability.
Q: For each informant, the lecture asks you to record their relationship to the patient, length of acquaintance and: = Reliability | Income | Religion | Education | Age only
> 'Informant(s) — relationship to patient and length of acquaintance/reliability.'

### Interviewing special groups
> - Children/adolescents: adjust to developmental stage; use play, drawings; see child alone and with parents; school reports; adolescents — HEADSSS (Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide, Safety); know child-protection law.
> - Older adults: check hearing and vision (aids in place), allow more time, screen cognition, polypharmacy, physical illness, elder abuse.
> - Intellectual disability / communication needs: simple short sentences, concrete questions, avoid leading questions (acquiescence), visual aids, involve carers; beware diagnostic overshadowing (attributing everything to the disability) — pain and physical illness often present as behaviour change.
> - Interpreters: use a trained, independent interpreter (not family); speak to the patient, brief the interpreter first.
> - Culture: explore the patient's explanatory model (spiritual attack, witchcraft), idioms of distress; DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview.
Q: The lecture asks what the caregivers or parents think caused the problem. This explores their: = Explanatory model of the illness | Insight | Intelligence | Premorbid personality | Risk
> 'What do the significant other/caregiver/parents think are the likely causes of the problem' — their explanatory model (e.g. spiritual, witchcraft, drugs).
Q: HEADSSS is a framework for interviewing: = Adolescents | Older adults | Dementia patients | Forensic patients | Interpreters
> Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide, Safety.

### Risk assessment
> - Domains: suicide/self-harm, harm to others/violence, self-neglect, exploitation/vulnerability, risk to children, absconding, driving.
> - Static factors (unchangeable — history of violence, male, past attempts) vs dynamic factors (modifiable — intoxication, psychosis, hopelessness, non-adherence, access to means).
> - Suicide: ideation, plan, intent, preparations, means, previous attempts, hopelessness, protective factors.
> - Violence: past violence (best predictor), substance misuse, command hallucinations, persecutory or jealous delusions, threats, specific victim, weapons. Tools: HCR-20.
> - Limitations: suicide and homicide are rare (low base rate) → prediction has low positive predictive value; risk fluctuates. NICE: don't use risk tools to predict or to decide who gets care — use a formulation and safety plan.
> - Document risk level, reasoning and the management plan.
Q: According to the lecture's goals, risk assessment should cover its components and: = Its limitations, including in specific populations | Its cost | Its history | Its legal status only | Nothing else
> 'Risk assessment: The components and limitations, including issues in specific populations, e.g. infants, children and adolescents, older people.'
Q: The single best predictor of future violence is: = Past violence | Schizophrenia diagnosis | Female sex | Old age | Anxiety
> Past violence.
Q: Why do risk tools predict suicide poorly? = Low base rate gives low positive predictive value | Suicide is common | Tools are too long | Patients always lie | Risk never changes
> Low base rate → many false positives. Use formulation and safety planning.

### Physical examination and investigations
> - Always examine: vital signs, BMI/waist, neurological (EPSE, focal signs, cerebellar), thyroid, stigmata of liver disease/alcohol, injection marks, self-harm scars, signs of infection (HIV, TB).
> - Baseline investigations: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, calcium, HIV, VDRL/syphilis, hepatitis B/C, urine drug screen, malaria parasite where relevant, pregnancy test.
> - Specific: ECG (QTc before antipsychotics, clozapine, lithium, ECT), EEG (epilepsy, delirium, CJD), CT/MRI (first-episode psychosis with atypical features, late onset, neurological signs, cognitive decline), prolactin, drug levels (lithium, valproate, clozapine).
> - Rating scales: BPRS/PANSS (psychosis), HAM-D/MADRS/BDI (depression), YMRS (mania), MMSE/MoCA (cognition) — record scores and interpret them.
Q: On abdominal examination, the lecture specifically asks you to note: = Scars and scarification marks | Tattoos only | Hair colour | Nail length | Shoe size
> 'Abdomen — appearance, shape, other features (scars, scarification marks etc.)' — relevant to traditional treatment.
Q: Which test of large-muscle coordination is suggested for younger children? = Hop on one foot and catch a ball | Romberg's test | Tandem walking blindfolded | Finger-nose with eyes closed | Grip strength dynamometer
> 'For younger children; catch a ball, hop on one foot, show hand (right and left).'
Q: Which is listed as a social investigation? = School visits and tutor comments | EEG | IQ testing | MRI | Urine toxicology
> 'Further Social Investigations — School visits and tutor comments; medical/other reports from different contexts.'
Q: Which is given as an example of an objective rating tool? = Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) | Rorschach | Tarot | Handwriting analysis | Polygraph
> 'e.g Brief Psychosis Rating Scale (BPRS), Mini Mental State (MMS), Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD).' Record scores and interpretation.

### Formulation — the heart of the long case
> - Summary: biodata, key features of the presentation, important positives and negatives.
> - Diagnosis (ICD-11 or DSM-5) with reasons for and against; differential diagnoses with reasons.
> - Aetiology — the 4 Ps × biopsychosocial grid:
> - Predisposing (genetic loading, birth complications, childhood adversity, personality)
> - Precipitating (life events, drugs, non-adherence, physical illness)
> - Perpetuating (ongoing stress, substance use, poor insight, high expressed emotion)
> - Protective (family support, employment, good premorbid functioning, insight)
> - Psychodynamic formulation: links early relationships, defence mechanisms, conflicts and the current presentation (e.g. loss → depression; attachment patterns → relationships with staff).
> - Management: short-term and long-term, biological–psychological–social, plus risk management and who does what.
> - Prognosis with reasons (good and poor prognostic factors).
Q: The lecture's psychodynamic formulation lists which aetiological factors? = Predisposing, precipitating and perpetuating | Genetic only | Biological and social only | Protective only | None
> 'Probable aetiological factors — Predisposing, Precipitating, Perpetuating.' (Add protective factors for the full 4 Ps.)
Q: Each differential diagnosis in the formulation should be given with: = Reasons for and reasons against | Its ICD code only | Its prevalence | Its treatment cost | Its history
> 'Differential diagnos(e)s (with reasons for and against).' Provisional diagnosis with reasons using DSM-5 or ICD-11.
Q: What is the first item under treatment planning in the lecture? = Aggression reduction/de-escalation methods in acute emergencies | Occupational therapy | Speech therapy | School placement | Supplements
> 'Aggression reduction/de-escalation methods in acute emergencies; other emergency interventions if required.'
Q: 'Leponex' on the prescription form refers to: = Clozapine (a second-line antipsychotic) | Haloperidol | Lithium | Fluoxetine | Diazepam
> '2nd Line Antipsychotics (Leponex)' — Leponex is a brand of clozapine.

### OSCE: Post-traumatic stress disorder: history | fps
> History taking station. Task: This patient was involved in a traumatic event and has been struggling since. Take a history to establish the diagnosis.
> - PTSD core: re-experiencing in the present, avoidance, persistent sense of current threat, lasting several weeks, with impairment.
> - Complex PTSD: the core PTSD features plus disturbances in self-organisation: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship difficulties. Usually follows prolonged or repeated trauma.
> Critical fail: Pressing for graphic trauma detail, or missing suicidal ideation.

> Examiner checks: Exposure to an extremely threatening or horrific event; perceived threat; onset (books: within 1–6 months).

### OSCE: Dissociative neurological symptom disorder (conversion): history and management | fps
> History taking station. Task: This woman suddenly lost her vision. Physical examination of the eyes is normal. Take a history, then explain the diagnosis and management.
> - Structure for explanations (FNPH DEEP SIT P): Definition, Epidemiology, Ethology (aetiology), Pathophysiology, Symptoms, Investigations, Treatment, Prognosis.
> - Abdulhakeem: also called functional neurological symptom disorder (DSM-5) and a dissociative disorder (ICD-11). Symptoms not intentionally produced; not limited to pain or sexual symptoms; gain is psychological, not monetary or legal. Treatment is usually spontaneous recovery, helped by insight therapy. Drugs depend on the presentation: a benzodiazepine for anxiety and muscle tension, antidepressants or serotonergic agents for obsessive rumination about symptoms. (Use benzodiazepines short-term only.)
> - Also note hypochondriasis (ICD-11: hypochondriasis/health anxiety) as a differential when the fear is of having a disease.
> Critical fail: Telling the patient she is faking it, or skipping exclusion of organic and mood causes.

Where were you and what were you doing? Which eye? Any pain, double vision? Are there things you can still see? Has… = Open and the symptom | Stressors and gain | Exclusions and background | Explain the diagnosis | Management and prognosis
> What to say: “Can you tell me what happened?” When did it start? Where were you and what were you doing? Which eye? Any pain, double vision? Are there things you can still see? Has it happened before? Any weakness elsewhere, or episodes of leaving home without knowing who you are? Test function informally: “Could you check the time for me?” Response to a sudden bright light.
> Examiner checks: Onset, setting, laterality, associated features; inconsistency on informal testing; fugue.
Q: Dissociative neurological symptom disorder (conversion): history and management, Open and the symptom: what is the examiner looking for? = Onset, setting, laterality, associated features; inconsistency on informal testing; fugue. | Temporal link to stressors; indifference is unreliable but expected in the local manual; secondary gain. | Organic causes (TIA, stroke, optic neuritis) need appropriate review; malingering and factitious disorder are differentials. | Validates the symptom; plain explanation; no blame. Safer than the book phrase “she does not know she is the one doing it”. | Biopsychosocial plan; graded rehabilitation; avoids unnecessary investigations once organic causes are excluded.

Q: Specific reading disorder (developmental learning disorder): assessment. Which phase is this line from? “Write some letters… write your name… write a simple sentence.” = Writing | Prepare | Reading | Arithmetic | Shapes and colours | Risk factors and differentials | Management
