### Bonus drill: Acronyms & screening tools
> Screening tools pick out who needs a full assessment. They do NOT make a diagnosis.
> For every tool, know: what the letters stand for, what it measures, how many items, the maximum score and the usual cut-offs.
Q: What does CAGE screen for? = Problem drinking (alcohol use disorder) | Severity of alcohol withdrawal :: CIWA-Ar rates withdrawal severity | Hazardous drinking in people who are not dependent :: CAGE misses many hazardous, non-dependent drinkers; AUDIT is better for that | Misuse of drugs other than alcohol :: CAGE-AID adapts it for drugs; CAGE itself is about alcohol
> CAGE (Ewing, 1984): four yes/no questions.
> - C: Have you ever felt you should CUT DOWN on your drinking?
> - A: Have people ANNOYED you by criticising your drinking?
> - G: Have you ever felt bad or GUILTY about your drinking?
> - E: Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover (EYE-OPENER)?
> Two or more "yes" answers is clinically significant. CAGE is quick but misses hazardous, non-dependent drinking; AUDIT is better for that.
L: CAGE = Cut down => Feeling that you ought to reduce how much alcohol you drink | Annoyed => Feeling irritated when other people criticise your drinking | Guilty => Feeling bad or remorseful about your drinking | Eye-opener => Having a morning drink to steady your nerves or relieve a hangover ~~ Craving => A strong urge to drink alcohol :: Not in CAGE. C is Cut down | Anxious => Feeling worried or tense :: Not in CAGE. A is Annoyed (by criticism of drinking) | Gambling => Betting money on uncertain outcomes :: Not in CAGE. G is Guilty | Early-morning waking => Waking earlier than intended and being unable to return to sleep :: Not in CAGE. E is Eye-opener (a morning drink)
> The E is the most specific item: a morning drink to treat withdrawal points towards dependence.
Q: How many CAGE "yes" answers are clinically significant? = 2 or more | 1 :: One "yes" deserves more questions, but the usual threshold is 2 | 3 or more :: Too high; 2 or more is significant | All 4 :: Too high; 2 or more is significant
> Two or more "yes" answers suggests an alcohol use disorder and needs a full alcohol history.
Q: What does AUDIT stand for? = Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test | Alcohol Use Disorders Inventory Test :: The I stands for Identification | Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Tool :: The T stands for Test | Alcohol Use and Drinking Identification Test :: It is Alcohol Use DISORDERS Identification Test
> AUDIT was developed by the WHO for use across cultures and in primary care.
Q: AUDIT screens for = Hazardous and harmful alcohol use | Alcohol dependence only :: AUDIT picks up hazardous and harmful use, not only dependence | Severity of alcohol withdrawal :: CIWA-Ar rates withdrawal severity | Lifetime alcohol exposure in units :: AUDIT asks mainly about the past year, and scores patterns and harm, not lifetime units
> AUDIT has 10 questions, each scored 0-4, for a maximum of 40.
> - Q1-3: consumption. Q4-6: dependence symptoms. Q7-10: alcohol-related harm.
> - Zones: 0-7 low risk. 8-15 hazardous. 16-19 harmful. 20 or more: possible dependence, so refer.
> - AUDIT-C is the short version, using only the first three (consumption) questions.
L: AUDIT sections in question order = Consumption (Q1-3) | Dependence symptoms (Q4-6) | Alcohol-related harm (Q7-10) ~~ Withdrawal seizures (Q11-12) :: AUDIT has only 10 questions | Family history (Q1-2) :: Not part of AUDIT | Craving scale :: Not an AUDIT section
> Remember the order: how much you drink, whether you are hooked, and what harm it is causing.
Q: AUDIT score suggesting possible dependence = 20 or more | 8 or more :: 8-15 is the hazardous zone | 16 or more :: 16-19 is the harmful zone | 40 :: 40 is the maximum score
> Zones: 0-7 low risk, 8-15 hazardous, 16-19 harmful, 20+ possible dependence.
Q: PHQ-9 screens for = Depression | Depression in older adults specifically :: That is the Geriatric Depression Scale | Postnatal depression specifically :: That is the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) | Generalised anxiety :: GAD-7 screens for generalised anxiety
> Patient Health Questionnaire-9: nine items that mirror the DSM depression criteria. Each is scored 0-3 for the last 2 weeks, so the maximum is 27.
> - Severity: 5 mild, 10 moderate, 15 moderately severe, 20 severe.
> - Item 9 asks about thoughts of death or self-harm. ANY positive answer needs a risk assessment.
> - PHQ-2 is the first two items (low mood and loss of interest), a quick pre-screen.
Q: PHQ-9 cut-off usually used for moderate depression = 10 | 5 :: 5 marks mild | 15 :: 15 marks moderately severe | 20 :: 20 marks severe
> 5, 10, 15, 20: mild, moderate, moderately severe, severe.
Q: GAD-7 screens for = Generalised anxiety | Depression :: PHQ-9 screens for depression | Panic disorder only :: It was built for GAD, and also picks up panic, social anxiety and PTSD | Health anxiety :: Not its purpose
> Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7: seven items scored 0-3 over 2 weeks, so the maximum is 21.
> - Cut-offs: 5 mild, 10 moderate, 15 severe. A score of 10 or more is a common referral threshold.
> - It also picks up panic disorder, social anxiety and PTSD reasonably well.
Q: Maximum MMSE score = 30 | 28 :: The MMSE is scored out of 30 | 26 :: 26 is the usual MoCA cut-off, not the MMSE maximum | 24 :: 24 is a commonly used MMSE cut-off, not the maximum
> Mini-Mental State Examination (Folstein, 1975):
> - Orientation 10 (time 5, place 5). Registration 3. Attention and calculation 5 (serial 7s or WORLD backwards). Recall 3.
> - Language and praxis 9: naming 2, repetition 1, three-stage command 3, reading 1, writing 1, copying pentagons 1.
> - 23 or below commonly suggests impairment; adjust for education and language. It is weak on executive function, where the MoCA is more sensitive for mild impairment.
S: MMSE sections = Orientation (10) | Registration (3) | Attention and calculation (5) | Recall (3) | Language and praxis (9) ~~ Abstract reasoning :: Not an MMSE section (the MoCA tests abstraction) | Insight :: Not a cognitive test item | Mood :: Not part of the MMSE
> 10 + 3 + 5 + 3 + 9 = 30.
Q: What does CIWA-Ar stand for? = Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised | Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Anxiety, revised :: The A is for Alcohol | Clinical Inventory of Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, rapid :: It is Institute, and r means revised | Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Addiction, rated :: It is Alcohol, revised
> The "-Ar" means Alcohol, revised.
Q: CIWA-Ar measures = Severity of alcohol withdrawal | Severity of opioid withdrawal :: Opioid withdrawal is rated with COWS | Risk of developing alcohol withdrawal later :: CIWA-Ar rates the signs and symptoms present NOW | Severity of alcohol dependence :: Dependence is judged from the ICD-11 features (or SADQ); CIWA-Ar rates withdrawal
> CIWA-Ar has 10 items: nausea and vomiting, tremor, paroxysmal sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile disturbances, auditory disturbances, visual disturbances, headache, and orientation (clouding of sensorium). Maximum 67.
> Commonly: under about 8-10 mild, 8-15 moderate, over 15 severe (higher risk of seizures and delirium tremens). It guides symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing.
Q: What does COWS stand for? = Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale | Clinical Opioid Withdrawal Score :: It is Opiate, and S is Scale | Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Survey :: S is Scale | Comprehensive Opiate Withdrawal Scale :: C is Clinical
> COWS rates opioid withdrawal signs: pulse, sweating, restlessness, pupil size, aches, runny nose and tearing, GI upset, tremor, yawning, anxiety and gooseflesh. It is the opioid counterpart of CIWA-Ar.
L: SAD PERSONS = Sex (male) => Being male | Age (under 19 or over 45) => Being younger than 19 or older than 45 | Depression => Persistent low mood or loss of interest and pleasure | Previous attempt => Having tried to end your life before | Ethanol use => Use of alcohol | Rational thinking loss => Impaired reality testing or reasoning | Social support lacking => Having few people to turn to for help | Organised plan => Having worked out a specific method for ending your life | No spouse => Having no marital partner | Sickness => Having a physical illness ~~ Female sex => Being female :: Male sex is the risk factor (S) | Employed => Having paid work :: Not in SAD PERSONS | Good social support => Having reliable people to turn to for help :: Lacking social support is the risk factor (S) | Married => Having a marital partner :: No spouse is the risk factor (N)
> Patterson et al. (1983) suicide-risk mnemonic; each item scores 1 point.
> The original guide was 0-2 low, 3-4 close follow-up, 5-6 consider admission, 7-10 admit.
> Modern guidance (for example NICE) warns AGAINST using risk scales to predict suicide or decide care. Use it as a memory aid for a full clinical risk assessment.
L: MSE order (ASEPTIC) = Appearance and behaviour => Observe dress, hygiene, eye contact, rapport and motor activity | Speech => Assess how quickly, loudly and how much the person talks | Emotion (mood and affect) => Ask about subjective mood and observe the range and reactivity of affect | Perception => Explore experiences such as hallucinations and illusions | Thought (form and content) => Assess the flow and content of ideas, including delusions | Insight and judgement => Explore awareness of illness and the ability to make sound decisions | Cognition => Test orientation, attention and memory ~~ Past psychiatric history => Ask about earlier episodes and treatment of mental illness :: That is part of the history, not the MSE | Family history => Ask about mental illness in relatives :: That is part of the history, not the MSE | Physical examination => Examine the body for medical signs :: Separate from the MSE | Diagnosis => Form the clinical conclusion after completing the assessment :: The diagnosis comes after the assessment, not inside the MSE
> - Appearance and behaviour: dress, hygiene, eye contact, rapport, psychomotor activity.
> - Speech: rate, volume, tone, quantity.
> - Emotion: mood (subjective, in the patient's words) and affect (observed: range, reactivity, congruence).
> - Perception: hallucinations, illusions.
> - Thought: form (flight of ideas, loosening of associations) and content (delusions, obsessions, suicidal or homicidal ideas).
> - Insight and judgement, then cognition (orientation, attention, memory).
> Many formats put thought before perception. Use the order your centre expects.
L: SIG E CAPS = Sleep => Changes in the amount or pattern of sleeping | Interest => Reduced enjoyment of usual activities | Guilt => Feelings of excessive blame or worthlessness | Energy => Reduced drive or increased fatigue | Concentration => Difficulty sustaining attention or making decisions | Appetite => Changes in eating or weight | Psychomotor change => Observable slowing or agitation | Suicidality => Thoughts of death or self-harm ~~ Elevated mood => An unusually high or expansive mood :: That is a manic symptom | Pressured speech => Rapid, excessive talking that is hard to interrupt :: That is a manic symptom | Grandiosity => An exaggerated sense of importance or ability :: That is a manic symptom | Hallucinations => Perception-like experiences without an external stimulus :: Not part of SIG E CAPS
> A memory hook ("prescribe SIG: Energy CAPSules") for the depressive symptoms other than low mood.
> DSM-5 needs 5 of 9: depressed mood or loss of interest, plus the rest from this list. ICD-11 uses 10 symptoms, adding hopelessness.
L: HPC five Cs (FNPH long case) = Complaint => The presenting problem in the patient’s own words | Course => How the problem began and changed over time | Cause (patient's perspective) => What the patient believes brought the problem on | Complications => Consequences arising from the presenting problems | Care so far => Help sought and treatment received up to this point ~~ Collateral history => Information about the patient obtained from someone else :: A separate section, not one of the five Cs | Cognition => Assessment of orientation, attention and memory :: That belongs to the mental state examination | Comorbidity => Another illness occurring alongside the main condition :: Not one of the five Cs
> FNPH style: write each presenting complaint as its own paragraph (complaint, course, cause from the patient's perspective, phenomenology).
> Complications and care so far come ONCE, at the bottom, after all the symptoms.
L: SPIKES (breaking bad news) = Setting up => Arrange privacy, sit down and involve family if wanted | Perception => Find out what the patient already understands | Invitation => Ask how much information the patient wants | Knowledge => Give a warning shot and explain the news in small, clear chunks | Emotions (respond with empathy) => Recognise the patient’s feelings and respond with empathy | Strategy and summary => Agree the plan and check the patient’s understanding ~~ Silence => A period without speaking :: Not a SPIKES step | Prognosis first => Discuss the likely outcome before checking what the patient knows :: First check what the person already knows (Perception) | Paperwork => Complete the written forms :: Not a SPIKES step
> Baile and Buckman (2000):
> - Setting: privacy, sit down, involve family if wanted.
> - Perception: what do they already know?
> - Invitation: how much do they want to know?
> - Knowledge: give a warning shot, use plain words, give small chunks.
> - Emotions: name the feeling and respond with empathy.
> - Strategy and summary: agree the plan and check understanding.
L: Stages of change (Prochaska and DiClemente) = Precontemplation | Contemplation | Preparation | Action | Maintenance ~~ Denial :: That is a Kubler-Ross grief stage | Bargaining :: That is a Kubler-Ross grief stage | Acceptance :: That is a Kubler-Ross grief stage
> The transtheoretical model (relapse can happen at any point). Match the intervention to the stage:
> - Precontemplation: raise doubt and give information.
> - Contemplation: explore ambivalence (decisional balance).
> - Preparation: make a plan. Action: support the change. Maintenance: relapse prevention.
> This is the backbone of motivational interviewing.

### Bonus drill: Anxiety, OCD & trauma
> ICD-11 groups these into three blocks:
> - Anxiety or fear-related (6B0-): 6B00 GAD, 6B01 panic, 6B02 agoraphobia, 6B03 specific phobia, 6B04 social anxiety, 6B05 separation anxiety, 6B06 selective mutism.
> - Obsessive-compulsive or related (6B2-): 6B20 OCD, 6B21 body dysmorphic, 6B22 olfactory reference, 6B23 hypochondriasis, 6B24 hoarding, 6B25 body-focused repetitive behaviour.
> - Specifically associated with stress (6B4-): 6B40 PTSD, 6B41 complex PTSD, 6B42 prolonged grief, 6B43 adjustment disorder.
Q: ICD-11 code for generalised anxiety disorder = 6B00 | 6B20 :: 6B20 is OCD | 6B40 :: 6B40 is PTSD | 6A70 :: 6A70 is single episode depressive disorder
> 6B0- is the anxiety block, and GAD is its first member.
Q: ICD-11 code for obsessive-compulsive disorder = 6B20 | 6B00 :: 6B00 is GAD | 6B40 :: 6B40 is PTSD | 6B41 :: 6B41 is complex PTSD
> 6B2- is the obsessive-compulsive block. It also includes BDD (6B21) and hoarding (6B24).
Q: ICD-11 code for PTSD = 6B40 | 6B41 :: 6B41 is complex PTSD | 6B20 :: 6B20 is OCD | 6B00 :: 6B00 is GAD
> 6B4- is the stress block. PTSD is 6B40 and complex PTSD is 6B41.
Q: ICD-11 GAD symptoms must last = At least several months, more days than not | At least 6 months, more days than not :: 6 months is the DSM-5 rule; ICD-11 says at least several months | At least 1 month, more days than not :: Too short | At least 2 weeks, most of the day :: That is the depressive episode pattern
> GAD = general apprehension or excessive worry about everyday matters, plus symptoms such as muscle tension, restlessness, sympathetic overactivity, poor concentration, irritability and sleep disturbance.
Q: Core feature of panic disorder = Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent worry about them | Recurrent expected panic attacks in feared situations :: Attacks tied to feared situations suggest a phobia or social anxiety | Recurrent unexpected panic attacks without worry about further attacks :: Persistent concern or behaviour change after the attacks is required | A single unexpected panic attack with lasting worry :: The attacks must be recurrent
> Panic attack: a sudden surge of intense fear peaking within minutes (palpitations, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, chest pain, fear of dying).
> Panic disorder needs UNEXPECTED recurrent attacks, plus persistent concern or behaviour change because of them.
Q: ICD-11 PTSD requires exposure to = An extremely threatening or horrific event or series of events | Any distressing event, including divorce or job loss :: Ordinary stressors fit adjustment disorder | An extremely threatening event experienced directly, not witnessed :: Witnessing such an event also counts | Prolonged, repeated trauma only :: Prolonged trauma is typical of complex PTSD; PTSD can follow a single event
> Then the three core elements must follow: re-experiencing in the present, avoidance, and a persistent sense of current threat. They must last at least several weeks and cause significant impairment.
S: ICD-11 PTSD core elements = Re-experiencing the event in the present | Avoidance of reminders | Persistent sense of current threat ~~ Low mood :: Common alongside PTSD, but not a core element | Obsessions :: Those belong to OCD | Hallucinations :: Not a core PTSD element
> Re-experiencing in ICD-11 means vivid intrusive memories, flashbacks or nightmares, felt as happening NOW, with strong emotion. Ordinary remembering is not enough.
S: Complex PTSD adds (disturbances in self-organisation) = Affect dysregulation | Negative self-concept | Difficulties in relationships ~~ Re-experiencing the event in the present :: Complex PTSD has this too, but it is a core PTSD element, not one of the additions | Avoidance of reminders :: Complex PTSD has this too, but it is a core PTSD element, not one of the additions | Grandiosity :: Not part of complex PTSD
> Complex PTSD (6B41) = all PTSD criteria PLUS these three "disturbances in self-organisation". It is usually after prolonged or repeated trauma that is hard to escape (torture, slavery, long-term abuse).
Q: First-line drug class for OCD = SSRIs, often at higher doses | SSRIs at the usual antidepressant dose, judged at 4 weeks :: OCD often needs higher doses and about 12 weeks to judge response | Low-dose antipsychotic :: Antipsychotics are only used to augment an SSRI in resistant OCD | Clomipramine :: Effective, but second line because of TCA side effects and overdose risk
> OCD often needs higher SSRI doses and a longer trial (about 12 weeks) than depression.
Q: Tricyclic with the best evidence in OCD = Clomipramine | Amitriptyline :: Less serotonergic; no specific OCD evidence. Clomipramine is the most serotonergic TCA | Imipramine :: No specific OCD evidence; clomipramine is the one | Nortriptyline :: Mainly noradrenergic; OCD needs strong serotonin reuptake inhibition
> Clomipramine is effective but has TCA side effects and is dangerous in overdose, so SSRIs come first.
Q: Psychological treatment of choice for OCD = CBT with exposure and response prevention | CBT with cognitive restructuring only :: Exposure and response prevention is the key ingredient | Exposure without response prevention :: Both parts are needed; carrying out the compulsion undoes the exposure | Thought-stopping techniques :: Not effective, and can strengthen the obsession
> ERP: face the trigger (exposure) without doing the compulsion (response prevention), so the anxiety falls on its own.
L: Exposure and response prevention for OCD = Psychoeducation | Build an exposure hierarchy | Graded exposure, starting low | Response prevention: resist the compulsion | Relapse prevention ~~ Reassurance seeking :: Reassurance is a compulsion that keeps OCD going | Start with the most feared situation :: Exposure is graded, starting low | Thought stopping :: Not part of ERP
> The hierarchy ranks triggers from least to most distressing (rated, for example, 0-100) and works upwards.

### Bonus drill: OSCE: history taking & risk | fps
> OSCE stations are marked against a checklist. Examiners reward structure, and they reward you for naming each domain out loud.
> - Open every station the same way: introduce yourself, confirm the patient's name, explain the task, get consent, and mention confidentiality and its limits.
> - Start with open questions, then funnel down to closed ones. Summarise back regularly. Close with a summary, the plan, and "Is there anything I haven't asked that you think is important?"
> - Global marks come from rapport, empathy statements, avoiding jargon, and keeping to time. Practise each checklist until you can produce the next domain without prompting.
L: OSCE: suicide risk assessment after an overdose = Introduce, consent, confidentiality and its limits | Open question: tell me what happened | Details of the act: method, planning, timing, precautions against discovery, final acts | Intent then: did you expect to die? Feelings about surviving | Current suicidal ideas, plans and access to means | Past self-harm or suicide attempts | Psychiatric symptoms now: depression, psychosis, substance use | Risk factors: social, physical illness, family history, recent loss | Protective factors: family, faith, children, future plans | Summarise, state the risk, safety plan and follow-up ~~ Promise to keep everything secret :: Never promise absolute confidentiality; risk to life overrides it | Avoid asking directly about suicide :: Asking directly does not increase risk and is expected by examiners | Discharge once medically fit :: Every self-harm presentation needs a psychosocial assessment first
> Examiners look for:
> - Direct questions: "Are you having thoughts of ending your life?"
> - High-intent markers: planning, isolation, precautions against discovery, a final act (note, will, goodbyes), a violent or lethal method, and regret at surviving.
> - Access to means (stored medicines, pesticides, firearms) and protective factors.
> - A clear risk statement at the end: low, moderate or high, with reasons, plus a safety plan.
L: OSCE: alcohol history = Introduce, consent, non-judgemental opening | Typical drinking day: what, how much, when, where, with whom | Quantity in standard drinks or units, and how it has changed | Dependence features: impaired control, precedence, tolerance and withdrawal | Withdrawal complications: seizures, delirium tremens, hallucinations | Consequences: physical, psychological, social, occupational, legal, financial | Previous treatment and longest period of abstinence | Other substances and smoking | Motivation and stage of change | Summarise and agree a plan ~~ Start with "Are you an alcoholic?" :: Labelling is confrontational and loses rapport | Skip the typical day :: The typical-day walk-through is the most reliable way to quantify drinking | Moralise about drinking :: Stay non-judgemental; motivational style scores higher
> Examiners look for:
> - The "typical day" technique and a quantity estimate.
> - Explicit ICD-11 dependence features (impaired control, precedence, physiological features) and withdrawal history, especially seizures and DTs, because they change detox safety.
> - Motivation assessed with the stages of change.
> Ask about drink-driving and about children at home: safeguarding.
L: OSCE: first-episode psychosis history = Introduce and consent | Presenting complaint and timeline (onset, duration, course) | Hallucinations: modality, person (2nd or 3rd), content, commands | Delusions: content, conviction, evidence the person gives | Passivity and thought alienation (insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting) | Negative symptoms | Mood symptoms (to separate from mania or psychotic depression) | Substance use, especially cannabis and stimulants | Risk: to self, to others, from others; command hallucinations | Insight | Past psychiatric, medical, family and personal history | Summarise and plan ~~ Argue with the delusion :: Never challenge or collude; explore it neutrally | Skip substance use :: Substances are a key cause and trigger of psychosis | Ask only yes/no questions :: Open questions first, then specific screens
> Examiners look for:
> - Screening each first-rank symptom with clear lay wording: "Do you ever hear your thoughts spoken aloud?" "Do you feel your thoughts are being taken out of your head?"
> - Command hallucinations and violence risk.
> - Cannabis.
> - Insight in its three parts.
> Close with differentials: schizophrenia, substance-induced psychosis, psychotic mood disorder, organic cause.
L: OSCE: collateral history from a relative = Introduce, explain your role, confirm the patient's consent or the reason to proceed without it | What changes have you noticed, and when did they start? | Timeline of the current episode | Specific behaviours: sleep, eating, self-care, speech, odd beliefs, aggression | Risk observed: self-harm, threats, violence, wandering, vulnerability | Substance use as they have seen it | Premorbid personality: what was he or she like before? | Past episodes and treatment response | Family history and social circumstances | Carer strain and support needs | Summarise and thank them ~~ Share all medical details freely :: Respect confidentiality; listen more than you disclose without consent | Skip premorbid personality :: Collateral is the best source of premorbid personality | Ignore carer strain :: Examiners reward asking how the carer is coping
> Collateral history adds what the patient cannot report: the true timeline, premorbid personality, risk behaviours, and the effect on the family. You can always listen to a relative even without consent. What you share depends on consent.
Q: In an OSCE risk assessment, asking directly about suicidal thoughts = Does not increase risk and is expected | Slightly increases risk but is still required :: Asking directly does NOT increase risk | Should be left to the end of the interview :: Ask when the history leads there, not as an afterthought | Is only needed if the patient is depressed :: Ask in every psychiatric assessment
> Asking directly and calmly is protective. It shows you take the person seriously and often brings relief.
Q: Which is a high-intent feature of a suicide attempt? = Taking precautions against being discovered | Taking an overdose in front of family :: Acting where help is likely suggests lower intent | Calling a friend soon afterwards :: Seeking help suggests lower intent | An impulsive overdose after an argument :: Impulsive acts can still be dangerous, but planning and concealment mark higher intent
> High-intent markers: planning, choosing a time when no one will find you, precautions against discovery, final acts (a note or will), believing the method would be lethal, and regret at surviving.

## Main Block | Mood disorders
> Mood disorders. Source: FEB 2026 MOOD DISORDERS FROM OWOEYE.ppt. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Mood vs affect — define both precisely
> - Mood: a pervasive, sustained feeling tone experienced internally, which colours behaviour and perception of self and the world ("climate").
> - Affect: the external, observed expression of emotion, moment to moment ("weather").
> - History: Aretaeus of Cappadocia linked melancholia and mania; Kraepelin — manic-depressive insanity (episodic, good inter-episode recovery, vs dementia praecox); Karl Leonhard (1957) split bipolar vs unipolar.
Q: The lecture defines mood as: = A pervasive and sustained feeling tone experienced internally that influences behaviour and perception of self and the world | The external expression of emotion | A brief emotional reaction to an event | The observed facial expression | A disorder of thought
> 'Mood — pervasive and sustained feeling tone that is experienced internally and that influences a person's behaviour, perception of self and the world. Affect — external expression of mood.'
Q: Mood (affective) disorders are conditions in which the most prominent feature is: = Elevation or depression of mood | Psychotic symptoms | Cognitive decline | Anxiety | Personality change
> '…a range of common clinical conditions in which the most prominent features are elevation or depression of mood.'
Q: The name 'bipolar' was introduced by: = Karl Leonhard (1957) | Emil Kraepelin | Aretaeus of Cappadocia | Eugen Bleuler | Aaron Beck
> 'Name bipolar → Karl Leonard, 1957.' Kraepelin described manic depressive insanity.

### ICD-11 mood disorders — the map
> - Bipolar or related disorders: 6A60 Bipolar type I, 6A61 Bipolar type II, 6A62 Cyclothymic disorder.
> - Depressive disorders: 6A70 Single episode depressive disorder, 6A71 Recurrent depressive disorder, 6A72 Dysthymic disorder, 6A73 Mixed depressive and anxiety disorder (new in ICD-11).
> - 6A80 ＝ qualifiers for episodes (anxiety, panic attacks, melancholia, seasonal pattern, rapid cycling, perinatal onset, current episode status).
> - Mood disorders are built from episodes (depressive, manic, hypomanic, mixed) — diagnose the episode, then the disorder from the lifetime pattern.
> - Premenstrual dysphoric disorder sits under depressive disorders (GA34.41, cross-listed).
Q: How are mood disorders diagnosed from episodes? = The type and pattern of episodes over time define the disorder | Each episode is a separate disorder | Only the current episode matters | Episodes are irrelevant to diagnosis | Only manic episodes count
> Mood disorders are built from episodes; their pattern over time (cycling) gives the disorder — e.g. depressive episodes only ＝ depressive disorder; any mania ＝ bipolar I.
Q: Which is an ICD-11 bipolar category? = Bipolar type 2 disorder | Bipolar disorder NOS | Bipolar III | Manic-depressive insanity | Bipolar IV
> ICD-11: bipolar type 1, bipolar type 2, cyclothymic, other specified, unspecified. 'NOS' is DSM-IV wording.

### ICD-11 depressive episode
> - ≥ 5 of 10 symptoms, most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥ 2 weeks, with at least one from the affective cluster.
> - Affective cluster: depressed mood; markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia).
> - Cognitive-behavioural cluster: reduced concentration/attention or indecisiveness; worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; hopelessness about the future (new in ICD-11); recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation or attempts.
> - Neurovegetative cluster: sleep disturbance; appetite/weight change; psychomotor agitation or retardation; reduced energy/fatigue.
> - In children/adolescents mood can present as irritability.
> - Must not be better explained by bereavement (ICD-11 keeps a bereavement caveat — DSM-5 removed the exclusion).
Q: A major depressive episode requires five or more symptoms, including at least: = Depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure | Sleep and appetite change | Suicidal thoughts | Fatigue and guilt | Psychomotor change
> 'Five or more of the following… including at least symptom 1 or 2' — depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure.
Q: The five symptoms must occur within the same: = Two weeks | Week | Month | Three months | Six months
> 'The five symptoms must occur in the same two weeks.'
Q: In the lecture's list, depressed mood may present as: = Sad, empty, weepy — or irritable and angry | Elation | Euphoria | Calmness | Grandiosity
> 'Depressed mood — sad, empty, weepy; irritable, anger.' Irritability is common, especially in young people.
Q: Which symptom is NOT in the lecture's list for a major depressive episode? = Grandiose self-esteem | Noticeable change in movement | Fatigue | Feelings of worthlessness or guilt | Impaired cognition or volition
> Grandiose self-esteem is a manic symptom. The depressive list: mood, interest, weight/appetite, sleep, movement, fatigue, worthlessness/guilt, cognition/volition, death/suicide.
Q: Which symptom was added to the depressive episode criteria in ICD-11? = Hopelessness about the future | Psychomotor retardation | Early-morning waking | Weight loss | Loss of libido
> Hopelessness — making 10 symptoms in ICD-11.

### ICD-11 severity — judged on intensity, function and psychosis
> - Mild: no symptom intense; some difficulty functioning; no delusions or hallucinations.
> - Moderate: several symptoms marked, or many milder ones; considerable difficulty functioning — with or without psychotic symptoms.
> - Severe: many/most symptoms marked; unable to function except to a very limited degree — with or without psychotic symptoms.
> - Note the change: in ICD-10, psychotic symptoms meant "severe"; in ICD-11 they can occur in moderate episodes.
> - Psychotic content is usually mood-congruent: guilt, poverty, nihilism (Cotard's), deserved punishment; hallucinations of accusing voices.
Q: In ICD-11, severity of a depressive episode is based on intensity of symptoms, difficulty with functioning and: = Presence of psychotic symptoms | Duration of illness | Family history | Number of episodes | Response to treatment
> 'Severity specifier in ICD-11: intensity of symptoms, degree of difficulty with functioning, and presence of psychotic symptoms.'
Q: Under ICD-11, psychotic symptoms cannot be present in which severity? = Mild | Moderate | Severe | Both moderate and severe | None — they can occur at any severity
> 'Mild — … no psychotic symptoms. Moderate — … there may be psychotic symptoms. Severe — … there may be psychotic symptoms.'

### Episode qualifiers (6A80) — and the old specifiers
> - With melancholia: pervasive anhedonia, lack of reactivity, early-morning waking, diurnal variation (worse in the morning), marked psychomotor change, appetite/weight loss, excessive guilt. Predicts response to antidepressants/ECT.
> - With prominent anxiety symptoms; with panic attacks.
> - Seasonal pattern: regular onset/remission at certain times of year (usually autumn–winter). Atypical features: hypersomnia, hyperphagia, carbohydrate craving, weight gain. Linked to melatonin and circadian shift → morning bright-light therapy (10,000 lux, 30 min).
> - Perinatal onset: during pregnancy or within about 6 weeks after delivery.
> - Rapid cycling (bipolar): ≥ 4 mood episodes in 12 months.
> - DSM-only labels you'll still meet: "atypical features" (mood reactivity, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity), "mixed features" specifier.
Q: Which is a feature of seasonal affective disorder given in the lecture? = Excessive sleep, weight gain and carbohydrate craving | Insomnia and weight loss | Elation in winter | Psychosis in summer | Anorexia
> 'Seasonal Affective Disorder — excessive sleep, weight gain, carbohydrate craving. Melatonin produced only in dark. Morning phototherapy.'
Q: Which feature suggests melancholia? = Early-morning waking with mood worst in the morning | Mood worse in the evening | Hypersomnia and hyperphagia | Marked mood reactivity | Leaden paralysis
> Melancholia: early-morning waking, worse in the morning, non-reactive mood, weight loss, guilt.

### Course of depression — numbers to quote
> - Mean onset mid-20s to late 20s (lecture: 27 years). Lifetime prevalence ≈ 10–20%; women ≈ 2:1.
> - Untreated episode lasts ~6–12 months; most remit, but ~15–20% become chronic.
> - Recurrence is the rule: after 1 episode ~50%, after 2 ~70%, after 3 ~90% will recur. Only ~5–15% have a single lifetime episode.
> - Continue antidepressant ≥ 6 months after remission; 2 years (or longer) if recurrent/high risk.
> - Suicide: classic figure ~15% lifetime in severe hospitalised depression (Guze & Robins); far lower in community samples.
Q: According to the lecture, the average onset of major depression is at: = 27 years | 15 years | 40 years | 55 years | 65 years
> 'Onset 27 years, with spontaneous remission in 9–12 months in 90%.'
Q: What proportion of people with major depression have only one lifetime episode? = 5–15% | 30% | 50% | 70% | 90%
> 'Episodic nature, only 5–15% one episode, average 5–6 episodes lifetime.'
Q: After two previous episodes, the chance of a third episode quoted in the lecture is: = 80% | 20% | 50% | 60% | 100%
> '50% recur within 2 years following 1st episode, 80% chance of 3rd episode if 2 previous.'

### Dysthymic disorder (6A72)
> - Persistent depressed mood, most of the day, more days than not, for ≥ 2 years (≥ 1 year in children/adolescents).
> - In the first 2 years there has never been a 2-week period meeting a full depressive episode.
> - Median duration ~5 years; can last decades. Early onset (< 21) → more chronic, poorer prognosis, more familial.
> - Double depression: a major depressive episode superimposed on dysthymia (~40% of dysthymics); worse outcome.
> - Cyclothymic disorder (6A62) is the bipolar counterpart (see bipolar point).
Q: Dysthymic disorder requires chronically depressed mood for: = 2 years | 6 months | 1 year | 5 years | 10 years
> 'Dysthymic disorder — two years of chronically depressed mood; two additional depression symptoms.'
Q: Early-onset dysthymia is defined as onset before age: = 21 | 12 | 16 | 30 | 40
> 'Early onset (before 21 years): greater chronicity, poorer prognosis, greater likelihood of familial transmission.'
Q: Double depression occurs in what proportion of people with dysthymia? = 42% | 5% | 15% | 61% | 90%
> 'Double depression — dysthymia & major depressive episodes — occurs in 42% of those with dysthymia; 61% do not recover within 2 years.'

### ICD-11 manic, hypomanic and mixed episodes
> - Manic episode: an extreme mood state (euphoria, irritability or expansiveness) AND increased activity or subjective energy — ICD-11 makes increased energy/activity a required core feature. Plus several of: rapid/pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, distractibility, impulsive/reckless behaviour, increased sexual drive. Lasts ≥ 1 week (or any duration if treatment is needed). Psychotic features may occur.
> - Hypomanic episode: milder version for several days; a clear change from usual, no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalisation.
> - Mixed episode (ICD-11 keeps it; DSM-5 replaced it with a "mixed features" specifier): several prominent manic and depressive symptoms, simultaneously or alternating very rapidly (day to day or within a day), for ≥ 2 weeks (lecture's DSM-IV figure: 1 week).
> - Mixed states carry the highest suicide risk in bipolar disorder.
Q: A manic episode in the lecture requires a high, expansive or irritable mood for at least: = 1 week | 1 day | 4 days | 2 weeks | 1 month
> 'At least one week of persistently high, expansive, or irritable mood, and 3 of: grandiose self-esteem, lower sleep need, overly talkative, racing thoughts, easily distracted, increased activity, high-risk activities.'
Q: A hypomanic episode lasts: = 4–7 days | 1–2 days | 2 weeks | 1 month | 6 months
> 'Four–seven days of manic episode symptoms; mood disturbance does not critically impair ability to work or maintain social responsibilities.'
Q: Which is listed as a common symptom of a mixed episode? = Thoughts of suicide | Euthymia | Hypersomnia without agitation | Calm mood | Normal appetite
> Mixed episode: one week of both manic and depressive symptoms with rapidly alternating moods — agitation, insomnia, irregular appetite, delusions, thoughts of suicide.
Q: The lecture says the hypomanic response pattern is: = Uncharacteristic — not euthymia | Characteristic of the person | Always psychotic | Always needs admission | Identical to mania
> 'Response pattern is uncharacteristic; not euthymia.' Others notice the change.
Q: In ICD-11, a manic episode requires which feature with the extreme mood state? = Increased activity or subjective energy | Psychotic symptoms | Grandiose delusions | Hospital admission | Decreased need for sleep
> Increased activity or energy is a required core feature in ICD-11.

### Bipolar types (ICD-11)
> - Bipolar I (6A60): ≥ 1 manic or mixed episode. Depressive episodes usual but not required. M ＝ F.
> - Bipolar II (6A61): ≥ 1 hypomanic + ≥ 1 depressive episode, and never a manic or mixed episode. More common in women. Not "milder" — more time depressed, high suicide risk.
> - Cyclothymic disorder (6A62): ≥ 2 years of unstable mood with numerous hypomanic and depressive periods that never meet full episode criteria; little euthymia; onset in adolescence; ~1/3 go on to bipolar disorder.
> - Bipolar III / IV (antidepressant-induced switching; depression with bipolar family history) are Akiskal's spectrum labels — not ICD-11 or DSM-5 categories.
> - An antidepressant-induced manic episode that persists beyond the drug's effect counts towards bipolar I in ICD-11.
Q: In Akiskal's spectrum, bipolar III refers to: = Treatment-induced mania or hypomania | Hypomania and depression | Depression with a bipolar relative | Mania only | Rapid cycling
> 'Bipolar III (treatment-induced mania or hypomania). Bipolar IV (relative with BPD, presents with only depression).' Not ICD-11 or DSM-5 categories.
Q: According to the DSM-5 summary in the lecture, bipolar II is: = Female > male | Male ＝ female | Male > female | Only in children | Defined by mania
> 'Bipolar II — one or more major depressive episodes accompanied by at least one hypomanic episode — FEMALE > MALE. Bipolar I — MALE ＝ FEMALE.'
Q: What proportion of people with cyclothymia develop bipolar disorder? = One-third | One-tenth | One-half | Two-thirds | All
> 'Cyclothymia — less severe than bipolar, lasting 2 years; little or no euthymia; modal onset 12–14 years; 1/3 will develop bipolar disorder.'

### Bipolar disorder — epidemiology and course
> - Lifetime prevalence ~1% (BP-I), 2–4% for the spectrum; M ＝ F for BP-I.
> - Onset ~18–22 years; new onset after 40 → look for an organic cause (secondary mania: steroids, stroke, MS, HIV, thyroid, tumour).
> - First episode is depressive in ~50% → 25–30% of "unipolar" patients later switch to (hypo)mania.
> - Depression dominates the course — patients spend ~3× more time depressed than manic.
> - Misdiagnosis ~70%, most often as unipolar depression; average delay to diagnosis ~10 years.
> - Rapid cycling (≥ 4 episodes/year): ~20%; mostly women; associated with hypothyroidism, antidepressants, substance misuse; lithium works less well.
> - Comorbidity: substance misuse > 50%, anxiety, ADHD. Suicide ~15% lifetime — risk up to 20–30× general population.
Q: Bipolar disorder is described as the _ leading cause of medical disability in developed nations: = 6th | 1st | 3rd | 10th | 20th
> 'Common illness affecting 1% of the world population… 6th leading cause of medical disability in the developed nations.'
Q: Typical onset of bipolar I and II respectively is at: = 18 and 22 years | 12 and 14 years | 30 and 35 years | 40 and 45 years | After 60
> 'Onset 18 & 22 years (Bipolar I & II, respectively), rarely after 40.'
Q: The median number of episodes in bipolar disorder quoted is: = 8 | 2 | 4 | 15 | 30
> 'Duration typically 4 months, depressed phase longer. Median # episodes is 8. Suicide common, 19%.'
Q: Regarding rapid cycling, which is true per the lecture? = 90% of rapid cyclers are female and it is associated with hypothyroidism | Defined as 2 episodes a year | First onset is usually mania | It affects 80% of patients | It is commoner in men
> 'Rapid cycling (4+ episodes in a year) — 20% experience; first onset usually depression; 90% female; commonly associated with hypothyroidism.'
Q: What proportion of first bipolar episodes are depressive? = 50% | 10% | 25% | 75% | 100%
> '50% of first bipolar episodes are depressive episodes.'
Q: Compared with mania, depressive episodes in bipolar disorder occupy: = About twice the amount of time | Half the time | The same time | Ten times the time | No time
> 'Depressive episodes dominate course of bipolar disorder (twice the amount of time as in mania).'
Q: Which is NOT listed by Akiskal as a predictor of suicide in bipolar disorder? = Euphoric mania | High impulsivity | Alcohol and substance abuse | Depression and mixed episodes | History of childhood abuse
> Predictors: impulsivity, alcohol/substance abuse, depression and mixed episodes, childhood abuse, exacerbated by incorrect treatment. Dysphoric (not euphoric) mania carries suicidality.
Q: The rate of misdiagnosis of bipolar disorder in the 2000 survey was: = 69% | 9% | 29% | 49% | 89%
> 'Rate of misdiagnosis — 1994: 73%; 2000: 69%. Most frequent misdiagnosis: unipolar depression.'

### Genetics — bipolar is more heritable than depression
> - Bipolar: heritability ~60–85%; MZ concordance ~40–70%, DZ ~5–25%. A child of one bipolar parent has ~10–25% risk of a mood disorder (lecture: 25–30%).
> - Unipolar depression: heritability ~35–40%; MZ ~46%, DZ ~20% (Kendler).
> - Polygenic; GWAS loci include CACNA1C (calcium channel), ANK3; shared genetic risk with schizophrenia.
> - Relatives of bipolar probands have more unipolar depression too; relatives of unipolar probands have little excess bipolar.
Q: If a parent has bipolar disorder, what proportion of offspring have it, per the lecture? = 25–30% | 1% | 5–10% | 50% | 90%
> '50% of patients with BPD have a parent with BPD. If a parent has BPD, 25–30% of offspring have BPD.'
Q: The MZ concordance for unipolar depression quoted in the lecture is: = 46% | 6% | 20% | 72% | 100%
> 'Unipolar MZ concordance ＝ 46%; unipolar DZ ＝ 20%. Bipolar MZ ＝ 43–72%; bipolar DZ ＝ 6–25%.'

### Biological theories
> - Monoamine hypothesis (Schildkraut 1965 — noradrenaline; Coppen — serotonin): reserpine depletes monoamines → depression; MAOIs/TCAs raise them → improvement. Weakness: drugs act in hours but mood improves over 2–4 weeks → current view ＝ receptor adaptation (down-regulation of β-adrenergic and 5-HT2 receptors, 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitisation) and neuroplasticity (BDNF).
> - HPA axis hyperactivity: raised cortisol, enlarged adrenals, raised CRH; dexamethasone suppression test — non-suppression in ~50% of severe/melancholic depression (Carroll). Not diagnostic, but predicts relapse/suicide.
> - Also: low CSF 5-HIAA (suicide/violence), blunted TSH response to TRH, shortened REM latency, inflammation (raised IL-6, CRP).
> - Imaging: reduced hippocampal volume; amygdala hyperactivity; subgenual anterior cingulate (Cg25 — target of deep brain stimulation).
Q: The current hypothesis of antidepressant action given in the lecture is that they: = Change the density or sensitivity of postsynaptic serotonin receptors | Block dopamine | Raise cortisol | Act only on GABA | Destroy serotonin
> 'Current hypothesis: antidepressant drugs change the density or sensitivity of postsynaptic serotonin receptors.'
Q: Which test is cited in the lecture as identifying major depressive episodes through HPA-axis function? = Dexamethasone suppression test | TRH stimulation test | Glucose tolerance test | Synacthen test | EEG
> 'High levels of cortisol correlate with depression; Dexamethasone Suppression Test identifies major depressive episodes.'

### Psychological and social theories — names and studies examiners want
> - Freud — "Mourning and Melancholia" (1917): loss + anger turned inward (introjection of the lost object). Abraham: oral fixation.
> - Beck's cognitive model: negative cognitive triad (self, world, future), negative schemas, cognitive errors — arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralisation, magnification/minimisation, personalisation, catastrophising. Basis of CBT.
> - Seligman — learned helplessness (dogs given inescapable shocks stop trying to escape). Abramson — reformulated / hopelessness theory: attributions that are internal, stable and global.
> - Lewinsohn — behavioural: loss of response-contingent positive reinforcement → basis of behavioural activation.
> - Interpersonal theory: rejection, poor social skills, excessive reassurance-seeking → basis of IPT.
> - Brown & Harris (1978), Camberwell women — vulnerability factors: ≥ 3 children under 14 at home, no employment outside the home, lack of a confiding relationship, loss of mother before age 11. Provoking agents ＝ severe life events.
Q: Which finding challenges the psychoanalytic view of depression as anger turned inward? = Dream themes of depressed patients are of loss and failure, not anger and hostility (Beck & Ward 1961) | Depressed people never express anger | Depression is genetic | Antidepressants work | Depression is commoner in women
> 'But dream themes of depressed patients are of loss and failure, not anger and hostility (Beck and Ward, 1961).'
Q: Which is NOT one of Beck's characteristic biases listed in the lecture? = Learned helplessness | Arbitrary inference | Selective abstraction | Overgeneralisation | Magnification and minimisation
> Biases: arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralisation, magnification/minimisation, catastrophisation. Learned helplessness is a behavioural theory.
Q: In the lecture's assessment of Beck's theory, which statement is made? = It is correlational, not causal | It is proven causal | CBT based on it does not help | Depressed people show no biases | Pessimism is always inaccurate
> 'Depressed people do show cognitive biases; their apparent pessimism, however, is accurate; the theory is correlational, not causal; treatment based on it (CBT) is helpful.'
Q: Behavioural theory explains depression mainly through: = Reduction in reinforcement leading to reduced activity | Unconscious conflict | Serotonin deficiency | Rejection by others | Loss of meaning
> 'Reduction in reinforcement leads to a reduction in activity; depressive behaviours are reinforced; depressed people take part in fewer pleasant events.'
Q: Brown and Harris's vulnerability factors include all EXCEPT: = Being the eldest child | Three or more children under 14 at home | Lack of a confiding relationship | Loss of mother before age 11 | No employment outside the home
> The four: ≥ 3 children under 14, no outside employment, no confidant, maternal loss before 11.

### Special populations
> - Elderly: more somatic and hypochondriacal complaints, agitation, insomnia, less reported sadness; depressive pseudodementia ("don't know" answers, patchy deficits, rapid onset, distress about memory) vs dementia. Vascular depression (white-matter lesions). Late-onset → screen for organic causes.
> - Children/adolescents: irritability, school refusal, somatic complaints, behavioural change; boys with conduct problems. Fluoxetine is the first-line antidepressant < 18 (with CBT/IPT-A). Suicide attempts rise sharply in adolescence.
> - Postpartum: blues 50–80% (days 3–5, resolve by 2 weeks, no treatment); postnatal depression ~10–15% (EPDS screen); puerperal psychosis ~1–2/1000, onset within 2 weeks, usually bipolar in nature — an emergency; recurrence risk ~50% in later pregnancies.
Q: According to the lecture, postnatal 'blues' affect: = 50–80% within 1–5 days | 1 in 1000 mothers | 10–15% within 6 weeks | All mothers | Only first-time mothers
> '50–80% blues within 1–5 days postpartum. 1/1000 psychotic depression or mania within 1–3 days postpartum.'
Q: A severe postpartum mood reaction: = Predicts similar reactions in future births | Never recurs | Only affects fathers | Means bipolar disorder is excluded | Requires sterilisation
> 'More severe reactions predict similar in future births.'
Q: Depression in the elderly is marked by: = Sleep difficulties, hypochondriasis and agitation | Early onset and brief course | Elation | Male predominance | No link with dementia
> 'Elderly — late onset common & chronic, marked by sleep difficulties, hypochondriasis, agitation; complicated by dementia; equal prevalence for men and women.'
Q: In very young children, depression shows as changes in: = Facial expression, eating, sleeping and play | Speech and reading | Handwriting | School grades only | Height
> 'Very young manifest changes in facial expression, eating, sleeping & play; older children mimic adults.'
Q: Which is true of mood disorders in young people, according to the lecture? = Depression and bipolar disorder peak in adolescence | Bipolar adolescents are cautious | Suicide attempts fall in adolescence | Conduct disorder never masks depression | Bipolar disorder starts after 40
> 'Depression & bipolar peak in adolescence; bipolar adolescents impulsive, accident-prone; conduct disorder for boys; skyrocketing suicide attempts.'

### Lithium — the most examined drug in mood disorders
> - Uses: acute mania (best in classic euphoric mania), prophylaxis of bipolar (gold standard — prevents mania and depression), augmentation in resistant depression. Only drug with strong anti-suicide evidence (with clozapine).
> - Less effective: mixed episodes, rapid cycling, comorbid substance misuse.
> - Levels: 12 h post-dose; 0.6–0.8 mmol/L maintenance (0.8–1.0 if relapsing); toxicity > 1.5, severe > 2.0.
> - Monitoring: level weekly after each dose change until stable, then 3-monthly in year 1, then 6-monthly; U&E/eGFR, TFT, calcium every 6 months; weight.
> - Side effects: fine tremor, polyuria/polydipsia (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), hypothyroidism (women), hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcaemia, weight gain, acne/psoriasis flare, T-wave flattening, CKD long-term. Ebstein's anomaly in pregnancy (risk smaller than once thought).
> - Raise levels: thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, dehydration, low-salt diet.
> - Toxicity: coarse tremor, vomiting/diarrhoea, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, seizures → stop, IV fluids, haemodialysis if severe.
> - Stopping abruptly → rebound mania; taper over ≥ 4 weeks.
Q: Lithium is less effective in: = Mixed mania episodes and rapid cycling | Euphoric mania | Prophylaxis | Bipolar depression | Acute mania
> 'Lithium appears to be effective for individuals with euphoric mania, but is less effective in mixed mania episodes and in rapid cycling bipolar disorders.'
Q: The lecture names which drug as first choice for maintenance that also reduces suicidality? = Lithium | Valproate | Lamotrigine | Olanzapine | Carbamazepine
> 'Lithium — first choice for maintenance treatment, and reduces suicidality.'
Q: Which drug is least likely to raise serum lithium? = Paracetamol | Bendroflumethiazide | Ibuprofen | Lisinopril | Losartan
> Thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and ARBs raise lithium; paracetamol is safe.
Q: Long-term lithium causes all EXCEPT: = Hyperprolactinaemia | Hypothyroidism | Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus | Hypercalcaemia | Psoriasis exacerbation
> Lithium does not raise prolactin.

### Anticonvulsant mood stabilisers
> - Valproate: acute mania, mixed episodes and rapid cycling (better than lithium there); rapid loading. Teratogenic (neural tube defects, ~10% malformations, ~30–40% neurodevelopmental harm) — must not be used in women/girls of childbearing potential unless a Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place (MHRA 2018); 2024 UK caution in men (possible fertility/offspring risk). Other effects: weight gain, tremor, hair loss, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, PCOS, hyperammonaemia. Enzyme inhibitor.
> - Carbamazepine: mania and prophylaxis (second line). Enzyme inducer — lowers its own level (auto-induction) and those of the pill, antipsychotics, warfarin. Risks: agranulocytosis/aplastic anaemia, hyponatraemia (SIADH), SJS/TEN (screen HLA-B*1502 in Han Chinese/SE Asian), teratogenic.
> - Lamotrigine: bipolar depression and prevention of depressive relapse; not effective for mania. Titrate slowly (25 mg/day) to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome; halve the dose with valproate.
> - Gabapentin, pregabalin, topiramate, levetiracetam, tiagabine — no proven mood-stabilising efficacy.
Q: An advantage of valproate over lithium listed in the lecture is: = Better tolerability, earlier onset and rapid loading | No teratogenicity | No drug interactions | Best evidence for prophylaxis | Safe in women of reproductive age
> 'Advantages — better tolerability and earlier onset than lithium; can be loaded rapidly; once-a-day formulation.' It's a hepatic enzyme inhibitor and teratogenic.
Q: Carbamazepine's main pharmacokinetic disadvantage is that it: = Reduces the plasma level of itself and other drugs | Inhibits liver enzymes | Is renally excreted | Has a long half-life | Cannot be given once daily
> 'Drug-drug interaction (reduces plasma level of itself and other drugs)' — auto-induction. Serious effects: bone marrow suppression, acute skin failure.
Q: Which anticonvulsant has no proven efficacy in bipolar disorder per the lecture? = Gabapentin | Valproate | Carbamazepine | Lamotrigine | None
> 'Gabapentin, Pregabalin, Levetiracetam, Tiagabine, Topiramate — NO PROVEN EFFICACY.'
Q: In the RCT evidence summary, lamotrigine is effective for: = Maintenance (and acute depression) but not acute mania | Acute mania | Nothing | Only rapid cycling | Only mixed episodes
> Lamotrigine: acute mania –, acute depression +, maintenance ++.

### Managing acute mania
> 1. Safety first: risk to self/others, finances, sexual disinhibition, driving; admission (often under mental health law); stop antidepressants; check for drugs/organic causes.
> 2. Not on a mood stabiliser: start an antipsychotic — haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone (NICE first line; onset 2–4 days). If ineffective, switch antipsychotic, then add lithium or valproate.
> 3. Already on lithium/valproate: check level and optimise dose, then add an antipsychotic.
> 4. Severe or mixed: combination (antipsychotic + valproate); lithium is weaker in mixed states.
> 5. Short-term benzodiazepine (lorazepam) for agitation and sleep.
> 6. Refractory: ECT, clozapine.
> - Maintenance: lithium first line; alternatives valproate, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole; LAIs (risperidone, paliperidone, aripiprazole) halve manic relapse in poor adherers — mainly prevent mania, not depression.
Q: The onset of action of atypical antipsychotics in acute mania is within: = 2–4 days | Hours | 2 weeks | 6 weeks | 3 months
> 'Convincing evidence for efficacy in acute treatment of mania… Onset of action within 2–4 days. Strong evidence for maintenance efficacy for olanzapine.'
Q: For a mixed episode, the APA guideline prefers: = Divalproex or an antipsychotic over lithium | Lithium | An SSRI | Lamotrigine | Benzodiazepine alone
> 'For mixed episodes, divalproex or antipsychotic is preferred over lithium.'
Q: For a breakthrough manic episode on maintenance, the first step is to: = Optimise the maintenance medication dose | Switch to clozapine | Start ECT | Add an SSRI | Stop all medication
> 'For breakthrough episodes, first optimize the maintenance medication dose; consider adding an antipsychotic… Clozapine or ECT for treatment-refractory patients.'
Q: Which LAIs have strong evidence for reducing manic relapse, per Maudsley? = Paliperidone, risperidone and aripiprazole LAI | Fluphenazine and haloperidol decanoate | Flupentixol only | Zuclopenthixol only | None
> 'Evidence on first-generation LAI is weak. Strong evidence for paliperidone, risperidone and aripiprazole LAI — relapse risk reduced by as much as 50%. No evidence of superiority over oral.'
Q: In emerging trends for acute mania, the lecture states that: = Combination treatment is the rule, not the exception | Monotherapy is the rule | Lithium is obsolete | Antidepressants are first line | ECT is first line
> 'Combination treatment the rule, not the exception; continued use of lithium and divalproex as cornerstones.'

### Bipolar depression — the trap is antidepressant monotherapy
> - First line (NICE/Maudsley): quetiapine, olanzapine + fluoxetine (combination), lurasidone, lamotrigine; lithium if not already on it (and for suicidality).
> - Antidepressants only with a mood stabiliser/antipsychotic — never alone in bipolar I. Monotherapy risks switch to mania, mixed states and rapid cycling (cycle acceleration).
> - Switch risk: high with TCAs, venlafaxine (SNRIs), MAOIs (> 10%); lower with SSRIs and bupropion.
> - Severe, psychotic or suicidal: add antipsychotic or ECT. Ketamine is an emerging second-line option.
> - Red flags for hidden bipolarity in a "depressed" patient: early onset (< 25), postpartum onset, psychotic or atypical features, very frequent episodes, family history of bipolar, antidepressant-induced (hypo)mania or agitation. → Ask about hypomania, involve the family, use a screen (MDQ, HCL-32).
Q: What proportion of patients first diagnosed with unipolar depression later have a manic or hypomanic episode? = 25–30% | 1–2% | 5–10% | 60% | 90%
> '25–30% of patients initially diagnosed with unipolar depression subsequently have a manic or hypomanic episode.'
Q: According to Berk & Dodd, antidepressants in bipolar disorder can induce: = Mixed states, rapid cycling and mania | Remission only | Dementia | Schizophrenia | Catatonia only
> 'Antidepressants can induce mixed states, rapid cycling, and mania… more likely to alternate with dysphoria… high impulsivity & irritability.'
Q: In the paroxetine studies, adding an antidepressant to lithium was better than lithium alone only when: = Lithium level was below 0.8 | The patient was male | Lithium level was above 1.2 | The patient had psychosis | Never
> 'Lithium alone as good as lithium combined with antidepressant… except at low lithium levels (< 0.8).'
Q: Which antidepressants have high switch rates (over 10%) even on mood stabilisers? = TCAs, venlafaxine and MAOIs | SSRIs and bupropion | Mirtazapine only | Agomelatine | None
> 'High rates of switch — TCAs, venlafaxine, MAOIs; low rates — bupropion, SSRIs; much higher if not on a mood stabilizer.'
Q: For a less severely ill bipolar depressed patient not on a mood stabiliser, APA advises starting: = Lithium or lamotrigine | An SSRI alone | Clozapine | ECT | Haloperidol
> 'For less severely ill patients — initiate lithium or lamotrigine; more severely ill — lithium and an antidepressant; psychosis or high suicide risk — add antipsychotic, ECT.'
Q: Which combination does Maudsley (14th ed.) present as probably the most effective treatment for acute bipolar depression? = Olanzapine + fluoxetine | Lithium + valproate | Haloperidol + sertraline | Lamotrigine + carbamazepine | Quetiapine + venlafaxine
> 'Emerging evidence for Olanzapine + Fluoxetine as the first choice and probably the most effective treatment of acute bipolar depression.'
Q: Treating bipolar disorder as unipolar depression can cause: = Switching into mania or cycle acceleration | Faster recovery | Dementia | Tardive dyskinesia | No harm
> 'Treatment as unipolar depression can lead to worsening of symptoms by switching into mania or cycle acceleration.'
Q: Which is NOT a step recommended to improve recognition of bipolar disorder? = Start antidepressants early to unmask mania | Educate physicians | Ask patients directly about bipolar symptoms | Involve family members | Screen depressed patients for bipolar disorder
> Steps: educate physicians, ask directly, involve family, increase awareness, screen for bipolar disorder especially in depressed patients. Unmasking mania with antidepressants is harmful.

### Treating unipolar depression (stepped care)
> - Mild: guided self-help, behavioural activation, group CBT, exercise; antidepressants not routine first line.
> - Moderate–severe: antidepressant + psychotherapy (CBT/IPT) combined is best. SSRI first line (sertraline, fluoxetine, escitalopram); review at 2 weeks (suicidality, especially < 25s); judge response at 4–6 weeks.
> - Non-response: increase dose → switch (other class: mirtazapine, SNRI, vortioxetine) → augment (lithium, an atypical antipsychotic — aripiprazole/quetiapine) → TCA/MAOI.
> - Psychotic depression: antidepressant + antipsychotic, or ECT.
> - ECT — fastest and most effective: severe depression with psychosis, stupor, refusal to eat/drink or high suicide risk; response ~70–80%.
> - Newer options: esketamine nasal spray (NMDA antagonist, rapid), vortioxetine (multimodal 5-HT), rTMS (left DLPFC), tDCS, psilocybin-assisted therapy (research); zuranolone/brexanolone for postpartum depression. Anti-inflammatory/antioxidant adjuncts (N-acetylcysteine, minocycline) are experimental.
Q: Which is listed as an antioxidant treatment under recent advances? = N-acetylcysteine | Ketamine | Vortioxetine | Psilocybin | rTMS
> 'Anti-oxidants — N-acetyl cysteine, Minocycline.' Ketamine and dizocilpine ＝ NMDA antagonists; vortioxetine ＝ serotonergic modulator.
Q: Which is a neuromodulation treatment listed in the lecture? = Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation | Psilocybin | Vortioxetine | Gene editing | Minocycline
> Neuromodulation: rTMS and transcranial direct current stimulation.

### Differentials — exclude organic and substance causes
> - Of depression: hypothyroidism, Cushing's/Addison's, anaemia, B12/folate deficiency, Parkinson's, stroke (left frontal), MS, dementia, HIV, cancer (pancreas); drugs — steroids, β-blockers, isotretinoin, interferon, reserpine, methyldopa, levetiracetam, alcohol, benzodiazepines; stimulant withdrawal. Psychiatric: adjustment disorder, bereavement, dysthymia, negative symptoms of schizophrenia, PTSD.
> - Of mania: hyperthyroidism, steroids, stimulants/cocaine, levodopa, antidepressants, HIV, syphilis, frontal lesions, right-hemisphere stroke, MS, Cushing's; schizophrenia, schizoaffective, ADHD, borderline personality disorder (mood shifts over hours, triggered by interpersonal events — not sustained episodes).
> - Work-up: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, B12/folate, HIV/VDRL, urine drug screen; CT/MRI if late onset or neurological signs.
Q: Which feature favours borderline PD over bipolar disorder? = Mood shifts over hours triggered by interpersonal events | Episodes lasting weeks | Decreased need for sleep with high energy | Grandiose delusions | Family history of bipolar
> BPD mood shifts are brief and reactive; bipolar episodes are sustained.

### Mixed questions: Mood disorders
> Questions from the lecture that are not tied to one summary point.
Q: Which is NOT one of the mood episodes listed in the lecture? = Psychotic episode | Depressive episode | Manic episode | Mixed episode | Hypomanic episode
> Episodes: depressive, manic, mixed, hypomanic — plus cycling patterns. Psychotic features are a specifier, not a mood episode.
Q: Which is listed as a social intervention in the lecture? = Carer needs assessment and support | CBT | Cognitive analytical therapy | Psychodynamic therapy | Interpersonal therapy
> Social interventions: patient needs assessment and interventions, support groups, carer needs assessment and support. The others are psychological treatments.
Q: Family therapy in mood disorders targets: = Family communication and relationship dynamics | Medication adherence only | Genetic counselling only | Financial support | Housing
> 'Family therapy — family communication and relationship dynamics.'

### OSCE: Depressive symptoms and cognitive errors | fps
> History taking station. Task: Assess a patient reporting low mood, identify depressive symptoms and elicit relevant cognitive errors. Summarise and address safety.
> Patient: “Amina”, 32, has felt low for 7 weeks after workplace criticism. Poor sleep, reduced appetite, fatigue, loss of interest, guilt and poor concentration. She thinks one mistake proves she is useless. Passive thoughts that life is not worth living, but no current plan or intent. No past mania.
> - FNPH Kaduna: open with “I understand you’ve been going through a lot. I am so sorry about that,” then “Can you tell me how things have been for you?” End by asking how they cope and about thoughts of killing themselves.
> - Abdulhakeem: begin with the cognitive triad (worthless, hopeless, helpless), screen for nihilistic delusions, then go through PLADMMOSC (personalisation, labelling, arbitrary inference, dichotomous thinking, magnification, minimisation, overgeneralisation, selective abstraction, catastrophising).
> - After the errors, screen mood symptoms, psychosis and substance use.
> Critical fail: Failing to assess suicide risk after a cue, or ending without an urgent safety response when intent/plan is present.

### OSCE: Explaining antidepressant treatment | fps
> Communication station. Task: Explain antidepressant treatment to this patient with a depressive episode.
> - The Abdulhakeem notes say antidepressants are “generally safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding”. Safer: “If you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding, tell us. We weigh the risks and benefits for you and the baby; some antidepressants are preferred, and you should not stop suddenly.”
> - Avoid describing depression as only a chemical imbalance.
> - Book prognosis: about a third respond fully, a third partially, a third not at all. Placebo response in trials is substantial.
> Critical fail: Not warning about the delay in effect, about stopping suddenly, or about early suicidal thoughts.
