### Bonus drill: ICD-11 depressive episode
> ICD-11 depressive episode: at least 5 of 10 symptoms, most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks. At least ONE must come from the affective cluster.
> - Affective (2): depressed mood; markedly diminished interest or pleasure.
> - Cognitive-behavioural (4): reduced concentration; worthlessness or excessive guilt; hopelessness; recurrent thoughts of death or suicide.
> - Neurovegetative (4): sleep disturbance; appetite or weight change; psychomotor agitation or retardation; reduced energy.
> Grade it mild, moderate or severe, with or without psychotic symptoms. A past manic or hypomanic episode makes it bipolar instead.
> Codes: 6A70 single episode, 6A71 recurrent, 6A72 dysthymic, 6A73 mixed depressive and anxiety disorder.
Q: Minimum duration of a depressive episode (ICD-11) = At least 2 weeks | At least 1 week :: One week is the usual minimum for a manic episode | At least 1 month :: One month is the ICD-11 duration for schizophrenia | At least 6 months :: Too long; a depressive episode needs at least 2 weeks
> Same 2-week threshold as DSM-5. Learn the duration ladder: hypomania several days, mania 1 week (less if hospitalised or treated), depressive episode 2 weeks, schizophrenia 1 month, dysthymia 2 years.
Q: Number of symptoms required for an ICD-11 depressive episode = At least 5 of 10 | At least 3 of 10 :: Too few; ICD-11 needs at least 5 of the 10 | At least 4 of 10 :: Too few; ICD-11 needs at least 5 of the 10 | At least 6 of 10 :: Too many; 5 of the 10 is enough
> ICD-11 has 10 symptoms because it adds HOPELESSNESS to the 9 DSM criteria. Both systems need 5.
Q: At least one of the symptoms must be = Depressed mood or markedly diminished interest or pleasure | Depressed mood or reduced energy :: Reduced energy is neurovegetative; the core pair is low mood and loss of interest | Diminished interest or hopelessness :: Hopelessness is cognitive-behavioural, not affective | Both depressed mood AND diminished interest :: Only ONE of the two is required
> These two make up the affective cluster. Without one of them, it is not a depressive episode, however many other symptoms there are.
Q: Which is NOT an ICD-11 depressive symptom? = Pressured speech | Hopelessness :: Hopelessness IS one of the 10 (ICD-11 added it) | Psychomotor agitation or retardation :: Agitation IS included (neurovegetative cluster) | Indecisiveness :: Indecisiveness IS included, with reduced concentration
> Pressured speech is a MANIC symptom. If manic and depressive symptoms mix within the episode, think of a mixed episode (bipolar).
Q: ICD-11 code for single episode depressive disorder = 6A70 | 6A71 :: 6A71 is recurrent depressive disorder | 6A20 :: 6A20 is schizophrenia | 6B00 :: 6B00 is generalised anxiety disorder
> The mood-disorder block: 6A60 bipolar I, 6A61 bipolar II, 6A62 cyclothymic, 6A70 single episode depressive, 6A71 recurrent depressive, 6A72 dysthymic, 6A73 mixed depressive and anxiety.
Q: ICD-11 code for recurrent depressive disorder = 6A71 | 6A70 :: 6A70 is single episode depressive disorder | 6A60 :: 6A60 is bipolar type I disorder | 6A72 :: 6A72 is dysthymic disorder
> "Recurrent" means at least two depressive episodes, separated by several months without significant mood disturbance.
Q: ICD-11 dysthymic disorder needs persistent low mood for at least = 2 years | 1 year :: 1 year is the DSM-5 rule for children and adolescents; ICD-11 uses 2 years | 6 months :: Too short for dysthymia | 3 years :: Too long; it is 2 years
> Dysthymic disorder (6A72): persistent depressive mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years, without full depressive episodes in the first 2 years.
L: ICD-11 depressive symptom clusters = Affective | Cognitive-behavioural | Neurovegetative ~~ Psychotic :: Not an ICD-11 depressive cluster | Manic :: Not an ICD-11 depressive cluster | Perceptual :: Not an ICD-11 depressive cluster
> Affective 2, cognitive-behavioural 4, neurovegetative 4 = 10 symptoms.
S: The 10 ICD-11 depressive episode symptoms = Depressed mood | Diminished interest or pleasure | Reduced concentration or indecisiveness | Low self-worth or excessive guilt | Hopelessness about the future | Recurrent thoughts of death or suicide | Disturbed sleep | Change in appetite or weight | Psychomotor agitation or retardation | Reduced energy or fatigue ~~ Pressured speech :: That is a manic symptom | Grandiosity :: That is a manic symptom | Increased goal-directed activity :: That is a manic symptom | Flight of ideas :: That is a manic symptom
> Group them as you shoot: 2 affective, 4 cognitive-behavioural, 4 neurovegetative.
L: Kubler-Ross stages of grief = Denial | Anger | Bargaining | Depression | Acceptance ~~ Contemplation :: That is a stage of change | Precontemplation :: That is a stage of change | Maintenance :: That is a stage of change
> From "On Death and Dying" (1969). People move back and forth; the stages are not strictly sequential.
> ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder (6B42): persistent longing or preoccupation with the deceased, with intense emotional pain, lasting at least 6 months after the loss and beyond cultural norms.
Q: ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder: minimum time since the loss = At least 6 months | At least 12 months :: 12 months is the DSM-5-TR rule for adults; ICD-11 uses 6 months | At least 3 months :: Too short | At least 2 years :: Too long; it is 6 months
> It must also clearly exceed what is expected in the person's social, cultural or religious context.
L: Starting an antidepressant (NICE outline) = Assess severity and suicide risk | Start an SSRI as first line | Review within 2 weeks (1 week if under 25 or at risk) | If little response at 4 weeks, adjust dose or switch | Continue for at least 6 months after remission | Taper gradually when stopping ~~ Stop abruptly when well :: Stopping suddenly risks discontinuation symptoms; taper | Start with an MAOI :: MAOIs are not first line | Review only after 3 months :: Far too late; review within 2 weeks
> Warn about early side effects, the 2-4 week delay in benefit, and possible early agitation or suicidal thoughts in young people.
> After remission, continue at least 6 months (longer if recurrent). Stop by tapering over weeks.

## NE Wing | Personality disorders
> Personality disorders. Source: PERSONALITY DISORDER 2026 AMOSU_081016.ppt. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Personality and personality disorder
> - Personality: the enduring pattern of perceiving, relating to and thinking about oneself and the environment; develops in childhood/adolescence, relatively stable, but adaptable.
> - Personality disorder (general criteria, all systems): an enduring, pervasive, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from cultural expectations, begins in adolescence or early adulthood, is stable over time, and causes distress or impairment.
> - Prevalence: ~4–10% of the general population; 40–50% of psychiatric outpatients/inpatients. Worsens the course of depression, substance use, eating disorders.
> - Social cost: crime, self-harm, substance misuse, homelessness, child abuse/neglect, unemployment — "an under-appreciated cause of morbidity and mortality".
Q: According to the ISSPD figure in the lecture, personality disorder affects: = 3–10% of the population | 0.1–0.5% of the population | 20–30% | 50% | Only psychiatric inpatients
> 'Affects 3–10% of the popln (ISSPD).'
Q: Which statement about PD is made in the lecture? = It may or may not be associated with subjective symptoms | It is always associated with subjective symptoms | It never affects the outcome of other disorders | It only distresses the patient | It is rare in psychiatric practice
> 'Unlike other diagnoses, may/may not be associated with subjective symptoms… Some PDs may produce distress in other people rather than in the patient.'
Q: The lecture describes PD as an under-appreciated cause of: = Social disruption, morbidity and mortality | Dementia | Psychosis | Epilepsy | Intellectual disability
> 'PD — underappreciated cause of social disruption, morbidity and mortality' — crime, DSH, homelessness, child abuse, delayed recovery from other illness.
Q: Zimbardo (2002) described personality as: = The thread of continuity in an individual in different situations | A set of symptoms | A brain region | A learned habit only | A temporary mood
> 'The psychological qualities that bring continuity to an individual's behaviour… It is the thread of continuity in an individual in different situations.'
Q: According to the lecture, personality: = Develops in childhood/adolescence and is relatively stable but adaptable | Develops in late adulthood | Changes completely with mood | Can be fully measured by one test | Has no influence on values
> 'Develops in childhood/adolescence; remains relatively stable in spite of mood changes, but is adaptable to environmental factors.' It is virtually impossible to measure with any single test.
Q: Which is NOT part of the DSM-IV-TR definition of PD quoted in the lecture? = Episodic with full recovery between episodes | Deviates markedly from the individual's culture | Pervasive and inflexible | Onset in adolescence or early adulthood | Leads to distress or impairment
> PD is stable over time, not episodic. The definition: deviates from culture, pervasive and inflexible, onset adolescence/early adulthood, stable, distress or impairment.

### History — names examiners ask for
> - Philippe Pinel (1801): "manie sans délire" — madness without delusion; reasoning intact.
> - James Cowles Prichard (1835): "moral insanity" — disordered feelings/conduct with intact intellect; first to treat enduring abnormal personality as a distinct group.
> - Kurt Schneider (1923): "psychopathic personalities" — abnormal personalities who suffer themselves or make society suffer. He described 10 types: hyperthymic, depressive, insecure (sensitive and anankastic), fanatical, attention-seeking, labile, explosive, affectionless, weak-willed, asthenic. First systematic classification.
> - Cleckley (1941) "The Mask of Sanity" → Hare's Psychopathy Checklist (PCL-R), 20 items, cut-off 30 (25 in UK).
Q: 'Manie sans délire' — madness with reasoning intact — was described by: = Pinel (1801) | Prichard | Schneider | Kraepelin | Cleckley
> 'Pinel (1801): Manie sans délire (madness without confusion of mind)… ability to reason intact; no loss of contact with reality.'
Q: Who first suggested that PD be constituted into a distinct diagnostic group? = Prichard | Pinel | Schneider | Freud | Zimbardo
> 'Pritchard — distinguished bw. transient psychopathological states and those with more enduring characteristics; first to suggest that PD be constituted into a distinct diagnostic group.'
Q: In Schneider's view (1923), an 'abnormal personality' is: = A deviation from the average range, not necessarily pathological | Always pathological | Always criminal | A psychotic disorder | Caused by brain damage
> 'Abnormal personality: a deviation (excess or deficiency, good or bad) from the range of average personality — being abnormal is not necessarily pathological.'
Q: How many variants of psychopathic personality did Schneider describe? = 10 | 4 | 6 | 12 | 16
> 10 variants — fanatical, depressive, hyperthymic, insecure (sensitive), insecure (anankast), affectionless, weak-willed, asthenic, attention-seeking, labile explosive — the first attempt at classifying PDs.

### Two ways to study personality
> - Idiographic — the uniqueness of the individual; clinical, descriptive; basis of ICD-10/DSM categories. Criticism: lacks objectivity.
> - Nomothetic — measures shared traits objectively (Eysenck, Cattell). Criticism: loses the individual.
> Trait models:
> - Hippocrates/Galen — 4 temperaments: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic.
> - Cattell (1957) — 16 Personality Factors (16PF), by factor analysis.
> - Eysenck — 3 dimensions (PEN): Psychoticism, Extraversion–introversion, Neuroticism–stability; measured with the EPQ.
> - Five-factor model ("Big Five", Costa & McCrae — OCEAN): Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism; measured with the NEO-PI-R.
> - Cloninger: temperament (novelty seeking, harm avoidance, reward dependence, persistence) + character.
Q: Sullivan's interpersonal theory holds that maladaptive behaviour results from: = Failure to progress satisfactorily through relationship stages from parents to marriage | Oral fixation | Low serotonin | Superego weakness | Classical conditioning
> 'Sullivan: interaction with parents → peer relationships → intimate relationships → marriage; failure to progress satisfactorily through the stages → maladaptive behaviour.'
Q: Which theorists are listed under the humanistic (self-growth) theories? = Maslow and Carl Rogers | Freud and Jung | Eysenck and Cattell | Pavlov and Skinner | Beck and Ellis
> 'Humanistic — John Maslow's holistic theory; Carl Rogers' person-centred theory.' Cattell ＝ trait (biological) theory.
Q: Which approach is the basis of both ICD and DSM classifications of PD? = Idiographic | Nomothetic | Psychometric | Projective | Behavioural
> 'Idiographic approach — emphasizes the uniqueness of the individual… basis of both ICD & DSM classifications of personality disorder. Criticism: lacks objective validity.'
Q: The main criticism of the nomothetic approach is that it: = Loses the individuality of the person | Lacks objective validity | Is too subjective | Cannot be measured | Ignores traits
> 'Criticism: loses the individuality of the person — e.g. 2 people could have the same score on the EPI and yet be viewed by others as quite different people.'
Q: Which ancient temperament is described as restless, aggressive, impulsive, optimistic? = Choleric | Sanguine | Melancholic | Phlegmatic | Hyperthymic
> 'Choleric: restless, aggressive, impulsive, optimistic.' Sanguine — outgoing, carefree; melancholic — moody, anxious; phlegmatic — careful, reliable.
Q: Cattell reduced thousands of trait names to how many personality factors? = 16 | 3 | 5 | 10 | 24
> 'Cattell (1957) — factor analysis: reduced thousands of trait names to 16 Personality Factors… measured using Cattell's 16-PF.'
Q: High scorers on Eysenck's psychoticism dimension are: = Cold, lacking empathy and tough-minded | Sociable and lively | Anxious and guilt-prone | Organised and responsible | Open to new ideas
> 'Psychoticism – superego control (high scorers: cold, lacking in empathy, tough minded).'
Q: In the Big Five, the tendency to be responsible and organised is: = Conscientiousness | Openness | Extraversion | Agreeableness | Neuroticism
> 'Conscientiousness – lack of direction: C — tendency to be responsible and organized.' Measured by the NEO Personality Inventory.

### ICD-11 — the big change: severity, not types
> - 6D10 Personality disorder, rated mild / moderate / severe by how much it impairs self-functioning (identity, self-worth, self-direction) and interpersonal functioning (intimacy, perspective-taking, managing conflict). Pattern present ≥ 2 years.
> - QE50.7 Personality difficulty — below the PD threshold (not a mental disorder).
> - Trait domain qualifiers (6D11) describe style: negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia — plus a borderline pattern qualifier (kept for clinical continuity).
> - The ICD-10 types are gone (paranoid, schizoid, dissocial, emotionally unstable, histrionic, anankastic, anxious, dependent). Schizotypal sits with psychotic disorders (6A22).
> - Rationale: types overlap heavily, are unreliable, and severity predicts outcome best. DSM-5 Section II stays categorical; its Section III "Alternative Model" is dimensional.
Q: In the ISSPD/ARPD survey, what proportion said PDs are better understood as variants of normal personality? = 80% | 20% | 40% | 60% | 100%
> '80% of respondents indicated that personality disorders are better understood as variants of normal personality than as categorical disease entities.'
Q: In DSM-IV, personality disorders were coded on: = Axis II | Axis I | Axis III | Axis IV | Axis V
> 'In DSM-IV multiaxial classification, PD was placed in Axis II (but not in DSM-5)' — DSM-5 uses a single axis.
Q: In ICD-11, personality disorder is primarily classified by: = Severity — mild, moderate, severe | Ten specific types | Three clusters A–C | Age of onset | Response to treatment
> ICD-11 6D10 is graded by severity, with optional trait domain qualifiers.
Q: Which is not an ICD-11 personality trait domain? = Psychoticism | Negative affectivity | Detachment | Dissociality | Anankastia
> ICD-11: negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia (+ borderline pattern).

### DSM-5 clusters — still essential for MCQs
> - Cluster A (odd, eccentric): paranoid (suspicious, grudges, litigious, jealous — not psychotic), schizoid (cold, solitary, indifferent to praise/criticism), schizotypal (magical thinking, ideas of reference, odd speech, social anxiety — genetically linked to schizophrenia).
> - Cluster B (dramatic, erratic): antisocial, borderline, histrionic (attention-seeking, seductive, shallow labile emotion, suggestible), narcissistic (grandiose, entitled, needs admiration, lacks empathy).
> - Cluster C (anxious, fearful): avoidant (wants relationships but fears rejection), dependent (needs others to decide, fears abandonment, submissive), obsessive-compulsive/anankastic (perfectionism, rigidity, can't delegate — ego-syntonic, unlike OCD).
> - ICD-10 equivalents: dissocial ＝ antisocial; emotionally unstable (impulsive or borderline type) ＝ borderline; anankastic ＝ OCPD; anxious (avoidant) ＝ avoidant. ICD-10 had no narcissistic and placed schizotypal with schizophrenia.
Q: Which personality disorder is in Cluster A? = Schizotypal | Histrionic | Avoidant | Borderline | Dependent
> Cluster A (odd, eccentric): paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal. B: histrionic, narcissistic, borderline, antisocial. C: avoidant, dependent, OCPD.
Q: The ICD-10 equivalent of DSM borderline PD is: = Emotionally unstable | Dissocial | Anankastic | Anxious | Histrionic
> ICD-10 emotionally unstable ＝ borderline; dissocial ＝ antisocial; anankastic ＝ obsessive-compulsive; anxious (avoidant) ＝ avoidant.
Q: Which DSM-IV personality disorder had no ICD-10 PD equivalent in the lecture's table? = Narcissistic | Paranoid | Dependent | Histrionic | Schizoid
> Narcissistic and schizotypal have no ICD-10 PD equivalent (schizotypal sits with schizophrenia).
Q: In the lecture's summary, paranoid PD is suspicious, jealous and distrustful but: = Not psychotic or unlawful | Psychotic | Always violent | Grandiose | Seductive
> 'Paranoid — suspicious, jealous, pervasive distrust, grudges but not psychotic or unlawful.'
Q: Which PD is summarised as 'needs people but fears relationships'? = Avoidant | Schizoid | Dependent | Paranoid | Narcissistic
> 'Avoidant — inhibited, inadequate, sensitive, avoids social activity, needs people but fears relationships.' Schizoid individuals are indifferent.
Q: The lecture describes obsessive-compulsive PD as: = Rigid, perfectionist and inefficient, can't delegate, detail-oriented | Unstable and chaotic | Dramatic and seductive | Cold and solitary | Grandiose
> 'Obsessive-Compulsive — rigid, perfectionist + inefficient, can't delegate, detail oriented.'

### Gender ratios
> - Male >> female: antisocial, paranoid, narcissistic, obsessive-compulsive.
> - Male > female: schizoid, schizotypal.
> - Equal: avoidant, dependent (dependent often diagnosed more in women clinically).
> - Female > male (clinical samples): borderline (~3:1 in clinics; near equal in community), histrionic.
Q: Which PD is listed as female much greater than male? = Borderline | Histrionic | Dependent | Avoidant | Paranoid
> 'F >> M: Borderline; F > M: Histrionic; M ＝ F: Avoidant, Dependent.'
Q: Which PD is listed as male much greater than female? = Antisocial | Borderline | Histrionic | Avoidant | Dependent
> 'M >> F: Paranoid, Antisocial, Narcissistic, Obsessive-compulsive.'

### Assessing personality
> - History from the patient AND an informant — longitudinal pattern: relationships, attitudes to self and others, moral/religious standards, mood variability, leisure, fantasy life, reactions to stress, forensic history.
> - Beware diagnosing PD during an acute illness (depression or mania distorts personality) and cultural norms.
> - Structured interviews: IPDE (WHO, International Personality Disorder Examination), SCID-5-PD, SIDP-IV; SAPAS (8-item screen).
> - Self-report: MMPI-2, MCMI-IV (Millon), NEO-PI-R, PDQ-4, PID-5 (for DSM-5 AMPD).
> - Projective: Rorschach, TAT. Psychopathy: PCL-R.
Q: When assessing personality, the lecture warns to beware of: = Distortion of personality by long psychiatric illness | Using informants | Asking about leisure | Structured interviews | Projective tests
> 'Beware: distortion of personality in long psychiatric illness.' Always use information from other sources.
Q: The IPDE is a: = Structured interview developed by the WHO | Self-report inventory | Projective test | Neuropsychological battery | Screening questionnaire for psychosis
> 'Structured interviews — IPDE – International PDs Evaluation (WHO), SCID-II, SIDP-IV.'
Q: Which is a self-report inventory listed in the lecture? = MCMI-IV | IPDE | SCID-II | TAT | Rorschach
> Self-report: MMPI-2, Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory (MCMI-IV), NEO-PI-R. TAT and Rorschach are projective.
Q: The integrative longitudinal perspective suggests PDs are: = Less stable over time than assumed, with stable traits and transient symptoms | Completely unchangeable | Purely state-dependent | Identical to mood disorders | Always lifelong without change
> 'Current evidence suggests these conditions are less stable than assumed… both stable temperamental traits and more specific, potentially transient symptoms.'

### Borderline PD / ICD-11 borderline pattern — most examined
> - Features (≥ 5 of 9, DSM-5): frantic efforts to avoid abandonment; unstable intense relationships (idealisation ↔ devaluation); identity disturbance; impulsivity (≥ 2 areas); recurrent self-harm/suicidal behaviour; affective instability (hours, reactive); chronic emptiness; intense anger; transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation.
> - Aetiology: childhood trauma/abuse (~70%), invalidating environment (Linehan's biosocial theory), genetics (~40%).
> - Course: better than thought — ~85% remit by 10 years (McLean study, Zanarini), though functioning lags. Suicide ~8–10%.
> - Treatment ＝ psychotherapy: DBT (Linehan) — reduces self-harm; mentalisation-based treatment (Bateman & Fonagy); schema therapy; transference-focused psychotherapy; STEPPS.
> - Drugs: NICE: no drug is licensed or recommended for the core disorder. Short-term (≤ 1 week) sedation in crisis; treat comorbidity. Older studies (as in the lecture) suggested SSRIs for impulsivity, low-dose antipsychotics for cognitive-perceptual symptoms and mood stabilisers (lamotrigine, topiramate) for affective dysregulation — evidence is weak.
Q: Which drug class does the lecture call the treatment of choice in borderline PD for impulsivity? = SSRIs | Typical antipsychotics | MAOIs | TCAs | Benzodiazepines
> 'Borderline PD: SSRIs — treatment of choice at present; reduces impulsive behaviour.' (NICE now advises against drugs for the core disorder — see high-yield.)
Q: The psychotherapy with the strongest evidence for reducing self-harm in borderline PD is: = Dialectical behaviour therapy | Psychoanalysis | Supportive counselling | Hypnotherapy | Exposure therapy
> DBT (Linehan). Mentalisation-based treatment is also effective.

### Antisocial (dissocial) PD
> - DSM-5: age ≥ 18, evidence of conduct disorder before 15, and ≥ 3 of: failure to conform to laws, deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability/aggression, reckless disregard for safety, irresponsibility, lack of remorse. Mnemonic CORRUPT.
> - ICD-10 dissocial: callous unconcern, irresponsibility, can't maintain relationships, low frustration tolerance, incapacity for guilt/learning from punishment, blames others.
> - Psychopathy (Hare) is narrower and more severe — affective features (callousness, shallow affect, no empathy) + antisocial lifestyle.
> - Comorbid substance misuse, ADHD. Tends to "burn out" after 40. Treatment: manage comorbidity, CBT-based offending programmes; NICE warns against drugs for the PD itself.
Q: A DSM-5 diagnosis of antisocial PD requires evidence of: = Conduct disorder before age 15 | ADHD in childhood | A criminal conviction | PCL-R ≥ 30 | Substance dependence
> Age ≥ 18 with conduct disorder before 15.

### Treatment principles for PD
> - Psychotherapy is the mainstay: supportive therapy, psychoeducation for families, CBT (social skills, contingency management), therapeutic communities (structured communal living — Henderson Hospital model), group therapy.
> - Schizotypal: low-dose antipsychotics help short-term (ideas of reference, odd perceptions); SSRIs if obsessive features.
> - Avoidant: CBT, social skills training, graded exposure (overlaps social anxiety disorder).
> - General rules: consistent team, clear boundaries, crisis plans, avoid long admissions (regression), treat comorbid mood/substance disorders.
Q: According to the lecture, the main way to treat personality disorder is: = Psychotherapy | Antipsychotics | ECT | Mood stabilisers | Admission
> 'Psychotherapy is the main way to treat PD. However, several types of psychiatric medication may help with various PD symptoms.'
Q: Interacting with others in a structured communal setting to force new patterns of behaviour describes: = Interpersonal (communal) treatment | Supportive therapy | Psychoeducation | Cognitive modification | Contingency management
> 'Interpersonal — interacting with others in a structured communal setting; interactions that force patients to engage in new patterns of behaviour in controlled settings.'
Q: In schizotypal PD, low-dose antipsychotics give: = An acute initial response, but doubtful long-term efficacy | No benefit | Cure | Worsening | Benefit only for depression
> 'Schizotypal PD: low doses of antipsychotics — an acute (initial) response; long-term efficacy doubtful. SSRIs may help obsessive-compulsive symptoms.'

### ICD-11 impulse control disorders (6C70–6C7Z)
> - 6C70 Pyromania — repeated fire-setting without an obvious motive (not money, revenge, political), with tension before and relief/gratification after, fascination with fire. More common in boys/men.
> - 6C71 Kleptomania — repeated stealing of objects not needed for personal use or monetary value; tension → gratification; more common in women; prevalence ~6 per 1000; ~5% of shoplifting.
> - 6C72 Compulsive sexual behaviour disorder — persistent failure to control intense sexual urges, ≥ 6 months, with impairment (new in ICD-11).
> - 6C73 Intermittent explosive disorder — repeated outbursts of aggression out of proportion to provocation.
> - The impulse cycle: impulse → rising tension → pleasure/relief on acting → (guilt may follow).
> - Not here in ICD-11: gambling disorder (6C50) and gaming disorder (6C51) are disorders due to addictive behaviours; trichotillomania (6B25.0) and skin-picking (6B25.1) are obsessive-compulsive or related disorders.
Q: Which is the correct order of the five behavioural stages of impulsivity? = Impulse, growing tension, pleasure on acting, relief, guilt | Guilt, impulse, tension, relief, pleasure | Tension, impulse, guilt, pleasure, relief | Pleasure, impulse, guilt, tension, relief | Relief, tension, impulse, pleasure, guilt
> 'An impulse, growing tension, pleasure on acting, relief from the urge and finally guilt (which may or may not arise).'
Q: DSM-5 placed impulse-control disorders in a new chapter titled: = Disruptive, impulse-control and conduct disorders | Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders | Addictive disorders | Personality disorders | Neurodevelopmental disorders
> 'DSM-5 (2013) includes a new chapter on Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders — problems in emotional and behavioral self-control.'
Q: Which is listed as a cause of pyromania? = Parental neglect and early abuse, and early observation of inappropriate fire use | Hypothyroidism | Head injury only | Schizophrenia | Alcohol only
> 'Causes include — parental neglect, early physical or emotional abuse, early observation of inappropriate fire usage.'
Q: Coccaro (2004) reported the lifetime prevalence of intermittent explosive disorder as: = 11.1% | 1–2% | 3.2% | 25% | 38%
> 'Coccaro and colleagues in 2004 reported about 11.1% lifetime prevalence and 3.2% one-month prevalence.'
Q: Kleptomania is characterised by stealing: = Items not needed and usually of little value, for gratification | Valuable items to sell | Only from family | On command of voices | For revenge
> 'Irresistible urge to steal items that aren't required and are usually of little value… purely for the sake of gratification. Commoner in women; 6 per 1000.'

### Behavioural addictions
> - ICD-11 gaming disorder (6C51) and gambling disorder (6C50): impaired control, increasing priority over other interests, continuation despite harm, usually evident for ≥ 12 months. ICD-11 is the first classification to include gaming disorder as a full diagnosis (DSM-5 lists internet gaming disorder only for further study).
> - "Internet addiction" is not a diagnosis in either system. Beard's criteria: all 5 (preoccupation, needing more time, failed attempts to cut back, irritability when cutting back, staying online longer than intended) plus ≥ 1 of: jeopardised relationship/job, lying about use, use to escape problems. Tools: Young's Internet Addiction Test, PIUQ, CIUS.
> - Compulsive buying: ~2–8% of adults, 80–95% women, onset late teens–20s.
> - Comorbidity: impulse-control problems occur in ~14–36% of Parkinson's patients on dopamine agonists (gambling, hypersexuality, shopping, binge eating). Link: ventral striatal (reward) circuit dysfunction shared with OCD and addiction.
Q: Regarding internet addiction, DSM-5: = Added it as a condition requiring more research, not a distinct disorder | Recognises it as a distinct disorder | Classifies it under OCD | Calls it gaming disorder | Ignores it completely
> 'Added to DSM-5 as a disorder that require more research; DSM-5 does not recognize it as a distinct dis.; ICD-11 recognises Gaming disorder (online or offline).'
Q: Under Beard's criteria, internet addiction requires all five core criteria plus at least one of: = Lying to conceal use, jeopardising a relationship/job, or using it to escape problems | Carpal tunnel syndrome | Dry eyes | Euphoria at the computer | Weight gain
> 'At least one of: has jeopardized a significant relationship, job or opportunity; has lied to conceal use; uses internet to escape problems or relieve dysphoric mood.'
Q: What proportion of compulsive buyers are female? = 80–95% | 20–30% | 50% | 60–70% | 100%
> 'Prevalence of compulsive buying in the US 2–8% of adults, with 80–95% of these cases being females.'
Q: Impulse control disorders occur in what proportion of Parkinson's patients? = 13.6–36% | 1–2% | 5% | 50–60% | 90%
> 'ICDs occur in 13.6–36.0% of Parkinson's patients (at least one form of ICD).'
Q: Which brain circuit may link OCD, ICDs and substance use disorders? = Ventral striatal circuit | Cerebellar circuit | Visual cortex | Brainstem | Hippocampal circuit only
> 'Dysfunction of the striatum may prove to be the link… progressive dysfunction of the ventral striatal circuit.'

### Treating impulse-control and related disorders
> - CBT is the best-supported approach (gambling, compulsive sexual behaviour, kleptomania); habit reversal for trichotillomania/skin-picking.
> - Drugs (lecture + standard evidence):
> - Gambling: naltrexone (opioid antagonist) has the best evidence; SSRIs (fluvoxamine, escitalopram) inconsistent.
> - Kleptomania: naltrexone; SSRIs.
> - Trichotillomania: clomipramine, N-acetylcysteine; fluoxetine inconsistent.
> - Skin-picking: fluoxetine.
> - Intermittent explosive disorder: fluoxetine reduces impulsive aggression.
> - Pyromania: CBT; SSRIs, antiandrogens in some cases.
> - Dopamine-agonist-induced gambling in Parkinson's → reduce or stop the agonist.
Q: In trichotillomania, which drug does the lecture say is effective? = Clomipramine | Fluoxetine | Lithium | Haloperidol | Escitalopram
> 'In trichotillomania, clomipramine has again been found to be effective; fluoxetine has not produced consistent positive results.'
Q: Which drug reduced the frequency and severity of impulsive aggression in intermittent explosive disorder? = Fluoxetine | Clomipramine | Fluvoxamine | Naltrexone | Diazepam
> 'Fluoxetine has also been evaluated in treating IED and demonstrated significant improvement in reducing frequency and severity of impulsive aggression.' Fluoxetine also helps skin-picking.
Q: In pathological gambling, which drugs reduced problems by up to 90%, per the lecture? = Fluvoxamine and clomipramine | Lithium and valproate | Haloperidol | Methylphenidate | Bupropion
> 'Fluvoxamine, clomipramine shown effective… reducing the problems of pathological gambling by up to 90%.' Escitalopram helped gambling with anxiety.
Q: The drug with the best evidence for gambling disorder is: = Naltrexone | Lithium | Haloperidol | Diazepam | Methylphenidate
> Naltrexone — also used for kleptomania.

### Sexual response cycle
> - Masters & Johnson (1966) — 4 phases (EPOR): Excitement, Plateau, Orgasm, Resolution (with a male refractory period).
> - Helen Singer Kaplan (1979) — triphasic: desire, arousal (excitement), orgasm — added desire; basis of the DSM dysfunction categories.
> - Physiology: arousal/erection ＝ parasympathetic (vasocongestion, nitric oxide); emission/ejaculation ＝ sympathetic ("point and shoot").
> - ICD-11: sexual dysfunctions and sexual pain disorders moved to a new Chapter 17 "Conditions related to sexual health" (HA00–HA0Z), no longer split into "organic" vs "non-organic" — with qualifiers for associated factors (medical, psychological, substance, relationship).
Q: Psychosexual disorders are defined as sexual problems that: = Are psychological in origin, in the absence of pathological disease | Have an organic cause | Only affect men | Are always paraphilic | Are untreatable
> 'Sexual problems that are psychological in origin and occur in absence of any pathological disease.'
Q: Kaplan's triphasic model of the sexual response comprises: = Desire, arousal and orgasm | Excitement, plateau, orgasm | Arousal, plateau, resolution | Desire, plateau, resolution | Excitement, orgasm, refractory
> 'Modified by Kaplan to a triphasic model of desire, arousal and orgasm.' Masters & Johnson: excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution.
Q: Vasocongestion causing erection is described as a: = Parasympathetic reaction | Sympathetic reaction | Somatic reflex | Hormonal surge | Cortical response only
> 'Vasocongestion, a parasympathetic reaction causing erection in men and labial-clitoral congestion in women.'

### Sexual dysfunctions — causes and treatment
> - Erectile dysfunction: most cases have an organic component (vascular, diabetes, neuropathy, drugs — antihypertensives, SSRIs, antipsychotics via prolactin). Preserved nocturnal/morning erections (nocturnal penile tumescence) suggest a psychogenic cause. Depression reduces NPT.
> - Premature ejaculation: Semans' stop-start and Masters & Johnson's squeeze techniques; SSRIs (dapoxetine); topical anaesthetics.
> - Women: most common are hypoactive sexual desire and orgasmic disorder; sexual pain (vaginismus/dyspareunia).
> - Drugs: PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) for ED — contraindicated with nitrates; intracavernosal alprostadil/papaverine; vacuum devices; prosthesis last.
> - Sensate focus (Masters & Johnson) — graded non-demand touching, banning intercourse at first; reduces performance anxiety. Treat the couple.
Q: In erectile dysfunction, evidence of nocturnal penile tumescence usually indicates: = A psychological cause | A vascular cause | Diabetes | Hypogonadism | Drug side effects
> 'A history of occasional erections — especially nocturnal penile tumescence — is usually evidence that the dysfunction is psychological in origin.'
Q: Decreased nocturnal penile tumescence occurs in some patients with: = Depression | Schizophrenia | Mania | OCD | Anorexia
> 'Decreased nocturnal penile tumescence occur in some depressed patients.'
Q: Which drugs are cited as organic causes of ejaculatory disturbance? = SSRIs and sympatholytics | Antibiotics | Antacids | Vitamins | Insulin
> 'Organic causes include interference with sympathetic nerve distribution (surgery or radiation) and pharmacologic agents (eg, SSRIs or sympatholytics).'
Q: In women, which is the most common form of sexual dysfunction named in the lecture? = Orgasmic disorder and hypoactive sexual desire disorder | Vaginismus only | Dyspareunia only | Hypersexuality | Gender dysphoria
> 'In women, the most common forms are orgasmic disorder and hypoactive sexual desire disorder.'
Q: Which is listed as a cause of reduced sexual desire? = Cyproterone acetate | Sildenafil | Testosterone replacement | Exercise | Bupropion
> 'Hormonal disorders, including hypogonadism or use of antiandrogen compounds such as cyproterone acetate, and chronic kidney disease.' Also alcohol, sedatives, opioids and cannabis.

### ICD-11 paraphilic disorders (6D30–6D3Z)
> - Defined by sustained, intense arousal focused on non-consenting persons (or with marked distress/risk of harm): exhibitionistic (6D30), voyeuristic (6D31), pedophilic (6D32), coercive sexual sadism (6D33), frotteuristic (6D34), other involving non-consenting individuals; other involving solitary behaviour or consenting individuals (only if marked distress or risk of injury/death).
> - Removed from ICD-11: fetishism, fetishistic transvestism and consensual sadomasochism — no longer disorders in themselves.
> - Sexual masochism can be dangerous (autoerotic asphyxia).
> - Treatment: CBT/relapse prevention; antilibidinal drugs — cyproterone acetate, medroxyprogesterone, GnRH analogues (leuprorelin, triptorelin); high-dose SSRIs. Better prognosis when motivation is personal rather than court-driven.
> - Gender incongruence (ICD-11 HA60/HA61) moved out of mental disorders into Chapter 17. DSM-5 "gender dysphoria" requires distress.
Q: Paraphilias become paraphilic disorders when they are associated with: = Distress, impairment or risk of harm | Any unusual interest | Marriage | Age over 40 | Alcohol use
> 'When paraphilias are associated with distress, impairment, or risk of harm, they become paraphilic disorders.'
Q: In both exhibitionism and voyeurism, excitation leads to: = Masturbation as a replacement for sexual activity | Assault | Cross-dressing | Pain infliction | Guilt only
> 'In both exhibitionism and voyeurism, excitation leads to masturbation as a replacement for sexual activity.'
Q: Why can sexual masochism be life-threatening? = Neck binding or partial asphyxiation may be part of the ritual | It involves drugs | It causes infection | It involves fire | It is always with children
> 'It may be life-threatening, since neck binding or partial asphyxiation usually forms part of the ritual. Much more common in men.'
Q: Gender dysphoria is a disorder only when there is: = Significant distress or impairment | Cross-dressing | Same-sex attraction | Hormonal abnormality | A request for surgery
> 'As a disorder, it is defined by significant distress or impairment; those experiencing this incongruence but without the distress would not meet criteria.'
Q: Prognosis in paraphilia treatment is much better when: = Motivation comes from the individual rather than the legal system | The court orders it | The person is older | Drugs are used alone | Onset is long-standing
> 'The prognosis is much better if the motivation comes from the individual rather than the legal system.' Recent-onset and superficial paraphilias respond better.
Q: Which drug is named in the lecture to suppress libido in men with paraphilic disorders? = Medroxyprogesterone acetate | Sildenafil | Testosterone | Diazepam | Fluoxetine
> 'Pharmacological — medroxyprogesterone acetate — suppress libido in men.'
Q: Which was removed as a disorder in ICD-11? = Fetishism | Pedophilic disorder | Exhibitionistic disorder | Coercive sexual sadism disorder | Voyeuristic disorder
> Fetishism, fetishistic transvestism and consensual sadomasochism were removed.

## Pink Quad | Schizophrenia
> Schizophrenia. Source: Schizophrenia NPMCN feb 2026.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Who named what — examiners love this
> - Kraepelin (1893/1899): "dementia praecox" — early onset, chronic deteriorating course, poor outcome. He separated it from manic-depressive insanity (the Kraepelinian dichotomy).
> - Bleuler (1911): "schizophrenia" (splitting of mental functions, not split personality). Fundamental symptoms ＝ the 4 As: Associations loosened, Affect inappropriate, Ambivalence, Autism. Hallucinations and delusions were only accessory.
> - Schneider (1938/1959): first- and second-rank symptoms.
Q: The term psychosis was originally introduced in: = 1845 | 1793 | 1893 | 1911 | 1938
> The lecture: 'The term psychosis has originally been introduced in 1845 and was used later on for severe mental disorders.' 1893 ＝ Kraepelin's dementia praecox; 1911 ＝ Bleuler; 1938 ＝ Schneider.
Q: Kraepelin's dementia praecox (1893) meant: = Premature loss of mind | Split mind | Madness without delusion | Moral insanity | Disordered association
> 'Dementia praecox (1893) Emil Kraepelin (premature loss of mind)' — early onset, chronic deteriorating course, poor outcome with permanent and pervasive impairment.
Q: Which feature was NOT part of Kraepelin's description of dementia praecox? = Variability in course and outcome | Onset in adolescence or early adulthood | Chronic and deteriorating course | Poor outcome with permanent impairment | Pervasive impairment of mental functions
> Variability in course and outcome was Bleuler's contribution (1911). Kraepelin emphasised early onset, deterioration and poor outcome.
Q: Bleuler derived the word schizophrenia from the Greek schizein and phren, meaning: = Splitting and soul/spirit/mind | Split and personality | Early and dementia | Divided and emotion | Broken and body
> '[from Greek Schizein (splitting) and Phren (soul, spirit, mind)]' — splitting of mental functions, not split personality.
Q: Bleuler's fundamental symptoms (Grundsymptome) included all of the following EXCEPT: = Hallucinations | Loosening of associations | Inappropriate affect | Ambivalence | Autism
> Fundamental: loss of associations, inappropriate affect, ambivalence, avolition, autism. Hallucinations and delusions were accessory symptoms.

### Schneider's first-rank symptoms (FRS) — 11 classically
> - Auditory: thought echo (Gedankenlautwerden), voices arguing/discussing in the 3rd person, running commentary.
> - Thought alienation: insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting.
> - Passivity: made feelings, made impulses, made actions, somatic passivity.
> - Delusional perception — the only two-stage FRS (normal percept → sudden delusional meaning).
> ICD-11 de-emphasises FRS: good specificity but poor sensitivity, and they occur in other psychoses (mania, ATPD). ICD-10 gave them special weight.
Q: In Schneider's scheme (1938), which is a second-rank symptom? = Visual hallucinations | Voices commenting on one's actions | Thought insertion | Delusions of being controlled | Thought withdrawal
> Lecture: '1st: hearing commenting or conversing voices, thoughts being inserted or withdrawn, delusions of being controlled… 2nd: other auditory hallucinations, visual hallucinations, delusional ideas.'
Q: Which classification emphasises first-rank symptoms? = ICD-10 | ICD-11 | DSM-5 | ICD-11 and DSM-5 | None
> 'First-rank symptoms — ICD-10: emphasises; DSM-5: does not emphasise; ICD-11: does not emphasise.'
Q: Regarding first-rank symptoms, the lecture states they have: = Limited diagnostic sensitivity but good specificity | High sensitivity and low specificity | No specificity at all | Perfect reliability | Value only in chronic schizophrenia
> 'Limited diagnostic sensitivity, but good specificity.' Bizarre delusions have poor reliability; FRS occur in other psychoses, but may aid early detection.

### ICD-11 Schizophrenia (6A20) — diagnostic requirements
> At least 2 symptoms, present most of the time for ≥ 1 month, and at least 1 must be from a–d (core):
> - a) persistent delusions
> - b) persistent hallucinations (usually auditory)
> - c) disorganised thinking (formal thought disorder)
> - d) experiences of influence, passivity or control
> - e) negative symptoms
> - f) grossly disorganised behaviour
> - g) psychomotor disturbances (including catatonia)
> Not due to another medical condition (e.g. brain tumour) or a substance/medication, including withdrawal.
Q: ICD-11 requires at least how many qualifying symptoms, for how long? = Two symptoms most of the time for at least 1 month | One symptom for 2 weeks | Three symptoms for 6 months | Two symptoms for 6 months | One first-rank symptom for 1 month
> 'At least two of these symptoms must be present most of the time for a period of at least 1 month.'
Q: At least one qualifying symptom must come from items a)–d). Which item is outside this core group? = Grossly disorganised behaviour | Persistent delusions | Persistent hallucinations | Disorganised thinking | Experiences of influence, passivity or control
> Core items a–d: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking, influence/passivity/control. e) negative symptoms, f) grossly disorganised behaviour, g) psychomotor disturbances are not core.
Q: Under ICD-11, schizophrenia should not be diagnosed when symptoms are: = Due to a brain tumour or substance withdrawal such as alcohol | Accompanied by cognitive impairment | Present for more than 1 month | Associated with psychosocial problems | Accompanied by negative symptoms
> 'Symptoms… are not a manifestation of another medical condition (e.g., a brain tumour) and are not due to… a substance or medication, including withdrawal effects (e.g., alcohol).'

### Duration — a classic MCQ trap
> - ICD-10: symptoms for ≥ 1 month.
> - ICD-11: ≥ 1 month.
> - DSM-5: active-phase symptoms 1 month, but total disturbance ≥ 6 months (including prodrome/residual). < 6 months ＝ schizophreniform disorder; < 1 month ＝ brief psychotic disorder.
> - Chapter names: ICD-10 "Schizophrenia, schizotypal and delusional disorders"; DSM-5 "Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders"; ICD-11 "Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders".
Q: Which system requires psychotic symptoms within a total disturbance of at least 6 months? = DSM-5 | ICD-10 | ICD-11 | All three | None
> Lecture table: ICD-10 — at least one month; ICD-11 — at least 1 month; DSM-5 — one month for section A; symptoms persist for at least 6 months.

### What's new in ICD-11 (5 changes)
> 1. First-rank symptoms de-emphasised.
> 2. Subtypes abolished (paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, simple, undifferentiated, residual) — poor stability, don't cluster in families, little prognostic value.
> 3. Cognitive symptoms added to the description — they predict functional outcome (neurocognition explains ~52% of variance in return to work/school).
> 4. Course qualifiers for all primary psychotic disorders.
> 5. Symptom qualifiers (dimensional ratings) replace subtypes.
Q: ICD-11 omitted the classical subtypes of schizophrenia because of: = Lack of evidence for prospective value and clinical stability | Patient preference | They were too difficult to code | WHO budget constraints | They were only used in Africa
> 'Omission of classical schizophrenia subtypes due to a lack of clinical evidence for prospective value and clinical stability.' They failed cluster analyses, didn't cluster in families, and had limited prognostic value.
Q: Neurocognitive factors predict what proportion of the variance in return to work or school? = 52% | 12% | 25% | 75% | 90%
> 'Neurocognitive factors predict 52% of the variance in return to work or school in schizophrenia' — the reason ICD-11 added cognitive symptoms.

### ICD-11 qualifiers
> - Course: first episode; multiple episodes (≥ 2 episodes with ≥ 3 months of partial/full remission between); continuous (symptoms for almost all of ≥ 1 year). Plus current status: currently symptomatic / partial remission / full remission (past month).
> - Six symptom domains, each rated 0 not present, 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3 severe (9 ＝ unable to rate):
> - positive, negative, depressive mood, manic mood, psychomotor (catatonia sits here), cognitive.
Q: The ICD-11 course qualifier 'continuous' means symptoms present for almost all of the course for at least: = 1 year | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 2 years
> 'Continuous — present for almost all of the course for at least one year.' Multiple episodes ＝ ≥ 2 episodes with ≥ 3 months of remission between.
Q: The cross-sectional course qualifiers in ICD-11 refer to the: = Past month | Past week | Past year | Lifetime | Current day
> 'Cross-sectional symptom status (i.e., past month): currently symptomatic / in partial remission / in full remission.'
Q: On the ICD-11 symptom qualifier scale, a rating of 9 means: = Unable to make a rating from available information | Severe | Very severe | Not present | In full remission
> '0 ＝ Not Present, 1 ＝ Present but mild, 2 ＝ Present and moderate, 3 ＝ Present and severe, 9 ＝ Unable to make a rating based upon available information.'
Q: Which is NOT one of the six ICD-11 symptom domains? = Anxiety symptoms | Positive symptoms | Negative symptoms | Manic mood symptoms | Cognitive symptoms
> Six domains: positive, negative, depressive mood, manic mood, psychomotor, cognitive. Anxiety is not a domain.
Q: When rating the depressive mood domain, which associated symptom does contribute to moderate/severe ratings? = Suicidal ideation or attempts | Anhedonia | Sleep change | Appetite change | Fatigue
> Only depressed mood and related symptoms (e.g. tearfulness) are rated — 'except for suicidal ideation/attempts, which contribute to ratings of moderate and severe.'
Q: Negative symptoms rated in ICD-11 must not be attributable to: = Depression, an under-stimulating environment, positive symptoms, medication or substances | Schizophrenia | Ageing | Male sex | Cognitive impairment
> 'Not attributable to depression, under-stimulating environment, positive symptoms, effects of medications or substance use' — i.e. exclude secondary negative symptoms.

### Symptom dimensions
> - Positive: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and behaviour, passivity.
> - Negative (the 5 As): Alogia, Affective blunting, Avolition, Anhedonia, Asociality. In ICD-11 they must not be explained by depression, an under-stimulating environment, positive symptoms, medication (EPS) or substances — that's secondary negative symptoms.
> - Cognitive: attention, working memory, processing speed, executive function, social cognition. Present before onset and the strongest predictor of functional outcome.
> - Crow (1980): Type I (positive, acute, good drug response, dopamine) vs Type II (negative, chronic, poor response, structural brain change).
Q: The lecture defines positive symptoms as: = Exaggerations or distortions of normal thoughts, emotions and behaviour | Symptoms that respond to treatment | Functioning below the normal level | Symptoms with a good prognosis | Mood-congruent symptoms
> 'Positive symptoms: exaggerations or distortions of normal thoughts, emotions, and behavior. Negative symptoms: symptoms that involve functioning below the level of normal behavior.'
Q: Which is listed in the lecture as a negative symptom? = Avolition | Delusions | Disorganised speech | Disturbed behaviour | Hallucinations
> Negative: restricted affect, avolition, a-sociality (also anhedonia, alogia). The others are positive.

### Epidemiology
> - Lifetime prevalence ≈ 0.5–1% (DSM-5: 0.3–0.7%). Incidence ~15 per 100,000/year.
> - Onset: men late teens–mid-20s; women late 20s, with a second peak after 45 (menopause, oestrogen hypothesis). Men slightly > women (≈ 1.4:1).
> - Risk factors: family history, urban birth/upbringing, migration (and ethnic minority status), winter/spring birth, obstetric complications, cannabis (especially high-potency, adolescent use), childhood adversity, advanced paternal age.
> - Mortality: life expectancy reduced by 15–20 years (cardiovascular disease, suicide ~5%).
Q: The lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia quoted in the lecture is: = 0.5–1.0% | 0.05–0.1% | 2–3% | 5% | 10%
> 'Lifetime prevalence: 0.5–1.0%; DSM-5: 0.3–0.7%.'
Q: The average age of onset in females is: = Early to late 20s | Teens to mid-20s | 30s | 40s | After menopause only
> 'Average age of onset — Males: teens to mid-20s; Females: early to late 20s; range early childhood to 50s/60s; male slightly > female.'

### Genetics — know the risk ladder (Gottesman)
> - General population 1% · sibling ~9% · one parent ~13% · DZ twin ~17% · both parents ~46% · MZ twin ~48%.
> - Heritability ≈ 80%. MZ concordance < 100% → environment matters.
> - Polygenic: hundreds of common variants (GWAS — e.g. C4 complement gene, MHC region) + rare CNVs, especially 22q11.2 deletion (velocardiofacial syndrome — ~25% develop psychosis).
> - Model: genetic vulnerability + environmental hits (stress–vulnerability).
Q: The lecture's aetiological equation for schizophrenia is: = Genetic vulnerability + environmental factors (intrauterine, post-natal) | Dopamine excess alone | Bad parenting | Cannabis use alone | Viral infection alone
> 'Genetic vulnerability + environmental factors (intrauterine, post-natal) ＝ Schizophrenia' — the stress–vulnerability model.
Q: The lifetime risk of schizophrenia in the child of two affected parents is closest to: = 46% | 1% | 9% | 13% | 80%
> ~46% (Gottesman). One parent ~13%, sibling ~9%, MZ twin ~48%. 80% is the heritability.
Q: Which chromosomal deletion carries about a 25% risk of psychosis? = 22q11.2 deletion | 5p deletion | 15q11–13 deletion | 7q11.23 deletion | 4p16 deletion
> 22q11.2 deletion (velocardiofacial) — the strongest single genetic risk factor.

### Dopamine hypothesis
> - Evidence: amphetamine causes psychosis; antipsychotic potency correlates with D2 blockade; antipsychotics cause parkinsonism.
> - Four pathways — learn their effects:
> - Mesolimbic — excess dopamine → positive symptoms. D2 block here ＝ antipsychotic effect.
> - Mesocortical — deficit → negative and cognitive symptoms (worsened by D2 block).
> - Nigrostriatal — D2 block → EPS, tardive dyskinesia.
> - Tuberoinfundibular — D2 block → hyperprolactinaemia (dopamine inhibits prolactin).
> - Modern version: presynaptic striatal dopamine synthesis capacity is raised (PET) — the "final common pathway" (Howes & Kapur).
Q: Researchers proposed that negative symptoms reflect: = Abnormalities in brain structure | Raised dopamine activity | Serotonin excess | Substance misuse | Depression
> 'Positive symptoms reflected activated dopamine levels… negative symptoms reflected abnormalities in brain structure.'
Q: Evidence for the dopamine hypothesis given in the lecture includes: = Antipsychotics cause parkinsonian symptoms and block D2 receptors | PCP causes psychosis | Low CSF 5-HIAA | Enlarged ventricles | Hypofrontality
> 'Psychotomimetic effect of dopaminergic drugs; antipsychotic medicines cause parkinsonian symptoms & block dopamine (D2) receptors.' PCP is the glutamate evidence.
Q: Mesocortical hypodopaminergia is linked to: = Negative and cognitive symptoms | Positive symptoms | Extrapyramidal side effects | Hyperprolactinaemia | Catatonia
> 'Mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia → positive symptoms; mesocortical hypodopaminergia → negative/cognitive symptoms.'
Q: Hyperprolactinaemia from antipsychotics results from D2 blockade in which pathway? = Tuberoinfundibular | Mesolimbic | Mesocortical | Nigrostriatal | Thalamocortical
> Tuberoinfundibular dopamine inhibits prolactin. Nigrostriatal → EPS.

### Glutamate (NMDA hypofunction) hypothesis
> - PCP and ketamine (NMDA antagonists) reproduce positive, negative AND cognitive symptoms — dopaminergic drugs only reproduce positive ones.
> - NMDA hypofunction on GABA interneurons → disinhibited glutamate → downstream dopamine dysregulation.
> - Clinical link: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with psychosis.
> - Minor systems: serotonin (5-HT2A — LSD; atypicals block 5-HT2A), GABA.
Q: The psychotomimetic drug cited as evidence for the glutamate/NMDA hypothesis is: = PCP (phencyclidine) | Amphetamine | LSD | Cocaine | Cannabis
> 'Psychotomimetic effect of PCP (NMDA antagonist); abnormalities in glutamate levels, release, receptors in schizophrenia.'

### Brain changes
> - Enlarged lateral ventricles — first on pneumoencephalography (1927), on CT by Johnstone et al. (1976). Linked to negative symptoms, cognitive deficits, poor prognosis.
> - Reduced volume: hippocampus/medial temporal lobe, prefrontal cortex, thalamus (mediodorsal nucleus), superior temporal gyrus; white-matter abnormalities; loss of normal asymmetry.
> - Microscopic: reduced neuropil (increased neuronal density, fewer dendritic spines) — no gliosis, which supports a developmental rather than degenerative process.
> - Functional: hypofrontality — DLPFC fails to activate during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (Weinberger).
Q: Enlarged ventricles in schizophrenia were first reported in 1927 using: = Pneumoencephalography | CT scanning | MRI | PET | Post-mortem histology
> 'Reported in 1927 (pneumoencephalography) — Jacobi & Winkler; replicated early in the CT era (Johnstone, Lancet 1976); replicated 100 times since with CT and MRI.'
Q: Enlarged ventricles are associated with all EXCEPT: = Good response to treatment | Poor prognosis | Negative symptoms | Cognitive deficits | Chronic course
> The lecture: 'Associated with poor prognosis, negative sx, cognitive deficits.'
Q: Which thalamic nucleus is singled out as reduced in volume? = Mediodorsal nucleus | Pulvinar | Ventral posterolateral nucleus | Lateral geniculate | Anterior nucleus
> 'Decreased volume: medial temporal (limbic) structures, prefrontal cortex, thalamus, esp. mediodorsal nucleus.'
Q: Hypofrontality in schizophrenia is: = Inconsistent at rest but robust during a prefrontal task such as the WCST | Robust at rest | Seen only in the occipital lobe | A feature of mania | Present only after treatment
> 'Hypoactivity of the frontal lobes, esp. DLPFC — inconsistent at rest, but robust during prefrontal task (e.g., Wisconsin Card Sorting Test).'

### Neurodevelopmental hypothesis (Weinberger, Murray)
> Abnormal brain development is present from birth (genes + obstetric complications, prenatal infection/famine, winter birth), but symptoms appear only when normal maturation — synaptic pruning in adolescence — "unmasks" the lesion.
> Supporting evidence: premorbid motor and cognitive delays, minor physical anomalies, no gliosis, structural changes already at first episode.
> The neurodegenerative view points to progressive grey-matter loss over time — the two are not mutually exclusive.
Q: The neurodevelopmental hypothesis proposes that aberrant neurodevelopment: = Is present at birth but manifests only with normal neuromaturation in the teens/early adulthood | Begins in old age | Is caused by antipsychotics | Is always visible on CT at birth | Occurs only after cannabis use
> 'Aberrant neurodevelopment present at birth, but does not manifest symptoms until normal neuromaturational events occur in teens/early adulthood.'

### Social factors
> - High expressed emotion (EE) in families — critical comments, hostility, emotional over-involvement — raises relapse risk (Brown, Vaughn & Leff). Family interventions reduce relapse.
> - Social drift (illness → downward mobility) vs social causation (poverty/urban stress → illness): both contribute; drift explains much of the class gradient.
> - WHO studies (IPSS, DOSMeD): outcome is better in developing countries — family support, less stigma.
Q: The sociocultural perspective links schizophrenia and low income through: = Social and economic 'downward drift' | Upward mobility | Genetic advantage | Better access to care | Urban protection
> 'Associated with environmental stressors of poverty — contracting the disease leads to social and economic downward drift.' Family factors: faulty communication, cognitive distortions, high expressed emotion.
Q: High expressed emotion includes all EXCEPT: = Warmth | Critical comments | Hostility | Emotional over-involvement | All are components
> High EE ＝ criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement. Warmth is protective. Family intervention reduces relapse.

### Prognosis — good vs poor
> - Good: female, acute onset, clear precipitant, late onset, prominent mood/positive symptoms, good premorbid functioning, married, short duration of untreated psychosis (DUP), good drug response, supportive family (low EE).
> - Poor: male, insidious onset, early onset, negative symptoms, cognitive impairment, poor premorbid adjustment, long DUP, substance misuse, enlarged ventricles, family history, high EE.
> - Rule of thumb: ~20% single episode/good recovery, majority relapsing course, ~15–20% chronic severe.
Q: Which is a good prognostic factor in schizophrenia? = Acute onset with a clear precipitant | Insidious onset | Prominent negative symptoms | Male sex | Long duration of untreated psychosis
> Good: acute onset, clear precipitant, female, late onset, mood symptoms, good premorbid function, short DUP, low expressed emotion.

### Exclude secondary psychosis first
> - Psychiatric: psychotic depression, mania, schizoaffective, delusional disorder, ATPD, OCD with poor insight, borderline PD (brief micro-psychotic episodes), dissociative disorders, dementia.
> - Substances: cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, alcohol withdrawal / hallucinosis, steroids, levodopa.
> - Medical: temporal lobe epilepsy, brain tumour, HIV, neurosyphilis, anti-NMDAR encephalitis, SLE, thyroid disease, Cushing's, Wilson's, Huntington's, B12 deficiency, delirium. In Nigeria also think cerebral malaria, typhoid encephalopathy.
> - Work-up: FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose, TFT, calcium, HIV/VDRL, urine drug screen, and CT/MRI or EEG if atypical features.
Q: Which personality disorder is singled out in the lecture as a psychiatric cause of psychosis? = Borderline | Schizoid | Dependent | Anankastic | Avoidant
> 'Personality disorders (esp BPD)' — brief stress-related psychotic symptoms. Other psychiatric causes: depression, mania, OCD, dementias, dissociative disorders, substance use.
Q: Which non-psychiatric cause of psychosis is highlighted with the abbreviation TLE? = Temporal lobe epilepsy | Thyroid lymphoma | Toxic liver encephalopathy | Tuberculous leptomeningitis | Transient limbic encephalitis
> 'Epilepsy (TLE)' — alongside mass lesions, metabolic disorders, encephalopathies, infection, autoimmune, nutritional, drugs and toxic states.
Q: A 22-year-old woman develops psychosis, seizures and orofacial dyskinesias after a flu-like illness. The key test is: = CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies | Urine drug screen | Serum prolactin | Thyroid function | Serum ceruloplasmin
> Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis — look for ovarian teratoma; CSF antibodies, MRI, EEG.

### Other ICD-11 primary psychotic disorders
> - Schizoaffective (6A21): meets schizophrenia and a mood episode at the same time, together for ≥ 1 month. In ICD-11 it describes the current episode only (not lifelong — unlike DSM-5).
> - Schizotypal (6A22): enduring odd speech, perception, beliefs; ≥ 2 years; not enough for a psychotic disorder.
> - ATPD (6A23): onset within 2 weeks, fluctuating symptoms, ≤ 3 months, no negative symptoms, full recovery usual. ICD-10's schizophrenia-like subtype moved out.
> - Delusional disorder (6A24): delusion(s) ≥ 3 months, no other psychotic symptoms (except related hallucinations), behaviour otherwise normal. ICD-10's induced delusional disorder (folie à deux) is now folded in here.
Q: ICD-11 acute and transient psychotic disorder has an onset within _ and lasts no longer than _: = 2 weeks; 3 months | 1 week; 1 month | 1 month; 6 months | 48 hours; 2 weeks | 3 months; 1 year
> 'Sudden onset (over no more than 2 weeks)… of brief duration (no longer than 3 months). Negative symptoms must not be present.'
Q: In ICD-11, schizoaffective disorder: = Applies only to the current episode | Is a lifelong diagnosis | Requires 6 months of symptoms | Excludes manic episodes | Requires first-rank symptoms
> 'Not longitudinal or lifelong in nature; the diagnosis only applies to the current episode of illness (different to DSM-5).' Requirements for schizophrenia and a mood episode met together for ≥ 1 month.
Q: ICD-11 schizotypal disorder requires symptoms for at least: = 2 years | 1 month | 6 months | 1 year | 5 years
> 'Symptoms are present continuously or episodically for at least 2 years.' Largely unchanged from ICD-10.
Q: ICD-11 delusional disorder typically requires the delusion to last at least: = 3 months | 2 weeks | 1 month | 6 months | 2 years
> 'Presence of a delusion or set of related delusions, typically for at least 3 months, with absence of other psychotic features (except possibly hallucinations consistent with delusional content).'

### Drug treatment
> - First episode: any antipsychotic except clozapine — choose by side-effect profile; lowest effective dose. Continue ≥ 1–2 years after a first episode; relapse risk is ~80% within 5 years if stopped.
> - FGAs (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine): more EPS, TD, prolactin. SGAs (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole): more metabolic problems (olanzapine, clozapine worst); aripiprazole is a partial D2 agonist (prolactin-sparing).
> - Treatment-resistant ＝ no response to 2 antipsychotics at adequate dose for 6–8 weeks each (one an SGA) → clozapine (Kane 1988). It also reduces suicide.
> - Clozapine monitoring: agranulocytosis (~0.8%) — FBC weekly for 18 weeks, then 2-weekly to 1 year, then monthly; myocarditis (first 2 months — troponin/CRP), seizures (dose-related), constipation/ileus (can kill), hypersalivation, weight gain, NMS.
> - Depots for poor adherence: fluphenazine decanoate, haloperidol decanoate, flupentixol, paliperidone palmitate, risperidone LAI, aripiprazole LAI.
Q: The consequences of neuroleptic treatment highlighted in the lecture are: = Extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia | Weight loss and insomnia | Hypertension and tachycardia | Hair loss and rash | Hypoglycaemia
> 'Neuroleptics — 'typical' or first generation, 'atypical' or second generation. Consequences: extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), tardive dyskinesia.'
Q: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as non-response to: = Two antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration | One antipsychotic for 2 weeks | Clozapine for 6 weeks | A depot for 3 months | Three typical antipsychotics
> ≥ 2 antipsychotics (one an SGA) at adequate dose for 6–8 weeks each → clozapine.
Q: Which clozapine adverse effect is most likely in the first two months? = Myocarditis | Tardive dyskinesia | Hyperprolactinaemia | Cataract | Hypothyroidism
> Myocarditis — monitor troponin and CRP. Agranulocytosis risk is highest in the first 18 weeks.

### Psychological and social treatment (NICE CG178)
> - CBT for psychosis (CBTp) — ≥ 16 sessions; offer to everyone.
> - Family intervention — 10+ sessions; targets expressed emotion, reduces relapse.
> - Early intervention in psychosis services — shorten DUP.
> - Assertive community treatment (ACT) — multidisciplinary team, small caseloads, outreach, for frequent relapsers.
> - Token economy (operant conditioning) for chronic institutional patients; cognitive remediation, social skills training, supported employment (IPS), arts therapies (negative symptoms).
> - Physical health: monitor weight, BP, glucose/HbA1c, lipids; smoking cessation.
Q: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) is described as: = A team of professionals from psychiatry, psychology, nursing and social work who reach out to clients | Inpatient electroconvulsive therapy | A token economy in hospital | Self-help groups | Family therapy only
> 'ACT: A team of professionals from psychiatry, psychology, nursing, and social work reach out to clients' — the lecture's sociocultural treatment.
Q: Which psychological treatment is NOT listed in the lecture? = Psychoanalysis | Token economy | Cognitive-behavioural therapy | Cognitive training | All are listed
> Psychological treatment: token economy, CBT, cognitive training. Psychoanalysis is not recommended for schizophrenia.

### Mixed questions: Schizophrenia
> Questions from the lecture that are not tied to one summary point.
Q: Psychosis nowadays denotes a clinical syndrome composed of: = Hallucinations, delusions and disordered thinking/behaviour | Anxiety, depression and insomnia | Memory loss, disorientation and confabulation | Obsessions and compulsions | Mania and depression
> 'Psychosis nowadays denotes a clinical syndrome — defined as being composed of hallucinations, delusions and disordered thinking/behaviour.'
Q: According to the lecture, psychotic disorders are currently defined by: = Clinical features — not (yet) by laboratory, genetic or neuroimaging techniques | Laboratory tests | Genetic testing | Neuroimaging | EEG findings
> 'Not (yet) defined by laboratory tests, genetic or neuroimaging techniques.' The diagnosis remains clinical. Psychoses are divided into primary and secondary.
Q: The broad category of schizophrenia includes disorders in which individuals experience: = Distorted perception of reality and impairment in thinking, behaviour, affect and motivation | Episodic elevation of mood only | Memory loss with preserved reality testing | Fear of specific objects | Physical symptoms without organic cause
> '…a set of disorders in which individuals experience distorted perception of reality and impairment in thinking, behavior, affect, and motivation.'
Q: Which is NOT listed in the lecture as an area disturbed in schizophrenia? = Level of consciousness | Content of thought | Form of thought | Sense of self | Interpersonal functioning
> Disturbances listed: content of thought, form of thought, perception, affect, sense of self, motivation, behaviour, interpersonal functioning. Consciousness is clear in schizophrenia — clouding suggests delirium.
Q: In ICD-11, schizophrenia belongs to the grouping: = Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders | Schizophrenia, schizotypal and delusional disorders | Schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders | Non-organic psychoses | Functional psychoses
> ICD-11: 'Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders' — schizophrenia, schizoaffective, schizotypal, ATPD, delusional disorder, other primary psychotic disorder. The first option is ICD-10; the second is DSM-5.
Q: Which is listed among the cognitive deficits of schizophrenia in the lecture? = Executive functions such as abstraction | Anhedonia | Hostility | Suicidality | Alogia
> Cognitive deficits: attention, memory, executive functions (e.g. abstraction). Anhedonia and alogia are negative; hostility sits with agitation; suicidality with mood symptoms.
Q: Loss of insight in schizophrenia is also termed: = Anosognosia | Alexithymia | Avolition | Abulia | Agnosia
> The lecture lists 'Loss of insight (anosognosia)' among the features — partly a neurocognitive deficit, not just denial.
Q: In ICD-11, ICD-10's induced delusional disorder is now classified under: = Delusional disorder | Schizophrenia | Acute and transient psychotic disorder | Schizotypal disorder | It was deleted
> The ICD-10 → ICD-11 map: persistent delusional disorder and induced delusional disorder → delusional disorder.
Q: Which is NOT listed among the lecture's goals of treatment? = Long-term institutional care | Early intervention | Psychoeducation | Pharmacogenomic testing | CBT-P
> Goals: 'Early intervention is important; psychoeducation; pharmacogenomic testing; CBT-P; outpatient care; medications.'

### OSCE: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia and clozapine | fps
> Communication station. Task: This patient’s schizophrenia has not responded to two antipsychotics. Assess, then explain clozapine.
> - FNPH explanations follow DR MS InterPOL: Definition, Rationale, Mechanism, Structure (dose), Investigations, Treatment, Prognosis, Other questions, Leaflet.
> - Smoking and stopping smoking change clozapine levels; mention it if relevant.
> Critical fail: Omitting blood monitoring or the warning to report fever or sore throat.
L: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia and clozapine: the phases of the station, in order = Check true resistance | Introduce clozapine | Monitoring | Starting and stopping | Side effects | Other options and close
Q: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia and clozapine. Which phase is this line from? “Can you tell me more?” “Have you had any issues with your current medication? Any side effects, and how much do they bother you?
