### Bonus drill: Schizophrenia: Diagnosis & Treatment Resistance
> ICD-11 schizophrenia (6A20): at least TWO of the following, at least one from a-d, for at least 1 month:
> - a. Persistent delusions. b. Persistent hallucinations. c. Disorganised thinking. d. Experiences of influence, passivity or control.
> - e. Negative symptoms. f. Grossly disorganised behaviour. g. Psychomotor disturbances, including catatonia.
> ICD-11 dropped the old subtypes (paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic). It uses symptom specifiers (positive, negative, depressive, manic, psychomotor, cognitive).
> Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS): non-response to at least TWO different antipsychotics (at least one second-generation) at adequate therapeutic dose for 6–8 weeks each. TRS is the primary indication for Clozapine.
Q: Minimum duration for schizophrenia (ICD-11) = 1 month | 6 months :: Six months is the DSM-5 total duration, not ICD-11 | 2 weeks :: Two weeks is the depressive episode duration | 3 months :: Not an ICD-11 threshold; it is 1 month
> Shorter psychotic presentations fit acute and transient psychotic disorder (6A23), which starts suddenly and typically resolves within 3 months.
Q: Symptom requirement for schizophrenia (ICD-11) = At least 2 symptoms, at least one from the core group | At least 2 symptoms from any of the groups :: At least one must come from the core group | At least 1 core symptom for 1 month :: Two symptoms are needed | At least 2 core symptoms :: Only one must be core; the second can be from any group
> Core group = delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder, and passivity experiences.
Q: How is Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia (TRS) defined? = Failure of at least 2 antipsychotics (≥1 SGA) at adequate dose for 6–8 weeks each | Failure of 1 antipsychotic for 2 weeks :: 2 weeks is too short to evaluate clinical response | Failure of typical antipsychotics only :: Current guidelines require at least one trial of a second-generation atypical | High dose depot for 6 months :: Resistance requires documented non-response to two distinct trials, not prolonged depot monotherapy
> Kane (1988) and McEvoy (2006): TRS requires failure of at least two antipsychotics at therapeutic doses for at least 6–8 weeks. It affects ~30% of patients and warrants Clozapine evaluation.
S: ICD-11 schizophrenia core symptoms = Persistent delusions | Persistent hallucinations | Disorganised thinking (formal thought disorder) | Experiences of influence, passivity or control ~~ Negative symptoms :: They count towards the diagnosis, but they are not in the core group | Grossly disorganised behaviour :: It counts towards the diagnosis, but it is not in the core group | Psychomotor disturbance (catatonia) :: It counts towards the diagnosis, but it is not in the core group
> At least one of these four must be present.
S: Schneider's first-rank symptoms = Audible thoughts (thought echo) | Voices arguing or discussing | Voices giving a running commentary | Somatic passivity | Thought insertion | Thought withdrawal | Thought broadcasting | Delusional perception | Made feelings, impulses or actions ~~ Visual hallucinations :: Not a first-rank symptom | Persecutory delusions :: Not a first-rank symptom; delusional perception is | Negative symptoms :: Not a first-rank symptom | Second-person command voices :: Not first-rank; the voices are third-person (arguing or commenting)
> Group them: 3 auditory hallucinations, 3 thought alienations (insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting), passivity (made feelings, impulses, actions, somatic), and delusional perception.
Q: Which antipsychotic is uniquely proven to reduce suicide in schizophrenia? = Clozapine | Olanzapine :: Olanzapine has strong metabolic effects but no unique anti-suicide licence | Haloperidol :: First-generation antipsychotic with high EPS; does not reduce suicide risk | Risperidone :: High EPS and prolactin; does not share clozapine's anti-suicide evidence
> Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with FDA and international approval for reducing suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder.

## Clozapine Clinic | Biological treatments
> Biological treatments. Source: BIOLOGICAL TREATMENT IN PSYCHIATRY.pptx (Dr Akinola). Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Choosing an antidepressant (Dr Akinola)
> - All antidepressants work about equally well: first trial — ~30% remit, ~50% respond. Pick by side-effect profile and comorbidity.
> - Activating → sedating: bupropion → venlafaxine/duloxetine → fluoxetine → sertraline/(es)citalopram → TCAs/paroxetine → trazodone, mirtazapine.
> - Weight gain: mirtazapine, paroxetine, TCAs. Weight loss: bupropion.
> - Pain: duloxetine, venlafaxine, TCAs. Migraine: amitriptyline.
> - No sexual dysfunction: bupropion, mirtazapine (SSRIs cause it in 25–70%).
> - Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold — avoid in epilepsy, eating disorders, electrolyte problems.
> - Paroxetine: CYP2D6 inhibitor, worst withdrawal. Fluoxetine: half-life in days. Citalopram: QTc, lower maximum dose.
> - TCAs cardiotoxic in overdose; MAOIs — tyramine crisis, 2–6 weeks' washout.
Q: Which condition is NOT appropriately treated with an antidepressant, according to the lecture? = Bipolar disorder | Panic disorder | Premenstrual dysphoric disorder | Obsessive-compulsive disorder | Dysthymia
> 'What conditions are not appropriately treated with antidepressants? Bipolar disorder, personality disorders.'
Q: After a first antidepressant trial, roughly what proportion of patients remit? = 30% | 10% | 50% | 70% | 90%
> 'About 30% of people will experience remission and 50% will have some response to a first trial.' (STAR*D)
Q: Which statement about antidepressant efficacy matches the lecture? = They all work about equally well, so choice is guided by side effects | SNRIs are twice as effective as SSRIs | TCAs are the most effective first-line drugs | MAOIs should be tried first | Efficacy rises with each failed trial
> 'Which antidepressant is the most effective? They all work about equally well.' They are chosen by an algorithm adjusted for side-effect profile.
Q: Which antidepressant is the most activating? = Bupropion | Mirtazapine | Trazodone | Paroxetine | Amitriptyline
> On the lecture's activating–sedating scale, bupropion sits at the activating end; trazodone and mirtazapine at the sedating end.
Q: A depressed patient's main complaint is insomnia. Which drug fits best? = Mirtazapine | Bupropion | Venlafaxine | Fluoxetine | Duloxetine
> Mirtazapine (and trazodone) are the most sedating; bupropion, venlafaxine and fluoxetine are activating.
Q: Which two antidepressants did the lecturer say he uses most commonly? = Sertraline and escitalopram | Amitriptyline and imipramine | Phenelzine and tranylcypromine | Paroxetine and fluvoxamine | Bupropion and trazodone
> 'Medications I commonly use: sertraline, escitalopram.'
Q: Which antidepressant is most likely to cause weight LOSS? = Bupropion | Mirtazapine | Paroxetine | Amitriptyline | Imipramine
> Bupropion — possible weight loss. Mirtazapine, paroxetine and TCAs cause more weight gain.
Q: A man stopped sertraline because of sexual dysfunction. Which alternative is least likely to cause it? = Mirtazapine | Paroxetine | Escitalopram | Fluoxetine | Venlafaxine
> 'To avoid sexual dysfunction (25–70% of all patients on an SSRI): bupropion, mirtazapine.'
Q: Bupropion should be avoided in a patient with: = Bulimia nervosa | Obesity | Nicotine dependence | Hypersomnia | Low energy
> Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold; avoid where seizures are possible, including eating disorders (electrolyte abnormalities).
Q: Which antidepressant is useful for both depression and chronic neuropathic pain? = Duloxetine | Bupropion | Mirtazapine | Escitalopram | Trazodone
> 'Useful for pain: duloxetine, venlafaxine, amitriptyline (and other TCAs).'
Q: Paroxetine interacts with many drugs and has a nasty withdrawal because it is a potent inhibitor and substrate of: = CYP2D6 | CYP1A2 | CYP3A4 | CYP2C19 | Monoamine oxidase
> 'Paroxetine is a potent inhibitor of CYP2D6, and a substrate of CYP2D6.'
Q: Why can a single dose of fluoxetine help when stopping another antidepressant? = Fluoxetine and norfluoxetine have half-lives measured in days | It is an MAOI | It blocks CYP3A4 | It has no serotonergic action | It is a mood stabiliser
> 'Both fluoxetine and norfluoxetine have half-lives measured in days' — useful to cover serotonin withdrawal, but side effects also last days.
Q: Citalopram now carries a warning that limits its maximum dose because of: = QTc prolongation | Hepatotoxicity | Agranulocytosis | Seizures | Hyperprolactinaemia
> 'Citalopram now carries a black box warning about potential QTc prolongation, and is effectively limited to half of the previous maximum dose.'
Q: When switching from another antidepressant to an MAOI, the washout recommended in the lecture is: = At least 2, up to 6 weeks | None | 24 hours | 3 days | 6 months
> MAOIs 'require at least 2, but up to 6 weeks of washout from other antidepressants due to risk of serotonin syndrome.'
Q: A 57-year-old man with a pacemaker, repeatedly shocked during AF, now has nightly attacks of racing heart and impending doom with normal ECGs. First-line drug? = Sertraline | Amitriptyline | Bupropion | Phenelzine | Lithium
> Panic disorder after cardiac shocks → sertraline or escitalopram (maybe fluoxetine). TCAs are cardiotoxic.
Q: A woman with recurrent depression failed maximum sertraline and escitalopram; she sleeps 16 h a day and has gained 35 lb. Which drug suits her best? = Bupropion | Mirtazapine | Paroxetine | Trazodone | Amitriptyline
> Hypersomnia, low energy and weight gain → an activating, weight-neutral drug: bupropion, venlafaxine or duloxetine.
Q: A veteran with PTSD, depression, combat nightmares and chronic leg pain has failed sertraline, venlafaxine and mirtazapine. Which drug targets his nightmares? = Prazosin | Bupropion | Lithium | Haloperidol | Zolpidem
> The lecture lists nortriptyline or another TCA, duloxetine, escitalopram and prazosin (for trauma nightmares).

### Treating bipolar disorder: four situations (Dr Akinola)
> - Most sensitive sign of mania: reduced sleep (only ~50% sensitive); patients forget manic episodes → get collateral. Rapid cycling ＝ ≥ 4 episodes/year.
> - Acute mania: olanzapine, valproate (oral load), lithium; all atypicals, carbamazepine. ~7 days to beat placebo. Not lamotrigine or topiramate.
> - Mania prophylaxis: lithium best; atypicals; valproate/carbamazepine (mixed).
> - Acute bipolar depression: quetiapine, olanzapine, lurasidone; lithium; lamotrigine (slow).
> - Depression prophylaxis: lamotrigine, quetiapine, olanzapine (± fluoxetine), lithium.
> - Avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I (ISBD). Use antidepressants only for comorbid anxiety, only with a mood stabiliser, and not in rapid cycling or mixed states.
> - Patients spend far more time depressed than manic — choose a drug that prevents both.
Q: According to the lecture, the single most sensitive symptom of mania is: = Sleep disturbance | Grandiosity | Pressured speech | Hypersexuality | Spending sprees
> 'The single most sensitive symptom of mania is sleep disturbance; it's only 50% sensitive.'
Q: Why is collateral history so important in diagnosing bipolar disorder? = Patients often cannot remember their manic episodes, especially when depressed | Mania is always obvious | Blood tests confirm bipolar disorder | Relatives always exaggerate | It is a legal requirement
> 'Many bipolar patients have trouble remembering their manic episodes, especially when they are depressed' — so you need collateral.
Q: Which is NOT one of the four treatment situations in bipolar disorder described in the lecture? = Prophylaxis against psychosis | Acute mania | Acute depression | Prophylaxis against mania | Prophylaxis against depression
> The four: acute mania, acute depression, prophylaxis against mania, prophylaxis against depression — each responds differently to drugs.
Q: Rapid cycling is defined as: = Four or more mood episodes in a year | Two episodes a year | Mood change within a day | Mania lasting under 4 days | Any mixed episode
> 'Rapid cycling: four discrete mood episodes per year.'
Q: Which drug does NOT work for acute mania, according to the lecture? = Lamotrigine | Olanzapine | Valproate | Lithium | Carbamazepine
> 'The only two medications... that do not have efficacy in acute mania are topiramate and lamotrigine (due to its slow titration).'
Q: Even aggressive treatment of acute mania takes about how long to separate from placebo? = 7 days | 1 day | 3 days | 4 weeks | 3 months
> 'Some patience is required, since even aggressive treatment takes 7 days to separate from placebo.'
Q: Which drug has the best evidence for preventing mania? = Lithium | Lamotrigine | Topiramate | Fluoxetine | Clonazepam
> 'Lithium has the best support for prophylaxis against mania, with studies suggesting that it is superior to other options.'
Q: If you use valproate for acute mania, the lecture advises: = Consider a loading dose regimen | Start at 125 mg and wait 6 weeks | Combine with an SSRI | Avoid blood levels | Give it only intramuscularly
> 'If you're going to use valproic acid, consider a loading dose regimen.'
Q: The ISBD Task Force recommendation on antidepressants in bipolar I disorder is: = Antidepressant monotherapy should be avoided | Use them first-line | Use them only in mania | Combine two antidepressants | Prefer TCAs
> 'Antidepressant monotherapy should be avoided in bipolar I disorder.' (ISBD 2013)
Q: When might an antidepressant reasonably be used in a bipolar patient? = For comorbid anxiety, with a mood stabiliser already on board | For bipolar depression as monotherapy | In rapid cycling | In mixed states | To prevent mania
> 'NOT for depression. For co-morbid conditions, typically anxiety disorders... only in patients who already have a mood stabilizer on board.'
Q: Which group has the best evidence for acute bipolar depression? = Quetiapine, olanzapine and lurasidone | SSRIs alone | Topiramate | Haloperidol | Benzodiazepines
> 'Atypical antipsychotics, especially quetiapine and olanzapine, and lurasidone.'
Q: Which drug is listed for preventing bipolar depression but takes a long time to reach a treatment dose? = Lamotrigine | Lithium | Olanzapine | Valproate | Carbamazepine
> Lamotrigine — effective for depression and its prevention, but slow titration (rash risk).
Q: A manic man settles on valproate, lithium and clonazepam. Which drug should be peeled off first? = Clonazepam | Lithium | Valproate | All three together | None ever
> 'Clonazepam first, then likely valproic acid' — keeping lithium for prophylaxis.
Q: Eight months later the same patient becomes depressed on lithium. Which option did the lecture recommend? = Augment with or switch to olanzapine or quetiapine, or add lamotrigine | Add sertraline alone | Start an MAOI | Stop all medication | Add haloperidol
> 'Augmentation with or a switch to olanzapine or quetiapine; augmentation with lamotrigine (although this may take a while).'
Q: A patient sets his car on fire as a sign to God, has not slept for 5 days and is pressured. Urine toxicology is negative. Most likely diagnosis? = Acute mania with psychotic features | Substance intoxication | Schizophrenia | Personality disorder | Delirium
> Reduced sleep, grandiosity, gambling, pressured speech, religious hallucinations, negative toxicology → acute mania.

### Mood-stabiliser safety (Dr Akinola)
> - Lithium — the only drug shown to reduce suicide in bipolar disorder. Early: sedation, weight, tremor, polyuria, nausea, leucocytosis, benign AV block. Late: nephrogenic DI, renal failure, hypothyroidism.
> - Lithium level 0.7–1.0 mEq/L (UK 0.6–1.0 mmol/L); monitor renal and thyroid. Toxicity: lethargy, coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea → confusion, dysarthria, nystagmus, ECG changes → seizures, renal failure, coma. Pregnancy: Ebstein's anomaly (risk now thought smaller).
> - Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonaemia, weight; level 50–100 µg/mL, FBC + LFTs; spina bifida.
> - Carbamazepine: CYP3A4 inducer; SJS/TEN 1–6/10,000 (10× in Asians); aplastic anaemia/agranulocytosis; spina bifida.
> - Lamotrigine: well tolerated; SJS ~0.1%, risk rises with fast titration → 25 mg steps every 2 weeks.
Q: Which is the only medication shown to decrease suicide rates in bipolar patients? = Lithium | Valproate | Lamotrigine | Quetiapine | Carbamazepine
> 'Lithium is the only medication demonstrated to decrease suicide rates in bipolar patients.'
Q: Which is a LATE-onset side effect of lithium? = Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus | Nausea | Fine tremor | Sedation | Leucocytosis
> Late: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal failure, thyroid failure. The others are early effects.
Q: Which sign suggests MODERATE lithium toxicity? = Nystagmus and dysarthria | Mild nausea | Fine tremor | Polyuria | Weight gain
> 'Moderate toxicity includes confusion, dysarthria, nystagmus, EKG changes.' Late: seizures, renal failure, coma.
Q: Lithium causes which white-cell change, so that it has been used for neutropenia? = Leucocytosis | Agranulocytosis | Lymphopenia | Eosinophilia | Aplastic anaemia
> 'Leukocytosis (Li is used in cases of neutropenia).'
Q: Which potentially fatal complications are specific risks of valproate? = Hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis | Agranulocytosis and myocarditis | Nephrogenic DI and hypothyroidism | Priapism and QTc | Tardive dyskinesia
> Valproate 'carries a risk of potentially fatal hepatotoxicity' and 'potentially fatal pancreatitis'; also hyperammonaemia.
Q: Carbamazepine interacts with many drugs because it: = Induces CYP3A4 | Inhibits CYP2D6 | Inhibits MAO | Blocks P-glycoprotein | Is renally cleared
> 'Induces CYP3A4, and therefore interacts with a long list of other medications.'
Q: The risk of carbamazepine-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome is much higher in: = People of Asian ancestry | Older men | Smokers | Pregnant women | Children
> 1–6/10,000, 'except in Asians, where the risk may be up to 10x higher' (HLA-B*1502).
Q: Why must lamotrigine be titrated slowly? = Because the risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome rises with faster dose increases | To avoid hyperammonaemia | To avoid QTc prolongation | Because it induces its own metabolism | To prevent lithium toxicity
> 'The risk [of SJS] is related to the rate of dose increase, so a slow schedule is required (25 mg every other week).'

### Antipsychotic side effects (Dr Akinola)
> - Efficacy: clozapine > olanzapine > the rest (small differences); typicals ＝ atypicals.
> - Three classes: dopaminergic, metabolic (antihistaminic), anticholinergic. Typicals: dopaminergic + anticholinergic. Atypicals: dopaminergic + metabolic.
> - Tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis). Nigrostriatal → EPS.
> - Rule of fours: dystonia (hours) → akathisia (days) → parkinsonism (weeks) → tardive dyskinesia (months–years).
> - Potency: haloperidol (high) — high EPS, low anticholinergic; chlorpromazine (low) — no EPS, very sedating/anticholinergic; perphenazine medium.
> - Risperidone: most prolactin and EPS of atypicals. Olanzapine: worst weight after clozapine. Quetiapine: almost no D2 block. Aripiprazole: partial agonist, akathisia up to 25%. Ziprasidone: weight-neutral, most QTc.
Q: Which is the most effective antipsychotic? = Clozapine | Haloperidol | Risperidone | Olanzapine | Aripiprazole
> 'Clozapine is the most efficacious of the antipsychotics. Olanzapine is the second most efficacious.'
Q: How do typical and atypical antipsychotics compare in overall efficacy? = No more or less effective than each other | Atypicals are clearly superior | Typicals are clearly superior | Atypicals don't treat positive symptoms | Typicals don't work in schizophrenia
> 'Typical antipsychotics are no more or less effective than atypical antipsychotics.'
Q: Which antipsychotic is specifically mentioned for aggression in autism? = Risperidone | Haloperidol | Clozapine | Ziprasidone | Chlorpromazine
> 'Aggression in autism (specifically risperidone).'
Q: Blocking dopamine in which pathway raises prolactin? = Tuberoinfundibular | Mesolimbic | Mesocortical | Nigrostriatal | Reticular
> Dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway (hypothalamus) inhibits prolactin release.
Q: By the 'rule of fours', which EPS typically appears around four DAYS after starting an antipsychotic? = Akathisia | Acute dystonia | Parkinsonism | Tardive dyskinesia | NMS
> Hours: dystonia. Days: akathisia. Weeks: parkinsonism. Months–years: tardive dyskinesia.
Q: Which is NOT a recognised consequence of hyperprolactinaemia? = Tardive dyskinesia | Galactorrhoea | Gynaecomastia | Osteoporosis | Amenorrhoea
> Hyperprolactinaemia: amenorrhoea, infertility, galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia, low libido, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis. TD is nigrostriatal.
Q: A low-potency typical such as chlorpromazine is most likely to cause: = Almost no EPS, but marked sedation and anticholinergic effects | High EPS, few anticholinergic effects | Weight loss | Akathisia in 25% | QTc shortening
> 'Chlorpromazine, a low potency agent (~400 mg/day): essentially no EPS, but very sedating and anticholinergic.'
Q: Haloperidol, a high-potency typical, is characterised by: = High EPS, low anticholinergic | Low EPS, high anticholinergic | Major weight gain | Agranulocytosis | No D2 affinity
> High potency (~5–15 mg/day): high potential for EPS, quite low anticholinergic effects.
Q: Anticholinergic drugs are particularly dangerous in which eye condition? = Acute angle-closure glaucoma | Cataract | Open-angle glaucoma | Myopia | Retinal detachment
> 'Increased intraocular pressure (dangerous in acute angle glaucoma).'
Q: Which atypical has the highest rates of hyperprolactinaemia and EPS? = Risperidone | Quetiapine | Clozapine | Aripiprazole | Olanzapine
> 'Risperidone: the most dopaminergic of the atypicals, with the highest rates of hyperprolactinemia and EPS.'
Q: Aripiprazole causes fewer dopaminergic side effects because it is a D2 partial agonist, but which side effect can reach 25%? = Akathisia | Weight gain | Sedation | Hyperprolactinaemia | Agranulocytosis
> 'Rates of akathisia are as high as 25% in some studies.'
Q: Which antipsychotic is weight-neutral but carries the highest QTc risk and must be taken with a meal? = Ziprasidone | Olanzapine | Quetiapine | Clozapine | Risperidone
> Ziprasidone: weight neutral, minimally sedating, highest QTc risk, take with a 500-calorie meal twice daily.
Q: Apart from clozapine, which antipsychotic causes the most weight gain and sedation? = Olanzapine | Aripiprazole | Haloperidol | Ziprasidone | Lurasidone
> 'Olanzapine causes significant weight gain and sedation, the worst of any antipsychotic other than clozapine.'

### Antipsychotic safety and choice (Dr Akinola)
> - NMS: rigidity, autonomic instability, delirium, catatonia; within a month of a change → stop the antipsychotic immediately.
> - All antipsychotics: lower seizure threshold; dementia mortality roughly doubles (2% → 4%/yr); QTc > 500 ms → torsade risk.
> - Choose with the patient (side effects, cost). Too psychotic to decide: olanzapine, risperidone or haloperidol.
> - Clozapine for resistance; depot for poor adherence.
> - Not responding at max dose → switch (olanzapine, clozapine). No antipsychotic polypharmacy, no high doses — beyond ~70% D2 occupancy only side effects rise.
> - Risperidone weight gain + amenorrhoea → aripiprazole/ziprasidone, or add metformin.
> - Delirium on dementia → antipsychotic only after an ECG, and warn the family about mortality.
Q: Antipsychotics in people with dementia roughly change annual all-cause mortality from: = 2% to 4% | 1% to 1.5% | 5% to 20% | 10% to 11% | No change
> 'The risk roughly doubles, from ~2% to ~4% annual mortality rate.'
Q: Above what QTc does the risk of torsade de pointes rise significantly? = 500 ms | 400 ms | 430 ms | 450 ms | 600 ms
> 'Above 500 ms, the risk of Torsade de Pointes increases significantly.'
Q: A patient with schizophrenia is not improving on the maximum dose of one antipsychotic. The evidence-based next step is: = Switch to another agent, e.g. olanzapine or clozapine | Add a second antipsychotic | Exceed the maximum dose | Add an SSRI | Stop treatment
> Switch. Antipsychotic polypharmacy and high doses are not supported — beyond ~70% D2 occupancy only side effects rise.
Q: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome usually begins: = Within a month of a medication change or dose adjustment | After years of treatment | Only after stopping the drug | Only with clozapine | Only in the elderly
> 'Onset is almost always within a month of a medication change or dose adjustment.' Stop the antipsychotic immediately.
Q: A woman on risperidone has gained 30 lb, has had no period for 2 years, and wants to conceive. Best option? = Switch to aripiprazole (or ziprasidone), or add metformin | Increase risperidone | Switch to haloperidol | Add a second antipsychotic | Stop all treatment
> Risperidone → prolactin and weight. Switch to aripiprazole or ziprasidone; metformin reduces weight gain and can reverse amenorrhoea.
Q: Before giving an antipsychotic to an agitated, dehydrated 76-year-old with dementia and electrolyte abnormalities, you should first get: = An ECG | An EEG | A brain MRI | A prolactin level | A lithium level
> An ECG (QTc), especially with electrolyte abnormalities — and warn the family about increased mortality.
Q: An acutely psychotic, violent patient in restraints needs an injectable antipsychotic. Which listed option is NOT injectable for acute use? = Risperidone | Olanzapine | Haloperidol | Chlorpromazine | Aripiprazole
> The lecture lists olanzapine and haloperidol, and 'risperidone (though it isn't injectable)' for acute agitation.

### Sedative-hypnotics (Dr Akinola)
> - Benzodiazepines: GABA-A modulators; potent, short-term, highly addictive, rebound anxiety. Uses: alcohol withdrawal, anxiety, anaesthesia, catatonia. Withdrawal like alcohol: seizures, DTs, death. Alone rarely stop breathing — dangerous with other sedatives.
> - Z-drugs (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone): less addictive sleep aids; may not beat placebo after ~30 days; complex sleep behaviours (sleep-eating, sleep-driving).
> - Trazodone: antihistaminic sleep aid; priapism ~1 in 10,000 men.
Q: Which is NOT a use of benzodiazepines listed in the lecture? = Long-term treatment of depression | Alcohol withdrawal | Catatonia | Anxiety | Anaesthesia
> Uses: 'alcohol withdrawal, anxiety, anaesthesia, and catatonia.' They are short-term and addictive.
Q: Zolpidem and other Z-drugs can cause: = Complex sleep behaviours such as sleep-driving and sleep-eating | Priapism | Agranulocytosis | Hypertensive crisis | Tardive dyskinesia
> 'Side effects include bizarre sleep behaviors; massive sleep eating, sleep driving, sleep sex.'
Q: Trazodone used as a sleep aid carries a rare risk (about 1 in 10,000 men) of: = Priapism | Agranulocytosis | SJS | Hepatotoxicity | Seizures
> '1/10,000 chance of priapism in men.'
Q: Benzodiazepine overdose is most dangerous when: = Combined with other sedatives such as alcohol or opioids | Taken alone | Taken with food | Taken in the morning | Taken by young adults
> Alone they rarely depress breathing, but 'in combination with other sedatives, they contribute significantly to respiratory depression.'

### Clozapine: the essentials
> - First atypical antipsychotic; synthesised 1958 (Wander AG); withdrawn 1975 after agranulocytosis deaths (8 in Finland); FDA-approved 1989 for treatment-resistant schizophrenia only.
> - Oral bioavailability 50–60% (first-pass); peak 2.5 h; food doesn't matter; half-life 12 h; metabolite norclozapine.
> - Metabolised by CYP1A2: smoking induces it (smokers may need double the dose); ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine inhibit it. Stopping smoking raises levels.
> - Mechanism: mainly D1 and D4 blockade, weak D2 (hence no EPSE or raised prolactin), plus 5-HT2 blockade (superior efficacy).
Q: Clozapine was synthesised in: = 1958 | 1952 | 1967 | 1975 | 1989
> 'Was synthesized in 1958 by Wander AG. Wander AG was acquired by Sandoz in 1967.'
Q: Clozapine was voluntarily withdrawn in 1975 because of: = Agranulocytosis that led to death in some patients | Seizures | Myocarditis | Weight gain | Diabetes
> '...shown to cause agranulocytosis, that led to death in some patients (eight deaths... in Finland).'
Q: In 1989 the FDA approved clozapine for: = Treatment-resistant schizophrenia only | All schizophrenia | Bipolar mania | Depression | Dementia
> 'The FDA approved clozapine's use but only for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.'
Q: Clozapine was: = The first of the atypical antipsychotics to be developed | The last typical antipsychotic | A partial D2 agonist | An MAOI | First used in 1995
> 'The first of the atypical antipsychotics to be developed.'
Q: The oral bioavailability of clozapine is: = 50–60% | 10–20% | 30–40% | 80–90% | 100%
> 'Absorption... almost complete, but the oral bioavailability is 50 to 60% due to first-pass metabolism.'
Q: Peak plasma concentration of clozapine is reached at about: = 2.5 hours | 30 minutes | 1 hour | 6 hours | 12 hours
> 'Peak concentration is 2.5 hours, and food does not appear to affect the bioavailability.'
Q: Clozapine is metabolised mainly by: = CYP1A2 | CYP2D6 | CYP3A4 | CYP2C19 | Glucuronidation only
> 'The cytochrome P450 isoenzyme 1A2 in the liver is primarily responsible for clozapine metabolism.'
Q: Compared with non-smokers, smokers may need: = Up to double the dose | Half the dose | The same dose | Ten times the dose | No clozapine
> 'Smokers require up to double the dose... to achieve an equivalent plasma concentration.' Smoke induces CYP1A2.
Q: The elimination half-life of clozapine is about: = 12 hours | 2 hours | 6 hours | 36 hours | 72 hours
> 'The elimination half-life is 12 hours.' The main metabolite is norclozapine.
Q: According to the lecture, clozapine mainly blocks: = D1 and D4 | D2 and D3 | H1 only | 5-HT1A only | NMDA
> 'Clozapine mainly blocks D1 and D4 receptors; its effects on D2 receptors are relatively less.'
Q: Clozapine's lack of EPSEs and hyperprolactinaemia is partly explained by: = Lower affinity for D2 receptors | High D2 affinity | GABA blockade | Muscarinic agonism | MAO inhibition
> 'The lower affinity of clozapine for D2 receptors may partially explain its lack of EPSEs and hyperprolactinaemia.'
Q: Its superior efficacy in resistant schizophrenia may be due to additional blockade of: = 5-HT2 receptors | H2 receptors | Beta receptors | Opioid receptors | Nicotinic receptors
> '...may be due to its additional blockade of 5HT2 receptors.'
Q: Which drug inhibits clozapine metabolism and so raises its level? = Ciprofloxacin | Carbamazepine | Rifampicin | Phenytoin | Phenobarbital
> CYP1A2 inhibitors: ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, macrolides, fluvoxamine, theophylline. The others are inducers.
Q: Which is a CYP1A2 inducer that lowers clozapine levels? = Rifampicin | Fluvoxamine | Cimetidine | Erythromycin | Ciprofloxacin
> Inducers: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin, rifabutin.
Q: Combining clozapine with antihypertensives risks: = Hypotension | Hypertension | Hyperthermia | Hypoglycaemia | Agranulocytosis
> 'Hypotension: concomitant use with antihypertensives.'
Q: Which class may enhance the adverse/toxic effect of clozapine, according to the lecture? = Benzodiazepines | Vitamins | Antacids | Paracetamol | Iron
> 'Benzodiazepines: may enhance the adverse/toxic effect of clozapine.'

### When to use clozapine, and when not
> - Treatment-resistant schizophrenia: failure of at least two different antipsychotics (McEvoy 2006).
> - Also: recurrent suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder; tardive dyskinesia and dystonia. Off-label: schizoaffective, bipolar, childhood psychosis, severe OCD, psychosis in Alzheimer's.
> - Contraindications: previous clozapine agranulocytosis, uncontrolled epilepsy, coma or severe CNS depression, paralytic ileus, myeloproliferative disorder or other marrow-suppressing drugs.
Q: Schizophrenia is labelled 'refractory' after failure to respond to at least: = Two different antipsychotics | One antipsychotic | Three depots | ECT | Six months of CBT
> '...failure of symptoms to respond satisfactorily to at least two different antipsychotics (McEvoy 2006).'
Q: Besides refractory schizophrenia, clozapine is used to reduce the risk of: = Recurrent suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder | Relapse of alcohol use | Migraine | Epilepsy | Postnatal depression
> '...used to reduce risk of recurrent suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder.'
Q: Which is listed as an unlabelled indication for clozapine? = Severe obsessive-compulsive disorder | Anorexia nervosa | Panic disorder | Insomnia | ADHD
> Unlabelled: schizoaffective, bipolar, childhood psychosis, severe OCD, psychosis/agitation in Alzheimer's.
Q: Why is clozapine not used routinely for schizophrenia? = Because of its adverse effects | It is ineffective | It is too expensive in all countries | It causes EPSE | It is only injectable
> 'It is not used routinely for treating schizophrenia because of its adverse effects.'
Q: Which is a contraindication to clozapine? = Paralytic ileus | Smoking | Previous EPSE | Hyperprolactinaemia | Tardive dyskinesia
> Contraindications include paralytic ileus, uncontrolled epilepsy, coma, previous clozapine agranulocytosis, myeloproliferative disorder.
Q: Clozapine is contraindicated with a history of: = Agranulocytosis or severe granulocytopenia with clozapine | Tardive dyskinesia | Suicide attempt | Treatment-resistant depression | Obesity
> 'History of agranulocytosis or severe granulocytopenia with clozapine.'

### Dosing clozapine
> - Start 12.5 mg once or twice daily, increase by 25–50 mg/day to 300–450 mg/day by 2 weeks; up to 900 mg/day maximum.
> - Suicidality: mean ~300 mg/day; treat 2 years then reassess; taper over 1–2 weeks.
> - Missed ≥ 48 hours → restart at 12.5–25 mg/day (can re-titrate faster unless there was cardiopulmonary arrest).
> - Stopping: taper over 1–2 weeks; abrupt stop → watch for psychosis and cholinergic rebound (headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea).
Q: The usual starting dose of clozapine in schizophrenia is: = 12.5 mg once or twice daily | 50 mg twice daily | 100 mg at night | 200 mg daily | 300 mg daily
> 'Initial: 12.5 mg once or twice daily.'
Q: The target dose after about 2 weeks of titration is: = 300–450 mg/day | 50–100 mg/day | 150–200 mg/day | 600–900 mg/day | 1,200 mg/day
> '...in increments of 25–50 mg/day to a target dose of 300–450 mg/day after 2 weeks.'
Q: The maximum daily dose of clozapine is: = 900 mg | 450 mg | 600 mg | 750 mg | 1,200 mg
> 'May require doses as high as 600–900 mg/day (max dose 900 mg/day).'
Q: For suicidal behaviour in schizophrenia, clozapine treatment duration is: = 2 years then reassess | 6 weeks | 6 months | Lifelong always | Until discharge
> 'Treatment duration 2 years then reassess need.' Mean dose ~300 mg/day.
Q: If clozapine doses are missed for 48 hours or more, therapy must be restarted at: = 12.5–25 mg/day | The previous dose | Half the previous dose | 100 mg/day | It must never be restarted
> 'If dosing is interrupted for ≥ 48 hours, therapy must be reinitiated at 12.5–25 mg/day.'
Q: After abrupt discontinuation of clozapine, monitor for psychosis and: = Cholinergic rebound | Serotonin syndrome | Hyperprolactinaemia | Tardive dyskinesia | Hypothyroidism
> '...monitor patient for psychosis and cholinergic rebound (headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea).'
Q: Planned termination of clozapine should be done by gradual reduction over: = 1–2 weeks | 1–2 days | 2–3 months | 6 months | 1 year
> '...gradual reduction in dose over 1–2 weeks period is recommended.'

### Clozapine blood monitoring
> - Register with CPMS; baseline WBC > 3500/mm³, neutrophils > 2000/mm³.
> - FBC weekly for 18 weeks, fortnightly to 1 year, then monthly indefinitely.
> - Green: WBC ≥ 3500 or ANC ≥ 2000 — continue.
> - Amber: WBC 3000–3500 or ANC 1500–2000 — test at least twice weekly.
> - Red: WBC < 3000 or ANC < 1500 — stop immediately, daily counts, haematology advice, watch for infection.
> - Rechallenge after WBC < 3.0 × 10⁹/L is off-label; G-CSF or lithium have been used, but lithium does not protect against agranulocytosis.
Q: Before starting clozapine, the neutrophil count must be above: = 2000/mm³ | 500/mm³ | 1000/mm³ | 1500/mm³ | 5000/mm³
> 'A normal leukocyte (WBC > 3500/mm³, neutrophils > 2000/mm³) count must precede treatment initiation.'
Q: Full blood counts on clozapine are done weekly for: = 18 weeks | 4 weeks | 8 weeks | 52 weeks | Life
> '...weekly intervals for 18 weeks and then fortnightly until 1 year... monthly indefinitely thereafter.'
Q: After the first year, blood monitoring on clozapine is: = Monthly indefinitely | Stopped | Yearly | Weekly for life | Only if symptomatic
> 'Blood monitoring should continue monthly indefinitely thereafter.'
Q: An amber result (caution) corresponds to: = WBC 3000–3500/mm³ or ANC 1500–2000/mm³ | WBC ≥ 3500/mm³ | WBC < 3000/mm³ | ANC < 500/mm³ | Any eosinophilia
> Amber: WBC 3000–3500 or ANC 1500–2000 — sample at least twice weekly until stable.
Q: A red result means: = STOP clozapine immediately and take daily blood samples | Continue with weekly tests | Halve the dose | Add lithium | Switch to depot
> 'Red light — STOP clozapine immediately (WBC < 3000/mm³ or ANC < 1500/mm³). Blood samples must be taken daily.'
Q: All patients on clozapine must be registered with: = The Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service | The police | A haematologist only | The NHIS | The WHO
> 'All patients must be registered with the Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service.'
Q: Agranulocytosis induced by clozapine is thought to be mediated by: = Direct toxic effect or an immune-mediated reaction | Vitamin B12 deficiency | Iron deficiency | Viral infection | Dopamine excess
> '...mediated either through a direct toxic effect or an immune-mediated reaction.'
Q: Patients whose WBC falls below which value are prohibited from further licensed clozapine? = 3.0 × 10⁹/L | 5.0 × 10⁹/L | 4.0 × 10⁹/L | 2.0 × 10⁹/L | 1.0 × 10⁹/L
> 'Patients with WBC test showing < 3.0 × 10⁹/L are prohibited from further licensed clozapine prescription.'
Q: When rechallenging clozapine with lithium, the lecture warns that lithium: = Does not protect against clozapine-related agranulocytosis | Fully protects against agranulocytosis | Must never be combined | Lowers clozapine levels | Prevents seizures
> '...close monitoring is essential as lithium does not protect against clozapine-related agranulocytosis.'
Q: Which agent has been used to mitigate repeat blood dyscrasia on clozapine rechallenge (Hagg 2003)? = Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor | Vitamin K | Iron | Steroids | Erythropoietin
> G-CSF (filgrastim) — Hagg 2003.

### Clozapine side effects to know
> - Common: constipation, hypersalivation, sedation, weight gain (~6.9 kg in 6 months), tachycardia, hypotension, nausea, enuresis.
> - Seizures: dose-related — < 300 mg 1%, 300–600 mg 2.7%, > 600 mg 4.4%. Reduce dose, EEG, levels, consider valproate.
> - Cardiac: myocarditis (IgE-mediated; low risk 0.015–0.188%), cardiomyopathy, pericarditis. Stop if persistent tachycardia in the first 2 months.
> - Metabolic: diabetes in 36.6% over 5 years (Henderson); M3 blockade on beta cells may contribute; raised triglycerides and cholesterol.
> - Rare/serious: agranulocytosis, paralytic ileus, pulmonary embolism (1 in 4,500), hepatic necrosis, interstitial nephritis, NMS, pancreatitis.
Q: Which is an anticholinergic side effect of clozapine listed in the lecture? = Constipation | Hypersalivation | Hypotension | Sexual dysfunction | Weight gain
> Anticholinergic: constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, difficulty passing urine. Hypotension is anti-adrenergic.
Q: Average weight gain on clozapine over 6 months in clinical trials was: = 6.9 kg | 1.2 kg | 3.5 kg | 12 kg | 20 kg
> 'The average weight gain in 6 months period with clozapine treatment was 6.9 kg.'
Q: Henderson et al. (2001) noted weight gain continuing for up to: = 46 months | 6 months | 12 months | 24 months | 10 years
> '...noted weight gain occurring for up to 46 months in some patients.'
Q: Which is a less common side effect of clozapine in the lecture? = Periodic catalepsy | Sedation | Constipation | Tachycardia | Hypersalivation
> Less common: fainting, gastric discomfort, small involuntary contractions, periodic catalepsy, enuresis.
Q: Seizure risk at clozapine doses above 600 mg/day is about: = 4.4% | 0.1% | 1.0% | 2.7% | 10%
> High > 600 mg: 4.4%; medium 300–600 mg: 2.7%; low < 300 mg: 1.0%.
Q: Which is not among the recommendations for clozapine-induced seizures? = Doubling the dose | Dose reduction | EEG | Plasma-level monitoring | Prophylactic antiepileptic
> Recommendations: dose reduction, EEG, plasma-level monitoring, prophylactic antiepileptic.
Q: Devinsky et al. found generalised tonic–clonic seizures in what percentage of clozapine patients? = 2.8% | 0.5% | 1.0% | 4.4% | 8%
> 'Devinsky et al. found that 2.8% of patients had generalized tonic clonic seizure.'
Q: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is thought to be caused by: = An IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction | Coronary spasm | Viral infection | Hypokalaemia | QT prolongation
> 'myocarditis — thought to be caused by immunoglobulin E mediated hypersensitivity reaction.'
Q: Clozapine should be discontinued if persistent tachycardia occurs: = In the first two months of treatment | After 1 year | Only above 150 bpm | Never | Only in smokers
> 'Discontinue if persistent tachycardia occurs in the first two months of treatment.'
Q: Orthostatic hypotension on clozapine is due to: = Alpha-adrenergic blockade | Anticholinergic activity | D2 blockade | H1 blockade | 5-HT3 blockade
> Tachycardia — anticholinergic; orthostatic hypotension — alpha-adrenergic blockade.
Q: In Henderson's (2001) 5-year study, the proportion developing diabetes on clozapine was: = 36.6% | 7% | 14% | 25% | 50%
> '...36.6% of the patient developed diabetes.'
Q: Sasaki et al. (2006) suggested clozapine-associated diabetes may result from blockade of: = M3 receptors on pancreatic beta cells | D2 receptors | H1 receptors in the hypothalamus | Alpha-1 receptors | GLP-1 receptors
> '...direct blockade of muscarinic, M3 receptors on the pancreatic beta cells.'
Q: The risk of fatal pulmonary embolism with clozapine is estimated at: = 1 in 4,500 | 1 in 100 | 1 in 1,000 | 1 in 100,000 | Nil
> 'The risk of fatal pulmonary embolism is estimated to be 1:4500 patients treated.'
Q: Which is listed among clozapine's rare serious side effects? = Fulminant hepatic necrosis | Hyperprolactinaemia | Tardive dyskinesia | Acute dystonia | Hypothyroidism
> Other side effects include fulminant hepatic necrosis, interstitial nephritis, ileus, priapism, NMS, pancreatitis.

### Fixing clozapine side effects
> - Hypersalivation → hyoscine hydrobromide (≤ 300 mcg tds) or pirenzepine (≤ 50 mg tds).
> - Constipation → fibre, fluids, aperients.
> - Enuresis → no evening fluids, change timing, desmopressin if severe.
> - Seizure → withhold 24 h, restart lower, add valproate.
> - Hypertension → slow titration, atenolol if persistent.
> - Nausea → anti-emetic, but avoid metoclopramide/prochlorperazine if previous EPSE.
> - Neutropenia → stop and admit.
> - Drugs added to clozapine: lithium raises the neutrophil count (useful in benign low counts, but it does not protect against agranulocytosis); sodium valproate as seizure prophylaxis once the dose is above 600 mg/day. Not carbamazepine — it adds marrow suppression.
Q: For clozapine hypersalivation, the lecture suggests: = Hyoscine hydrobromide or pirenzepine | Metoclopramide | Atenolol | Desmopressin | Valproate
> 'Consider use of hyoscine hydrobromide (up to 300 mcg tds), pirenzepine (up to 50 mg tds).'
Q: For severe nocturnal enuresis on clozapine, consider: = Desmopressin | Lithium | Haloperidol | Diazepam | Metformin
> 'Avoid fluids in the evening, alter dose scheduling, if severe consider use of desmopressin.'
Q: After a seizure on clozapine, the lecture advises: = Withhold for 24 hrs, recommence at a lower dose, consider prophylactic anticonvulsant (e.g. valproate) | Stop clozapine for ever | Double the dose | Add carbamazepine | Switch to depot haloperidol
> 'Withhold clozapine for 24 hrs, recommence at lower dose, consider prophylactic anticonvulsant (e.g. valproate).'
Q: For nausea on clozapine in a patient with previous EPSEs, avoid: = Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine | Ondansetron | Domperidone | Cyclizine | Ginger
> '...avoid metoclopramide and prochlorperazine if previous problems with EPSEs.'
Q: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis in an outpatient on clozapine is managed by: = Stopping clozapine and admitting to hospital | Halving the dose | Adding lithium | Repeating the test in a month | Giving iron
> 'Stop clozapine, if outpatient admit to hospital.'

### Antipsychotics (core notes)
> - High-potency FGA (haloperidol): EPSE. Low-potency (chlorpromazine): sedation, anticholinergic, hypotension.
> - Olanzapine/clozapine: weight and metabolic. Risperidone/amisulpride: prolactin. Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist, akathisia.
> - D2 occupancy 60–80% treats; > 80% gives EPSE.
> - Dystonia → IM procyclidine; akathisia → propranolol; TD → reduce/switch, clozapine, VMAT2 inhibitors.
> - Monitor weight, BP, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, ECG (QTc).
Q: Which antipsychotic is most associated with hyperprolactinaemia? = Risperidone | Aripiprazole | Quetiapine | Clozapine | Olanzapine
> Risperidone (and amisulpride). Aripiprazole is a partial agonist and tends to lower prolactin.
Q: Acute dystonia after starting haloperidol is best treated with: = IM procyclidine | Propranolol | Valbenazine | Lithium | Bromocriptine
> Acute dystonia → IM procyclidine (or benztropine). Propranolol is for akathisia; VMAT2 inhibitors for TD.
Q: Extrapyramidal side effects usually appear when D2 occupancy exceeds about: = 80% | 20% | 40% | 60% | 100%
> Antipsychotic effect at 60–80%; EPSE above ~80%.

### Antidepressants (core notes)
> - SSRIs: sertraline safest after MI; citalopram/escitalopram QTc; paroxetine worst discontinuation; fluoxetine longest half-life.
> - TCAs: dangerous in overdose (wide QRS, arrhythmia, seizures); clomipramine for OCD.
> - MAOIs: tyramine → hypertensive crisis.
> - Mirtazapine: sedation, weight. Bupropion: seizures. Venlafaxine: raises BP.
> - Response in 2–4 weeks; continue ≥ 6 months after remission (2 years if recurrent); taper to stop.
> - Watch hyponatraemia in the elderly, bleeding with NSAIDs, switch to mania.
Q: Which antidepressant is considered safest after a myocardial infarction? = Sertraline | Amitriptyline | Citalopram | Venlafaxine | Phenelzine
> Sertraline (SADHART). TCAs are cardiotoxic; citalopram prolongs QTc; venlafaxine raises BP.
Q: A patient on phenelzine eats mature cheese and develops severe headache and very high BP. This is: = A tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis | Serotonin syndrome | NMS | Lithium toxicity | Anticholinergic toxicity
> MAOIs + tyramine → noradrenaline release → hypertensive crisis.
Q: A first episode of depression has remitted on an SSRI. Continue treatment for at least: = 6 months | 2 weeks | 6 weeks | 5 years | Life
> At least 6 months after remission; 2 years or more if recurrent.

### Mood stabilisers (core notes)
> - Lithium level 0.6–1.0 mmol/L (12 h post-dose); toxic > 1.5. Monitor level 3-monthly, U&E/eGFR and TFT 6-monthly.
> - Lithium side effects: tremor, polyuria (nephrogenic DI), hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, weight, renal impairment.
> - NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, dehydration raise lithium.
> - Valproate: teratogenic — avoid in women who could become pregnant.
> - Carbamazepine: enzyme inducer, hyponatraemia, SJS, agranulocytosis.
> - Lamotrigine: bipolar depression prevention; slow titration (rash); valproate doubles its level.
Q: Which drug is most likely to raise lithium levels? = Ibuprofen | Paracetamol | Theophylline | Caffeine | Sodium bicarbonate
> NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides raise lithium. Theophylline and caffeine lower it.
Q: Polyuria and polydipsia on lithium are mainly due to: = Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus | Diabetes mellitus | Psychogenic polydipsia | Hypercalcaemia only | SIADH
> Lithium blocks ADH action in the collecting duct → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Q: Valproate should be avoided in women who could become pregnant mainly because of: = Teratogenicity, including neural tube defects and developmental delay | Weight gain | Hair loss | Tremor | Thrombocytopenia
> Valproate is highly teratogenic — use only under a pregnancy-prevention programme, if at all.
Q: Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly mainly to reduce the risk of: = Serious rash (Stevens–Johnson syndrome) | Weight gain | Hypothyroidism | Agranulocytosis | Hyponatraemia
> Slow titration reduces serious rash/SJS. Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels.

### ECT and other physical treatments (core notes)
> - ECT for: severe depression with psychosis, stupor, refusal to eat/drink or high suicide risk; catatonia; resistant mania; NMS.
> - Twice weekly, ~6–12 sessions; anaesthetic + suxamethonium; bilateral or right unilateral; dose by seizure threshold.
> - Side effects: headache, confusion, memory loss (more with bilateral).
> - No absolute contraindications; high risk with raised ICP, recent MI/stroke.
> - rTMS (left DLPFC), ketamine/esketamine, VNS, DBS, bright light (seasonal).
Q: Which is the strongest indication for urgent ECT? = Depressive stupor with refusal to eat or drink | Mild depression | Generalised anxiety | Insomnia | Personality disorder
> Life-threatening depression — stupor, food/fluid refusal, psychosis, high suicide risk — and catatonia.
Q: The muscle relaxant usually used in modified ECT is: = Suxamethonium | Diazepam | Baclofen | Dantrolene | Atropine
> Suxamethonium, after a short anaesthetic (e.g. propofol or methohexital).

### OSCE: ECT counselling: beginning to end | fps
> Communication station. Task: Counsel a patient with severe depression about electroconvulsive therapy, including procedure, benefits, risks, alternatives, preparation, consent and follow-up.
> Patient: “Maryam”, 45, has severe depression with psychotic symptoms and poor oral intake. She fears electrocution and permanent memory loss. Capacity is intact. She asks whether she will be awake and whether she may refuse.
> - The senior-resident material emphasises: explore ideas; explain anaesthesia, electrical stimulus and convulsion; about twice-weekly treatment; a typical 8–12 course; benefits; headache, muscle pain, nausea and memory effects; rare serious risk; consent.
> - For safe modern counselling, do not describe depression as merely a chemical imbalance, promise a fixed response rate, use a universal mortality statistic, or say the family simply decides for an incapable adult.
> - Both books order the talk as DR MS InterPOL: Definition, Rationale, Mechanism, Structure, Investigations/Treatment, Prognosis, Other questions, Leaflet.
> - FNPH wording: “Imagine it like a hard reset of your computer or phone.” Consent form signed; pros and cons explained because “your opinion about your treatment is of utmost importance”; anaesthetist reviews fitness; fast overnight (the book says 6–8 hours, so follow the unit’s instruction); vital signs in the ECT suite; asleep; electrodes on the temples; a seizure lasting a few seconds; wakes within minutes and is escorted back to the ward. Other medicines continue.
> - Abdulhakeem wording: “Your form of depression is treated with physical (biological) and psychosocial treatment; ECT is a physical treatment.” Benefits: mood improves faster (within 1–2 weeks); works best combined with an antidepressant; also used in schizophrenia and catatonia. Respect autonomy: “You have full autonomy to decide and your decision will be respected. You need not decide now; you may discuss it with your family, and we will give you a leaflet.”
> Critical fail: Coercion, dismissing memory concerns, or telling her the family decides.

### OSCE: ECT electrode placement explanation | fps
> Practical skills station. Task: On a head model, demonstrate and explain the placements expected in the local practical manual; compare efficacy, speed, dose and cognitive effects; estimate hemispheric dominance.
> Patient: FNPH scenario: “Demonstrate on Mr Oliver, a ward attendant, ECT electrode placement for (a) unilateral, (b) bifrontal and (c) bitemporal positions. Explain to Prof Rogers.”
> - Bitemporal, front view: lateral canthus —— midpoint —— external auditory meatus; electrode ≈ 4 cm above the midpoint; mirror on the other side.
> - Right unilateral, right side view: E1 ≈ 4 cm above the canthus–meatus midpoint; E2 ≈ 10 cm superior to E1.
> - Bifrontal, front view: electrode ≈ 5 cm above each lateral canthus, symmetrically over the frontal regions.
> - Source ambiguity: one older page uses “bitemporal” inconsistently after describing “bilateral”. Name the configuration before demonstrating it.
> - FNPH indications for unilateral: when avoiding memory problems is the priority (e.g. existing cognitive impairment), when speed of response matters less, or after a previous good response to it.
> - FNPH indications for bilateral: when speed of recovery is the priority, or after failure of unilateral ECT. More cognitive side effects, usually reversible. Bifrontal is described as having fewer cognitive side effects than bitemporal.
> - Both books expect: most cognitive side effects ＝ bilateral; most rapid response ＝ bilateral; dominance without special tests ＝ hand for writing/throwing/catching, foot for kicking.
> Critical fail: Guessing landmarks without measuring, or demonstrating without clarifying an ambiguous “bilateral” command.
