### Bonus drill: OSCE: Clozapine Initiation & Blood Monitoring | fps
> CANDIDATE BRIEF: A 28-year-old patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is referred after failing olanzapine and risperidone. Counsel the patient and their sister, explain the CPMS monitoring traffic lights, outline baseline tests, and take informed consent.
> CRITICAL FAIL: Failing to explain that fever or sore throat requires an immediate emergency hospital check; or combining clozapine with carbamazepine.
L: Clozapine Counselling Protocol (OSCE) = 1. Validate distress over past medication failures and define treatment resistance | 2. Explain Clozapine's superior efficacy and proven suicide-reduction evidence | 3. Explain mandatory blood monitoring: Weekly for 18 weeks, 2-weekly to 1 year, then monthly | 4. Explain the Traffic Light system: Green (continue), Amber (re-test 2x/wk), Red (stop immediately) | 5. Warn about emergency red flags: Fever, sore throat, severe constipation, and chest pain | 6. Address smoking impact (CYP1A2 induction: stopping smoking spikes clozapine levels) ~~ Promise blood tests will stop after 1 month :: Monitoring is indefinite (monthly after 1 year) | State clozapine has zero side effects :: Frank discussion of metabolic, seizure, and bowel side effects is required for valid consent | Recommend adding Carbamazepine for mood stability :: Carbamazepine is contraindicated with clozapine due to additive bone marrow suppression
S: Mandatory Baseline Pre-Clozapine Workup = Full Blood Count with Differential (WBC > 3500, ANC > 2000) | Baseline 12-lead ECG (QTc interval) | Troponin and C-Reactive Protein (CRP) | Fasting blood glucose and lipid profile | Urea, Electrolytes and Liver Function Tests | Baseline weight, BMI and waist circumference ~~ Lumbar puncture :: Not indicated unless an infectious or autoimmune encephalitis is suspected | Therapeutic drug monitoring blood level :: TDM is performed after steady-state titration, not as a baseline test | Bone marrow biopsy :: Not indicated prior to clozapine initiation
Q: CPMS Blood Monitoring Thresholds: When does a count require RED ALERT immediate cessation? = WBC < 3000/mm³ or Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) < 1500/mm³ | WBC < 4000/mm³ or ANC < 2500/mm³ :: These are normal safe ranges (Green category) | WBC < 3500/mm³ or ANC < 2000/mm³ :: This is the Amber category: continue treatment but increase monitoring to twice weekly | Platelets < 150,000/mm³ only :: Clozapine monitoring focuses primarily on leukocyte and absolute neutrophil counts
> Green: WBC ≥ 3500, ANC ≥ 2000. Amber: WBC 3000–3500, ANC 1500–2000 (test twice weekly). Red: WBC < 3000, ANC < 1500 (STOP clozapine immediately; daily counts; admit). Note: In Benign Ethnic Neutropenia (BEN), Red is ANC < 1000/mm³.
Q: What is the management if a patient on Clozapine misses doses for 48 hours or more? = Restart at 12.5 mg once or twice daily and re-titrate | Resume at their previous full maintenance dose :: Resuming a full dose after 48h carries high risk of fatal collapse, severe hypotension and seizures | Double the next dose to compensate :: Extremely dangerous; clozapine must be re-titrated from 12.5 mg | Switch immediately to another antipsychotic :: Missing 48 hours only requires safe re-titration, not abandonment of effective therapy
> Because tolerance to alpha-1 adrenergic and histaminic blockade is rapidly lost, missing ≥48 hours requires restarting at 12.5 mg and re-titrating to prevent syncope and cardiac arrest.

### Bonus drill: Lithium & mood stabilisers
> Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is excreted unchanged by the kidneys. Anything that reduces renal clearance raises the level: dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, thiazides, renal impairment.
> Know the targets and timing, baseline tests, the monitoring schedule, toxicity signs and management, and long-term effects: hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD, hyperparathyroidism with high calcium, weight gain, tremor.
> Other stabilisers: valproate (highly teratogenic), carbamazepine (enzyme inducer, hyponatraemia, Stevens-Johnson), lamotrigine (slow titration for rash).
Q: Usual maintenance lithium level = 0.6-1.0 mmol/L | 0.4-0.6 mmol/L :: Subtherapeutic for most people | 1.0-1.5 mmol/L :: Above the usual range and close to toxicity | 1.5-2.0 mmol/L :: That is the toxic range
> Many guidelines aim for 0.6-0.8 mmol/L for maintenance, going up to 1.0 if needed. Older people often need lower levels.
Q: Lithium level is taken how long after the last dose? = 12 hours | 2 hours :: Near the peak, so the level would read falsely high | 24 hours :: Not standard; levels are standardised at 12 hours | 6 hours :: Not standard; levels are standardised at 12 hours
> A "12-hour trough": give the evening dose, then take the blood the next morning.
Q: Lithium toxicity usually appears above = 1.5 mmol/L | 1.0 mmol/L :: 1.0 is the top of the usual therapeutic range | 0.8 mmol/L :: 0.8 is therapeutic | 3.0 mmol/L :: Toxicity starts well before 3.0; that is severe, life-threatening
> Toxicity can occur even at "normal" levels in older or physically ill people. Treat the patient, not just the number.
S: Baseline tests before lithium = Renal function (U&E, eGFR) | Thyroid function | Calcium | ECG if cardiac risk | Weight or BMI | Pregnancy test if relevant ~~ EEG :: Not a routine lithium baseline test | Chest X-ray :: Not a routine lithium baseline test | CT head :: Not a routine lithium baseline test
> Each test is there for a reason: kidneys (excretion and nephrotoxicity), thyroid (hypothyroidism), calcium (hyperparathyroidism), heart (conduction effects), weight (gain), pregnancy (Ebstein's anomaly).
L: Lithium level monitoring after starting = Check level 1 week after starting (12 h after dose) | Repeat weekly until stable | Every 3 months for the first year | Every 6 months after that if stable ~~ Check 2 hours after the dose :: Levels are taken 12 hours after the dose | Once a year only :: Far too infrequent | Only if toxic symptoms appear :: Routine monitoring is required
> Recheck the level after every dose change, a new interacting drug, or an illness with vomiting or dehydration. Check renal and thyroid function every 6 months.
S: Signs of lithium toxicity = Coarse tremor | Vomiting and diarrhoea | Ataxia | Dysarthria | Confusion | Seizures ~~ Fine tremor :: A fine tremor is a common side effect at normal levels; a COARSE tremor suggests toxicity | Weight gain :: A side effect, not toxicity | Hypothyroidism :: A long-term effect, not acute toxicity
> The usual progression is GI upset, then coarse tremor and cerebellar signs (ataxia, dysarthria), then confusion, seizures, arrhythmias and coma.
Q: Drugs that raise lithium levels = NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazide diuretics | NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, theophylline :: Theophylline LOWERS lithium | Thiazides, sodium bicarbonate, NSAIDs :: Sodium bicarbonate LOWERS lithium | ACE inhibitors, acetazolamide, caffeine :: Acetazolamide and caffeine LOWER lithium
> Common traps: ibuprofen for pain, starting an ACE inhibitor or thiazide, and dehydration from heat or diarrhoea.
Q: Classic cardiac defect linked to lithium in pregnancy = Ebstein's anomaly | Ebstein's anomaly of the mitral valve :: Ebstein's anomaly involves the TRICUSPID valve | Neural tube defects :: Neural tube defects are linked to valproate and carbamazepine | Tetralogy of Fallot :: Not the classic lithium-associated defect
> Ebstein's anomaly is a downward displacement of the tricuspid valve. The absolute risk is small; counsel before conception rather than stopping abruptly.
Q: Valproate in women who could become pregnant = Avoid unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place | Use with any form of contraception :: It needs a formal pregnancy prevention programme with highly effective contraception | Avoid only in the first trimester :: Harm includes neurodevelopmental effects throughout pregnancy | Safe if high-dose folic acid is given :: Folic acid does not remove valproate's risk
> Exposed pregnancies carry about a 10% risk of major malformations, with neurodevelopmental problems in up to 30-40% of children.
Q: Long-term lithium can cause = Hypothyroidism and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus | Hyperthyroidism and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus :: Lithium causes HYPOthyroidism | Hypothyroidism and cranial diabetes insipidus :: Lithium causes NEPHROGENIC diabetes insipidus | Hypothyroidism and hypocalcaemia :: Lithium causes HYPERcalcaemia (via hyperparathyroidism)
> Also watch for hyperparathyroidism (raised calcium), weight gain, acne and psoriasis flares, and a slow decline in eGFR.
Q: Mood stabiliser that needs slow titration because of rash (Stevens-Johnson) = Lamotrigine | Carbamazepine :: It carries a Stevens-Johnson risk (screen HLA-B*1502), but slow titration for rash is the lamotrigine rule | Valproate :: The concerns with valproate are teratogenicity and liver toxicity | Lithium :: The concern with lithium is toxicity, not rash
> Valproate DOUBLES lamotrigine levels, so use an even slower titration when they are combined.
Q: Carbamazepine commonly causes which electrolyte problem? = Hyponatraemia (SIADH) | Hypernatraemia :: The opposite: carbamazepine causes hyponatraemia | Hyponatraemia through a diuretic effect :: The mechanism is SIADH (water retention), not diuresis | Hypokalaemia :: Not typical of carbamazepine
> Carbamazepine also induces liver enzymes (it lowers levels of the contraceptive pill and many other drugs) and can cause agranulocytosis. Screen for HLA-B*1502 in people of Asian ancestry.

### Bonus drill: OSCE: explaining treatment | fps
> Explanation stations are marked on structure and on checking understanding. Use the same frame every time:
> - Find out what they know and what they want to know (avoid lecturing).
> - Give information in small chunks, in plain language. Check understanding with teach-back ("Can you tell me in your own words…?").
> - Cover benefits, risks, alternatives, and what happens if they do nothing.
> - Invite questions, offer a leaflet, and agree a follow-up.
L: OSCE: explaining lithium to a patient = Introduce, check what they already know and want to know | What lithium is and why it is recommended (prevents relapse, reduces suicide risk) | How to take it and how long before it works | Blood tests: level 12 hours after a dose, then regular checks | Common side effects: thirst, passing more urine, fine tremor, weight gain, stomach upset | Toxicity warning signs: vomiting, diarrhoea, coarse tremor, unsteadiness, confusion: stop and seek help | Avoid dehydration; avoid NSAIDs; tell every doctor you take lithium | Pregnancy and contraception | Long-term monitoring of kidneys, thyroid and calcium | Check understanding, give a leaflet and lithium card, invite questions ~~ Say it has no side effects :: Inaccurate and loses marks for honesty | Skip toxicity warning signs :: Toxicity counselling is the most heavily weighted point | Tell them to stop suddenly if they feel well :: Stopping abruptly raises the risk of rebound mania
> Examiners look for: a clear toxicity safety-net, the dehydration and NSAID warnings, the 12-hour blood level, pregnancy counselling, and teach-back.
> Common fail: listing side effects without explaining what to DO about them.
L: OSCE: explaining clozapine = Check understanding: why clozapine (when 2 antipsychotics have not worked) | Benefits: often works when others have not, reduces suicide risk | Blood monitoring: weekly for 18 weeks, then fortnightly, then monthly, because of low white cells | Report infection signs urgently: sore throat, fever | Common side effects: drowsiness, drooling, constipation, weight gain, dizziness | Constipation can be serious: report it, take laxatives | Heart warning signs early on: chest pain, breathlessness, fast heartbeat | Smoking changes clozapine levels: tell us if you stop or start | Missed doses for 48 hours or more need re-titration | Check understanding and invite questions ~~ Blood tests are optional :: Monitoring is mandatory to continue clozapine | Constipation is harmless :: Clozapine constipation can cause fatal bowel obstruction | Smoking makes no difference :: Smoking induces CYP1A2; stopping smoking can raise clozapine levels sharply
> Examiners look for: the reason for monitoring (neutropenia), sore throat or fever as an emergency, constipation, myocarditis warning signs, the smoking interaction, and what to do about missed doses.
L: OSCE: explaining ECT = Check understanding and concerns | What ECT is: a brief, controlled seizure under general anaesthetic | Why it is recommended (severe or psychotic depression, catatonia, not eating or drinking) | What happens: fasting, anaesthetic, muscle relaxant, monitoring, recovery | How many: usually twice weekly, often 6 to 12 treatments | Benefits: often works faster than medication in severe illness | Side effects: headache, muscle aches, confusion afterwards, memory problems | Alternatives and the right to refuse or withdraw consent at any time | Address myths, check understanding, invite questions ~~ Say it is painful and done awake :: ECT is given under general anaesthetic with a muscle relaxant | Promise no memory effects :: Memory problems can occur and must be discussed honestly | Say consent cannot be withdrawn :: Consent can be withdrawn at any time
> Myths to address: it is not a punishment, they will be asleep, it does not change personality, and the amount of electricity is carefully controlled.
L: OSCE: explaining a diagnosis of schizophrenia to a relative = Check consent and what they know | Explain the illness simply: changes in thinking and perception | Common symptoms they may see | Causes: a mix of genes, brain chemistry, stress and drugs like cannabis (not bad parenting or a curse) | Treatment: medication, talking therapies, family support, rehabilitation | Outlook: many recover well, and relapse can be prevented | Early warning signs of relapse | How the family can help: low expressed emotion, adherence support | Support services and carer support | Check understanding and invite questions ~~ Blame the family :: Blaming causes harm and is factually wrong | Say it is untreatable :: Outcomes improve with treatment; give realistic hope | Confirm it is a spiritual attack :: Respect beliefs, but explain the medical model clearly
> Cultural sensitivity scores marks: acknowledge the family's beliefs (spiritual or traditional explanations), then explain the medical view without dismissing them. High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, over-involvement) predicts relapse, so family psychoeducation is evidence-based.
Q: Best way to check understanding in an explanation station = Ask the patient to explain it back in their own words (teach-back) | Ask "Do you have any questions?" :: This invites questions but does not check understanding | Ask "Do you understand?" :: A closed question; patients usually just say yes | Summarise the key points for them yourself :: Your summary does not show what THEY understood
> Teach-back is the single most rewarded technique in explanation stations.

## Emergency Resus | Emergency psychiatry | race
> Emergency psychiatry. Source: EMERGENCY PSYCHIATRY LECTURE REVISION COURSE PART I 19TH FEBRUAY 2026.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### What a psychiatric emergency is
> - Emergency psychiatry ＝ the clinical application of psychiatry in emergency settings (AAEP).
> - A psychiatric emergency ＝ a situation needing immediate, rapid assessment and intervention to prevent harm — acute disturbance of thought, mood, behaviour or relationships, as defined by the patient, family or social unit (Wheat et al., 2016).
> - It involves behavioural disturbance, threat of it, physiological disturbance and high-risk assessment.
> - Rising because of violence, socio-economic instability, more awareness of mental illness, and more substance use.
Q: Emergency psychiatry is defined by the AAEP as: = The clinical application of psychiatry in emergency settings | Psychiatry practised only in prisons | Care of the elderly | Liaison psychiatry | Forensic assessment
> 'Emergency psychiatry (EP) is the clinical application of psychiatry in emergency settings' — AAEP.
Q: Wheat et al. (2016) say the need for immediate intervention in a psychiatric emergency is defined by: = The patient, family or social unit | The police | The court | The ED nurse only | The psychiatrist alone
> '...require immediate intervention as defined by the patient, family or social unit...'
Q: Which is not given as a reason for rising numbers of psychiatric emergencies? = Fewer substance-related disorders | Violence | Socio-economic instability | Increased awareness of mental illness | Increased alcohol and drug disorders
> The lecture cites more substance-related disorders, not fewer.
Q: A psychiatric emergency involves behavioural disturbance, threat of it, physiological disturbance and: = High-risk assessment | Financial assessment | Genetic assessment | Occupational assessment | Imaging
> 'PE involves behavioural disturbance, threat of behavioural disturbance, physiological disturbance and high-risk assessment.'

### Who comes, and how often
> - Three categories: acute episode of a chronic illness; an underlying medical/toxic cause (intoxication, delirium, drug interactions); normal people overwhelmed by an event.
> - 6–9% of ED visits are primarily mental health; no gender difference; single > married.
> - 40% need admission; 20% are suicidal; 10% are violent.
> - Commonest: psychosis, mood disorders, alcohol and SUDs; mostly nights and weekends (more seclusion).
> - ED pitfalls: tempers flare while waiting; medical problems minimised once labelled "psychiatric".
Q: A recognised problem in the ED is 'minimisation of medical issues', meaning: = Patients labelled psychiatric get too little attention to medical symptoms | Patients exaggerate symptoms | Doctors over-investigate | Nurses refuse to triage | Patients refuse tests
> '...labelled as psychiatric rather than medical i.e. not enough attention to medical symptoms.'
Q: Which is a role of the psychiatrist in the ED? = Assessing the potential lethality of the situation or dangerousness of the patient | Performing surgery | Running the pharmacy | Discharging all patients | Billing
> Roles: expert, assess lethality/dangerousness, help with difficult cases, decide inpatient/outpatient and voluntary/involuntary care.
Q: What proportion of ED visits (USA) involve a primary mental health diagnosis? = 6–9% | 1–2% | 20–25% | 40% | 60%
> '6–9% of all emergency department (ED) visits involve patients with primary mental health diagnosis.'
Q: Of psychiatric emergency patients, the proportion who are suicidal is about: = 1 in 5 | 1 in 2 | 2 in 5 | 1 in 10 | 1 in 100
> 40% need admission; 1 in 5 (20%) are suicidal; 1 in 10 are violent.
Q: Psychiatric emergencies present mostly: = At nights and weekends | Weekday mornings | During clinic hours | In the rainy season only | On public holidays only
> 'Presentation mostly at nights & weekend — less manpower... increased risk of use of seclusion.'
Q: A previously well person overwhelmed by the sudden discovery of a serious illness belongs to which ED category? = Essentially normal psychological balance with an overwhelming event | Acute episode of chronic illness | Medically induced psychiatric symptoms | Personality disorder | Malingering
> Third category: 'essentially normal psychological balance but overwhelming event...'
Q: Which is listed as a medication-related cause of delirium/emergency? = Neuroleptic malignant syndrome | Paracetamol | Vitamin C | Iron | Antacids
> Medication side effects: serotonin crisis, acute dystonia, akathisia, NMS.

### The emergency process
> - Triage → assessment → differential diagnosis → manage acute symptoms → discharge planning.
> - Triage: how urgent; real emergency or not; medical, psychiatric or both; ensure safety; ask about suicidal/homicidal ideation.
> - Assessment: life-threats first; collateral before seeing the patient; organic causes as priority.
> - Goals: risk to self/others, diagnosis, biopsychosocial factors, premorbid function, strengths and protective factors, treatment goals, level of care, follow-up.
> - Work-up: vitals, E/U/Cr, glucose, lipids, LFT, FBC (+ malaria), urinalysis, urine toxicology, ECG; EEG and CT/MRI only when indicated.
Q: The FIRST goal of evaluating a psychiatric emergency is to: = Determine whether the patient is at impending risk of harm to self or others | Make a full ICD-11 diagnosis | Arrange psychotherapy | Take a family tree | Start antipsychotics
> Goal 1: 'To determine if the patient is at impending risk of harm to self or others.'
Q: Which is among the goals of emergency evaluation? = Identify strengths, supports and protective factors | Complete psychoanalysis | Prescribe long-term depot | Arrange marriage counselling | Do a sleep study
> 'To identify the strengths, supports, and protective factors that may reduce distress & risk.'
Q: The correct order of emergency psychiatric care is: = Triage → assessment → differential diagnosis → management → discharge planning | Treatment → triage → assessment | Admission → triage → discharge | Assessment → admission → triage | Discharge → follow-up → triage
> Triage → Assessment → Differential diagnosis → Management → Discharge planning.
Q: In assessment, the lecture advises gathering information from others: = Before seeing the patient | Never | Only after discharge | Only with a court order | Only from the police
> 'Gather information from others b4 seeing the patient.'
Q: In the differential diagnosis, which disorders take priority? = Organic disorders | Personality disorders | Anxiety disorders | Dissociative disorders | Sleep disorders
> '...Differential Diagnosis - (Organic disorders priority).'
Q: CT or MRI in the emergency work-up should be done: = Only when indicated, for traumatic brain injury or intracranial mass | In every patient | Never | Instead of history | Before triage
> 'Assess for traumatic brain injury and intracranial mass (ONLY WHEN INDICATED).'
Q: Which test is used to assess for certain types of substance use? = Urine toxicology | ECG | Lipid profile | EEG | Thyroid function
> 'Urine toxicology — assess for certain types of substance use.'
Q: During triage, staff must find out about: = Suicidal or homicidal ideation | Educational history | Hobbies | Religious practice | Developmental milestones
> '...find out suicidal or homicidal ideation that could endanger the patient or others.'

### Initial treatment — four categories
> - Environmental: safe space, quiet room/time-out, seclusion with close nursing monitoring, respite care, emergency placement of a child.
> - Medication — but remember: the diagnosis may be wrong, labs incomplete, sedation masks medical illness, and follow-up won't be by the ED doctor. Benzodiazepines, antipsychotics.
> - Crisis intervention: ventilation, alternatives, clarifying roles, interpreting meaning, empathic listening.
> - Education: removes guilt, shame and hopelessness.
> - Discharge: level of care, willingness to seek treatment, timing of follow-up, communication.
Q: Which is not one of the four categories of emergency intervention? = Psychoanalysis | Environmental management | Medical intervention | Crisis intervention | Education
> Categories: environmental, medical, crisis intervention, education.
Q: Before giving medication in the ED, the lecture warns that sedation can: = Mask signs of medical illness | Cure delirium | Speed discharge | Improve history-taking | Replace investigations
> 'Medication sedation — can mask signs of medical illness.' Also: diagnosis may be wrong, labs incomplete, follow-up not by ED doctor.
Q: A seclusion room is used to reduce the potential for violence and absconding, and requires: = Close monitoring by nursing staff | No supervision | A court order each time | Family consent only | Police presence
> 'Seclusion room to reduce potential for violence & absconding — close monitoring required by nursing staff.'
Q: Which is a crisis (psychological) de-escalation technique listed in the lecture? = Ventilation | Restraint | Rapid tranquillisation | ECT | Seclusion
> Crisis interventions: ventilation, identifying alternatives, clarifying roles, interpreting meaning, empathic listening.
Q: Discharge planning from the ED depends mainly on: = The resources available | The patient's income | The weather | The day of the week | The nurse's preference
> 'Discharge planning — depends on the resources available.'

### Ethics and involuntary care
> - Balance autonomy, safety and confidentiality against immediate, sometimes involuntary, intervention; follow beneficence, non-maleficence, justice.
> - Tensions: autonomy vs beneficence; restraint (trauma, dignity, liberty); confidentiality vs duty to warn; capacity for consent; cultural bias (behaviour misread as aggression); fair resource allocation.
> - Involuntary admission: risk to self, risk to others, or unable to care for self due to mental illness.
> - Psychiatric patients have the same right to refuse as medical patients.
Q: Which three ethical principles does the lecture say must be adhered to? = Beneficence, non-maleficence and justice | Profit, speed, efficiency | Secrecy, obedience, loyalty | Autonomy only | Paternalism, control, restraint
> 'NB: Need to adhere to the ethical principles of beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice.'
Q: The tension between a patient's privacy and the need to protect others from a homicidal patient is: = Confidentiality vs safety (duty to warn or protect) | Autonomy vs beneficence | Justice vs resources | Capacity vs consent | Culture vs bias
> 'Confidentiality & Safety: Patient privacy & duty to warn or protect others — homicidal patient.'
Q: Involuntary admission is justified by risk to self, risk to others, or: = Inability to care for self due to mental illness | Poor school grades | Refusing to pay | Unemployment | Family request alone
> '...risk to self — suicidality, risk to others — homicidal, unable to care for themselves due to MI.'
Q: Regarding refusal of treatment, patients with psychiatric disorders: = Have the same right to refuse treatment as those with medical conditions | Have no right to refuse | Can refuse only with a lawyer | Must always be sedated | Need police approval
> 'Patient with psychiatric disorders have the same right to refuse treatment like those with medical condition.'
Q: 'Cultural competence and bias' refers mainly to the risk of: = Misinterpreting behaviour as aggressive | Over-billing | Language exams | Excess medication cost | Loss of records
> '...potential for misinterpreting behavior as aggressive — diagnosis & Mx.'

### Models of emergency psychiatric care
> - Consultation in the ED (can be chaotic); dedicated mental health wing of the ED.
> - Crisis stabilisation unit — outside the ED, cannot admit, psychiatrist round the clock (on-call/telepsychiatry).
> - Psychiatric Emergency Services (PES) — patients pre-screened and medically cleared; 24/7, calmer.
> - Mobile crisis team — goes to the patient; may avoid hospital.
> - Walk-in crisis centre (less stigma); acute diversion units in real houses (not dangerous patients).
> - Contemporary: 23-hour observation; verbal de-escalation before medication; oral before parenteral antipsychotics.
Q: A crisis stabilisation unit (CSU): = Is not usually in the ED and cannot provide admission | Is always inside the ED and admits patients | Replaces the psychiatric hospital | Treats only children | Is run by police
> 'CSU — Not usually located in ED... not able to provide admission; Pt assessed initially at ED then referred there.'
Q: In Psychiatric Emergency Services (PES), patients are: = Pre-screened and medically cleared before referral | Never medically assessed | Only voluntary | Only children | Seen by surgeons
> 'Psychiatric Emergency services (PES) — Pts are pre screened and medical clearance is done prior referral.'
Q: A team that travels to the patient's location to provide on-site crisis intervention is a: = Mobile crisis team | Crisis stabilisation unit | Regional PES | Consultation service | Day hospital
> 'Mobile Crisis Team — Mental health team travel to site to see a patient in crisis...'
Q: Acute diversion units (crisis residential) are suitable for patients who: = Are not dangerous to self or others and will join group activities | Are violent | Need ICU care | Are in prison | Have delirium
> 'Patients are willing to participate in group activities. The patients are not dangerous to self or others.'
Q: Contemporary emergency care manages agitation by prioritising: = Verbal de-escalation, and oral rather than parenteral antipsychotics | Immediate restraint | IV benzodiazepines first | Seclusion first | ECT
> 'Prioritizes verbal de-escalation rather than medication and use of oral antipsychotics rather than parenteral meds.'
Q: Modern short-term emergency treatment often uses an observation period of: = 23 hours | 1 hour | 6 hours | 7 days | 1 month
> 'Short term treatment... 23-hour observation periods, discharge to community is aimed.'

### Deliberate self-harm (DSH)
> - Definition: deliberate destruction of body tissue without conscious suicidal intent. A less stigmatising term.
> - Includes: cutting, burning, pins/needles, biting, punching, head-banging, scratching. Excludes: piercing/tattoos, overdose, substance use, eating disorders, learning-disability self-injury, self-harm with suicidal intent.
> - Up to 4–5 in 10 later die by suicide (UK).
> - Repeat predictors: previous episodes, personality disorder, unemployment, alcoholism, unmarried, violence, criminal record, low social class.
> - Signs of real suicidal intent: isolation, timing to avoid discovery, precautions, suicide note, anticipatory acts (will, gifts), dangerous method. Rate with C-SSRS (18 items, 4 sections).
> - Brown and Stanley safety plan: warning signs → internal coping → people/places for distraction → people to ask for help → professionals/lifelines → make the environment safe.
Q: Deliberate self-harm is defined as deliberate destruction of body tissue: = Without conscious suicidal intent | With clear suicidal intent | Only by overdose | Only in children | Caused by others
> 'The direct, deliberate destruction or alteration of the body tissue without conscious suicidal intent...'
Q: Which is excluded from the lecture's definition of DSH? = Overdose/self-poisoning | Cutting | Burning | Head-banging | Severe scratching
> DSH does not include piercing/tattooing, overdose/self-poisoning, substance abuse, eating disorders, LD self-injury, or self-harm with suicidal intent.
Q: After DSH, the UK figure quoted is that as many as how many eventually kill themselves? = 4 or 5 in 10 | 1 in 100 | 1 in 20 | 9 in 10 | None
> '...as high as 4 or 5 in ten people with the disorder end up succeeding in killing themselves (UK).'
Q: Which predicts repeat DSH? = Presence of personality disorder features | Being married | High social class | Employment | No alcohol use
> Predictors: previous episodes, personality disorder, unemployment, alcoholism, unmarried, violence, criminal record, lowest social class.
Q: Which feature indicates suicidal intent? = Writing a suicide note | Telling a friend immediately | Self-harm in a crowded room | Seeking help straight away | Minor scratch
> Intent: isolation, timing, precautions, suicide note, anticipatory acts, dangerous method.
Q: The C-SSRS used to assess the seriousness of suicidal intent has: = 18 items in 4 sections | 5 items in 1 section | 10 items in 2 sections | 30 items in 6 sections | 100 items
> 'Columbia-Suicide severity rating scale (C-SSRS)... (18 items in 4 section).'
Q: The FIRST element of the Brown and Stanley safety plan is: = Warning signs suggesting a crisis may be developing | Contacting professionals | Making the environment safe | Calling the police | Admission
> Order: warning signs → internal coping → people/settings for distraction → people to ask for help → professionals → safe environment.
Q: 'Internal coping strategies' in a safety plan are things the patient can do: = Without contacting another person | With a psychiatrist | Only in hospital | Only with medication | With the police
> 'Internal coping strategies — (things they can do to take mind off their problems) without contacting another person.'

### Suicide
> - > 720,000 deaths a year; 3rd leading cause of death at 15–19; 73% in LMICs (WHO).
> - Previous attempt ＝ the most important risk factor. 4 in 5 saw a doctor in the previous 2 weeks.
> - Nigeria: still criminalised, under-reported; Asuni 1962 17.3/100,000; World Bank 2021 4.99/100,000; South-West highest, North-East lowest (Oyedeji 2021).
> - Females attempt more; males complete more.
> - SAD PERSONS: Sex (male), Age, Depression, Previous attempt, Ethanol, Rational thinking loss, Social support lacking, No spouse, Sickness.
> - High-risk symptoms: command hallucinations, depression with hopelessness.
Q: According to WHO, how many people die by suicide each year? = More than 720,000 | About 72,000 | About 7 million | About 1,000 | About 70 million
> '>720,000 die by suicide/year.'
Q: Suicide is the leading cause of death in which rank among 15–19-year-olds? = 3rd | 1st | 2nd | 5th | 10th
> 'Suicide — 3rd leading cause of death among 15–19-year-olds.'
Q: The most important risk factor for suicide is: = A previous suicide attempt | Male sex | Unemployment | Old age | Living alone
> 'Previous suicide attempt — Most important risk factor.'
Q: About how many people who die by suicide saw their doctor in the preceding 2 weeks? = 4 in 5 | 1 in 10 | 1 in 4 | 1 in 2 | All
> 'About 4 in 5 have seen their doctor within the preceding 2-weeks before the event (Be warned).'
Q: Asuni (1962) reported a Nigerian suicide rate of: = 17.3/100,000 | 0.27/100,000 | 4.99/100,000 | 6.9/100,000 | 50/100,000
> 'Rate: 17.3/100,000 in Nigeria (Asuni 1962).' World Bank 2021: 4.99.
Q: In Oyedeji et al. (2021), the Nigerian region with the highest completed suicide rate was: = South-West | North-East | North-West | South-South | South-East
> South-West 0.27, NC 0.22, SE 0.21, SS 0.19, NW 0.07, NE 0.04 per 100,000.
Q: Regarding sex differences in suicide: = Women attempt more but more men succeed | Men attempt more and complete more | No difference | Women complete more | Only men attempt
> 'Sex (females — more attempts, but more male succeed).'
Q: In SAD PERSONS, the 'R' stands for: = Rational thinking loss (psychosis) | Religion | Recent loss | Race | Rural residence
> R — Rational thinking loss (psychosis). E — Ethanol; N — No spouse; S — Sickness.
Q: What percentage of global suicides occur in LMICs? = 73% | 23% | 50% | 90% | 99%
> '73% of global suicide occur in LMIC.'
Q: Which is the strongest single predictor of eventual suicide after self-harm? = High suicidal intent at the time of the act | Female sex | Young age | Married status | Living with family
> High intent (and repetition, male sex, older age, mental illness) predict completed suicide.

### Homicidal ideation
> - The desire to kill another person with a mental plan to do it.
> - Risk: young male, past violence, conduct problems; victim usually someone close; weapons; schizophrenia, SUDs, antisocial PD; command hallucinations.
> - Tarasoff v Regents of the University of California (1976): a duty to protect people at risk.
> - Action: ask directly; inform police if serious; warn potential victims; admit (involuntarily if needed); treat the illness.
Q: The legal ruling requiring clinicians to protect people at risk from a patient with homicidal intent is: = Tarasoff v Regents of the University of California (1976) | McNaughton (1843) | Bolam (1957) | Gillick (1985) | Montgomery (2015)
> Tarasoff (1976) — the duty to protect/warn.
Q: In homicide, the victim is most often: = Somebody close to the perpetrator, e.g. a family member | A stranger | A police officer | A doctor | A child unknown to them
> 'Victim: Often somebody close to perpetrator e.g. family member or close associate.'
Q: Which is a management precaution for a patient with serious homicidal intent? = Make efforts to warn potential victims | Discharge home | Ignore it | Prescribe sleeping tablets only | Tell no one
> Inform police if serious; warn potential victims (Tarasoff); inpatient/involuntary admission; treat the illness.
Q: In Nigeria, emergency involuntary admission is now governed by: = The National Mental Health Act 2021 | The Lunacy Act 1958 only | The Penal Code only | No law | The Child Rights Act
> The Mental Health Act 2021 replaced the old Lunacy Act framework.

### Delirium in the emergency setting
> - Ask: fluctuating consciousness? Abnormal vitals? Infection? Abnormal labs? Beware lucid intervals and sundowning.
> - Treat the cause, plus: consistent minimal staff, family at the bedside, clocks and calendars, daylight, daytime activity, less noise.
> - Low-dose drugs: oral quetiapine/risperidone; IM olanzapine/chlorpromazine; IV haloperidol or lorazepam.
Q: Which environmental measure helps a delirious patient? = Family at the bedside and clocks and calendars | Frequent staff changes | Keeping the room dark all day | Loud background music | Encouraging daytime sleep
> Consistent staff, family at bedside, clocks/calendars, daylight, daytime activity, less noise.
Q: Which IV drugs are listed for delirium? = Haloperidol or lorazepam | Morphine | Phenytoin | Insulin | Diazepam only
> Oral quetiapine/risperidone; IM olanzapine/chlorpromazine; IV haloperidol or lorazepam (low doses).
Q: Worsening of confusion in the evening in delirium is called: = Sundowning | Lucid interval | Twilight state | Fugue | Clouding
> '...be aware of lucid interval, sundowning effect...'
Q: In delirium tremens, the drug of choice is: = A benzodiazepine (e.g. chlordiazepoxide or lorazepam) plus parenteral thiamine | Haloperidol alone | Naltrexone | Disulfiram | Acamprosate
> Alcohol withdrawal delirium: benzodiazepines plus parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) to prevent Wernicke's.

### Lithium toxicity
> - Monovalent, like sodium; narrow therapeutic index.
> - Half-life 12–27 h (≈ 36 h in the elderly); target 0.7–1.2 mEq/L; toxic ≥ 1.5 mEq/L; take the level after an overnight fast.
> - Types: acute (lithium-naive), acute-on-chronic, chronic (therapeutic).
> - Mild: weakness, fine tremor, mild confusion. Severe: coarse tremor, fasciculation, choreoathetosis, hyperreflexia, clonus, opisthotonos, seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse.
> - Treat: supportive, IV fluids, whole-bowel irrigation, avoid hypernatraemia, Kayexalate, lithium levels every 4 h, haemodialysis if severe.
Q: Lithium toxicity occurs at a serum level of: = 1.5 mEq/L or more | 0.4 mEq/L | 0.7 mEq/L | 1.0 mEq/L | 5 mEq/L only
> 'Desired serum levels of 0.7–1.2 mEq/L. Toxicity level is 1.5 mEq/L or more.'
Q: In the elderly, the half-life of lithium increases to about: = 36 hours | 6 hours | 12 hours | 24 hours | 72 hours
> 'Half-life increases to approximately 36 hours in elderly.'
Q: Progressive lithium toxicity in a patient on long-term lithium therapy is called: = Chronic (therapeutic) poisoning | Acute poisoning | Acute-on-chronic poisoning | Idiosyncratic | Allergic
> Chronic or therapeutic poisoning. Acute ＝ lithium-naive; acute-on-chronic ＝ overdose while on lithium.
Q: Which is a feature of severe lithium toxicity? = Opisthotonos and seizures | Fine resting tremor only | Mild weakness | Polyuria only | Weight gain
> Severe: severe tremor, fasciculation, choreoathetosis, hyperreflexia, clonus, opisthotonos, stupor, seizures, coma.
Q: During treatment of lithium toxicity, serum lithium is monitored: = Every 4 hours | Once only | Daily | Weekly | Not at all
> 'Serial serum lithium monitoring 4 hourly — declining tendency monitoring.'
Q: Renal dialysis in lithium toxicity is indicated: = In severe cases | In all cases | Never | Only in children | Only if level < 1.0
> 'Renal dialysis indicated in severe cases.'
Q: Activated charcoal in lithium overdose: = Does not bind lithium | Is the treatment of choice | Increases lithium excretion tenfold | Is contraindicated in all overdoses | Replaces dialysis
> Charcoal doesn't bind lithium; whole-bowel irrigation, fluids and dialysis are used.

### Serotonin syndrome, NMS and EPSE
> - Serotonin syndrome: excess synaptic 5-HT, especially with MAOIs; triad altered mental state + neuromuscular hyperactivity + autonomic instability. Causes: SSRIs, SNRIs, trazodone, TCAs, lithium, tramadol/codeine/fentanyl, cocaine/amphetamine/ecstasy, ginseng, nutmeg, cannabinoids. Stop the drug, fluids, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine, dantrolene for intractable hyperthermia.
> - NMS: 0.02% on antipsychotics; rigidity, autonomic dysfunction, fever, altered consciousness; raised CPK, metabolic acidosis, leucocytosis. Stop the drug, hydrate, cool; dopamine agonists or ECT. Don't confuse with catatonia.
> - Akathisia 5–36% (beta-blockers); acute dystonia 25–40%, within 48 hours.
Q: Serotonin syndrome occurs more commonly with drug interactions, especially with: = Monoamine oxidase inhibitors | Antacids | Antihistamines | Statins | Insulin
> '...inadvertent drug interaction especially with monoamine oxidase inhibitors.'
Q: Which pain medication is listed as a cause of serotonin syndrome? = Tramadol | Paracetamol | Aspirin | Ibuprofen | Diclofenac
> Opioids: codeine, fentanyl, tramadol.
Q: Which herbal supplements are listed as possible causes of serotonin syndrome? = Ginseng and nutmeg | Garlic and ginger | Vitamin C and zinc | Aloe and honey | Moringa and bitter leaf
> 'Herbal supplements: e.g. ginseng, nutmeg.'
Q: Which drug is used for hyperthermia in serotonin syndrome that is difficult to control? = Dantrolene | Paracetamol | Aspirin | Haloperidol | Lithium
> 'Dantrolene — for hyperthermia that is difficult to control.' Cyproheptadine is the 5-HT antagonist.
Q: NMS occurs in about what percentage of patients on antipsychotics (per the lecture)? = 0.02% | 2% | 10% | 25% | 40%
> 'Occur in 0.02% of patient on antipsychotics.'
Q: Which laboratory finding is a marker of NMS? = Elevated CPK (rhabdomyolysis) | Low CPK | Low white cell count | Metabolic alkalosis | High lithium
> Markers: elevated CPK, metabolic acidosis, leucocytosis.
Q: The lecture warns NMS may be confused with: = Catatonia | Mania | Panic attack | Dementia | Malingering
> 'NMS may be confused with catatonia — Oversight may be fatal.'
Q: Acute dystonia from antipsychotics usually begins within: = 48 hours of starting | 2 weeks | 3 months | 1 year | 5 years
> '...begins within 48 hrs of commencing the medication.' Occurs in 25–40%.
Q: Which may help akathisia? = Beta-blockers | Increasing the antipsychotic dose | Caffeine | Stimulants | Antihistamine eye drops
> 'Stop or reduce dose of offending medication, beta-blockers may be helpful.'
Q: Which clinical sign best distinguishes serotonin syndrome from NMS? = Clonus and hyperreflexia (vs lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia in NMS) | Fever | Confusion | Tachycardia | Sweating
> Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, rapid onset. NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, slower onset.

### Agitation, stupor, overdose and disasters
> - Agitation: don't restrain or medicate immediately — de-escalate first, then limit-setting. Restraint types: mechanical/physical (Pinel), chemical, environmental. Never disarm an armed patient yourself.
> - Stupor: almost entirely unresponsive except to intense (painful) stimuli; organic or functional causes.
> - Overdose: children and elderly most at risk; prevent with disposal of old drugs, no sharing, dosette boxes; common illicit overdose is opioids.
> - Disaster psychiatry: with or without warning; help new cases and those with pre-existing illness (prevent relapse).
> - Medico-legal: document everything; involuntary admission, confidentiality, duty to warn.
Q: Faced with an agitated patient, the FIRST step is: = De-escalation | Immediate physical restraint | Immediate IM medication | Seclusion | Call the family to leave
> 'DO NOT restrain or medicate patient immediately. DE-ESCALATION.'
Q: A violent patient is holding a weapon. You should: = Call security personnel or police — don't attempt to disarm | Disarm them yourself | Give oral lorazepam | Leave them alone in the ED | Restrain them alone
> 'Do not attempt to physically disarm a violent patient with weapon (security personnel or police needed).'
Q: A Pinel restraint is an example of: = Mechanical/physical restraint | Chemical restraint | Environmental restraint | Verbal de-escalation | Seclusion
> 'Mechanical/physical restraints (e.g. Pinel restraint).'
Q: In stupor, the person responds only to: = Intense stimuli such as pain | Normal conversation | Written questions | Music | Bright light only
> '...almost entirely unresponsive and responds only to intense stimuli such as pain.'
Q: Which group is most at risk of medication overdose, according to the lecture? = Children and the elderly | Young adults | Athletes | Pregnant women only | Health workers
> 'Children/Elderly more at risk.'
Q: Which is a preventive measure against medication overdose? = Using dosette boxes | Sharing medicines with family | Keeping expired medicines | Buying in bulk | Hiding medicines in food
> Dispose of unwanted/expired medicines, don't share, dosette boxes.
Q: In disaster psychiatry, people with pre-existing mental illness need help mainly to: = Reduce relapse or new morbidity | Claim compensation | Leave the area | Testify in court | Avoid treatment
> 'Those with pre-existing mental illness will also need help to reduce relapse or development of new morbidity.'
Q: Which is not listed as a key legal area in emergency psychiatry? = Patent law | Involuntary patients | Confidentiality | Duty to warn | Documentation of decision-making
> Legal areas: involuntary patients, confidentiality, duty to warn — and document everything.
Q: For rapid tranquillisation when oral medication is refused, a common NICE option is: = IM lorazepam, or IM haloperidol with IM promethazine | IV diazepam bolus | IM chlorpromazine high dose | Oral lithium | IV phenytoin
> NICE: IM lorazepam, or IM haloperidol + IM promethazine (ECG first for haloperidol).

### OSCE: Serotonin syndrome and management
> Emergency station. Task: Recognise serotonin toxicity, identify the culprit combination, assess severity and initiate urgent management.
> Patient: “Bello”, 40, takes sertraline; tramadol was added yesterday. He is agitated, sweaty, febrile, tachycardic, has diarrhoea, tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible ankle clonus.
> - Book: stop all medicines; manage jointly with other specialists; cooling blankets for pyrexia; clonazepam for myoclonus; nifedipine for hypertension; ventilation for respiratory insufficiency; anticonvulsants for seizures.
> - Book also lists IM chlorpromazine for pyrexia. Safer modern wording: avoid chlorpromazine and other antipsychotics unless toxicology advises, because of hypotension, a lowered seizure threshold and confusion with NMS. Use benzodiazepines and active cooling.
> - Treat hypertension cautiously with short-acting agents under monitoring; the autonomic picture can swing quickly to hypotension.
> Critical fail: Continuing the offending medicines, using antipyretics as the main cooling strategy, or overlooking severe hyperthermia/status.

I would stop serotonergic drugs, call for senior/emergency help and assess airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, glucose and… = Immediate approach | Focused medication history | Recognise the triad | Book’s switching questions | Examine deliberately | Management
> What to say: “This may be an acute toxic syndrome. I would stop serotonergic drugs, call for senior/emergency help and assess airway, breathing, circulation, temperature, glucose and consciousness while monitoring vital signs.”

### OSCE: Psychological first aid
> Communication station. Task: Explain psychological first aid to a group of students (or demonstrate it with a survivor of a disaster).
> - FNPH RAPID: Rapport, Assessment, Prioritisation, Intervention, Disposition.
> - Abdulhakeem C²LIP F²ISHR²: Comfort/consolation, Coping styles, Link with help, Identify those needing help (triage), Protect, Facilitate a sense of control, Food, Immediate physical care, Share the experience (don’t force), Social support, Help reunite, Refer, Return to normal functioning.
> - WHO principle: Look, Listen, Link. Goals: safety, calm, connectedness, self-efficacy, hope.
> Critical fail: Forcing survivors to recount the trauma (psychological debriefing), or neglecting safety and basic needs.
L: Psychological first aid: the phases of the station, in order = Define it | Safety first | Rapport (R) | Assess (A) | Prioritise (P) | Intervene (I) | Disposition (D)
Q: Psychological first aid. Which phase is this line from? “Psychological first aid is a humane, supportive response to someone exposed to a traumatic event. It aims to reduce distress and support short- and long-term adaptive… = Define it | Safety first | Rapport (R) | Assess (A) | Prioritise (P) | Intervene (I) | Disposition (D)
> What to say: “Psychological first aid is a humane, supportive response to someone exposed to a traumatic event. It aims to reduce distress and support short- and long-term adaptive functioning and coping. It can be given by trained people: mental-health professionals, emergency responders, firefighters, volunteers and humanitarian workers.”
> Examiner checks: Clear definition; who delivers it; not a clinical treatment.
