### Bonus drill: OSCE / Emergency: Clozapine Neutropenia & Red Alert Protocol
> CANDIDATE BRIEF: Week 8 of Clozapine therapy. The patient presents to casualty with a temperature of 38.6°C, shivering, and a sore throat. Urgent FBC reveals: WBC 2.2 × 10⁹/L, Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) 850/mm³.
> CRITICAL FAIL: Reducing the clozapine dose instead of immediately stopping it; or discharging the patient with oral antipyretics.
L: Clozapine Red Alert Emergency Sequence = 1. Immediately cease Clozapine permanently (do not taper or reduce dose) | 2. Immediate hospital admission under reverse barrier nursing isolation | 3. Urgent blood, throat and urine cultures followed by empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics | 4. Daily FBC with differential and urgent Haematology consult for G-CSF (filgrastim) | 5. Monitor vital signs for septic shock; never re-challenge clozapine without expert multidisciplinary approval ~~ Taper clozapine slowly over 2 weeks to avoid withdrawal :: In severe neutropenia (ANC < 1000) or agranulocytosis, immediate cessation is mandatory | Prescribe oral paracetamol and send patient home :: Neutropenic fever is a medical emergency with high mortality requiring inpatient admission | Re-challenge clozapine once fever clears :: Re-challenging after a Red Alert agranulocytosis carries fatal recurrence risk
S: Life-Threatening Clozapine Emergencies requiring Immediate Intervention = Agranulocytosis / Severe Neutropenic Sepsis (ANC < 1000) | Acute Myocarditis (persistent resting tachycardia, chest pain, raised troponin/CRP in first 2 months) | Paralytic Ileus / Severe Gastrointestinal Hypomotility (constipation, vomiting, abdominal distension) | Dose-related generalized tonic-clonic seizures (especially at doses >600 mg/day) | Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability) ~~ Mild transient hypersalivation :: A common benign anticholinergic/adrenergic side effect treated with hyoscine | Benign transient tachycardia without chest pain or troponin rise :: Common during titration; managed with slow titration or a beta-blocker | Mild sedation during evening dosing :: Common histaminic effect managed by dosing adjustments
> Severe constipation from clozapine causes paralytic ileus, bowel necrosis, and toxic megacolon, which has caused more deaths in some national registries than agranulocytosis! Always prescribe laxatives proactively.
Q: Examiner Viva: Under what circumstance may Clozapine be re-challenged after a Red Alert? = Never routinely; only in exceptional treatment-refractory cases under a specialist hematology/psychiatry panel with G-CSF support | As soon as the neutrophil count returns above 2000 :: Spontaneous recovery does not remove the risk of lethal recurrence upon re-exposure | Whenever the patient's psychosis worsens :: Worsening psychosis must be managed with alternative strategies, not unmonitored clozapine re-exposure | If the patient switches from smoking cigarettes to non-smoking :: Smoking affects CYP1A2 metabolism, but has no relation to autoimmune agranulocytosis
> Agranulocytosis re-challenge carries a mortality rate of up to 30%. Routine re-challenge is contraindicated. Formal specialist registries and haematology co-management with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) are mandatory for rare off-label exceptions.

### Bonus drill: Antipsychotic emergencies
> Three reactions you must not miss:
> - NMS: dopamine blockade, slow onset over days. Lead-pipe rigidity, high fever, autonomic instability, confusion, very high CK.
> - Serotonin syndrome: serotonin excess, fast onset within 24 hours. Clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, agitation, diarrhoea, dilated pupils.
> - EPS timeline: acute dystonia (hours to days), akathisia (days to weeks), parkinsonism (weeks), tardive dyskinesia (months to years).
> Clozapine: agranulocytosis, myocarditis (first 2 months), dose-related seizures, constipation and ileus, hypersalivation, metabolic syndrome.
L: NMS features (FEVER) = Fever | Encephalopathy | Vital signs unstable | Elevated CK (enzymes) | Rigidity ~~ Clonus :: Clonus points to serotonin syndrome | Hyperreflexia :: Hyperreflexia points to serotonin syndrome | Diarrhoea :: Diarrhoea points to serotonin syndrome
> FEVER: Fever, Encephalopathy (confusion), Vitals unstable (BP, pulse, sweating), Elevated enzymes (CK, white cells), Rigidity (lead-pipe).
> Risk factors: high-potency or depot antipsychotics, rapid dose increases, dehydration, agitation.
Q: Lab marker most associated with NMS = Raised creatine kinase | Raised troponin :: Troponin points to myocarditis (e.g. clozapine) | Raised amylase :: That points to pancreatitis (e.g. valproate) | Low white cell count :: NMS usually RAISES the white cell count
> CK can be in the thousands from muscle breakdown, which risks acute kidney injury. Also check white cells, U&E, LFTs and myoglobinuria.
S: Serotonin syndrome triad = Altered mental state | Autonomic hyperactivity | Neuromuscular abnormality (clonus, hyperreflexia) ~~ Lead-pipe rigidity :: That is typical of NMS | Bradycardia :: Serotonin syndrome causes tachycardia | Onset over days to weeks :: That slow onset fits NMS
> Hunter criteria centre on clonus (spontaneous, inducible or ocular) in someone taking a serotonergic drug.
Q: Clonus and hyperreflexia point to = Serotonin syndrome | NMS :: NMS has lead-pipe rigidity, slow onset and reduced reflexes | Anticholinergic toxicity :: Hot, dry, flushed, delirious, with large pupils, but no clonus | Malignant hyperthermia :: Triggered by anaesthetic agents, with rigidity rather than clonus
> Quick differentiator: serotonin syndrome is fast, hyperkinetic and "jumpy" (clonus). NMS is slow, rigid and "stiff".
Q: Onset of serotonin syndrome is usually = Within 24 hours of the drug change | Within 1 week of the drug change :: Usually much faster: within 24 hours, often within hours | Over days to weeks :: That slower onset fits NMS | Only after an overdose :: It can occur at normal doses, especially with drug combinations
> Classic triggers: SSRI plus tramadol, MAOI plus SSRI, linezolid, triptans, St John's wort.
L: Serotonin syndrome management = Stop the serotonergic drugs | Supportive care: IV fluids and cooling | Benzodiazepines for agitation | Cyproheptadine if moderate to severe | ICU care if severe hyperthermia ~~ Increase the SSRI :: The SSRI is the cause; stop it | Physical restraint :: Restraint worsens hyperthermia and acidosis | Add another serotonergic drug :: That makes it worse
> Most mild cases settle within 24 hours of stopping the drug.
Q: Most serious blood risk with clozapine = Agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia) | Thrombocytopenia :: Not the key clozapine risk | Eosinophilia :: Eosinophilia can occur but is usually benign | Aplastic anaemia :: That is a rare risk of carbamazepine
> The risk is highest in the first 18 weeks, which is why monitoring starts weekly. Any sore throat or fever needs an urgent FBC.
Q: Clozapine FBC monitoring (UK schedule) = Weekly for 18 weeks, fortnightly to 1 year, then monthly | Weekly for 6 weeks, fortnightly to 1 year, then monthly :: Weekly lasts 18 weeks | Weekly for 18 weeks, then monthly :: Fortnightly checks continue to 1 year before going monthly | Fortnightly for 18 weeks, then monthly :: The first 18 weeks are WEEKLY
> Results follow a traffic-light system (green, amber, red). A red result means stop clozapine.
Q: Clozapine myocarditis risk is highest = In the first 2 months | In the first 6 months :: Most cases are in the first 2 months | After the first year :: Myocarditis is an early complication | Only above 600 mg/day :: It is not mainly dose-related
> Monitor pulse, temperature, BP, troponin and CRP in the early weeks. Persistent tachycardia, fever, chest pain or breathlessness means stop and assess.
S: Serious clozapine adverse effects = Agranulocytosis | Myocarditis or cardiomyopathy | Seizures | Severe constipation (ileus) | Hypersalivation | Metabolic syndrome ~~ Raised prolactin :: Clozapine is prolactin-sparing | Tardive dyskinesia :: Clozapine has a very low risk | Hypothyroidism :: That is linked to lithium
> Constipation from clozapine can be fatal (ileus), so always ask about bowels and prescribe laxatives early.
L: Order of onset of extrapyramidal side effects = Acute dystonia (hours to days) | Akathisia (days to weeks) | Parkinsonism (weeks) | Tardive dyskinesia (months to years) ~~ NMS (always first) :: NMS is not an EPS stage; it is a separate emergency | Serotonin syndrome :: Not an antipsychotic EPS | Chorea in Huntington's :: Not drug-induced
> Rule of 4s: about 4 hours for acute dystonia, 4 days for akathisia, 4 weeks for parkinsonism, 4 months for tardive dyskinesia.
Q: Treatment of acute dystonia = IM or IV anticholinergic (e.g. procyclidine, biperiden) | IM benzodiazepine first line :: An anticholinergic is first line | Oral propranolol :: Propranolol is used for akathisia | Stop the antipsychotic and wait for it to pass :: Acute dystonia is distressing and can affect the airway; treat it promptly
> Acute dystonia includes oculogyric crisis, torticollis and laryngeal dystonia (an airway emergency). It is commoner in young men on high-potency drugs.
L: Acute dystonia management = Recognise the dystonia and reassure | IM or IV anticholinergic (e.g. procyclidine) | Repeat the dose if needed | Short oral anticholinergic course | Review the antipsychotic dose or choice ~~ Give more haloperidol :: The antipsychotic caused it | Propranolol first :: Propranolol is for akathisia | Wait and watch only :: It is distressing and can affect the airway; treat it
> IM or IV anticholinergics usually work within minutes.
Q: First steps for akathisia = Reduce the antipsychotic dose; consider propranolol | Add procyclidine as first line :: Anticholinergics help little in akathisia | Increase the antipsychotic dose :: That makes akathisia worse | Add a second antipsychotic :: That adds to the problem
> Akathisia (inner restlessness, pacing) is often mistaken for agitation or psychosis and wrongly treated with more antipsychotic. It is linked to suicide risk.
Q: Which drug class worsens tardive dyskinesia? = Anticholinergics (e.g. procyclidine) | VMAT2 inhibitors (e.g. valbenazine) :: These TREAT tardive dyskinesia | Clozapine :: Clozapine has a very low risk and may help | Beta blockers :: Not known to worsen it
> Management of TD: review the need for antipsychotics, consider clozapine or quetiapine, stop anticholinergics, and consider a VMAT2 inhibitor.

### Bonus drill: Emergency protocols
> Emergencies are examined as sequences. The same principles run through all of them: safety first, the least restrictive option, treat the medical cause, monitor, document, and debrief.
L: Rapid tranquillisation steps = Verbal de-escalation | Offer oral medication | IM medication (e.g. lorazepam, or haloperidol with promethazine) | Monitor vital signs afterwards | Debrief patient and staff ~~ Physical restraint first :: Use the least restrictive option first | Electroconvulsive therapy :: Not part of rapid tranquillisation | IV haloperidol first :: Start with de-escalation, then oral, then IM
> If there is no ECG, or there is cardiac disease or a long QT, use IM lorazepam rather than haloperidol.
Q: Vital signs after IM rapid tranquillisation = At least hourly until no concerns; every 15 minutes if high dose, asleep or physically unwell | Every 15 minutes for the first hour, then stop if calm :: Continue at least hourly until there are no concerns | Hourly for the first hour only :: Monitoring continues until there are no concerns | Every 4 hours :: Too infrequent
> Monitor pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and level of consciousness. A sleeping patient needs closer, not looser, observation.
Q: Avoid haloperidol for rapid tranquillisation when = There is no ECG, or there is cardiac disease or a prolonged QT | The patient is very agitated :: Agitation is the indication | The patient has taken antipsychotics before :: Previous antipsychotic exposure makes haloperidol MORE suitable | The patient has asthma :: Not a contraindication to haloperidol
> Haloperidol prolongs QT. Promethazine is added to reduce dystonia and add sedation.
> NICE also advises IM lorazepam if there is not enough information to choose, or if the person has never taken an antipsychotic.
Q: Drug to reverse benzodiazepine respiratory depression = Flumazenil | Naloxone :: Naloxone reverses opioids | Procyclidine :: Procyclidine treats acute dystonia | Atropine :: Atropine treats bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning
> Flumazenil can trigger seizures in people dependent on benzodiazepines or after mixed overdoses. Give it carefully, with airway support first.
L: NMS management = Stop the antipsychotic | Supportive care: cooling and IV fluids | Monitor CK, renal function and vital signs | Transfer to medical or ICU care | Consider benzodiazepine, bromocriptine or dantrolene | Wait at least 2 weeks before a cautious rechallenge ~~ Increase the antipsychotic dose :: The antipsychotic is the cause; stop it | Add a second antipsychotic :: Makes NMS worse | Give IM haloperidol :: An antipsychotic would worsen NMS
> On rechallenge, use a low-potency or atypical drug, start low, go slow, and monitor temperature and CK.
L: Alcohol detox essentials = Assess severity (CIWA-Ar) | Give thiamine before glucose | Benzodiazepine reducing regimen (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) | Watch for seizures and delirium | Plan relapse prevention ~~ Give glucose before thiamine :: Wrong order; thiamine first to avoid Wernicke's | Start disulfiram during acute withdrawal :: Disulfiram is for relapse prevention after detox, never during withdrawal | Stop all fluids :: No role
> Relapse prevention options: acamprosate (reduces craving), naltrexone (reduces the reward), disulfiram (aversive). Add psychosocial support and AA.
Q: Why give thiamine before glucose? = To avoid precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy | To prevent refeeding syndrome :: Thiamine is part of refeeding care, but the reason here is Wernicke's | To prevent hypoglycaemia :: Glucose prevents hypoglycaemia; thiamine is about Wernicke's | To prevent Korsakoff syndrome only :: It prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy, which can then lead to Korsakoff's
> Glucose metabolism uses up thiamine. In a depleted drinker, glucose alone can tip them into Wernicke's.
L: Lithium toxicity management = Stop lithium | Check lithium level, U&E and ECG | IV fluids and correct electrolytes | Consider haemodialysis if severe ~~ Give NSAIDs for pain :: NSAIDs RAISE lithium levels | Add a thiazide diuretic :: Thiazides RAISE lithium levels | Give the next lithium dose :: Stop lithium first
> Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium. Consider haemodialysis for severe toxicity, a very high level, or renal failure.
L: ECT procedure = Informed consent | Pre-ECT work-up (examination, bloods, ECG, anaesthetic review) | Nil by mouth | General anaesthetic and muscle relaxant | Deliver the electrical stimulus | Monitor the seizure (EEG and motor) | Recovery observation ~~ Give lithium before ECT :: Lithium with ECT raises the risk of prolonged confusion | Benzodiazepine just before :: Raises the seizure threshold | Skip consent :: Consent (or the legal process) is always required
> Indications: severe depression (especially psychotic, or with refusal of food and fluids), catatonia, treatment-resistant mania.
> Common side effects: headache, muscle aches, transient confusion and memory impairment (mostly around the treatment period).
Q: Commonest cognitive side effect of ECT = Short-term memory impairment around the treatment period | Permanent loss of all memories from before ECT :: Not typical; effects are mostly around the treatment period | Impaired procedural memory (skills) :: Procedural memory is usually preserved | Lasting aphasia :: Not an ECT effect
> Right unilateral electrode placement causes less memory impairment than bilateral, but may be slightly less effective.

## U-Block | Substance use disorders
> Substance use disorders. Source: PPT Part 1 Revision course.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Epidemiology terms
> - Incidence ＝ new cases ÷ population at risk over a period — reflects risk.
> - Prevalence ＝ all existing cases at a point (point prevalence) or over a period ÷ total population — reflects burden; depends on incidence × duration (P ≈ I × D). Falls with recovery or death.
> - Drug use prevalence is shaped by culture and social norms, legal controls, availability and price, individual stress and neurobiological vulnerability.
Q: According to the lecture, incidence is taken to represent: = The risk of a disease | The public health burden | Mortality | Duration | Recovery
> 'Incidence: No of new cases/at-risk population over a given period. It is taken to represent the risk of a disease.'
Q: Prevalence takes into account incidence and: = Duration of the disease | Cost | Age only | Gender only | Treatment
> 'It takes into account both incidence and duration of the disease… affected by degree of recovery and death… an indicator of the public health burden.'
Q: Which is NOT listed as affecting the prevalence of drug intake? = Blood group | Cultural patterns and norms | Legal requirements and prohibitions | Environmental and social factors | Neurobiological risk factors
> Influences: individual stress, cultural patterns/norms, legal requirements, environmental/social factors, neurobiological risk factors.

### Drug use in Nigeria — National Drug Use Survey (UNODC/NBS, 2018; data 2017), ages 15–64
> - Past-year drug use: 14.4% (~14.3 million) — about 3× the global average (~5.5%).
> - Men 21.8% vs women 7.0% — but 1 in 4 users is a woman.
> - Cannabis 10.8% (~10.6 million) — the most used drug.
> - Pharmaceutical opioids (tramadol, codeine, morphine) 4.7% (~4.6 million) — the second; heroin only ~0.1%. Codeine cough syrup and tramadol misuse are a Nigerian hallmark (codeine syrup banned for import 2018).
> - High-risk drug use ~0.4% (~376,000); people who inject drugs ~80,000.
> - Highest prevalence in the South-West and South-South; most users first use in adolescence/early 20s.
Q: The national annual prevalence of any drug use in Nigeria (2017) was: = 14.4% | 4.7% | 10.8% | 21.8% | 30%
> 'Any drug use — men 21.8, women 7.0, national 14.4 (14,300,000).'
Q: The most commonly used drug in Nigeria (2017) was: = Cannabis | Pharmaceutical opioids | Cough syrups | Cocaine | Tranquilisers
> Cannabis 10.8% (≈ 10.6 million), then pharmaceutical opioids 4.7%, cough syrups 2.4%.
Q: Which drug category had a similar prevalence in women and men in the Nigerian data? = Cough syrups | Cannabis | Heroin | Cocaine | Amphetamines
> Cough syrups — men 2.3%, women 2.5% — unlike cannabis (men 18.8%, women 2.6%).
Q: The estimated number of people who inject drugs in Nigeria (2017) was about: = 80,000 | 8,000 | 376,000 | 800,000 | 3 million
> 'People who inject drugs — national 0.08% (80,000).' High-risk drug use ≈ 376,000.

### ICD-11 substance use disorders (6C40–6C4H; behaviours 6C50–6C51)
> - Episode of harmful psychoactive substance use — a single episode causing harm.
> - Harmful pattern of use — repeated use causing damage to physical or mental health, or harm to others' health (new in ICD-11), over ≥ 12 months (episodic) or ≥ 1 month (continuous).
> - Substance dependence — ≥ 2 of 3 central features, over ≥ 12 months (or ≥ 1 month if use is continuous/daily):
> 1. impaired control over use (onset, amount, stopping);
> 2. increasing precedence of use over other interests and responsibilities, continuing despite harm;
> 3. physiological features — tolerance, withdrawal, or repeated use to prevent/relieve withdrawal.
> - Plus substance-induced states: intoxication, withdrawal, delirium, psychotic disorder, mood, anxiety, OCD-related and impulse-control disorders, and amnestic disorder/dementia.
> - Hazardous substance use (QE10) — risky use without harm yet (not a mental disorder).
> - DSM-5 differs: a single "substance use disorder" with 11 criteria, severity by count (2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, ≥ 6 severe); no separate abuse/dependence.
Q: ICD-11 substance dependence requires at least how many of its three central features? = Two | One | Three | Four of six | Six of eleven
> ≥ 2 of 3: impaired control; increasing precedence; physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal).
Q: Which is new in ICD-11's 'harmful pattern of use'? = It includes harm to others' health | It requires dependence | It requires withdrawal | Only alcohol | Requires legal problems
> Harm to other people's health now counts.

### New psychoactive substances (NPS)
> - UNODC definition: substances of abuse not controlled by the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs or the 1971 Convention on Psychotropic Substances, but posing a public health threat. "New" ＝ newly available, not newly invented. > 600 reported worldwide.
> - Six groups:
> - synthetic cannabinoids ("spice", "K2", Yucatan fire) — full CB1 agonists, much more psychosis, seizures, agitation than cannabis;
> - synthetic cathinones ("bath salts", mephedrone) — stimulants;
> - ketamine and other dissociatives;
> - phenethylamines (PMMA — an ecstasy substitute, dangerous hyperthermia);
> - piperazines (BZP, TFMPP);
> - plant-based — khat (cathinone), kratom, Salvia divinorum.
> - Sold online and in "head shops"; effects and toxicity often unknown; standard urine drug screens miss most of them.
Q: Per UNODC (2017), new psychoactive substances are those not controlled by: = The 1961 Single Convention and the 1971 Convention on Psychotropic Substances | Nigerian law only | The WHO essential medicines list | The FDA | Any law at all
> '…not controlled by the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs or the 1971 Convention on Psychotropic Substances, but which may pose a public health threat.'
Q: 'Bath salts' belong to which NPS category? = Synthetic cathinones | Synthetic cannabinoids | Piperazines | Phenethylamines | Plant-based substances
> 'Synthetic cathinones (e.g. bath salts)'. Spice/Yucatan fire ＝ synthetic cannabinoids.
Q: Which is a plant-based NPS listed in the lecture? = Kratom | Spice | Benzylpiperazine | PMMA | Ketamine
> 'Plant-based substances (e.g. khat, kratom, Salvia divinorum).'
Q: Approximately how many NPS have been reported globally? = 600 | 60 | 200 | 6,000 | 60,000
> 'Global phenomenon — 600 substances have been reported.'

### Neurobiology of addiction
> - Mesolimbic reward pathway: ventral tegmental area (VTA) → nucleus accumbens (NAc). All drugs of abuse raise dopamine in the NAc — 5–10× more, and longer, than natural rewards (food, sex).
> - Direct dopamine action: cocaine (blocks DAT), amphetamines (release + block reuptake), MDMA. Indirect: opioids (inhibit GABA interneurons on VTA neurons via μ receptors), alcohol and benzodiazepines (GABA-A), nicotine (nicotinic receptors on VTA neurons), cannabis (CB1).
> - Prefrontal cortex — chronic use impairs it → poor inhibitory control, impulsivity, poor decisions. Amygdala — conditioned cues, stress, craving. Hippocampus — drug-context memories.
> - Low striatal D2 receptor availability (PET, Volkow) is associated with vulnerability and is found in addicted people.
> - Addiction is a developmental disorder: adolescents' reward systems mature before the prefrontal control system → more risk-taking; early onset predicts dependence.
Q: Which brain region is the origin of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway? = Ventral tegmental area | Nucleus accumbens | Amygdala | Hippocampus | Prefrontal cortex
> 'Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA) — origin of mesolimbic dopamine pathway — reward and motivation. Nucleus accumbens — primary target.'
Q: In the lecture, the amygdala in addiction is linked to: = Negative emotions and cravings during withdrawal | Poor decision-making | Memory deficits | Motor control | Reward prediction only
> 'Amygdala is affected leading to negative emotions and cravings during withdrawal.' PFC → poor decisions/impulsivity; hippocampus → memory.
Q: Drugs of abuse raise dopamine longer and more than natural reinforcers by about: = 5–10-fold | Equal amounts | 2-fold | 100-fold | 1000-fold
> 'Longer and larger dopamine 5–10 folds than natural reinforcers (food, sex).'
Q: Which drug works indirectly on dopamine, via other receptors, per the lecture? = Nicotine | Cocaine | Ecstasy | Amphetamine | ATS
> 'Some stimulants inhibit reuptake/promote release (cocaine, ATS, ecstasy). Others work indirectly (nicotine, alcohol, opiates and marijuana).'
Q: Why are adolescents at higher risk of addiction, according to the lecture? = Incomplete brain development with risk-taking and novelty-seeking | They metabolise drugs faster | They have more money | They have more D2 receptors | They never experience withdrawal
> 'Normal adolescent behaviors — risk taking, novelty seeking, response to peer pressure… incomplete development of brain region… different neuroadaptation.'

### Koob's allostatic model (Koob & Le Moal)
> - Allostasis ＝ "achieving stability through change". With repeated use the reward set-point shifts.
> - Three-stage cycle:
> 1. Binge/intoxication — reward, positive reinforcement — basal ganglia (NAc);
> 2. Withdrawal/negative affect — loss of reward plus recruitment of the "anti-reward" stress systems (CRF, dynorphin, noradrenaline) in the extended amygdala;
> 3. Preoccupation/anticipation (craving) — prefrontal cortex dysfunction.
> - The driver shifts from positive reinforcement (getting high) to negative reinforcement (relieving dysphoria) → compulsive use.
> - Defining features of addiction: compulsion, reinforcement, loss of control, persistence despite harm, long-lasting brain change, chronic relapsing course.
Q: Allostasis is defined as: = The process of achieving stability through physiological and behavioural change | Total abstinence | Tolerance | A withdrawal syndrome | Genetic predisposition
> '…'the process of achieving stability through physiological and behavioral change' (George, Le Moal & Koob, 2012).'
Q: In Koob's model, continued drug use leads to: = The recruitment of anti-reward and a rise in the brain's stress system | Strengthened reward | Reduced stress | Normal reward | Brain growth
> 'The brain's reward system begins to dysfunction, leading to 'the recruitment of antireward'… an increase in the brain's stress system… leading to compulsive drug use.'
Q: Loss of reward plus recruitment of the stress system creates what Koob calls: = An opponent motivational process | A positive feedback loop | Tolerance | Sensitisation | Extinction
> '…creates an 'opponent motivational process' that drives addiction (Koob & Le Moal, 2008).'
Q: Which statement about addiction is made in the lecture? = It is fundamentally a brain disease, but not just a brain disease | It is purely a moral failing | It is purely social | It never changes the brain | It is always voluntary
> 'Addiction is fundamentally a brain disease, but it's not just a brain disease.' Characteristics: compulsive, reinforcing, loss of control.

### Genetic factors — 40–60% of vulnerability
> - Protective:
> - ALDH2*2 / ADH1B variants (East Asian flushing reaction) — protect against alcoholism;
> - CYP2A6 slow metabolisers — less nicotine dependence (nicotine lasts longer, fewer cigarettes);
> - CYP2D6 poor metabolisers — can't convert codeine to morphine → protected against codeine misuse (but no analgesia).
> - Risk:
> - CHRNA5–A3–B4 nicotinic receptor cluster → nicotine dependence, heavy smoking;
> - GABA-A receptor (GABRA2) variants → alcoholism;
> - DRD2 (dopamine D2) variants → addiction vulnerability.
> - Twin heritability: cocaine/opioids ~60–70%, alcohol ~50%.
Q: What proportion of vulnerability to addiction is attributed to genetic factors? = 40–60% | 5–10% | 20–30% | 80–90% | 100%
> 'It is estimated that 40% to 60% of the vulnerability to addiction is attributable to genetic factors.'
Q: Genetic alterations of cytochrome P450 2A6 protect against: = Nicotine abuse | Alcoholism | Codeine abuse | Cocaine abuse | Cannabis abuse
> 'CYP2A6 — protective from nicotine abuse; CYP2D6 — protective against codeine abuse; alcohol dehydrogenase — protective against alcoholism.'
Q: The CHRNA5/A3/B4 gene cluster is associated with: = Nicotine dependence | Alcohol dependence | Opioid dependence | Cocaine dependence | Gambling
> 'The CHRNA5/A3/B4 gene cluster is associated with nicotine dependence.' GABA-A variants predispose to alcoholism.

### Environmental and social factors
> - Micro-level: parents/family (parenting, monitoring, parental substance use, abuse), school, peers (strongest adolescent influence).
> - Macro-level: cultural norms, poverty, unemployment, inequality, availability and price, media/advertising, laws and enforcement.
> - Risk: low socioeconomic status, poor parental support, drug availability, childhood trauma, early conduct problems.
> - Classic primate study (Morgan, Nader et al., 2002): monkeys that became socially dominant gained D2 receptors and self-administered less cocaine — environment changes brain biology.
Q: After the family, the lecture calls which the next major influence? = The school | Media | Religion | Government | Hospital
> 'After the family, the next major influence is the school and/or other education-related groups.'
Q: Which is a macro-level influence on substance use? = Economic environment — poverty, unemployment, affordability | Parenting skills | Peer relationships | Sibling rivalry | School grades
> Macro: cultural norms, economic environment (poverty, unemployment, availability, affordability, inequality), technology and media, laws and policies.
Q: Evidence-based family-focused prevention interventions have been shown to: = Reduce problem behaviours in both parents and children | Have no effect | Increase drug use | Only help parents | Only work in adults
> 'Evidenced-based family-focused prevention interventions have been shown to reduce problem behaviors and negative outcomes in both parents and their children.'
Q: Which environmental factor is NOT listed as consistently linked to drug self-administration? = High educational attainment | Low socioeconomic class | Poor parental support | Drug availability | All are listed
> 'Low socioeconomic class, poor parental support, and drug availability.'
Q: In non-human primates, animals that achieved dominant status showed: = More D2 receptors and less drug consumption | Fewer D2 receptors and more drug use | No change | More dopamine transporters | Fewer opioid receptors
> 'Animals that achieve a dominant status show increased numbers of D2 receptors; high D2 receptor levels lead to marked decreases in drug consumption.'

### Comorbidity (dual diagnosis)
> - Substance misuse is far more common in people with mental illness (e.g. ~50% of people with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder at some point).
> - Explanations: shared genetic, environmental and neurobiological risk; self-medication hypothesis (Khantzian) — drugs chosen to relieve specific distress; drugs causing psychiatric disorder (cannabis → psychosis; alcohol → depression).
> - Implication: screen everyone, treat both disorders together (integrated treatment), and treat mental illness early to prevent addiction that starts as self-medication.
Q: The lecture proposes comorbidity may partly be due to: = Using drugs to self-medicate mental illness | Hospital admission | Old age | High income | Physical exercise
> 'It has been proposed that comorbidity might be due to the use of the abused drugs to self-medicate the mental illness.'
Q: The lecture's preventive message from comorbidity is: = Early evaluation and treatment of mental illness prevents addiction that starts as self-medication | Avoid treating mental illness | Only treat addiction | Ban all drugs | Admit all patients
> '…highlights the relevance of the early evaluation and treatment of mental diseases — an effective strategy to prevent drug addiction that starts as self-medication.'

### Adolescents
> - Incomplete development of judgement, planning, self-control circuits; peer pressure; high-risk transitions (moving to secondary school, entering university).
> - Risk factors — girls: depression, tobacco use, maternal substance problems, low parental attachment/monitoring, childhood sexual abuse, chaotic home. Boys: early aggression, peer problems, conduct disorder, genetics.
> - Protective: personal and social competence, optimism, pro-social activities, problem-solving skills, school connectedness.
> - Screening: CRAFFT — Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble; ≥ 2 'yes' ＝ high risk (validated for 12–21-year-olds).
> - Compared with adults, adolescents hide use more, report fewer withdrawal symptoms, and believe they can stop. Treat with the family; behavioural therapies (family therapy, CBT, contingency management, MI) work; address schooling and legal issues.
Q: According to the WHO definition cited, a child is a person: = 19 years or younger | Below 12 years | Below 16 years | Below 21 years | Below 8 years
> 'UN/UNICEF: below 18 years. WHO: 19 years or younger. UNESCO: early childhood ＝ birth to 8 years.'
Q: The Suitcase for Life (CHILD intervention) has how many modules? = 8 | 3 | 5 | 12 | 20
> 'There are eight modules that comprise the Suitcase for Life' — mindfulness, DBT, relapse prevention, motivational interviewing, art therapy techniques.
Q: In treating children with substance use, the lecture stresses that treatment usually needs to: = Include caregivers | Exclude parents | Use only medication | Avoid play | Be purely verbal
> 'Treatment usually needs to include caregivers — children have adults in their lives upon which they depend.' Structured play is important.
Q: Which is an individual risk factor for substance use in boys listed in the lecture? = Aggressiveness in first grade | Childhood sexual abuse | Maternal drug problems | Depression | Unstructured home
> Boys: aggressiveness in first grade, peer difficulties, conduct disorder, genetics. Girls: depression, tobacco, maternal drug problems, low attachment, sexual abuse.
Q: Which validated screening tool for adolescent substance use is named in the lecture? = CRAFFT | CAGE | AUDIT | ASI | ASSIST
> 'The CRAFFT tool is a validated screening tool for substance use of adolescents.'
Q: Which is a high-risk transition for adolescent substance use? = Entering high school or college | Getting a driving licence | Learning to swim | Turning 13 | Joining a choir
> 'High risk periods: moving from primary school to middle school; entering high school; entering college.'
Q: Compared with adults, adolescents are more likely to: = Hide their substance use and say they can stop when they want | Identify withdrawal symptoms | Experience withdrawal symptoms | Seek treatment early | Have no complaints from others
> Adolescents are more likely to hide use and say they can stop when they want; less likely to identify or experience withdrawal.

### Women, pregnancy and the post-partum period
> - Women "telescope" — progress faster from first use to dependence and to injecting; are often introduced by a partner; relapse with interpersonal problems; more trauma.
> - Opioids in pregnancy — do NOT detoxify: WHO (2014) — offer opioid maintenance (methadone or buprenorphine) rather than withdrawal; detox risks fetal distress, miscarriage, preterm labour and maternal relapse.
> - Neonatal abstinence syndrome (neonatal opioid withdrawal): CNS irritability (high-pitched cry, tremor, hypertonia, poor sleep, seizures), GI (poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhoea), autonomic (sweating, fever, sneezing, nasal stuffiness, yawning); scored (Finnegan) and treated.
> - Alcohol: benzodiazepine-assisted withdrawal; avoid disulfiram and acamprosate in pregnancy; thiamine.
> - Tobacco: NRT is safer than smoking; behavioural support (5 As).
> - Benzodiazepines: gradual taper with a long-acting agent, aiming to be benzodiazepine-free at delivery.
> - Stimulants: no proven drugs — CBT, contingency management, motivational interviewing.
> - Encourage breastfeeding (except with HIV or ongoing high-risk use); never discharge from treatment because of pregnancy.
Q: Which is true of young women and substance use, per the lecture? = They accelerate to injecting drugs faster than men | They progress to injecting more slowly than men | They never start through relationships | The gender gap is widening | They are unaffected by caregiving
> 'Women accelerate to injecting drugs at a faster rate than men… more likely to initiate through significant relationships… gender gap is narrowing.'
Q: What barrier to treatment did the lecture highlight for young women? = Sobriety requirements for treatment entry | Too many beds | Free treatment | Male-only staff | Short waiting lists
> 'Sobriety requirements for treatment entry create barriers… Women engaged in creative strategies, such as claiming they were suicidal, to access treatment.'
Q: When involving a partner in treatment, the primary consideration is: = Safety and the partner's willingness to participate | Cost | The partner's job | Religion | Distance
> 'Primary consideration should be given to safety and to the partner's willingness to participate in treatment.'
Q: WHO (2014) recommends that pregnant women dependent on opioids be encouraged to: = Use opioid maintenance treatment rather than detoxification | Detoxify rapidly | Stop abruptly | Use naltrexone implants | Switch to alcohol
> 'Pregnant women dependent on opioids should be encouraged to use opioid maintenance treatment whenever available rather than to attempt opioid detoxification.'
Q: Which drugs should be avoided for alcohol use disorder in pregnancy? = Acamprosate and disulfiram | Diazepam and thiamine | NRT | Methadone | Folic acid
> 'Avoid using acamprosate and disulfiram during pregnancy due to risk to the fetus.' Withdrawal uses a benzodiazepine (e.g. diazepam).
Q: Benzodiazepine dependence in pregnancy is managed by: = Gradual taper with a long-acting benzodiazepine, aiming to be benzodiazepine-free at birth | Abrupt cessation | Switching to alcohol | Increasing the dose | ECT
> 'Gradual taper with a long-acting benzodiazepine with the goal of being benzodiazepine-free at birth.'
Q: The 5 As brief intervention for tobacco are: = Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange | Avoid, Abstain, Accept, Adapt, Act | Alert, Advise, Admit, Aid, Approve | Ask, Assure, Attend, Act, Assess | Abstain, Apply, Assess, Advise, Accept
> '5As (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) is a Brief Intervention.'
Q: The biggest concern with opioid agonist medication in pregnancy is: = Neonatal abstinence syndrome — a treatable condition | Fetal malformation | Maternal death | Preterm labour always | Breastfeeding failure
> 'Biggest concern… is the potential for neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) – a treatable condition.'
Q: Which is an autonomic sign of neonatal opioid withdrawal listed in the lecture? = Nasal stuffiness | Irritability | Vomiting | Sleep disturbance | Uncoordinated sucking
> Neurological: hyperactivity, irritability, sleep disturbance. GI: uncoordinated sucking/swallowing, vomiting. Autonomic: fever, sweating, nasal stuffiness.
Q: Which statement about women-only treatment is made in the lecture? = It was effective, with its strongest effect on pregnancy outcomes | It was ineffective | It increased relapse | It is illegal | It only helped men
> 'Women-only treatment was effective and its strongest effect was on pregnancy outcomes.' Pregnant women should not be turned away.

### Older adults — hidden problem
> - Triggers: retirement, empty nest, bereavement, isolation, chronic pain, medical illness.
> - Signs of alcohol misuse: self-neglect, neglected home/bills, falls, confusion, blackouts, many doctors and prescriptions, unexplained health complaints, depression, suicidal thoughts.
> - Higher sensitivity to alcohol (less body water, slower metabolism, drug interactions — benzodiazepines, opioids, z-drugs).
> - Women develop alcohol-related diseases at lower intake and earlier.
> - Older adults do as well or better in treatment than younger people; respectful, direct approach; address grief; behavioural activation for depression.
Q: Middle adulthood in the lecture is defined as ages: = 40–64 | 20–39 | 30–50 | 50–70 | 65+
> 'A person in the middle adulthood stage ages from 40 to 64.' Young adult ＝ 20–39.
Q: Which is described as a danger in middle-adult treatment needs? = Increased prescription usage | Too much exercise | Too much sleep | High income | Social media
> 'Increased prescription usage is a danger.' Challenges: misdiagnosis, ageism, other health issues, no time for treatment.
Q: Which is a behavioural sign of alcohol use disorder in an older person, per the lecture? = Empty food cupboards and many doctors and prescriptions | Improved hygiene | Weight gain | More social outings | Better finances
> 'Neglected appearance, neglect of home/bills/pets, empty food cupboards, self-isolation, many physicians and prescriptions, falls, unexplained pain.'
Q: How do older adults fare in treatment compared with younger adults? = Outcomes as good as or better | Much worse | They cannot be treated | They need only individual therapy | They always relapse
> 'Older adults in treatment are more likely to complete treatment and have outcomes as good or better than younger adults. No evidence they need individual approaches.'
Q: Which is NOT recommended in the treatment response for older adults? = Dig up painful events from the past | Be direct | Talk patiently without pressure | Address grief | Behavioural activation for depression
> 'Do not dig up painful events from the past.'

### Assessment
> - Goals: establish presence and severity of a disorder, readiness to change, strengths, risks, and the right level of care.
> - Addiction Severity Index (ASI) — McLellan, 1980 (University of Pennsylvania); 7 domains: medical, employment/support, drug use, alcohol use, legal, family/social, psychiatric. 5th edition 1992; ASI-Lite 1997.
> - Thorley's model (1980) — three types of problem: problems of Intoxication (accidents, aggression, overdose), Regular use (health, finance, relationships, child neglect) and Dependence (impaired control, drug-centred behaviour, withdrawal).
> - Zinberg's "drug, set and setting" — the interactive model: effects depend on the drug (dose, route, purity), the individual (mood, expectations, tolerance) and the environment (social context, legality, culture).
> - Physical investigations: LFT (GGT, AST:ALT > 2 in alcohol), MCV, FBC, U&E, glucose, HIV, hepatitis B and C, VDRL, ECG, imaging as indicated.
Q: The Addiction Severity Index was developed in 1980 by: = A. Thomas McLellan | Koob | Prochaska | Thorley | Khantzian
> 'Originally developed in 1980 by A. Thomas McLellan and colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania… 5th edition 1992; ASI Lite 1997.'
Q: Which is NOT one of the ASI's seven problem areas? = Educational status | Medical status | Legal status | Psychiatric status | Family/social status
> Seven: medical, employment and support, drug use, alcohol use, legal, family/social, psychiatric.
Q: Which investigation is listed in the lecture's work-up? = Retroviral screening, hepatitis B and C, VDRL | Bone marrow biopsy | Lumbar puncture | Echocardiogram only | Skin biopsy
> 'Liver function test; HBV, HCV, RVS, VDRL, FBC, U/E/Cr; urinalysis; RBS, FBS; imaging.'
Q: Thorley's model classifies drug problems into problems of: = Intoxication, regular use and dependence | Drug, set and setting | Binge, withdrawal and preoccupation | Precontemplation to maintenance | Physical, psychological, social
> Thorley: Intoxication, Regular (excessive) use, Dependence (I, R, D).
Q: In Thorley's model, child neglect is a problem of: = Regular (excessive) use | Intoxication | Dependence | Withdrawal | None
> 'Regular — excessive use — health, finances, relationships, child neglect.'
Q: In the interactive model of drug use, tolerance, expectations and mood belong to: = The individual | The drug | The environment | The law | The dealer
> Individual: physical/emotional reaction, mood, health, age, tolerance, knowledge, beliefs, memories, expectations.
Q: In the interactive model, legality, culture and peers belong to: = The environment | The drug | The individual | Genetics | Neurobiology
> Environment: where, when, who, how, social context, supply, peers, legality, culture, media, advertising.

### Drug testing
> - Matrices: urine (commonest), blood, saliva, sweat, hair (longest window ~90 days), breath (alcohol).
> - Urine: immunoassay screen (fast, cheap, false positives) → confirm with gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS).
> - Approximate urine detection windows:
> - cannabis ~3 days after single use, up to 30 days in heavy daily users (fat-soluble THC);
> - cocaine (benzoylecgonine) 2–4 days; amphetamines 2–3 days;
> - heroin/morphine 1–3 days (6-MAM ＝ heroin specifically, < 24 h);
> - methadone ~1 week; benzodiazepines days to weeks (long-acting);
> - alcohol hours (EtG metabolite up to ~80 h).
> - Tramadol, fentanyl and most NPS are not detected on standard opiate screens.
Q: Which is NOT one of the five primary drug-testing samples listed? = Cerebrospinal fluid | Urine | Hair | Saliva | Sweat
> 'Five primary ways: urine (immunoassay, GC/MS), blood, hair, saliva, sweat.'
Q: A positive urine immunoassay should be confirmed by: = GC-MS | Repeat immunoassay | Breathalyser | Serum ethanol | History alone
> GC-MS — the confirmatory gold standard.
Q: Which drug is not detected by a standard urine opiate immunoassay? = Tramadol | Morphine | Codeine | Heroin (as morphine) | Diamorphine metabolites
> Tramadol (and fentanyl, methadone) need specific assays.

### Treatment principles
> - Stages of change (Prochaska & DiClemente): precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (→ relapse). Match the intervention to the stage.
> - Motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) — OARS (Open questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, Summaries); express empathy, develop discrepancy, roll with resistance, support self-efficacy.
> - Brief intervention — FRAMES: Feedback, Responsibility, Advice, Menu of options, Empathy, Self-efficacy. Effective for hazardous/harmful alcohol use in primary care.
> - Psychosocial: CBT, relapse prevention (Marlatt), contingency management (best evidence for stimulants), 12-step facilitation, family therapy, therapeutic communities.
> - Harm reduction: needle and syringe programmes, opioid substitution, naloxone.
> - Pharmacological (by substance — see the drug-specific topics): alcohol (chlordiazepoxide, thiamine, acamprosate, naltrexone, disulfiram), opioids (methadone, buprenorphine, lofexidine, naltrexone), tobacco (NRT, varenicline, bupropion).
Q: Which is NOT a principle of motivational interviewing? = Confront denial directly | Express empathy | Develop discrepancy | Roll with resistance | Support self-efficacy
> MI avoids confrontation.
Q: The psychosocial treatment with the strongest evidence for stimulant use disorders is: = Contingency management | Psychoanalysis | Hypnosis | Aversion therapy | Group counselling
> Contingency management.

### OSCE: Opioid withdrawal: assessment and treatment | fps
> Emergency station. Task: This man uses opioids and is now in withdrawal. Assess him and discuss management.
> - Book options include accelerated detox (naltrexone plus clonidine, shortening detox by 4–5 days) and ultra-rapid detox under general anaesthesia. Ultra-rapid detox is not recommended: serious adverse events and deaths have occurred without better outcomes.
> - Book notes levomethadyl (LAAM) causes torsades de pointes. Methadone also prolongs QTc, so check an ECG if there are risk factors.
> - Overdose risk is highest after detox because tolerance is lost. Warn the patient and offer naloxone.
> Critical fail: Unsupervised high-dose methadone, or discharging after detox without overdose warning or naloxone.
