### Bonus drill: Substance dependence (ICD-11)
> Walk the ICD-11 pathway for every substance, and show whether each requirement is present or absent. Don't force the diagnosis.
> - Is there a single episode of harmful use, or a harmful pattern of use (episodic or continuous) causing damage to health?
> - Dependence: at least 2 of 3 central features, usually over 12 months (or 3 months if use is continuous): impaired control; increasing precedence over other interests; physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal, use to relieve withdrawal).
> - Then add what else is present: intoxication, withdrawal, substance-induced disorders.
> Codes: 6C40 alcohol, 6C41 cannabis, 6C43 opioids, 6C44 sedatives, 6C45 cocaine, 6C46 stimulants. Suffixes: .0 episode of harmful use, .1 harmful pattern, .2 dependence, .3 intoxication, .4 withdrawal.
L: ICD-11 substance diagnosis pathway (FNPH) = Clerk the patient fully | Check single episode of harmful use | Check harmful pattern of use | Check dependence (2 of 3 central features) | Add intoxication, withdrawal or induced disorders present ~~ Decide the diagnosis first :: Clerk first, then follow the pathway | Count ICD-10 criteria (3 of 6) :: That is the old ICD-10 rule | Skip harmful use if dependent :: Dependence takes precedence, but state that you checked each level
> In the long case, say each step out loud: "Impaired control: present, because... Physiological features: absent, because..."
S: ICD-11 dependence: the 3 central features = Impaired control over use | Increasing precedence of use over other interests | Physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal) ~~ Legal problems :: Not an ICD-11 dependence feature | Harm to other people :: That relates to harmful use, not dependence | Use of an illegal drug :: Legality is not a criterion
> - Impaired control: onset, amount, circumstances, termination; often with craving.
> - Precedence: use takes priority over health, responsibilities and interests, and continues despite harm.
> - Physiological: tolerance, withdrawal, or repeated use to prevent or relieve withdrawal.
Q: Features needed for ICD-11 dependence = At least 2 of the 3 central features | All 3 features :: Only two are needed | Any 1 feature :: One is not enough; two are needed | 3 of 6 features :: That was the ICD-10 rule (3 of 6)
> Two of three, usually evident over 12 months.
Q: Usual time frame for ICD-11 dependence = 12 months, or 3 months if use is continuous (daily or almost daily) | 12 months, or 1 month if use is continuous :: Continuous use needs at least 3 months | 6 months, or 1 month if use is continuous :: The usual period is 12 months, or 3 months if continuous | 12 months in every case :: It can be shortened to 3 months if use is continuous
> "Usually evident over a period of at least 12 months, but the diagnosis may be made if use has been continuous (daily or almost daily) for at least 3 months."
Q: ICD-11 physiological features include = Tolerance, withdrawal, or use to relieve withdrawal | Tolerance and craving :: Craving belongs to impaired control | Tolerance, withdrawal, or neglect of other interests :: Neglect of other interests belongs to increasing precedence | Withdrawal only after stopping completely :: Withdrawal can follow a reduction too, and using to relieve withdrawal also counts
> Physiological features alone are not dependence (for example, tolerance to prescribed opioids for pain). You still need a second feature.
Q: ICD-11 harmful pattern of substance use means = Use that damages health, without dependence | Use that damages health, with features of dependence :: If dependence is present, dependence is the diagnosis | A single episode of use that damages health :: That is an episode of harmful use, not a pattern | Use that causes social problems only, with no damage to health :: A harmful pattern requires damage to physical or mental health
> The harm can be physical or mental (including harm caused by intoxication), and in ICD-11 it can include harm to the health of others.
Q: ICD-11 code for alcohol dependence = 6C40.2 | 6C40.1 :: 6C40.1 is harmful pattern of use of alcohol | 6C40.3 :: 6C40.3 is alcohol intoxication | 6C41.2 :: 6C41.2 is cannabis dependence
> The suffix pattern repeats for every substance: .2 is always dependence.
Q: ICD-11 code for alcohol withdrawal = 6C40.4 | 6C40.3 :: 6C40.3 is alcohol intoxication | 6C40.2 :: 6C40.2 is alcohol dependence | 6C43.4 :: 6C43.4 is opioid withdrawal
> .3 intoxication, .4 withdrawal. 6C43 is opioids.
L: Alcohol withdrawal timeline (earliest first) = Tremor, sweating, anxiety (6-12 h) | Withdrawal seizures (12-48 h) | Delirium tremens (48-72 h) ~~ Korsakoff syndrome :: A chronic amnestic state, not a withdrawal stage | Hepatic encephalopathy :: Caused by liver failure, not a withdrawal stage | Wernicke's encephalopathy :: Caused by thiamine deficiency, not a withdrawal stage
> Alcoholic hallucinosis (usually auditory, in clear consciousness) can also appear in the first 1-2 days.
> Delirium tremens: confusion, vivid visual hallucinations, tremor and autonomic overactivity. It is a medical emergency.
S: Wernicke's encephalopathy triad = Confusion | Ataxia | Ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus ~~ Amnesia with confabulation :: That is Korsakoff syndrome | Peripheral neuropathy :: Not part of the triad | Seizures :: Not part of the triad
> Caused by thiamine (B1) deficiency. The full triad is present in a minority, so treat on suspicion with parenteral thiamine.
> Untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome.
Q: Korsakoff syndrome is mainly = Profound anterograde amnesia with confabulation | Profound retrograde amnesia with intact new learning :: Anterograde amnesia (poor new learning) is the hallmark | Acute confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia :: That triad is Wernicke's encephalopathy | Amnesia with confabulation caused by vitamin B12 deficiency :: It is caused by thiamine (B1) deficiency
> Consciousness and other cognitive functions are relatively preserved, but new learning is severely impaired. Mammillary bodies and thalamus are involved.
S: Opioid overdose triad = Pinpoint pupils | Respiratory depression | Reduced consciousness ~~ Dilated pupils :: Dilated pupils suggest stimulants, anticholinergics, or opioid WITHDRAWAL | Hyperthermia :: Not part of the opioid triad | Hypertension :: Opioid overdose tends to cause hypotension
> Pinpoint pupils plus slow breathing plus drowsiness: think opioid and give naloxone.
L: Opioid overdose management = Support airway and breathing | Give naloxone | Repeat naloxone as needed | Observe for several hours, as naloxone wears off before many opioids ~~ Give flumazenil :: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids | Discharge after one dose :: Naloxone is short-acting; the patient can re-sedate | Induce vomiting :: No role
> Naloxone lasts about 60-90 minutes, which is shorter than methadone and many other opioids. Watch for re-sedation and consider an infusion.

## Sports Field | Genetics
> Genetics. Source: Feb 2026 NPMCN - Genetics in Child and Psychiatry.pdf. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Genes and variation
> - 23 pairs of chromosomes; DNA wound on histones; nucleosides A, G, C, T; exons expressed, introns not.
> - Central dogma: DNA → (transcription) RNA → (translation) protein.
> - Humans are 99.9% genetically similar.
> - Mendelian (single gene, large effect): phenylketonuria 1 in 23,930. Polygenic (many small common variants): schizophrenia 1 in 100.
> - SNP example: sickle cell — GAG (Glu) → GTG (Val) on β-globin (HbS ＝ α2βS2).
> - CNV example: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion).
Q: Human somatic cells contain: = 23 pairs of chromosomes | 22 pairs of chromosomes | 46 pairs of chromosomes | 23 single chromosomes | 48 chromosomes
> 'The genetic material is condensed into 23 pairs of chromosomes in the nuclei human somatic cells.'
Q: The non-expressed DNA within a gene is called: = Intron | Exon | Codon | Histone | Promoter
> 'A gene is a section of the DNA that codes for a specific product (Exon), non-expressed DNA — intron.'
Q: In the central dogma, DNA is transcribed into: = RNA | Protein | Histone | Amino acids directly | Chromosomes
> 'DNA is transcribed into RNA and codons are translated into proteins.'
Q: Chromosomal DNA is supercoiled on itself and fixed on: = Histone proteins | Ribosomes | Mitochondria | Microtubules | Lipids
> '...supercoiled on itself and fixed histone proteins.'
Q: How genetically similar are humans to one another? = 99.9% | 50% | 75% | 90% | 100%
> 'Humans are 99.9% genetically similar to one another.'
Q: Which disorder is given as an example of 'Mendelian-type' inheritance? = Phenylketonuria | Schizophrenia | Depression | ADHD | Anxiety
> 'Relatively rarer disorders (e.g., phenylketonuria — 1:23,930 live births) follow a Mendelian type inheritance.'
Q: Schizophrenia is described in the lecture as: = Polygenic — many common variants each of small effect | Mendelian | Mitochondrial | Caused by one CNV | Not heritable
> '...more common traits (e.g., schizophrenia — 1:100) are polygenic i.e., influenced by multiple and common genetic variants each of small effect.'
Q: In sickle cell disease, the β-globin codon change is: = GAG (Glu) → GTG (Val) | GTG → GAG | CAG repeat expansion | CGG repeat expansion | Deletion of exon 3
> GAG codon for Glu → GTG codon for Val — a single nucleotide polymorphism.
Q: DiGeorge syndrome is the lecture's example of: = A copy number variant | A SNP | Trisomy | Imprinting | A mitochondrial disorder
> Copy number variant — DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion).

### Population (quantitative) genetic designs
> - Family studies: clustering in relatives (Gottesman 1991); can't separate genes from family environment.
> - Adoption studies: biological vs adoptive relatives; Tienari & Wynne (1994) — more schizophrenia in adopted-away children of affected parents. Controls family environment; limits: records, selective placement.
> - Twin studies: MZ 100%, DZ 50% shared genes, equal environments assumed. ACE model — Additive genetics, Common environment, non-shared Environment (Rijsdijk & Sham 2002).
> - All population designs: heritability is a population statistic (not individual) and they don't identify specific genes.
Q: Population genetics is also known as: = Biometric or quantitative genetics | Molecular genetics | Epigenetics | Statistical genetics | Pharmacogenomics
> 'Also known as biometric or quantitative genetics.'
Q: The main limitation of family studies is that they: = Cannot distinguish genetic influences from family-environment influences | Need huge samples | Need DNA samples | Only work for twins | Are too expensive
> 'Cannot distinguish between genetic influences and family environment influences.'
Q: Clustering of schizophrenia in different relatives was shown by: = Gottesman (1991) | Caspi (2003) | Tienari (1994) | Sullivan (2017) | Demontis (2023)
> 'Clustering of schizophrenia in different relatives (Gottesman, 1991).'
Q: In adoption studies, genetic influence is suggested by: = Higher prevalence in biological than adoptive families | Higher prevalence in adoptive than biological families | Equal prevalence | Lower prevalence in twins | Higher prevalence in step-parents
> 'Logic: Higher disease prevalence among biological compared adoptive families suggests genetic influences.'
Q: The main advantage of adoption studies is that they: = Control for confounding by family environment | Identify specific genes | Need no records | Are cheap | Measure epigenetics
> 'Advantages — Controls for confounding by family environment.'
Q: A limitation of adoption studies is: = Selective placement during adoption | They cannot study schizophrenia | Linkage disequilibrium | Multiple testing | They need twins
> Limitations: detailed record keeping and bias from selective placement.
Q: Increased schizophrenia in adopted-away children of affected probands was reported by: = Tienari and Wynne (1994) | Gottesman (1991) | Seeman (1983) | Jones (2013) | Kato (2022)
> Tienari and Wynne, 1994.
Q: The classical twin design assumes DZ twins share what proportion of their genes? = 50% | 25% | 75% | 100% | 0%
> 'Mz twins are 100% genetically identical while dz twins are only 50%.'
Q: In the ACE model, 'C' stands for: = Common (shared) environment | Chromosome | Candidate gene | Copy number | Cortisol
> A additive genetics, C common environment, E non-shared environment.
Q: Which is a 'difference factor' between twins in the ACE model? = Non-shared environment | Additive genetics | Common environment | Shared genes | Family income
> A and C are similarity factors; E (non-shared environment) is the difference factor.
Q: An overall limitation of population genetic designs is that heritability: = Is a population statistic, not informative at the individual level | Applies to each individual | Identifies the exact gene | Is always 100% | Cannot be estimated
> 'Not informative at the individual level — heritability is a population statistic.' They also don't identify specific genes.
Q: Twins have more birth complications than singletons; the lecture says these effects: = Do not persist | Persist for life | Double heritability | Cause schizophrenia | Invalidate all twin studies
> 'High birth complications may make twins different from singletons but these do not persist.'
Q: Heritability of schizophrenia from twin studies is roughly: = 80% | 10% | 30% | 50% | 100%
> About 80% (twin estimates), with MZ concordance ~40–50%.

### Finding the genes
> - Candidate-gene studies: case-control tests of theory-chosen SNPs — BDNF, COMT, neuregulin 1, dysbindin, AKT1, DRD2, DISC1. Not replicable, weak rationale, linkage disequilibrium, low power.
> - GWAS: test the whole genome at once; Manhattan plot; genome-wide significance p < 5 × 10⁻⁸.
> - GWAS show disorders are polygenic, find novel genes, and give polygenic scores — for research, not yet clinical prediction.
> - Common disorders → common SNPs of small effect; rare disorders → rare CNVs of large effect (Manolio 2010).
> - ADHD GWAS (Demontis 2023); ADHD symptoms GWAS 17 new loci (van der Laan 2025).
Q: A candidate-gene study is essentially a: = Case-control design testing a theory-chosen variant | Cohort study | Twin study | Randomised trial | Adoption study
> 'Essentially a case-control design... Genetic variant is selected based on theory.'
Q: Which was a popular schizophrenia candidate gene? = COMT | MECP2 | FMR1 | HBB | PAH
> BDNF, COMT, neuregulin 1, dysbindin, AKT1, DRD2, DISC1 (Sullivan 2017).
Q: The main problem with candidate-gene findings was that they: = Were not replicable | Were too large | Used whole genomes | Had too much power | Studied twins
> 'Findings were not replicable' — plus weak gene selection, linkage disequilibrium, low power.
Q: The genome-wide significance threshold used in GWAS is: = p < 5 × 10⁻⁸ | p < 0.05 | p < 0.01 | p < 0.001 | p < 1 × 10⁻²
> 'To correct for multiple testing, p set at p < 5×10⁻⁸.'
Q: GWAS results are typically displayed as a: = Manhattan plot | Kaplan-Meier curve | Forest plot | Funnel plot | Bland-Altman plot
> Manhattan plot (e.g. social skills, Jones et al. 2013).
Q: According to the lecture, polygenic scores are currently: = Useful for clinical research but not clinical prediction | Used for routine diagnosis | Banned | Only for Mendelian disorders | More accurate than history
> 'Only useful for clinical research now but not clinical prediction.'
Q: GWAS overcame candidate-gene weaknesses by: = Testing variants across the whole genome simultaneously | Studying one gene in depth | Using only twins | Ignoring statistics | Testing only CNVs
> '...simultaneously testing variants across the whole genome.'
Q: According to Manolio (2010), commoner disorders like depression are influenced mainly by: = Common variants like SNPs with individually small effects | Rare CNVs of large effect | Single genes | Mitochondrial DNA | Imprinting
> Commoner disorders → common SNPs, small effects; rarer disorders → rare CNVs, larger effects.
Q: The van der Laan (2025) ADHD symptoms GWAS identified how many new loci? = 17 | 3 | 50 | 102 | None
> 'Identified 17 new loci including transcription factors, microRNA.'
Q: A limitation of genome-wide approaches mentioned in the conclusion is that they: = Require large samples | Are too small | Identify no genes | Ignore SNPs | Are cheap
> 'Genome-wide approaches require large samples.' Population approaches don't identify specific genes.

### Gene–environment interplay and overlap
> - G×E: genetic effects depend on environment — stress-diathesis.
> - Caspi et al. (2003): short 5-HTTLPR allele (risk) + stressful life events → more depression; long/long protected.
> - Genetic overlap between psychiatric disorders (Romero 2022) and with neurological disorders (Peall 2026) — shared synaptic, dendritic and calcium mechanisms.
> - Metabolic pathways (Kopylov 2023): complement, cholesterol, thyroxine, vitamin D3.
Q: Network analyses (Romero 2022) showed genetic associations between psychiatric disorders based on: = Common genetic variants (SNPs) | Rare CNVs | Mitochondrial genes | Epigenetic marks | Karyotypes
> '...based on common genetic variants (SNPs) (Romero et al., 2022).'
Q: Peall et al. (2026) describe shared mechanisms in rare genetic brain disorders including altered: = Calcium homeostasis and signalling | Bone density | Liver enzymes | Skin pigment | Red cell shape
> Synaptic release and receptor signalling, dendritic arbour complexity, and calcium homeostasis.
Q: In the stress-diathesis framework, genetic risk for depression manifests more strongly: = In stressful contexts | In calm environments | Only in twins | Only in men | Only after 60
> '...genetic risk for psychopathology like depression manifests more strongly in stressful contexts.'
Q: In Caspi et al. (2003), the 5-HTTLPR risk allele is the: = Short allele | Long allele | Null allele | Duplicated allele | Mitochondrial allele
> 's ＝ short 5HTTLPR variant — risk allele.'
Q: Caspi's study is the classic example of: = Gene–environment interaction | Genomic imprinting | Linkage disequilibrium | Anticipation | Mosaicism
> G×E — the effect of stressful life events on depression depended on 5-HTTLPR genotype.

### Epigenetics and imprinting
> - Epigenetics ＝ change in gene function without change in DNA sequence; heritable and reversible: DNA methylation, histone modification, non-coding RNA.
> - Prader-Willi: 15q11.2–q13, paternal deletion (Angelman if maternal).
> - PWS mechanisms: paternal deletion 60%, maternal uniparental disomy 36%, imprinting defects.
> - PWS features: learning disability, skin picking, obesity (failure of satiety), psychosis risk in young adulthood.
Q: Epigenetics refers to changes in gene function that: = Are not based on changes to the underlying DNA sequence | Alter the DNA sequence | Are always permanent | Only occur in cancer | Cannot be inherited
> 'Changes in gene function that are not based on changes to the underlying DNA sequence. Can be inherited and reversible.'
Q: Which is an example of an epigenetic process? = DNA methylation | Point mutation | Trisomy | CGG expansion | Translocation
> DNA methylation, histone modification, non-coding RNA regulation.
Q: A 15q11.2–q13 deletion inherited from the mother causes: = Angelman syndrome | Prader-Willi syndrome | Rett's syndrome | Fragile X | DiGeorge syndrome
> Paternal deletion → Prader-Willi; 'Angelman syndrome if maternally inherited'.
Q: Maternal uniparental disomy accounts for what proportion of Prader-Willi cases? = 36% | 5% | 15% | 60% | 90%
> Paternal deletion 60%, maternal uniparental disomy 36%, imprinting defects the rest.
Q: Obesity in Prader-Willi syndrome is due to: = Failure of satiety | Hypothyroidism | Steroid use | Low activity only | Insulin excess
> 'Obesity — failure of satiety.' Also LD, skin picking, psychosis risk in young adulthood.

### Genetic syndromes to know
> - Down's (trisomy 21): 1 in 800–1,000; advanced maternal age; 8% of learning disability; non-disjunction, unbalanced translocation, mosaicism; hypothyroid depression, early-onset Alzheimer's.
> - Fragile X: 1 in 4,000 males; CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 (Xq27.3); normal ≤ 45, > 200 ＝ full mutation; anticipation (X-linked); poor eye contact, sensory sensitivity, stereotypies, autism.
> - Rett's: girls; MECP2 on X; normal to 6–18 months then regression; severe LD, scoliosis, breathing problems, anxiety (hand-wringing).
> - Types: chromosomal, microdeletion, CNV, single-gene (Rett, PKU), mitochondrial, polygenic (ADHD, depression), multifactorial.
Q: Down's syndrome occurs in about: = 1 in 800–1,000 live births | 1 in 100 births | 1 in 4,000 males | 1 in 23,930 | 1 in 100,000
> '1/800–1000 live births.'
Q: Down's syndrome accounts for what proportion of learning disability? = 8% | 1% | 25% | 50% | 80%
> 'Accounts for 8% of Learning disability.'
Q: Which psychiatric presentation is linked with Down's syndrome in the lecture? = Early-onset Alzheimer's dementia | Anorexia nervosa | Gambling | Kleptomania | Pyromania
> 'Hypothyroidism-depression, early onset of Alzheimer's dementia.'
Q: Rett's syndrome is classified in the lecture as a: = Single-gene disorder | Chromosomal disorder | Polygenic disorder | Mitochondrial disorder | Copy number variant
> 'Single gene disorders — Rett's syndrome, Phenylketonuria.'
Q: Which is NOT a mechanism of Down's syndrome given in the lecture? = Uniparental disomy | Non-disjunction | Unbalanced translocation | Mosaicism | All of these are mechanisms
> Down's: non-disjunction, unbalanced translocation, mosaicism. Uniparental disomy is a Prader-Willi mechanism.
Q: Fragile X syndrome affects about: = 1 in 4,000 males | 1 in 800 births | 1 in 100 | 1 in 23,930 | Only girls
> '1 in 4000 males.'
Q: Fragile X results from expansion of which repeat, beyond how many copies? = CGG, > 200 | CAG, > 40 | CTG, > 50 | GAA, > 100 | CGG, > 20
> 'Expansion of CGG repeats... Usually up to 45 repeats; > 200 results in Fragile X.'
Q: Rett's syndrome is caused by mutations in which gene? = MECP2 | FMR1 | COMT | DISC1 | HTT
> MECP2 on the X chromosome.
Q: In Rett's syndrome, development is normal until about: = 6–18 months | Birth | 1–2 months | 5 years | Puberty
> 'Normal development till 6–18 months, then regression — loss of motor/communication skills.'
Q: Rett's syndrome is rarely compatible with life in: = Boys | Girls | Twins | Adults | Africans
> 'Mostly seen in girls, rarely compatible with life in boys.'
Q: Anticipation (worsening severity in successive generations) is classically seen in: = Huntington's disease and Fragile X (trinucleotide repeat disorders) | Down's syndrome | Prader-Willi | Phenylketonuria | Turner syndrome
> Anticipation is typical of trinucleotide repeat disorders: Huntington's (CAG), Fragile X (CGG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG).
Q: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome carries a lifetime risk of schizophrenia of about: = 25% | 1% | 5% | 75% | 100%
> About 25% — the strongest known single genetic risk factor for schizophrenia.
Q: Which gene on chromosome 21 links Down's syndrome to early Alzheimer's disease? = APP (amyloid precursor protein) | APOE | PSEN1 | MAPT | HTT
> An extra copy of APP on chromosome 21 → more amyloid → early-onset Alzheimer's.
Q: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) is characterised by: = Over-friendliness ('cocktail party' personality), anxiety and supravalvular aortic stenosis | Social withdrawal | Self-mutilation of lips | Hyperphagia | Hand-wringing
> Williams: hypersociability, anxiety, visuospatial weakness, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcaemia.
Q: Self-mutilation (biting lips and fingers) with hyperuricaemia suggests: = Lesch-Nyhan syndrome | Rett's syndrome | Fragile X | Prader-Willi | Down's syndrome
> Lesch-Nyhan — X-linked HGPRT deficiency, severe self-injury, gout.

### Genetic testing in practice
> - Why: closure for families, risk to relatives, identify risk (e.g. 22q11.2 deletion → psychosis).
> - When: intellectual disability (cause found in 40–50%), dysmorphic features, early-onset schizophrenia, family history of a risk CNV, congenital anomalies.
> - Tests: chromosomal microarray, whole-genome sequencing, Fragile X.
> - Treatment: genetic tests for clozapine neutropenia risk exist; pharmacogenomics (antidepressant metaboliser status) is not yet adequate for personalised treatment.
Q: In intellectual disability, genetic testing finds a cause in about: = 40–50% | 5% | 10–15% | 90% | 100%
> 'Intellectual disability (40–50% of cases)/dysmorphic features.'
Q: Which is an indication for genetic testing in psychiatry listed in the lecture? = Early-onset schizophrenia | Late-onset depression | Insomnia | Adjustment disorder | Specific phobia
> Indications: intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, early-onset schizophrenia.
Q: A 22q11.2 deletion is important in psychiatry because it raises the risk of: = Psychosis | Dementia | Eating disorders | Gambling | Insomnia
> 'For psychiatric e.g., 22q11.2 deletion (Di George syndrome) — psychosis.'
Q: The lecture's view of pharmacogenomic antidepressant selection is that it is: = Not yet adequate for personalised treatment | Standard care | Proven superior | Banned | Only for children
> '...not yet adequate for personalized treatment.'

## West Courtyard | Perinatal psychiatry
> Perinatal psychiatry. Source: Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry (no lecture). Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Classification
> - Perinatal ＝ pregnancy + first postnatal year.
> - ICD-11 6E20 (without psychotic symptoms) / 6E21 (with psychotic symptoms) — onset within ~6 weeks of delivery, when no other specific disorder fits.
> - DSM-5-TR: "with peripartum onset" (pregnancy or 4 weeks postpartum).
> - Spectrum: blues → postnatal depression → puerperal psychosis.
Q: The perinatal period in psychiatry refers to: = Pregnancy and the first year after birth | Pregnancy only | The first 6 weeks after birth only | Labour only | The first 5 years of the child's life
> Perinatal ＝ pregnancy and the first postnatal year.
Q: In ICD-11, a postpartum psychotic syndrome not meeting criteria for another specific disorder is coded under: = 6E21 | 6E20 | 6A20 | 6A60 | 6B40
> 6E21 — mental or behavioural disorders associated with pregnancy, childbirth or the puerperium, with psychotic symptoms; 6E20 ＝ without psychotic symptoms.
Q: ICD-11 puerperal disorders (6E2x) apply to syndromes beginning after delivery within about: = 6 weeks | 48 hours | 6 months | 1 year | 2 years
> Onset within about 6 weeks after delivery.
Q: The DSM-5-TR specifier for depression starting in pregnancy or soon after birth is: = With peripartum onset (pregnancy or within 4 weeks after delivery) | With postpartum onset (within 6 months) | With seasonal pattern | With melancholic features | With catatonia
> DSM-5-TR: 'with peripartum onset' — during pregnancy or within 4 weeks of delivery.
Q: If a postpartum woman meets full criteria for bipolar disorder, ICD-11 advises: = Code the specific disorder (bipolar disorder) | Code 6E21 only | Use no diagnosis | Code baby blues | Code adjustment disorder
> 6E2x is used only when no other specific disorder is diagnosable; otherwise code the specific disorder.

### Baby blues
> - 50–80%; day 3–5; tearful, labile, anxious.
> - Resolves by ~day 10–14; reassure, no drugs.
> - > 2 weeks → think postnatal depression.
Q: Baby blues affects approximately what proportion of new mothers? = 50–80% | 1–2 per 1,000 | 5% | 10–15% | 100%
> 50–80% — very common.
Q: Baby blues typically begins on: = Day 3–5 | The day of delivery | Week 3 | Month 3 | Month 6
> Day 3–5, coinciding with hormone fall and onset of lactation.
Q: The correct management of baby blues is: = Reassurance and support | SSRI | Admission | ECT | Lithium
> Self-limiting by about day 10–14 — reassurance, support, rest.
Q: Low mood that persists beyond about 2 weeks postpartum should prompt consideration of: = Postnatal depression | Normal adjustment | Baby blues | Sheehan's syndrome only | Couvade syndrome
> Blues resolve by ~2 weeks; persistence suggests postnatal depression.

### Postnatal depression
> - 10–15%; onset usually within 3 months; guilt about mothering, worry about baby, intrusive harm thoughts.
> - Risks: past/family depression, antenatal depression, poor support, marital conflict/IPV, life events, unwanted pregnancy, preterm/ill infant.
> - EPDS: 10 items, no somatic items, ≥ 13 probable depression; item 10 ＝ self-harm. Whooley questions.
> - Harms mother–infant interaction, child development; fathers 8–10%.
Q: The prevalence of postnatal depression is approximately: = 10–15% | 1–2% | 50% | 80% | 0.1%
> About 10–15% of mothers.
Q: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale has how many items? = 10 | 5 | 9 | 17 | 21
> 10 items, self-rated over the past 7 days.
Q: A distinctive design feature of the EPDS is that it: = Omits somatic items that overlap with normal postpartum changes | Is clinician-rated only | Measures mania | Includes infant weight | Requires a blood test
> It deliberately omits somatic items (sleep, appetite, energy) that are altered after birth anyway.
Q: The commonly used EPDS cut-off for probable depression is: = ≥ 13 | ≥ 3 | ≥ 7 | ≥ 20 | ≥ 30
> ≥ 13 probable depression (≥ 10 possible in many services).
Q: Item 10 of the EPDS asks about: = Thoughts of self-harm | Sleep | Appetite | Bonding | Partner support
> Item 10 — thoughts of harming oneself; any positive response needs assessment.
Q: Which is the strongest predictor of postnatal depression? = Past history of depression or depression in pregnancy | Breastfeeding | Caesarean section alone | Maternal age over 30 | Having a girl
> Previous depression and antenatal depression are among the strongest predictors, with poor support and conflict.
Q: Paternal postnatal depression affects approximately: = 8–10% of fathers | < 1% of fathers | 50% of fathers | None | All fathers briefly
> About 8–10%, more likely when the mother is depressed.
Q: Neonaticide is the killing of a baby: = Within 24 hours of birth | Under 12 months | Under 5 years | In utero | By a stranger
> Within 24 hours of birth — often by young mothers who concealed or denied the pregnancy.
Q: Resnick's classification of filicide includes all EXCEPT: = Economic-compulsive | Altruistic | Acutely psychotic | Unwanted child | Spousal revenge
> Resnick: altruistic, acutely psychotic, unwanted, accidental (fatal maltreatment), spousal revenge.
Q: Untreated maternal depression in low-income settings is associated in the infant with: = Poor growth (stunting) and developmental problems | Faster growth | Higher IQ | No effect | Macrocephaly
> Linked to stunting, insecure attachment and developmental delay.
Q: A carer fabricating or inducing illness in a child is now termed: = Fabricated or induced illness | Munchausen's syndrome | Ganser syndrome | Couvade | Factitious disorder imposed on self
> Fabricated or induced illness (formerly Munchausen's by proxy; DSM: factitious disorder imposed on another).

### Puerperal psychosis
> - 1–2 per 1,000; abrupt, within 2 weeks; insomnia early.
> - Manic/mixed/psychotic depression, confusion and perplexity, delusions about the baby.
> - Bipolar I → 25–50% risk; after a puerperal psychosis, ~50% recurrence in later pregnancy; primiparity.
> - Emergency — suicide, infanticide. Admit (mother-and-baby unit); exclude organic causes; antipsychotic, lithium, ECT.
> - Prevention: care plan; prophylactic lithium/antipsychotic after delivery; protect sleep.
Q: The incidence of puerperal psychosis is about: = 1–2 per 1,000 deliveries | 1 in 10 | 1 in 2 | 1 per 100,000 | 50–80%
> 1–2 per 1,000 deliveries.
Q: Puerperal psychosis typically begins: = Abruptly within the first 2 weeks after delivery | In the first trimester | At 6 months postpartum | Gradually over a year | Only after weaning
> Abrupt onset, usually within 2 weeks (often days 3–10).
Q: Puerperal psychosis is most closely linked to which disorder? = Bipolar disorder | Schizophrenia | OCD | Panic disorder | Personality disorder
> Mostly an affective (bipolar-spectrum) psychosis — mania, mixed states, psychotic depression.
Q: A woman with bipolar I disorder has approximately what risk of postpartum psychosis? = 25–50% | 1% | 5% | 90% | Same as general population
> About 25–50%, higher with previous puerperal psychosis or a family history.
Q: A feature that distinguishes puerperal psychosis from non-puerperal psychosis is: = Confusion, perplexity and rapidly fluctuating symptoms | Gradual onset | Prominent negative symptoms | Absence of mood symptoms | Onset after 1 year
> Confusion, perplexity and fluctuation ('delirium-like') with prominent mood features.
Q: After one episode of puerperal psychosis, the recurrence risk after a subsequent delivery is about: = 50% | 5% | 15% | 90% | 0%
> About 50%.
Q: The preferred setting for admission of a mother with puerperal psychosis is: = Mother-and-baby unit | General adult ward without the baby | Maternity ward with no psychiatric input | Home without support | Prison
> A mother-and-baby unit keeps mother and infant together with specialist care.
Q: A rapidly effective treatment for severe puerperal psychosis with food refusal is: = ECT | Psychodynamic therapy | Watchful waiting | St John's wort | Hormone replacement only
> ECT acts quickly and is highly effective in severe puerperal illness.
Q: An early warning sign of puerperal psychosis is: = Severe insomnia | Excessive sleep | Weight gain | Craving sweets | Good appetite
> Insomnia is often the earliest sign; protecting sleep is preventive.
Q: Which factor increases the risk of puerperal psychosis? = Primiparity (first delivery) | Multiparity | Older paternal age only | Breastfeeding | Epidural anaesthesia
> First deliveries, bipolar history, family history and sleep loss raise risk.

### In pregnancy
> - Antenatal depression/anxiety → preterm birth, low birth weight, predicts PND.
> - Tokophobia (fear of childbirth): primary/secondary.
> - Hyperemesis → Wernicke's (thiamine).
> - Pseudocyesis (false pregnancy with physical signs) vs delusion of pregnancy vs couvade (partner's symptoms).
> - Denial of pregnancy → risk of neonaticide.
Q: Intense fear of childbirth is called: = Tokophobia | Pseudocyesis | Couvade | Hyperemesis | Gynophobia
> Tokophobia — primary (no previous birth) or secondary (after traumatic birth).
Q: A false belief of being pregnant WITH physical signs such as abdominal distension and amenorrhoea is: = Pseudocyesis | Delusion of pregnancy | Couvade syndrome | Denial of pregnancy | Tokophobia
> Pseudocyesis — physical signs present; a delusion of pregnancy has no physical signs.
Q: Couvade syndrome is: = The partner experiencing pregnancy symptoms | Denial of pregnancy | Fear of childbirth | Delusion of infidelity | Postnatal psychosis in fathers
> Couvade — the expectant father develops pregnancy-like symptoms.
Q: Severe hyperemesis gravidarum can cause which neuropsychiatric complication? = Wernicke's encephalopathy | Huntington's disease | NMS | Serotonin syndrome | Tardive dyskinesia
> Vomiting → thiamine deficiency → Wernicke's encephalopathy.
Q: Untreated antenatal depression is associated with: = Preterm birth and low birth weight | Post-term pregnancy only | Macrosomia | Twins | No effects
> Linked to preterm birth, low birth weight, and later postnatal depression.
Q: Denial of pregnancy is particularly associated with a risk of: = Neonaticide and unassisted delivery | Twin pregnancy | Hyperemesis | Tokophobia | Gestational diabetes
> Concealed/denied pregnancy → unassisted birth and neonaticide risk.
Q: Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder features include: = Smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures, growth and cognitive impairment | Macrocephaly | Ebstein's anomaly | Polydactyly | Cleft foot
> Classic facial triad: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures, plus growth and neurodevelopmental problems.

### Drugs in pregnancy
> - Valproate: avoid (NTD, ~10% malformations, ↓IQ, autism) — pregnancy prevention programme; folic acid 5 mg on antiepileptics.
> - Carbamazepine: NTD ~1%; induces → OCP failure.
> - Lithium: Ebstein's anomaly (small absolute risk); foetal echo; levels fall in pregnancy, rise after delivery → reduce/withhold in labour; neonatal toxicity, hypothyroidism.
> - Lamotrigine: relatively safe; levels fall in pregnancy.
> - SSRIs (sertraline); paroxetine → cardiac defects; late exposure → neonatal adaptation syndrome, PPHN.
> - Antipsychotics: olanzapine/clozapine → gestational diabetes.
> - Benzodiazepines: ?cleft palate; floppy infant, withdrawal.
> - Never stop abruptly on discovering pregnancy; lowest effective dose, monotherapy.
Q: A woman with bipolar disorder on lithium discovers she is 8 weeks pregnant. The best immediate advice is: = Do not stop abruptly; urgent specialist review to weigh relapse vs foetal risk | Stop lithium abruptly today | Double the dose | Switch to valproate | Terminate the pregnancy
> Abrupt cessation sharply raises relapse risk; review urgently and plan with the woman.
Q: The general principle for psychotropic prescribing in pregnancy is: = Lowest effective dose of the agent with the best safety record, preferably monotherapy | Polypharmacy at high doses | Always stop all drugs | Use newest drugs first | Switch drugs every trimester
> Lowest effective dose, best-known safety, monotherapy, with multidisciplinary planning.
Q: Pre-conception counselling for women with severe mental illness mainly aims to: = Plan the balance of relapse risk against medication risk before conception | Discourage all pregnancy | Start valproate | Arrange sterilisation | Avoid antenatal care
> Plan ahead: relapse risk vs medication risk, folic acid, and a perinatal care plan.
Q: Which antipsychotic-related complication should be monitored for in pregnant women on olanzapine or clozapine? = Gestational diabetes | Hypocalcaemia | Hyperkalaemia | Thrombocytosis | Hypothyroidism
> Gestational diabetes and weight gain — monitor glucose.
Q: Valproate exposure in pregnancy is associated with: = Neural tube defects and reduced IQ/autism | Ebstein's anomaly | Grey baby syndrome | Tooth discolouration | No risk
> NTDs, ~10% malformations, lower IQ, autism, ADHD — avoid in women of childbearing potential.
Q: Lithium in the first trimester is linked to: = Ebstein's anomaly | Spina bifida | Cleft lip only | Phocomelia | Anencephaly
> Ebstein's anomaly (tricuspid malformation) — small absolute risk; offer foetal echocardiography.
Q: During pregnancy, serum lithium levels tend to: = Fall, because renal clearance increases | Rise | Stay exactly the same | Become unmeasurable | Rise only in the first week
> Clearance rises → levels fall; monitor more often. After delivery levels rise sharply.
Q: At the onset of labour, a woman on lithium should: = Have lithium reduced or withheld and levels checked, because levels rise after delivery | Double the dose | Start valproate | Stop all fluids | Take an extra dose
> Post-delivery fluid shifts → toxicity risk; withhold/reduce at labour and recheck.
Q: Which SSRI is associated with first-trimester cardiac septal defects and is usually avoided in pregnancy? = Paroxetine | Sertraline | Citalopram | Fluoxetine | Escitalopram
> Paroxetine — cardiac malformations; sertraline is often preferred.
Q: Late-pregnancy SSRI exposure is associated with: = Neonatal adaptation syndrome and a small risk of PPHN | Ebstein's anomaly | Neural tube defects | Floppy infant syndrome only | Foetal alcohol syndrome
> Neonatal adaptation syndrome (mild, brief) and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (small risk).
Q: Women taking antiepileptic mood stabilisers who may conceive should take folic acid at a dose of: = 5 mg daily | 400 micrograms | 50 mg daily | None | 1 g weekly
> High-dose folic acid 5 mg daily.
Q: Benzodiazepines used late in pregnancy can cause: = Floppy infant syndrome and neonatal withdrawal | Ebstein's anomaly | Neural tube defects | Gestational diabetes | Grey baby syndrome
> Floppy infant syndrome, neonatal withdrawal; possible small cleft-palate risk (evidence inconsistent).
Q: Carbamazepine in a woman using the combined oral contraceptive may cause: = Contraceptive failure via enzyme induction | Increased contraceptive levels | No interaction | Lithium toxicity | Hyperprolactinaemia
> Enzyme induction → reduced OCP efficacy; also NTD risk (~1%) in pregnancy.
Q: Lamotrigine levels during pregnancy typically: = Fall, because clearance increases | Rise sharply | Do not change | Become toxic in the first trimester | Cannot be measured
> Clearance increases → levels fall; may need dose adjustment and post-delivery reduction.

### Breastfeeding
> - Sertraline, paroxetine — low infant levels (preferred); avoid fluoxetine (long half-life).
> - Olanzapine, quetiapine OK; clozapine — avoid (agranulocytosis).
> - Lithium — avoid or monitor infant closely.
> - Short-acting benzodiazepines; caution in premature infants.
> - Share night feeds to protect sleep in bipolar disorder.
Q: Which antidepressants are preferred during breastfeeding because of low infant levels? = Sertraline and paroxetine | Fluoxetine and doxepin | Phenelzine | Lithium | Bupropion and doxepin
> Sertraline and paroxetine — very low infant levels. Avoid fluoxetine (long half-life) and doxepin.
Q: Which antipsychotic should be avoided in breastfeeding because of agranulocytosis risk to the infant? = Clozapine | Olanzapine | Quetiapine | Haloperidol | Aripiprazole
> Clozapine — risk of infant agranulocytosis and sedation.
Q: Lithium during breastfeeding is: = Generally avoided, or used only with close infant monitoring | Completely safe without monitoring | Preferred first line | Safe only in premature babies | Required for all bipolar mothers
> Infant levels can be substantial — avoid or monitor closely (levels, thyroid, renal, hydration).
Q: For a breastfeeding mother with bipolar disorder, a useful practical measure is to: = Share night feeds (expressed milk/formula) to protect her sleep | Do all night feeds herself | Stop all sleep | Stop breastfeeding immediately in every case | Use caffeine at night
> Protect sleep — sleep loss triggers relapse.
Q: Infants needing extra caution when the mother takes psychotropics while breastfeeding are those who are: = Premature or unwell | Over 6 months and healthy | Formula-fed | Male | Twins only
> Premature or sick infants metabolise drugs less well.

### Treatment and context
> - Mild–moderate: CBT, IPT, support; moderate–severe: + antidepressant; ECT safe.
> - WHO Thinking Healthy Programme — CBT by community health workers (Pakistan).
> - Brexanolone (IV) / zuranolone (oral) — GABA-A modulators for PPD.
> - Perinatal OCD: ego-dystonic harm thoughts — very low risk; CBT/ERP.
> - Postpartum thyroiditis, Sheehan's (PPH), eclampsia, CVST, sepsis — organic mimics.
> - Nigeria: spiritual attributions, stigma; omugwo support; EPDS at antenatal/immunisation visits; task-shifting (mhGAP).
Q: First-line treatment for mild-to-moderate postnatal depression is: = Psychological therapy such as CBT or IPT | ECT | Lithium | Antipsychotics | Admission
> Psychological therapy (CBT, IPT), guided self-help and support; add an antidepressant if moderate–severe.
Q: The WHO Thinking Healthy Programme is: = A CBT-based intervention for perinatal depression delivered by community health workers | A drug trial | An inpatient programme | A screening tool | A breastfeeding guide
> CBT-based, delivered by community health workers; first tested in Pakistan.
Q: Brexanolone and zuranolone, licensed for postpartum depression, act as: = GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulators | SSRIs | Dopamine antagonists | NMDA agonists | MAO inhibitors
> Neurosteroid analogues — GABA-A positive allosteric modulators; brexanolone IV, zuranolone oral.
Q: Regarding ECT in pregnancy: = It is safe and can be used for severe illness | It is absolutely contraindicated | It causes miscarriage in most | It is only allowed after delivery | It requires termination first
> ECT is safe in pregnancy and the puerperium with obstetric and anaesthetic input.
Q: A new mother has distressing, unwanted intrusive thoughts of harming her baby, which horrify her, and she avoids bathing the baby. The most likely diagnosis and risk is: = Perinatal OCD; very low risk of acting on the thoughts | Puerperal psychosis; high risk | Psychopathy; high risk | Baby blues; no treatment | Delusional disorder
> Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts ＝ perinatal OCD; the risk of acting is very low. Treat with CBT/ERP ± SSRI.
Q: Failure of lactation and amenorrhoea after a major postpartum haemorrhage suggests: = Sheehan's syndrome | Postpartum thyroiditis | Baby blues | Couvade | Pseudocyesis
> Sheehan's syndrome — pituitary infarction after PPH.
Q: A woman develops anxiety and palpitations at 3 months postpartum, then low mood and fatigue at 5 months. The investigation to do is: = Thyroid function tests | EEG | Lumbar puncture | Chest X-ray | Urine drug screen only
> Postpartum thyroiditis — hyperthyroid then hypothyroid phase; check TFTs.
Q: Which organic cause must be excluded in postpartum confusion with headache and seizures? = Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or eclampsia | Baby blues | Tokophobia | Couvade | Perinatal OCD
> Eclampsia, CVST, sepsis, drug withdrawal are key organic mimics.
Q: A useful point for screening Nigerian mothers for perinatal depression is: = Antenatal clinic and infant immunisation visits | Only at psychiatric hospitals | Only at church | At school enrolment | During labour
> Antenatal and immunisation visits reach most mothers; use the EPDS and link to care.
Q: Expanding access to perinatal mental health care in Nigeria with few specialists relies on: = Task-shifting to trained primary health workers and midwives | Building more asylums | Only private psychiatrists | Ignoring mild cases | Herbal remedies only
> Task-shifting (e.g. WHO mhGAP, Thinking Healthy-type programmes).
Q: The Igbo postpartum practice in which the mother's mother comes to help is called: = Omugwo | Ogbanje | Iwa | Juju | Egungun
> Omugwo — practical support that can protect against postnatal depression.

## Long Red Ward | Old age psychiatry
> Old age psychiatry. Source: National-Old Age Psychiatry-02-2026.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Amnestic syndrome
> - Specific impairment of episodic memory with functional impairment; medial temporal lobe ± thalamus/diencephalon damage.
> - Anterograde ＝ can't learn new; retrograde ＝ can't recall past.
> - Transient: transient global amnesia, head injury, alcoholic blackout, post-ECT, PTSD, fugue, crime-related amnesia.
> - Persistent: Korsakoff (most common), encephalitis, posterior cerebral artery/thalamic stroke, head injury.
> - Potentially reversible: Wernicke's from thiamine deficiency — low red-cell transketolase; MRI thalamus and mammillary bodies. Give thiamine urgently, rehydrate, feed, treat withdrawal.
Q: 'Organic mental disorders' are now better known as: = Neurocognitive disorders | Functional disorders | Psychotic disorders | Neurodevelopmental disorders | Somatoform disorders
> 'Organic Mental Disorders: Now better known as Neurocognitive disorders.'
Q: Which is listed as a common mental health need in older people? = Delirium | ADHD | Conduct disorder | Anorexia nervosa | Enuresis
> Depression, dementia, delirium, comorbidities.
Q: Amnestic syndrome is a specific impairment of: = Episodic memory | Semantic memory | Procedural memory | Working memory only | Sensory memory
> 'Specific impairment in episodic memory leading to impairment in functioning.'
Q: The pathology of amnestic syndrome involves the medial temporal lobe and: = Thalamus or other diencephalic structures | Cerebellum | Occipital cortex | Spinal cord | Pons
> 'Damage to the medial temporal lobe... Thalamus or other diencephalic structures are also implicated.'
Q: Inability to learn new information is: = Anterograde amnesia | Retrograde amnesia | Confabulation | Agnosia | Aphasia
> Anterograde: unable to learn new information. Retrograde: unable to recall past events.
Q: The most common type of persistent amnestic syndrome is: = Korsakoff syndrome | Transient global amnesia | Post-ECT amnesia | Dissociative fugue | Alcoholic blackout
> 'Korsakov syndrome (Most common type).'
Q: Which is a cause of transient amnesia in the lecture? = Post-ECT | Encephalitis | Korsakoff syndrome | Posterior cerebral artery stroke | Alzheimer's
> Transient: head injury, alcoholic blackout, post-ECT, PTSD, dissociative fugue, crime-related amnesia.
Q: A stroke in which territory can cause persistent amnesia? = Posterior cerebral artery or thalamus | Anterior cerebral artery | Middle cerebral artery only | Basilar tip only | Spinal artery
> 'Stroke (posterior cerebral artery, or thalamus).'
Q: A laboratory marker of thiamine deficiency is reduced: = Red-cell transketolase | Serum B12 | Ferritin | Folate | Albumin
> 'Reduced RBC transketolase level (Marker for thiamine deficiency).'
Q: MRI in Wernicke's encephalopathy shows symmetrical signal changes in the thalamus and: = Mammillary bodies | Frontal poles | Occipital lobes | Cerebellar hemispheres only | Corpus callosum only
> 'Symmetrical signal abnormalities in areas of the thalamus, mammillary bodies, other midline brain structures.'
Q: In suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy you should: = Treat urgently with thiamine while awaiting investigation results | Wait for MRI before treatment | Give glucose first | Start donepezil | Give haloperidol
> 'Treat urgently with thiamine while awaiting investigation results.'
Q: The lecture stresses that amnestic syndrome is: = Potentially reversible | Always permanent | Always psychogenic | Untreatable | Only in the young
> 'Amnestic syndrome is potentially reversible! Investigate the cause.'

### Dementia: types and numbers
> - Progressive cognitive impairment that affects everyday function (ADL/IADL); behaviour and personality change with progression.
> - Alzheimer's 60–65%, vascular 20–25%, Lewy body 15%, FTLD < 5%.
> - Natural history: cognition → function → behaviour → institutionalisation and death.
> - Indianapolis 4.8% vs Ibadan 2.3%; prevalence doubles every 5 years after 65.
> - SSA (Ojagbemi 2021): pooled prevalence 5% (West Africa 2%, East/Central 6%), incidence 2%; age ＝ dominant risk, low education ＝ dominant modifiable risk. Low rates may reflect premature mortality and a resilient survivor population.
> - Scales: ADCS-ADL, MMSE, MoCA, NPI; trajectories — slow, stepwise (vascular), rapidly progressive.
Q: Alzheimer's disease accounts for what proportion of dementia? = 60–65% | 10–15% | 20–25% | 40% | 90%
> AD 60–65%, vascular 20–25%, Lewy body 15%, FTLD < 5%.
Q: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration accounts for: = < 5% | 15% | 25% | 40% | 60%
> 'Frontotemporal lobal degeneration (< 5%).'
Q: The final stage in the natural history of dementia is: = Institutionalisation and death | Cognitive impairment | Functional disability | Behavioural disturbance | Recovery
> 1. Cognitive → 2. Functional → 3. Behavioural → 4. Institutionalisation and death.
Q: For a diagnosis of dementia, the cognitive impairment must lead to: = Impairment in everyday functioning (ADL/IADL) | Psychosis | Depression | Hospital admission | Seizures
> '...the cognitive impairment should lead to impairment in physical functioning (i.e., IADL or ADL).'
Q: A 'stepwise' trajectory of decline is most typical of: = Vascular dementia | Normal ageing | Alzheimer's disease | Depression | Delirium
> Stepwise decline with each vascular event — vascular dementia.
Q: In the Indianapolis–Ibadan comparison, dementia prevalence in Ibadan was: = 2.3% | 0.5% | 4.8% | 10% | 15%
> Indianapolis 4.8% vs Ibadan 2.3% — may be commoner in more developed societies.
Q: After age 65, dementia prevalence: = Doubles every 5 years | Stays constant | Halves every 5 years | Doubles every 20 years | Falls
> 'Prevalence doubles every 5 years after the age of 65 years.'
Q: The pooled prevalence of dementia in sub-Saharan Africa (Ojagbemi 2021) was: = 5% | 1% | 2% | 10% | 20%
> Pooled prevalence 5% — 2% in West Africa, 6% in East and Central Africa; incidence 2%.
Q: In SSA, the dominant modifiable risk factor for dementia is: = Low education | Smoking | Alcohol | Obesity | Air pollution
> 'Age as the dominant risk factor; Low education as the dominant modifiable factor.'
Q: A key possible driver of relatively low dementia rates in SSA is: = Premature mortality | Better diet | Genetic immunity | More screening | Lower stress
> 'Premature mortality a problem in SSA — potential key driver of relatively low rates of dementia.'
Q: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations and parkinsonism suggest: = Dementia with Lewy bodies | Alzheimer's disease | Vascular dementia | FTD | Korsakoff
> Core DLB features: fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder. Avoid typical antipsychotics (severe sensitivity).
Q: Early disinhibition and personality change with relatively preserved memory suggests: = Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia | Alzheimer's | Lewy body dementia | Vascular dementia | Delirium
> bvFTD — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, hyperorality; memory relatively spared early.
Q: Depressive pseudodementia is suggested by: = 'Don't know' answers, rapid onset and prominent mood symptoms | Insidious onset over years | Confabulation | Visual hallucinations | Stepwise decline
> Pseudodementia: rapid onset, 'don't know' answers, patient complains of memory loss, depressive features; improves with treatment.

### Preventing dementia
> - Lancet Commission 2024: 45% preventable by tackling 14 modifiable factors — diabetes, LDL cholesterol, hypertension, smoking, obesity, air pollution, head injury, depression, inactivity, alcohol, low education, hearing loss, vision loss, social isolation.
> - SSA prevalent dementia: older age, family history, poor social engagement, hypertension, early parental loss, recent change of residence, female sex, no education.
> - SSA incident dementia: low formal education (biggest), low cognitive reserve, rural residence, hypertension, cholesterol, smoking.
Q: The Lancet Commission (2024) estimated that what proportion of dementia could be prevented? = 45% | 10% | 25% | 75% | 90%
> '45% of dementia could be prevented by eliminating 14 modifiable risk factors.'
Q: How many modifiable risk factors does the 2024 Lancet Commission list? = 14 | 9 | 12 | 20 | 5
> 14 — including the newer additions LDL cholesterol and vision loss.
Q: Which is one of the Lancet Commission's modifiable risk factors? = Hearing loss | Older age | Female sex | Family history | APOE e4
> Hearing loss (and vision loss, isolation, air pollution...). Age, sex and genes are not modifiable.
Q: In the SSA meta-analysis, the factor carrying most weight for incident dementia was: = Low formal education | Smoking | Cholesterol | Rural residence | Hypertension
> Low formal education (32.6%), then low cognitive reserve (20.5%), rural residence (9.6%).
Q: Which was associated with prevalent dementia in SSA? = Early parental loss | High education | Urban residence only | Male sex | Vegetarian diet
> Older age, family history, poor social engagement, hypertension, early parental loss, recent change of residence, female sex, no education...

### Imaging in dementia
> - Uses: exclude pseudodementia; tell AD, FTD, DLB apart.
> - CT: atrophy, ventricular enlargement; vascular vs Alzheimer's.
> - MRI: hippocampal atrophy (AD), caudate/putamen (Huntington's), temporal lobe (FTLD).
> - SPECT: posterior temporo-parietal hypoperfusion (AD); patchy multiple defects (vascular).
> - PET: reduced glucose metabolism in AD and DLB.
Q: On MRI, Alzheimer's disease characteristically shows atrophy of the: = Hippocampus | Caudate | Cerebellum | Occipital lobe | Pons
> 'Hippocampal atrophy in AD, putamen/caudate atrophy in Huntington's, temporal lobe in FTLD.'
Q: SPECT in Alzheimer's typically shows perfusion defects in the: = Posterior temporal and parietal lobes | Frontal poles | Occipital lobes | Cerebellum | Brainstem
> 'Asymmetrical perfusion defect in the posterior temporal and parietal lobes in Alzheimer's.'
Q: Multiple patchy perfusion defects on SPECT suggest: = Vascular dementia | Alzheimer's | FTD | Normal ageing | Depression
> '...multiple patchy perfusion defects in vascular dementia.'
Q: One use of neuroimaging in suspected dementia is to: = Eliminate pseudodementia | Prove depression | Measure IQ | Diagnose personality disorder | Replace history
> 'May be used to eliminate pseudodementia; to distinguish between AD, FTD and DLB.'
Q: Which imaging type measures cerebral glucose metabolism? = PET | CT | MRI | SPECT | EEG
> PET — reduced local cerebral glucose metabolism in AD and DLB.

### Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD)
> - Up to 97% (Steinberg 2008); distressing; worsen outcome.
> - NPI: 12 domains, frequency (1–4) × severity (1–3) ＝ 1–12 each, total 0–144; carer distress 0–5 (total 0–60).
> - Apathy ~50% — no dysphoria or vegetative symptoms; responds to cholinesterase inhibitors (depression responds to SSRIs).
> - Depression 40–50% (10–20% moderate–severe); may predate dementia; carers stay depressed up to 5 years after the death.
> - Psychosis 41% in AD (Ropacki & Jeste): 23% delusions, 5% hallucinations, 13% both.
> - Aripiprazole best efficacy–safety balance; olanzapine least benefit; USA: no licensed antipsychotic; only risperidone licensed in UK/EU/Canada.
> - Most burdensome: screaming, aggression, wandering, night-time waking, uncooperativeness, suspiciousness.
Q: Prevalence of BPSD may reach: = 97% | 20% | 50% | 75% | 100% always
> 'Prevalence of BPSD may reach up to 97% (Steinberg 2008).'
Q: The Neuropsychiatric Inventory assesses behavioural disturbance in how many domains? = 12 | 6 | 10 | 20 | 30
> 12 domains, from a caregiver interview.
Q: The maximum NPI total frequency × severity score is: = 144 | 12 | 36 | 60 | 200
> 12 domains × (4 × 3 ＝ 12) ＝ 144.
Q: Apathy in dementia differs from depression in that apathy lacks: = Dysphoria and vegetative symptoms | Reduced motivation | Withdrawal | Reduced activity | Flat affect
> 'Similar to depression, but without dysphoria and vegetative symptoms.'
Q: Apathy in dementia responds best to: = Cholinesterase inhibitors | SSRIs | Benzodiazepines | Antipsychotics | Lithium
> 'Apathy responds to cholinesterase inhibitors while depression responds to antidepressants.'
Q: Depressive symptoms occur in what proportion of people with dementia? = 40–50% | 5–10% | 80% | 97% | 1%
> 'Depression symptoms occur in 40–50% of dementia, 10–20% moderate to severe.'
Q: Depression in caregivers of people with dementia may persist for up to: = 5 years after death | 1 month after death | 6 months after death | Only during caring | 20 years
> '...continues to be present up to 5 years after death of the subject.'
Q: Prevalence of psychosis in Alzheimer's disease (Ropacki & Jeste 2005) is: = 41% | 5% | 15% | 70% | 90%
> 41% — 23% delusions, 5% hallucinations, 13% both.
Q: Which antipsychotic appears to give the best balance of efficacy and safety in dementia? = Aripiprazole | Olanzapine | Haloperidol | Chlorpromazine | Clozapine
> 'Aripiprazole appears to provide the best balance between efficacy and safety. Olanzapine provide the least benefit.'
Q: Which antipsychotic is indicated for psychosis/agitation in dementia in the UK, EU and Canada? = Risperidone | Quetiapine | Olanzapine | Aripiprazole | None
> 'Only risperidone is indicated in the UK, EU and Canada.' In the USA, none is licensed.
Q: Which BPSD is listed among those most associated with caregiver burden? = Screaming | Euphoria | Hyperphagia | Hypersomnia | Talkativeness
> Screaming, physical aggression, wandering, depression, uncooperativeness, suspiciousness, not sleeping at night.
Q: The commonest delusions in Alzheimer's psychosis are: = Persecutory and misidentification | Grandiose | Nihilistic only | Erotomanic | Religious
> '23% delusions (persecutory and misidentification).'
Q: Antipsychotics in people with dementia increase the risk of: = Stroke and death | Hypoglycaemia | Hair loss | Cataract | Hearing loss
> Antipsychotics in dementia raise stroke and mortality risk — lowest dose, shortest time, regular review.

### Treating dementia
> - Kitwood's person-centred care — keep "personhood"; see the person, not the disease.
> - Structured psychological approach: diagnosis, course, driving, legal and property matters; share caregiving (not just the oldest female).
> - Cholinesterase inhibitors: donepezil, rivastigmine (licensed for Lewy body and Parkinson's dementia), galantamine (mild–moderate).
> - Memantine — NMDA blocker, reduces excitotoxicity and agitation.
> - Anti-amyloid antibodies (aducanumab, lecanemab, donanemab): mild AD, questionable efficacy, brain microhaemorrhages.
> - BPSD: first exclude pain, constipation, infection, dehydration, delirium; carer ＝ second patient; walks, music, photos; drugs — risperidone (psychosis/aggression), brexpiprazole (agitation), citalopram/memantine (agitation), methylphenidate (apathy).
> - Therapies: reminiscence, validation, reality orientation, cognitive stimulation (theme) / training (domain) / rehabilitation (impairment), doll therapy, Snoezelen, music.
Q: Person-centred care in dementia was developed by: = Tom Kitwood | Kraepelin | Bleuler | Folstein | Alzheimer
> Tom Kitwood — maintaining 'personhood'.
Q: The goal of person-centred care is to: = Maintain 'personhood' despite declining capacity | Slow the disease | Reduce costs | Increase medication | Avoid families
> 'The goal... is to maintain personhood in the face of diminishing intellectual and functional capacity.'
Q: On caregiving, the lecture emphasises that it should: = Be shared and not left to a single individual | Be left to the oldest female | Be done only by nurses | Be avoided | Be paid for
> '...caregiving should be shared and not left to a single individual (who in many cases is the oldest female).'
Q: Which cholinesterase inhibitor is approved for Lewy body and Parkinson's disease dementia? = Rivastigmine | Donepezil | Galantamine | Memantine | Lecanemab
> 'Rivastigmine (Exelon): Approved for Lewy body and Parkinson's disease dementia.'
Q: Memantine works by: = Blocking glutamate (NMDA) receptors, reducing excitotoxicity | Inhibiting cholinesterase | Removing amyloid | Blocking dopamine | Raising serotonin
> 'Glutamate receptor blocker: memantine (Reduces neuronal excitotoxicity leading to reduce agitation).'
Q: A recognised side effect of anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) is: = Brain microhaemorrhages | Weight gain | Agranulocytosis | Hyperprolactinaemia | QT prolongation
> 'Brain microhaemorrhages as side effects.' Approved for mild AD; questionable efficacy.
Q: Galantamine is approved for: = Mild to moderate dementia | Severe dementia only | Lewy body dementia only | Delirium | Depression
> 'Galantamine (approved for mild to moderate dementia).'
Q: Before treating BPSD with drugs, which should be excluded? = Pain, constipation, infection, dehydration, delirium | High IQ | Good appetite | Family support | Hearing aids
> Consider pain, constipation/faecal impaction, infection, injury, dehydration, nutrition, delirium.
Q: The lecture describes the caregiver as: = Potentially a second patient | A nuisance | Irrelevant to treatment | Responsible for the illness | A legal guardian only
> 'The caregiver is potentially a second patient.'
Q: Which drug may be beneficial for apathy in dementia? = Methylphenidate | Haloperidol | Diazepam | Lithium | Carbamazepine
> 'Methylphenidate may be beneficial for Apathy.'
Q: Which drug is named for agitation in dementia? = Brexpiprazole | Fluoxetine | Donepezil | Lamotrigine | Clonazepam
> 'Brexpiprazole for agitation.' Also citalopram and memantine may help agitation.
Q: Guided practice with memory aids such as calendars and diaries is: = Cognitive training | Cognitive stimulation | Cognitive rehabilitation | Reminiscence therapy | Validation therapy
> Cognitive training — related to a cognitive domain. Stimulation ＝ theme; rehabilitation ＝ impairment.
Q: Teaching a person to cook a meal because they have lost the ability is: = Cognitive rehabilitation | Cognitive stimulation | Cognitive training | Reality orientation | Aromatherapy
> 'Cognitive rehabilitation (Related to an impairment: e.g., Teaching the person to cook a meal).'
Q: The 'life story approach' is a form of: = Reminiscence therapy | Snoezelen | Doll therapy | Aromatherapy | Acupuncture
> 'Reminiscence therapy (e.g., life story approach).'
Q: Snoezelen is a: = Multisensory environment therapy for BPSD | Drug | Memory test | Brain scan | Herbal remedy
> Snoezelen — a multisensory room; one of the novel non-pharmacological approaches to BPSD.
Q: A common contraindication/caution for cholinesterase inhibitors is: = Bradycardia / heart block | Hypertension | Diabetes | Hypothyroidism | Obesity
> Cholinergic effects → bradycardia, heart block, syncope; also GI upset, vivid dreams.

### Psychosis and personality in later life
> - Primary psychosis ~0.5%; causes: dementia ~40%, depression 33%, delirium ~7%, mania ~5% (often medical), delusional disorder 2%, schizophrenia 1%.
> - Earlier-onset schizophrenia in old age: 80–85% began before 45; ~50% improve, only ~15% worsen; cognition worsens.
> - Very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis (≥ 60): neurodegenerative, female, brain abnormalities, persecutory and partition delusions, visual/tactile/olfactory hallucinations, sensory impairment, tardive dyskinesia risk.
> - Personality disorder stable or less in old age but rigidity/suspicion increase; triggered by loss, long-term care, trauma re-enactment, alcohol/prescription drugs.
> - Approach: tailor; MDT; few need admission; continuity with the same team.
Q: The commonest cause of psychosis in older people is: = Dementia | Schizophrenia | Delirium | Mania | Delusional disorder
> 'Dementia is the commonest cause of psychoses in older people (~40%).'
Q: What proportion of older people with schizophrenia had onset before age 45? = 80–85% | 20–25% | 50% | 100% | 10%
> '80–85% of older people with schizophrenia had onset before age 45 years.'
Q: With ageing, what proportion with earlier-onset schizophrenia recover or improve? = ~50% | ~15% | ~30% | ~85% | None
> '~50% attain recovery or show improvement in old age. Only ~15% get worse.'
Q: Very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis begins at age: = ≥ 60 | ≥ 30 | ≥ 45 | ≥ 80 | Any age
> ≥ 60 years, considered neurodegenerative.
Q: Which is characteristic of very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis? = Partition delusions and sensory abnormalities | Male preponderance | Negative symptoms dominate | No hallucinations | Neurodevelopmental cause
> Female preponderance, brain abnormalities, persecutory and partition delusions, visual/tactile/olfactory hallucinations, sensory abnormalities, TD risk.
Q: Which cognitive feature tends to change with ageing in schizophrenia? = Cognitive symptoms often worsen | Cognition always improves | IQ rises | Memory normalises | No change
> 'Cognitive symptoms often worsen with ageing.'
Q: In later life, personality disorders tend to: = Remain stable or decrease, though rigidity or suspicion may increase | Get much worse | Disappear completely | Become psychotic | Change type
> 'Personality disorders tend to remain stable or decrease in later life — Rigid behaviour or suspicion may increase.'
Q: Which is a reason personality disorder may present clinically in later life? = Moving to long-term care | Getting a promotion | Marriage | Starting school | Puberty
> Loss of a significant other, stabilising situation or social roles, trauma re-enactment, alcohol/prescription drugs, move to long-term care.
Q: In the general approach to older patients, admission is needed for: = Only a minority — severe behavioural disturbance or immediate risk | Most patients | All dementias | All depression | Anyone over 80
> 'Only a minority of older people will require hospital admission — severe behavioural disturbances, immediate risk.'
