### Bonus drill: Delirium & dementia
> Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, with cognitive change, caused by a medical condition, a substance, or withdrawal.
> - Subtypes: hyperactive, hypoactive (most often missed) and mixed.
> Dementia is a chronic, progressive decline in two or more cognitive domains, enough to impair independence. Delirium on top of dementia is common.
> Know each dementia by its signature: Alzheimer's (early memory loss), vascular (stepwise decline), Lewy body (fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism), frontotemporal (behaviour and language first).
Q: Hallmark of delirium = Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness | Acute, stable impairment of memory with clear consciousness :: Delirium fluctuates, and attention and awareness are impaired | Gradual disturbance of attention over months :: Delirium develops over hours to days | Acute psychosis in clear consciousness :: Clear consciousness points away from delirium
> Inattention is the core sign. Test it with months of the year backwards or digit span.
S: CAM (Confusion Assessment Method) features = Acute onset and fluctuating course | Inattention | Disorganised thinking | Altered level of consciousness ~~ Visual hallucinations :: Common in delirium but not a CAM feature | Memory loss over months :: That suggests dementia | Low mood :: Not a CAM feature
> CAM-positive = feature 1 + feature 2 + either feature 3 or feature 4.
Q: Bedside delirium screening tool = CAM (Confusion Assessment Method) | AMTS :: The Abbreviated Mental Test is a cognitive screen, not delirium-specific | MoCA :: The MoCA screens cognition, not delirium | GCS :: The Glasgow Coma Scale rates level of consciousness only
> The 4AT is another quick tool: Alertness, AMT4, Attention (months backwards), and acute change.
Q: Delirium subtype most often missed = Hypoactive | Hyperactive :: Agitation makes this one obvious | Mixed :: Fluctuating agitation usually gets noticed | Catatonic :: Not a standard delirium subtype
> A quiet, withdrawn older patient may be labelled depressed. Hypoactive delirium has the worse outcomes.
Q: Commonest cause of dementia = Alzheimer's disease | Vascular dementia :: Second commonest | Lewy body dementia :: Less common than Alzheimer's | Frontotemporal dementia :: More common in younger-onset dementia, but not overall
> Alzheimer's pathology: amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles. It starts in the medial temporal lobe (hippocampus), so early memory loss is typical.
S: The 4 As of Alzheimer's disease = Amnesia => Impaired memory | Aphasia => Impaired language | Agnosia => Failure to recognise familiar objects despite adequate sensation | Apraxia => Difficulty performing learned purposeful actions despite adequate motor ability ~~ Ataxia => Impaired coordination of movement :: Not one of the 4 As | Alogia => Reduced quantity of speech :: A negative symptom of schizophrenia | Anhedonia => Loss of pleasure in previously enjoyable activities :: A depressive symptom | Akathisia => Subjective inner restlessness with a need to move :: An antipsychotic side effect
> Amnesia (memory), aphasia (language), agnosia (recognition), apraxia (skilled movement).
S: Core features of dementia with Lewy bodies = Fluctuating cognition | Recurrent visual hallucinations | REM sleep behaviour disorder | Parkinsonism ~~ Early prominent memory loss :: Typical of Alzheimer's disease | Stepwise decline :: Typical of vascular dementia | Chorea :: Typical of Huntington's disease | Early disinhibition :: Typical of frontotemporal dementia
> McKeith 2017 consensus: two or more core features = probable DLB.
Q: Severe antipsychotic sensitivity is a red flag for = Dementia with Lewy bodies | Alzheimer's disease :: Antipsychotics carry risk, but severe sensitivity is the DLB hallmark | Vascular dementia :: Not the classic association | Delirium tremens :: DTs is treated with benzodiazepines; not this red flag
> Up to half of DLB patients react badly to antipsychotics (rigidity, falls, NMS-like reactions). Avoid typical antipsychotics.
Q: Pick's disease is a form of = Frontotemporal dementia | Vascular dementia :: Vascular dementia is caused by cerebrovascular disease | Prion disease :: Prion disease is CJD | Lewy body dementia :: Lewy bodies are a different pathology
> FTD presents earlier (often before 65), with behaviour change (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy) or language problems, while memory is relatively spared at first.
Q: Stepwise decline with focal signs suggests = Vascular dementia | Alzheimer's disease :: Alzheimer's shows a gradual, steady decline | Lewy body dementia :: DLB fluctuates, with hallucinations and parkinsonism | Huntington's disease :: Huntington's shows chorea and is autosomal dominant
> Look for vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, smoking, AF) and earlier slowing and executive problems.
S: Normal pressure hydrocephalus triad = Gait disturbance | Urinary incontinence | Cognitive decline ~~ Visual hallucinations :: Not part of the triad | Seizures :: Not part of the triad | Chorea :: Not part of the triad
> "Wet, wobbly and wacky". A potentially reversible cause of dementia: think of it when gait problems come FIRST.
L: Delirium management = Identify and treat the underlying cause | Review and stop offending drugs | Non-drug measures: reorientation, lighting, family, sleep | Short-term low-dose antipsychotic only if distressed or a risk | Follow up cognition after recovery ~~ Start an antipsychotic first :: Treat the cause first; drugs are a last resort | Routine benzodiazepines :: They can worsen delirium (except alcohol withdrawal) | Physical restraint :: Avoid; it worsens agitation and injury risk
> Common causes: infection, drugs (anticholinergics, opioids, sedatives), metabolic problems, hypoxia, urinary retention, constipation, pain, withdrawal.

## Round Huts | Psychiatry of later life
> Psychiatry of later life. Source: PSYCHIATRIC OF LATER LIFE 2026 - Copy.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Old age psychiatry: history and scope
> - Psychogeriatrics ＝ care of the psychologically ill elderly; gerontology ＝ study of ageing.
> - Originated in the UK, early 1940s; subspecialty in the 1950s; UK DoH separate specialty 1989; APN Old Age Psychiatry Interest Group; SASOP subgroup 2007.
> - Elderly depressed women were killed as witches (Murphy 1995). Ageism ＝ seeing age, not the person.
> - Cut-off 65 internationally, 60 in Nigeria/LMICs; "graduates" ＝ younger patients ageing into the service.
> - Unique features: atypical presentation, comorbidity, polypharmacy, "start low, go slow", psychosocial losses, elder abuse, capacity and guardianship issues.
Q: Gerontology is: = The study of ageing, including biological, social and psychological changes | Care of psychologically ill elderly | General medical care of the elderly | Old age psychiatry in Nigeria | Study of dementia only
> Gerontology ＝ study of ageing. Psychogeriatrics ＝ psychiatric care of the elderly; geriatric medicine ＝ general medical care.
Q: Old age psychiatry is generally accepted to have originated in: = United Kingdom | USA | Nigeria | Germany | South Africa
> 'It is generally accepted that Old Age Psychiatry originated from the United Kingdom.'
Q: The UK Department of Health recognised old age psychiatry as a separate specialty in: = 1989 | 1945 | 1959 | 1975 | 2007
> 'Old Age Psychiatry was recognized by the UK Department of Health as a separate specialty in 1989.'
Q: Before World War II, older people's mental health conditions were mostly assumed to be: = Degenerative, 'senile' and not treatable | Infectious | Psychogenic | Genetic only | Caused by malnutrition
> '...most conditions being assumed to be degenerative "senile" and not amenable to treatment.'
Q: Prejudice and discrimination based on negative stereotypes of older people is: = Ageism | Racism | Elder abuse | Stigma by association | Gerontophobia only
> Ageism — seeing a person by chronological age rather than as an individual.
Q: According to Murphy (1995), depressed elderly women were sometimes: = Killed because they were regarded as witches | Honoured as elders | Sent abroad | Given ECT | Made chiefs
> '...the depressed elderly females were killed because they were regarded as witches...'
Q: In Nigeria and most LMICs, the geriatric age threshold is pragmatically set at: = 60 years | 50 years | 55 years | 65 years | 70 years
> '...often pragmatically set at 60 years, in line with national life expectancy and retirement policies.' (65 internationally.)
Q: 'The graduates' in old age psychiatry are: = Patients diagnosed younger who are now crossing the 60–65 cut-off | New consultants | Medical students | Nurses | Discharged patients
> 'Those with psychiatric diagnoses at younger age now crossing over 60–65 years cut-off.'
Q: Anxiety disorders in older people are often under-recognised because of: = Somatic overlap | Low prevalence | Good coping | Lack of tests | Dementia only
> 'Anxiety disorders, often under recognized due to somatic overlap.'
Q: The prescribing principle for older people because of pharmacokinetic changes is: = Start low and go slow | Start high, hit hard | Use injections | Avoid all drugs | Double the adult dose
> '...necessitate the principle of "start low and go slow".'

### Assessing an older person
> - Same aims (diagnosis, care plan) but longer, more than one interview, more reliance on informants, wider psychosocial view, carers' needs, and a big role for physical examination and investigations.
> - Comprehensive, longitudinal, context-sensitive, non-ageist — symptoms are not normal ageing.
> - Home (domiciliary) assessment is internationally recommended — real-life function, environment, no travel disorientation, informants.
> - Settings: home, nursing home (medical care) vs residential home (24-h personal care), memory clinic, inpatient → liaison old age psychiatry.
> - History: onset and course (fluctuating, stepwise), depression presenting with somatic complaints, UTI/malaria, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, herbal drugs, education (for test interpretation).
Q: Compared with younger patients, assessment of older adults: = Takes longer, often needs more than one interview and relies more on informants | Is shorter | Never needs informants | Excludes physical examination | Ignores carers
> 'The assessment takes longer time requiring more than one interview with a greater reliance on the informants.'
Q: Physical examination and investigations play a large role in older people because: = Organic causes of psychiatric symptoms are more prevalent | They are cheaper | Older people prefer it | Psychiatrists must do surgery | It is the law
> '...because of the greater prevalence of organic disorders as a cause of psychiatric symptoms in the elderly.'
Q: 'Non-ageist' assessment means recognising that: = Psychiatric symptoms are not normal ageing | Older people never get ill | Age is irrelevant to dosing | All elderly have dementia | Families are unreliable
> 'Non-ageist — psychiatric symptoms are not normal ageing.'
Q: When interviewing informants, the focus should be on: = Change from baseline, functional decline, behaviour change and medication adherence | Their own health | Family finances only | The patient's childhood only | Legal matters
> Focus on change from baseline, functional decline, behavioural changes, medication adherence.
Q: Which assessment setting is internationally recommended? = Home-based (domiciliary) assessment | Emergency department | Prison | Police station | Telephone only
> 'Home-based assessment (Domiciliary Service) — Internationally recommended.'
Q: Which is an advantage of home assessment? = Avoids disorientation from travelling to hospital | Allows blood tests on the spot | Needs no informants | Is faster | Allows ECT
> Real-life information, environment assessment, avoids excessive disorientation from travel, good access to informants.
Q: A residential care home differs from a nursing home in that it provides: = Home-style accommodation with 24-hour supervised staff for personal care | Intensive medical care | ECT | Surgery | Only day care
> Nursing home — special medical care. Residential home — home-style live-in accommodation with 24-hr staff for personal care.
Q: A memory clinic (outpatient) is best suited to: = Early dementia, functional illness in the physically fit, and mobile patients | Severely disturbed patients | Delirium | Terminal care | Acute mania
> Outpatient/memory clinic: functional illness but physically fit, early dementia, younger and less impaired, mobile patients.
Q: Inpatient assessment of older people in general hospital beds led to: = Liaison old age psychiatry services | Forensic services | Child services | Prison services | Addiction services
> 'This has led to Specialist Liaison Old Age Psychiatric Services.'
Q: In older people, depression often presents with: = Somatic complaints | Grandiosity | Euphoria | Hyperactivity | Thought disorder
> 'Mood symptoms — depression often presents with somatic complaints.'
Q: Why is education important in the personal history of an older patient? = For interpreting cognitive test results | For pension rights | For choosing antidepressants | For legal capacity | It is not important
> 'Education (important for cognitive testing interpretation).'
Q: Which infections are singled out as relevant in Nigeria in the medical history? = UTI and malaria | TB and leprosy | Measles and mumps | HIV only | Typhus
> 'Infections (UTI, Malaria — relevant in Nigeria).'
Q: A 'stepwise' course in the presenting complaint suggests: = Vascular disease | Alzheimer's disease | Depression | Normal ageing | Anxiety
> Course: progressive (AD), fluctuating (delirium/DLB), stepwise (vascular).

### Mental state in older people
> - Assess for parkinsonism in every new patient (DLB); retardation may be bradykinesia.
> - Speech: loud/garrulous ＝ FTD or mania; dysphasia ＝ early dementia, never depression; deafness mimics receptive dysphasia.
> - Mood: depression with prominent anxiety; catastrophic reaction to tasks.
> - Formal thought disorder rare in late-onset schizophrenia; delusions of theft common in dementia.
> - Misidentification: Capgras (double), mirror sign (doesn't recognise own reflection), phantom boarder (strangers living in the house).
> - Delirium: all kinds of hallucinations. DLB: complex, enduring visual hallucinations of people and animals. Charles Bonnet: complex visual hallucinations without cognitive impairment (may progress to dementia).
Q: Why should parkinsonism be assessed in every new older patient? = It is common and diagnostically important for dementia with Lewy bodies | It is always caused by drugs | It indicates depression | It is required by law | It excludes dementia
> 'The high prevalence of Parkinsonism... and the diagnostic importance of this in dementia (DLB) means it is good practice to assess for parkinsonism in every new patient.'
Q: Loud and garrulous speech in an older person is consistent with: = FTD or mania | Depression | Alzheimer's | Delirium | Parkinson's
> 'Loud and garrulous is consistent with FTD or mania — quiet and impoverished speech as in degenerative dementias and depression.'
Q: Dysphasia is a key feature of early dementia that: = Does not occur in depression | Is common in depression | Means delirium | Is always due to stroke | Indicates mania
> 'Dysphasia is another key feature of early dementing illness and one which does not occur in depression.'
Q: An explosion of emotion when given a task the patient cannot do is a: = Catastrophic reaction | Panic attack | Manic switch | Dissociative episode | Seizure
> 'Catastrophic reaction — task causes explosion of emotions.'
Q: Depression in older people is often accompanied by more prominent: = Anxiety | Euphoria | Grandiosity | Hallucinations | Aggression
> 'Lowering of mood in depression is often accompanied by a more prominent anxiety.'
Q: Formal thought disorder in late-onset schizophrenia is: = Rare | Universal | Diagnostic | Always severe | Caused by dementia
> 'Formal thought disorder is rare in late onset schizophrenia.'
Q: Which paranoid delusion is very common in dementia? = Delusion of theft | Delusion of grandeur | Nihilistic delusion | Erotomania | Religious delusion
> 'Paranoid delusions, especially of theft very common in dementia.'
Q: The belief that extra people are living in the house is called: = Phantom boarder syndrome | Capgras syndrome | Mirror sign | Fregoli syndrome | Cotard syndrome
> Phantom boarder syndrome — perhaps after failing to recognise relatives.
Q: A patient who cannot recognise their own image in the mirror shows: = The mirror sign | Prosopagnosia only | Capgras | Charles Bonnet | Anosognosia
> 'Mirror sign: patient cannot recognise his image in the mirror.'
Q: Complex, enduring visual hallucinations of people and animals are a core feature of: = Dementia with Lewy bodies | Alzheimer's disease | Vascular dementia | Depression | FTD
> Core feature of DLB (McKeith 2005).
Q: Persistent complex visual hallucinations without cognitive impairment or altered consciousness describe: = Charles Bonnet syndrome | Delirium | DLB | Schizophrenia | Korsakoff
> Charles Bonnet syndrome — may later progress to dementia.
Q: Auditory, olfactory, visual and tactile hallucinations are common in: = Delirium | Depression | Anxiety | Personality disorder | Normal ageing
> 'Auditory, Olfactory, visual and tactile hallucinations are common in delirium.'
Q: The commonest cause of acute confusion in an elderly inpatient is: = Delirium from a medical cause (e.g. infection, drugs) | Dementia | Schizophrenia | Mania | Malingering
> Acute confusion in the elderly ＝ delirium until proven otherwise — infection, drugs, metabolic.

### Cognitive examination
> - Attention: days of week backwards, serial 7s, digit span 6 ± 1.
> - Episodic memory — hippocampal–diencephalic; semantic — anterior temporal lobe; working memory — dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Avoid the term "short-term memory".
> - Tests: 3 items / name and address, route to hospital, hidden objects, recent president.
> - Semantic dementia: progressive naming loss + object agnosia, left anterior temporal atrophy.
> - Language: naming, comprehension, repetition ("no ifs, ands or buts"), reading ("close your eyes"); pure alexia ＝ letter-by-letter.
> - Dressing/constructional apraxia ＝ visuospatial; prosopagnosia ＝ occipito-temporal.
> - Capacity: understand, appreciate, reason, express a stable choice.
Q: Normal digit span is about: = 6 ± 1 | 3 ± 1 | 9 ± 2 | 12 | 15
> 'Normal digit span 6 ± 1 — depends on age and intellectual ability.'
Q: Semantic memory depends mainly on the: = Anterior temporal lobe | Hippocampus | Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex | Cerebellum | Occipital lobe
> 'The normal substrate for semantic memory is the anterior temporal lobe.'
Q: Working memory uses the: = Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex | Hippocampus | Thalamus | Amygdala | Occipital cortex
> 'Working memory uses dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.'
Q: The lecture advises avoiding which memory term because it is confusing? = Short-term memory | Episodic memory | Semantic memory | Working memory | Procedural memory
> 'Short term memory is applied to a number of different memory problems, confusing and better avoided.'
Q: Episodic memory depends on the: = Hippocampal–diencephalic system | Cerebellar system | Basal ganglia | Brainstem | Spinal cord
> 'Episodic memory depends on hippocampal-diencephalic system.'
Q: Impaired naming with object agnosia, relentlessly progressive, suggests: = Semantic dementia (left anterior temporal atrophy) | Alzheimer's | Depression | Delirium | Normal ageing
> 'Impaired naming in semantic dementia is relentlessly progressive... due to atrophy of the left anterior temporal lobe.'
Q: Dressing and constructional apraxias are best considered as: = Visuospatial impairments | Motor impairments | Language disorders | Memory disorders | Psychogenic
> '...best considered as visuospatial rather than motor impairment.'
Q: Prosopagnosia is due to a lesion in the: = Occipito-temporal region | Frontal lobe | Cerebellum | Brainstem | Parietal lobe only
> 'Prosopagnosics cannot recognize familiar faces. An occipito-temporal lesion underlies this.'
Q: Which is NOT one of the 4 aspects of capacity? = Agreeing with the doctor | Understanding the information | Appreciating it for one's situation | Reasoning | Expressing a stable choice
> Capacity: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, expression of a stable choice.
Q: Letter-by-letter reading is called: = Pure alexia | Agraphia | Acalculia | Aphasia | Dyslexia
> 'Pure alexia: letter by letter reading.'
Q: The lecture advises recording insight as: = A brief description of its extent | A single word ('full') | A number out of 10 | Nothing | Only in dementia
> Record a brief description rather than a summary phrase like 'full insight'.

### Cognitive scales
> - MMSE: /30, ≤ 24 abnormal; Nigeria ≤ 16 (Gureje 2006); memory/attention-weighted, no executive testing; insensitive to frontal, subcortical, MCI; culture-bound.
> - Floor effects (poorly educated) reduce specificity; ceiling effects (MCI, highly educated) reduce sensitivity. Fix with education-adjusted norms.
> - Hearing loss lowers verbal scores; visual loss lowers even non-visual items.
> - ACE-R: /100, 5 domains; 88 ＝ sensitive, 82 ＝ specific.
> - MTS: 10 items, ≤ 6 abnormal, only advantage speed.
> - MoCA: /30, ≤ 26 impaired, +1 if ≤ 12 years education, better for MCI and executive function, 10–15 min.
> - Mini-Cog: 3-word recall + clock; recall 0 ＝ dementia likely, 3 ＝ unlikely, 1–2 ＝ use the clock; 3–5 min.
Q: The Nigerian MMSE cut-off (Gureje et al. 2006) is: = ≤ 16 | ≤ 30 | ≤ 24 | ≤ 20 | ≤ 10
> 'Nigeria cut-off ≤ 16 (Gureje et al, 2006).' Standard: ≤ 24 abnormal.
Q: The MMSE includes no testing of: = Executive performance | Memory | Attention | Orientation | Language
> 'No testing of executive performance.'
Q: MMSE floor effects are frequent in persons with poor education and they: = Reduce specificity | Reduce sensitivity | Have no effect | Increase accuracy | Only affect men
> Floor effects reduce specificity; ceiling effects reduce sensitivity.
Q: MMSE ceiling effects are frequent in: = MCI and highly educated people | The illiterate | Severe dementia | Delirium | Children
> 'MMSE-CE are frequently seen in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and in highly educated people.'
Q: The MMSE is relatively insensitive to: = Frontal and subcortical pathology and MCI | Alzheimer's disease | Severe dementia | Disorientation | Memory loss
> 'Quite insensitive in the context of frontal, and subcortical pathology as well as mild cognitive impairment.'
Q: The ACE-R is scored out of: = 100 | 10 | 30 | 144 | 28
> 100-point scale with 5 domain subscores.
Q: An ACE-R cut-off of 82 gives: = Very high specificity at the cost of sensitivity | High sensitivity, low specificity | No diagnostic value | Only MCI detection | Delirium screening
> 88 ＝ high sensitivity; 82 ＝ very high specificity.
Q: On the MoCA, a score suggesting impairment is: = ≤ 26 | ≤ 30 | ≤ 20 | ≤ 16 | ≤ 6
> '≤ 26 suggests impairment; add 1 point if education ≤ 12 years.'
Q: The Mini-Cog consists of: = 3-word recall and clock drawing | 30 items | Serial 7s only | Digit span and naming | 10 questions
> 3-word recall + clock drawing; 3–5 minutes.
Q: On the Mini-Cog, recall of 1–2 words means: = Use the clock drawing to decide | Dementia certain | Dementia unlikely | Repeat in a year | Delirium
> Recall 0 → dementia likely; 3 → unlikely; 1–2 → use clock drawing.
Q: On the 10-item Mental Test Score, an abnormal score in the elderly is: = ≤ 6 | ≤ 9 | ≤ 3 | ≤ 24 | ≤ 16
> 'A score of 6 or less is abnormal.'

### Functional assessment
> - ADL ＝ basic self-care (eat, groom, bathe, toilet, dress). IADL ＝ independent living (medication, money, meals).
> - Ask whether they ever did the task.
> - Reasons: criterion for dementia diagnosis, snapshot, baseline, policy evidence, who will benefit.
> - Katz ADL (1963): bathing → dressing → toileting → transferring → continence → feeding (order of loss).
> - Lawton–Brody IADL: 8 domains; women 0–8, men 0–5; used in Tanzania.
> - Blessed Dementia Scale (1968): 22 items, 0–28 (cognitive subscale 0–17).
> - African tools: CHIF (Ibadan–Indianapolis), IDEA-IADL (Tanzania).
Q: Which is an instrumental activity of daily living? = Managing finances | Bathing | Dressing | Toileting | Eating
> IADL: managing medication, finances, preparing meals. The others are basic ADLs.
Q: On the Lawton–Brody IADL scale, the score range for women is: = 0–8 | 0–5 | 0–28 | 0–30 | 0–100
> 0–8 for women; historically 0–5 for men.
Q: According to the Katz index, the first function usually lost is: = Bathing | Feeding | Continence | Transferring | Toileting
> Order: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feeding.
Q: The CHIF functional interview was developed in the: = Ibadan–Indianapolis Dementia Project | Tanzania project | UK Biobank | WHO SAGE | Lancet Commission
> CHIF — Hendrie et al. 2006, Ibadan–Indianapolis Dementia Project.
Q: Which is a reason given for functional assessment? = It is a criterion for the diagnosis of dementia | It replaces cognitive tests | It measures IQ | It diagnoses depression | It determines pension
> '1. It's a criterion for the diagnosis of dementia.'

### Social care, risk and Diogenes
> - Target social situations: retirement, widowhood, poverty, disability, loneliness, changing family roles, dependency.
> - Nigeria: National Policy on Ageing 2021; Renewed Hope ₦200,000 grant for 65+; National Senior Citizens Centre; NHIS; proposed Older Persons Rights and Privileges Bill; pensions. Problem: policy lacuna (not implemented).
> - NGOs: COSROPIN, HelpAge, El-Aged Care, DewDrop (dementia), GAPA (grandmothers raising orphans).
> - Risk assessment: social services lead; risks ＝ falls, wandering, malnutrition, self-neglect, elder abuse, drug side effects.
> - Falls: postural hypotension, psychotropics, hazards, sensory loss → hip fracture, head injury.
> - Diogenes syndrome: self-neglect, squalor, hoarding rubbish, lack of shame; 0.005% UK; linked to schizotypal/OCPD, schizophrenia, mania, FTD; not in DSM-5 (hoarding is).

### Treating older people
> - ECT: faster and possibly safer than drugs in the frail; best with psychomotor change and psychosis; relapse high — continue drugs; twice weekly; no fixed high-dose — use age-based dosing; stop benzodiazepines/anticonvulsants/anticholinergics; capacity may change during the course.
> - Prescribing: review and stop unneeded drugs; liquids if swallowing is hard; nervous system more sensitive; reduced renal clearance; side effects ＝ confusion, constipation, postural hypotension, falls; start at ~50% of the adult dose; once or twice daily; "start low, go slow".
> - Dementia drugs: donepezil, galantamine (also nicotinic agonist), rivastigmine (PD and AD); memantine — moderate to severe AD. Review at ~3 months; up to 50% slow decline; stop non-responders and retest at 4–6 weeks.
> - CAM: ginkgo biloba (most studied), huperzine A, melatonin, vitamin E, omega-3.
> - Psychotherapy: brief problem-solving; losses and the past; Erikson's integrity vs despair; behaviour therapy not in dementia; reality orientation, reminiscence, validation.
Q: Neuroimaging findings in elderly dementia usually show: = Quantitative severity and a mixture of age-related changes | Clear qualitative hallmarks of each disease | Normal brains always | Only tumours | Only strokes
> 'Findings rather demonstrate "quantitative" severity and mixture of prevalent age-associated brain changes.'
Q: In complex cases, the lecture recommends: = A case conference so everyone is 'singing from the same hymn sheet' | Immediate admission | Discharging the patient | Only drug treatment | Referral abroad
> '...a case conference to facilitate exchange of information and to ensure that everyone involved is singing from the same hymn sheet.'
Q: Compared with drugs, ECT in frail older patients: = Works faster and may be safer | Is slower and riskier | Is never used | Has no relapse | Needs no anaesthetic
> 'It works faster, and may be safer than pharmacotherapy for frail, older patients.'
Q: After a course of ECT in older people: = Continuing pharmacotherapy is mandatory because relapse rates are high | No further treatment is needed | Repeat ECT weekly for life | Stop all drugs | Start benzodiazepines
> 'Relapse rates are high once treatment stops. Continuing pharmacotherapy is mandatory.'
Q: The recommended ECT frequency for older people is: = Twice weekly | Daily | Three times weekly | Monthly | Once only
> 'Twice weekly ECT is adequate.'
Q: Regarding ECT dosing in older people: = Fixed-dose high-energy treatment is not acceptable; use age-based formulae | Fixed high-energy dosing is standard | Lowest possible dose always | Dose by weight only | No dosing needed
> 'Fixed-dose, high energy treatments not acceptable. Alternative strategies include age-based formulae.'
Q: ECT works best in older patients with: = Psychomotor changes and psychotic symptoms | Mild anxiety | Personality disorder | Dementia alone | Insomnia
> 'ECT works better in patients with psychomotor changes and psychotic symptoms.'
Q: When prescribing for older people, a reasonable starting dose is about: = 50% of the younger adult dose | The full adult dose | Double the adult dose | 10% of the dose | Whatever the family asks
> 'Reduce dose (start with about 50% of the younger adult dose).'
Q: Common adverse effects of drugs in older people include: = Confusion, constipation, postural hypotension and falls | Euphoria | Weight loss only | Hyperactivity | Improved memory

Q: Memantine is licensed for: = Moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease | Mild Alzheimer's only | Depression | Delirium | Lewy body only
> 'Licensed for treating moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease.'
Q: Benefit from anti-dementia drugs is assessed by repeating cognitive testing at about: = 3 months | 2 weeks | 1 year | 5 years | Never
> 'Benefit is assessed by repeating cognitive assessment around 3 months.' Up to 50% slow decline.
Q: The most studied biological supplement for dementia is: = Ginkgo biloba | Ginseng | Green tea | Melatonin | Vitamin C
> Ginkgo biloba (120–240 mg/day) — most studied and most widely used.

Q: Erikson's psychosocial stage relevant to older people is: = Ego integrity vs despair | Trust vs mistrust | Identity vs role confusion | Intimacy vs isolation | Industry vs inferiority

Q: Reality orientation originated from: = Resocialisation technique | Psychoanalysis | CBT | Hypnosis | ECT
> 'Reality Orientation — Originated from resocialisation technique.'
Q: Validation therapy focuses on: = The emotional state underlying the behaviour | Correcting false beliefs | Memory drills | Medication adherence | Physical exercise
> 'Validation — It looks to the emotional state which underlies the person's behaviour.'
Q: Which antidepressant class is generally first-line in older adults? = SSRIs (e.g. sertraline) | TCAs | MAOIs | Benzodiazepines | Lithium
> SSRIs — watch hyponatraemia and bleeding; avoid anticholinergic TCAs.
Q: The Beers criteria list: = Potentially inappropriate medications in older adults | Dementia scales | ECT doses | Capacity tests | Pension rules
> Beers criteria (and STOPP/START) — drugs to avoid or use cautiously in older people.

## South Ward | Neurology I
> Neurology I. Source: 2026 Psychiatry Update Course _ Neurology 1 _ Rufus Akinyemi.pdf. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Brain health and burden
> - WHO 2022: capacitance to function across cognitive, sensory, socio-emotional, behavioural and motor domains, to actualise full potential over the life course, irrespective of disorder.
> - Top neurological diseases in Africa: stroke, epilepsy, migraine, Alzheimer's/related dementias, meningitis, Parkinson's.
> - Neural stem cells → neuronal progenitors (neurons) or glial progenitors (glia).
Q: The WHO (2022) defines brain health as function across cognitive, sensory, socio-emotional, behavioural and motor domains: = Irrespective of the presence or absence of disorders | Only in the absence of disease | Only in adulthood | Measured by IQ alone | Only after neuroimaging
> '...actualize their full potential over life's course irrespective of the presence or absence of disorders.'
Q: Which is listed FIRST among the top neurological diseases in Africa? = Stroke | Epilepsy | Migraine | Meningitis | Parkinson's disease
> Top in Africa: stroke, epilepsy, migraine, Alzheimer's and related dementias, meningitis, Parkinson's.
Q: Which of these is NOT on the lecture's list of top neurological diseases in Africa? = Multiple sclerosis | Migraine | Meningitis | Parkinson's disease | Epilepsy
> The six: stroke, epilepsy, migraine, AD/related dementias, meningitis, Parkinson's. MS is not listed.
Q: The approach to brain disorders promoted by Akinyemi et al. (Nat Rev Neurol 2021) is: = A life course approach | A single-gene approach | A purely curative approach | An age-65-plus approach | A hospital-only approach
> 'A Life Course Approach to Brain Disorders.'
Q: Neural stem cells: = Have the potential to generate all neural cell types | Generate only neurons | Generate only glia | Are found only in adults | Arise from glial cells
> 'Neural stem cells have the potential to generate all neural cell types.'
Q: Glial cells arise from: = Glial progenitors | Neuronal progenitor cells | Microglia from the bone marrow only | Neurons | Ependymal cells only
> Stem cells → neuronal progenitors (→ neurons) or glial progenitors (→ glial cells).
Q: The sum of environmental exposures across life acting on the brain is termed the: = Exposome | Genome | Connectome | Proteome | Phenome
> The lecture shows the exposome alongside development and brain ageing.

### Reserve (Stern 2020) ＝ difference between clinical picture and neuropathology
> - Brain reserve — numbers of neurones and synapses.
> - Brain maintenance — genetics/lifestyle reducing pathology over time.
> - Cognitive reserve — adaptability preserving function despite pathology.
> - Trajectory: normal ageing → CIND/MCI → dementia; non-clinical → pre-clinical → clinical phases.
Q: Reserve is a concept accounting for: = The difference between an individual's clinical picture and their neuropathology | Brain weight at birth | IQ score | Speed of nerve conduction | Amount of CSF
> 'Reserve is a concept accounting for the difference between an individual's clinical picture and their neuropathology.' (Stern 2020)
Q: 'Numbers of neurones and synapses at a given timepoint' describes: = Brain reserve | Cognitive reserve | Brain maintenance | Neuroplasticity | Compensation
> Brain reserve (e.g. numbers of neurones and synapses at a given timepoint).
Q: Neurobiological capital, based on genetics or lifestyle, that reduces brain changes and pathology over time is: = Brain maintenance | Brain reserve | Cognitive reserve | Neurogenesis | Apoptosis
> Brain maintenance — '...based on genetics or lifestyle reducing brain changes and pathology development over time.'
Q: Adaptability that preserves cognition or everyday function in spite of brain pathology is: = Cognitive reserve | Brain reserve | Brain maintenance | Resilience to stress | Plasticity failure
> Cognitive reserve — 'adaptability enabling preservation of cognition or everyday functioning in spite of brain pathology.'
Q: On the trajectory of cognition, the stage between normal ageing and dementia is: = CIND / MCI | Delirium | Pseudodementia | Encephalopathy | Amnestic syndrome
> Normal ageing → CIND / MCI → dementia (after the threshold for dementia).

### Synapses and neurotransmitters
> - Two modalities: chemical and electrical — their interaction is needed for normal function; electrical-synapse dysregulation → cognitive impairment.
> - Homeostasis: balanced release/reuptake; glutamate vs GABA; LTP/LTD → learning and memory; MAO, COMT, SERT clear transmitters; astrocytes and microglia help.
> - Excess glutamate → excitotoxicity. Low GABA → seizures. Dopamine/serotonin → mood, motivation, memory.
Q: The two main modalities of synaptic transmission are: = Chemical and electrical | Fast and slow | Axonal and dendritic | Excitatory and modulatory | Central and peripheral
> 'Two main modalities of synaptic transmission: chemical and electrical.'
Q: Dysregulation of electrical synapses by neurotransmitters could contribute to: = Cognitive impairment | Muscle hypertrophy | Peripheral oedema | Hypertension | Anaemia
> 'Dysregulation of electrical synapses by neurotransmitters could contribute to cognitive impairment.'

> 'Cell death – Excitotoxicity and Apoptosis.'

### Myelin autoantibodies and mutations
> - MBP, MOG → multiple sclerosis.
> - GQ1b → Miller Fisher variant of GBS.
> - GM1 → multifocal motor neuropathy.
> - PMP22 → hereditary liability to pressure palsies; PLP (slide: CMT; textbook: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher).
> - Cell death: excitotoxicity, apoptosis, ferroptosis (iron-dependent). Neuro-infection → epilepsy.

### n1 dementia
> Mechanisms of dementia: neuronal/synaptic loss (genes, abnormal cytoplasmic deposits), ischaemia, transmitter deficiency, metabolic/electrolyte, vitamin deficiency, chronic infection, toxins.
> - Vascular risk factors (+ APOE ε4, eNOS) → vessel wall change → chronic hypoperfusion (oligaemia), SVD, microinfarcts, white matter lesions → VaD, mixed, AD.
> - Vascular change may exacerbate Alzheimer pathology.
> - Stroke and dementia are risks for each other and share risk factors.
Q: Which is NOT listed among the mechanisms of dementia? = Excess dopamine | Ischaemia | Vitamin deficiencies | Chronic infections | Toxins
> Listed: neuronal/synaptic loss, ischaemia, transmitter deficiency, metabolic/electrolyte, vitamins, chronic infections, toxins. Excess dopamine is not listed.
Q: Vascular disease risk factors lead to cerebral vessel wall changes and a chronic hypoperfusive state termed: = Oligaemia | Hyperaemia | Anoxia | Vasculitis | Hypercapnia
> 'Chronic Hypoperfusive State (Oligaemia)' (SVD and microinfarcts).
Q: Genetic factors listed in the vascular-neurodegeneration model are: = APOE ε4 and eNOS | HTT and SOD1 | BRCA1 and BRCA2 | FMR1 and MECP2 | DISC1 and COMT
> 'Other factors: Genetic — APOE E4 / eNOS.'
Q: The relationship between stroke and dementia is that they: = Are risks for each other and share vascular risk factors | Are unrelated | Only stroke causes dementia | Dementia protects against stroke | Share only genetic risks
> 'Stroke and Dementia are risks for each other and also share vascular risk factors.'
Q: Kalaria, Akinyemi and Ihara (2012) proposed that vascular changes: = May exacerbate Alzheimer pathology | Protect against Alzheimer pathology | Are irrelevant in Alzheimer's | Only occur after age 90 | Cause Parkinson's
> 'Vascular Changes May Exacerbate Alzheimer Pathology.'
Q: Which hereditary small vessel disease is shown among dementia pathologies? = CADASIL | Wilson's disease | Friedreich's ataxia | Tay-Sachs | Fabry's only
> Pathologies shown: AD, Pick's, HD, DLB and CADASIL.
Q: CADASIL is caused by mutations in: = NOTCH3 | APP | PSEN1 | HTT | MAPT
> NOTCH3 on chromosome 19: migraine with aura, mood disorder, subcortical strokes, dementia; anterior temporal WM lesions.
Q: Vascular cognitive impairment typically affects which domain earliest? = Executive function and processing speed | Episodic memory only | Language only | Visual perception only | Praxis only
> VCI is typically dysexecutive with slowed processing, often with a stepwise course.

### Abnormal sensation
> - Negative ＝ reduced pathway activity → numbness; abnormal exam/NCS/SSEPs.
> - Positive ＝ excess discharge/lowered threshold → tingling, burning, lancinating; exam normal.
> - Allodynia: non-painful stimulus → pain. Hyperalgesia: mildly noxious → severe pain. Hyperaesthesia ↑, hypoaesthesia ↓, anaesthesia absent, dysaesthesia abnormal.
> - Exam: touch, pain, temperature, JPS/vibration, Romberg, cortical — compare sides.
Q: Negative sensory phenomena are due to: = Reduced activity in sensory pathways | Excessive discharges | Lowered thresholds | Psychological causes | Muscle spasm
> 'Negative Phenomena — due to reduced activity in sensory pathways.' Example: numbness.
Q: In positive sensory phenomena, the sensory examination is typically: = Normal | Grossly abnormal | Showing complete anaesthesia | Showing absent reflexes | Impossible
> 'Sensory examination, however, remains normal.'
Q: A non-painful stimulus producing excruciating pain is: = Allodynia | Hyperalgesia | Hypoalgesia | Dysaesthesia | Anaesthesia
> Allodynia — non-painful stimulus → excruciating pain.
Q: A mildly noxious stimulus producing severe pain is: = Hyperalgesia | Allodynia | Hyperaesthesia | Paraesthesia | Hypoaesthesia
> Hyperalgesia — mildly noxious stimulus → severe pain.
Q: Which is an example of a NEGATIVE sensory phenomenon? = Numbness | Tingling | Burning | Lancinating pain | Band-like pain
> Numbness is the lecture's example of a negative phenomenon; the rest are positive.
Q: The prefix 'dys' in dysaesthesia means: = Not normal | Absent | Increased | Reduced | Painful
> 'the Greek word "dys," means "not-normal".'

### Localising sensory loss
> - Parietal cortex: agraphaesthesia, astereognosis, lost two-point discrimination; cortical seizures.
> - Thalamus: Dejerine–Roussy thalamic pain.
> - Brainstem: face one side, body the other.
> - Cord: transection, Brown-Séquard (hemicord), central cord → dissociated loss.
> - Nerve/root: polyneuropathy, mononeuropathy, radiculopathy.
Q: In sensory examination, which is described as crucial? = Comparison of response on one side with the other | Testing only one side | Using only vibration | Avoiding subjective responses | Testing with eyes open
> 'Comparison of response on one side to the other side is crucial.'

Q: Dejerine-Roussy syndrome is a pain syndrome of the: = Thalamus | Parietal cortex | Spinal root | Brainstem | Peripheral nerve
> Thalamus — thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy).
Q: Sensory loss on one side of the face and the other side of the body localises to the: = Brainstem | Thalamus | Parietal cortex | Cauda equina | Peripheral nerve
> Brainstem — crossed sensory loss.
Q: Dissociated sensory loss is typical of: = Central cord syndrome | Parietal lesion | Mononeuropathy | Thalamic stroke | Radiculopathy
> 'Central Cord Syndrome (dissociated sensory loss).'
Q: Brown-Séquard syndrome is a lesion of: = Half of the spinal cord (hemicord) | The thalamus | The whole brainstem | A single nerve root | The parietal lobe
> 'Hemicord (Brown Sequard Syndrome).'
Q: First-line drug treatment for central post-stroke (thalamic) pain includes: = Amitriptyline or gabapentinoids | Paracetamol alone | Morphine first line | Haloperidol | Steroids
> Amitriptyline, pregabalin/gabapentin (neuropathic pain agents).

### Stroke burden
> - 2019: >101.4 m survivors, 12.2 m new, 6.5 m deaths. 2050: >200 m, 25 m, 13 m.
> - Africa: leading cause of medical admission; incidence ≤316/100,000; prevalence ≤1,460/100,000; 3-year fatality ≤84%.
> - African ancestry: onset 60s (vs 70s/80s); ICH 34% vs 9%; SVD 30% vs 19%; heritability 0.35 vs 0.16; worse outcomes; cost US$145–4,860.
> - ICH from Charcot–Bouchard aneurysms; SAH from berry aneurysms. Hereditary: CADASIL, CARASIL, RVCL.

### Risk factors
> - 90% of stroke burden is from preventable risk factors — behavioural, metabolic, environmental (household solid-fuel smoke, particulates, lead).
> - ≥12 servings of vegetables/week → less hypertension (esp. men, young adults).
> - Hypertensives cluster near roads, dense areas, little green vegetation.
> - Infections: HIV, H. pylori, periodontitis, Chlamydia, CMV/EBV/HSV/HZV → inflammation and atherogenesis.
> - SIREN GWAS: genome-wide significant loci on chromosome 3.
Q: Globally, what proportion of the stroke burden is attributable to preventable risk factors? = 90% | 30% | 50% | 70% | 99%
> 'Globally, 90% of the burden of stroke are attributable to preventable risk factors.'
Q: Which is listed as an ENVIRONMENTAL risk factor for stroke? = Household air pollution from solid fuels | Low physical activity | Raised BMI | Raised fasting glucose | Smoking
> Environmental: household air pollution from solid fuels, ambient particulate matter, lead exposure.
Q: Indigenous Africans were significantly less likely to be hypertensive if they ate at least how many servings of vegetables per week? = 12 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 21
> '...consumed at least 12 servings of vegetables per week were significantly less likely to be found hypertensive.'
Q: Diagnosed hypertensives were found to cluster: = Closer to road networks, in dense areas with little green vegetation | Far from roads | In forested areas | Only in rural farms | Randomly
> Clustering: closer to road networks, higher population density, little or no green vegetation.
Q: Infections such as HIV, H. pylori and periodontitis are linked to stroke through: = Inflammation and atherogenesis | Direct haemorrhage only | Hypoglycaemia | Hypercalcaemia | Vitamin excess
> '...associated with inflammation, atherogenesis.'
Q: The first African stroke GWAS (SIREN) found genome-wide significant loci on chromosome: = 3 | 1 | 9 | 19 | 22
> 'genome-wide significant (p<5.0E-8) SNPs associations of loci on chromosome 3.'
Q: The genome-wide significance threshold used in the SIREN GWAS was: = p < 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ | p < 0.05 | p < 0.001 | p < 10⁻³ | p < 0.01
> p < 5.0 × 10⁻⁸.
Q: A stated implication of African-ancestry-specific genetic variants is: = New risk prediction, biomarkers and novel therapeutics | No clinical relevance | Proof that stroke is purely genetic | That hypertension is irrelevant | That treatment is impossible
> 'implications for future discoveries of new risk prediction, biomarkers ... and novel therapeutics.'

### Stroke by mechanism
> - Haemorrhage ≈ 20% (SAH ≈ 5%); ischaemic ≈ 80%.
> - Ischaemic: atherosclerotic 20%, lacunar (penetrating artery) 25%, cardioembolic 20%, cryptogenic 30%, other 5%.
> - Causes: arteries/veins, blood (clots too fast/slow), heart, genes.
Q: Approximately what proportion of strokes are ischaemic? = 80% | 20% | 50% | 65% | 95%
> Haemorrhage ≈ 20%, ischaemic ≈ 80%.
Q: In the classification of ischaemic stroke by mechanism, the LARGEST single category is: = Cryptogenic stroke | Atherosclerotic disease | Lacunes | Cardiogenic embolism | Other unusual causes
> Atherosclerotic 20%, lacunes 25%, cardioembolic 20%, cryptogenic 30%, other 5%.
Q: Penetrating artery disease ('lacunes') accounts for about what proportion of ischaemic stroke? = 25% | 5% | 15% | 35% | 50%
> Penetrating artery disease (lacunes) ≈ 25%.
Q: Subarachnoid haemorrhage accounts for about what proportion of strokes? = 5% | 1% | 15% | 20% | 30%
> Subarachnoid ≈ 5%.
Q: Which is listed as a cardiac source of embolic stroke? = Atrial fibrillation | Dissection | Arteritis | Migraine | Prothrombotic state
> Cardiogenic embolism: atrial fibrillation, valve disease, ventricular thrombi.

### n1 eval
> Care phases: acute days 1–7; early sub-acute weeks 2–4; late sub-acute months 2–6; long-term month 7+ (community).
> - 4 Ps imaging: Parenchyma (rule out bleed on unenhanced CT), Pipes, Perfusion (CBV, CBF, MTT), Penumbra.
> - CT/MRI ＝ structure; PET/SPECT/EEG/MEG ＝ function.
> - NIHSS ＝ Class I (AHA/ASA 2018).
> - Bloods (glucose, FBC, PT/aPTT, HbA1c, U&E, lipids), ECG, TTE, carotid Doppler at minimum, Hb electrophoresis, HIV.
Q: Acute (emergency) stroke care covers which period from onset? = Days 1–7 | First 24 hours | Weeks 2–4 | Months 2–6 | Month 7 onwards
> Acute care: 1st–7th day, assessment and early supportive care, in hospital.
Q: Long-term (chronic) stroke care from month 7 onwards is preferably located in the: = Community | ICU | Hospital ward | Stroke unit | Emergency department
> Long-term care: rehab, psychological and social support, prevent recurrence — in the community.
Q: In the '4 Ps' of acute stroke imaging, 'Penumbra' refers to: = Tissue at risk of dying if ischaemia continues without recanalisation | The carotid arteries | Cerebral blood volume | Haemorrhage | The ventricles
> 'Penumbra: assess tissue at risk of dying if ischemia continues without recanalization.'
Q: Ruling out haemorrhage with unenhanced CT is part of which 'P'? = Parenchyma | Pipes | Perfusion | Penumbra | Prognosis
> 'Parenchyma: assess early signs acute stroke, R/o hemorrhage (unenhanced CT).'
Q: Perfusion imaging in acute stroke assesses: = CBV, CBF and MTT | Only carotid flow | Haematoma volume | White matter tracts | EEG activity
> 'Perfusion: Assess CBV, CBF, and MTT.'
Q: Use of a formal stroke scale such as the NIHSS in the 2018 AHA/ASA guideline is a: = Class I recommendation | Class IIb recommendation | Class III (harm) | Research-only tool | Not recommended
> 'Use of formal stroke scales (e.g. NIHSS) is a Class I recommendation.'
Q: Which brain imaging technique is listed as assessing FUNCTION rather than structure? = SPECT | CT | MRI | Plain skull X-ray | CT angiography
> Structure: CT, MRI/MRS. Function: PET, SPECT, EEG, MEG.
Q: The minimum vascular imaging recommended in the lecture is: = Carotid Doppler ultrasound | Digital subtraction angiography | MR venography | PET | CT perfusion
> 'Carotid doppler ultrasound at the minimum.'

### Services
> - Door-to-needle ≤60 min in ≥50% ＝ Class I.
> - Primary stroke centre: imaging, teams, protocols, ED, lab, neurosurgery, stroke unit, QI.
> - Nigeria (Ogbole 2015): median 24 h, none within 3 h, ~69% after 12 h.
> - Causes: transport, sociocultural beliefs, poor awareness. Nigerian health workers: 30% couldn't name the brain; 14% blamed evil spirits; 13% preferred spiritual healing.
> - ASO survey: 45/54 countries; only 29% admitted to stroke units.

### Management
> - Ischaemic: lower BP by 15% if DBP >120 or SBP >220; treat glucose >140 mg/dl; rtPA within 4.5 h; early mobilisation; carotid endarterectomy.
> - ICH: no anticoagulant for 3–4 days; IPC/TED; rFVIIa; surgery; anticonvulsants as indicated.
> - ENOS: 5 mg transdermal GTN. INTERACT: early gentle BP lowering → less haematoma growth.
> - Antiplatelets: clopidogrel ＝ aspirin + dipyridamole > aspirin. DOACs; statins.
> - Watch for chameleons; exclude mimics.
Q: In acute ischaemic stroke, the lecture advises lowering BP by 15% if: = DBP > 120 or SBP > 220 | SBP > 140 | SBP > 160 or DBP > 100 | Any elevation | Never
> 'BP management principle; lower by 15% if DBP > 120, SBP > 220.'
Q: In ischaemic stroke, blood glucose should be treated if above: = 140 mg/dl | 100 mg/dl | 200 mg/dl | 250 mg/dl | 300 mg/dl
> 'Treat blood glucose >140 mg/dl.'
Q: The time window for recombinant tPA thrombolysis in the lecture is: = 4.5 hours | 1 hour | 3 hours | 12 hours | 24 hours
> 'recombinant Tissue Plasminogen Activator (4.5 hr window).'
Q: In intracerebral haemorrhage, anticoagulants for DVT prevention should be avoided for: = The first 3–4 days or until bleeding stops | The first 24 hours | 6 weeks | 3 months | Life
> 'avoid anticoagulant in the 1st 3-4 days or until bleeding stops, IPCD, TED stockings.'
Q: The INTERACT trial suggested that in acute ICH: = Early gentle BP reduction improves outcome and reduces haematoma growth | BP should not be lowered | Aggressive anticoagulation helps | Steroids reduce haematoma | Surgery is always needed
> 'early gentle reduction of BP produces better outcome and reduction of haematoma growth.'
Q: The ENOS trial tested: = 5 mg transdermal glyceryl trinitrate | IV labetalol | Oral nimodipine | IV mannitol | Recombinant factor VII
> 'ENOS: Efficacy of Nitric Oxide in Stroke — 5mg of transdermal Glyceryl Trinitrate.'
Q: According to the lecture's ranking of antiplatelets for stroke prevention: = Clopidogrel ＝ aspirin + dipyridamole > aspirin | Aspirin > clopidogrel | Dipyridamole alone is best | Aspirin ＝ warfarin | Antiplatelets are not used
> 'Antiplatelets: clopidogrel ＝ ASA + dipyridamole > ASA.'
Q: Managing stroke requires a high index of suspicion for stroke chameleons and: = Exclusion of stroke mimics | Routine steroids | Avoiding imaging | Immediate anticoagulation | Lumbar puncture in all
> 'High index of suspicion for stroke chameleons; Exclusion of stroke mimics.'

### After stroke (Nigeria, Akinyemi 2014)
> - CIND 39.9%; post-stroke dementia 8.4%.
> - Risks: low education OR 5.09, pre-stroke decline 4.51, MTLA 2.25, age 1.05.
> - Daily fish intake protective (OR 0.39).
> - MTLA correlates with WMH (r ＝ 0.461) → vascular basis.
> - Psychiatry: post-stroke depression ~1 in 3; emotionalism responds to SSRIs.

> 39.9% CIND; 8.4% post-stroke dementia.
Q: The strongest risk factor for post-stroke cognitive impairment in that cohort (highest OR) was: = Low education | Older age | Pre-stroke cognitive decline | Medial temporal lobe atrophy | Female sex

Q: Which pre-stroke habit was protective against post-stroke cognitive impairment? = Daily fish intake | Daily alcohol | Smoking cessation only | Coffee | Night shifts

> Post-stroke emotionalism responds well to SSRIs (e.g. citalopram).

### OSCE: Temporal lobe epilepsy: diagnosis and seizure management | fps
> History taking station. Task: Take a focused seizure history, identify features suggesting temporal lobe epilepsy, address immediate safety and outline management.
> Patient: “Musa”, 24. Episodes begin with a rising epigastric sensation and déjà vu, then staring, lip-smacking and impaired response for 1–2 minutes. He is confused for 15 minutes afterward. Three attacks in two months. One occurred after sleep deprivation. No fever or drug use.
> - Shared selection of an antiseizure medicine according to seizure type, comorbidity, interactions, pregnancy potential and local guidance; specialist-led initiation where required.
> - Adherence, sleep, alcohol/recreational drugs, medication interactions and individual triggers.
> - No driving until medically reviewed and local legal requirements are met; caution with heights, open flames, machinery, unsupervised swimming and bathing.
> - If drug-resistant after adequate trials, refer to an epilepsy service for diagnostic review and surgical/device/dietary options.
> - Acute convulsive status: ABC, urgent help, glucose, first-line benzodiazepine per protocol, then second-line antiseizure treatment and cause management.
> Critical fail: Unsafe first-aid advice, missing status criteria, or casually clearing the patient to drive.
L: Temporal lobe epilepsy: diagnosis and seizure management: the phases of the station, in order = Characterise the event | Temporal-lobe clues | Book sequence: recent seizures | Aura and post-ictal phase | Background history | Differentials and causes | Safety and status | Focused examination and investigations | Explain and plan
Q: Temporal lobe epilepsy: diagnosis and seizure management. Which phase is this line from? “Please describe exactly what happens before, during and after an episode. What is the last thing you remember? What did a witness see?” = Characterise the event | Temporal-lobe clues | Book sequence: recent seizures | Aura and post-ictal phase | Background history | Differentials and causes | Safety and status | Focused examination and investigations | Explain and plan

> What to say: “I heard you have been having some strange experiences lately. ### OSCE: Frontal lobe assessment | fps
> Physical examination station. Task: Perform and explain a focused bedside assessment of frontal-lobe function.
> - Dorsolateral prefrontal: planning, working memory, set shifting, verbal fluency; dysexecutive syndrome.
> - Orbitofrontal: inhibition and socially appropriate behaviour; disinhibition and poor judgement.
> - Medial frontal/anterior cingulate: initiation and motivation; apathy, abulia or akinetic mutism.
> - Dominant frontal language areas may affect speech production; medial lesions may affect continence and gait.
> - Book mnemonics: Abdulhakeem VALID CMV PS (Verbal fluency, Abstraction, Luria, Inhibition, Digit span, Cognitive estimate, Motor, Visual field, Primitive reflexes, Speech), or VAC²DOVS. FNPH: FACED SPV (Fluency, Abstraction, Coordination, Estimate, Digit span, Speech, Primitive reflexes, Visual field).
> Critical fail: Diagnosing a focal frontal lesion from one bedside sign without considering confounders or completing the neurological examination.
L: Frontal lobe assessment: the phases of the station, in order = Opening | Observation | Orientation and baseline | Verbal fluency | Abstract thinking | Cognitive flexibility | Inhibitory control | Motor programming | Digit span and cognitive estimate | Speech and visual fields | Frontal release signs | Closure

> What to say: “Good morning, I am , a resident here for the examination. The frontal lobe is the part of the brain that controls intellect, impulses, movement and personality, among other things. I will test some of these by asking you questions and giving you tasks. Can I go on?” First ask: any pain anywhere, any problem with sight or hearing, and level of education.
> Examiner checks: Explains purpose in plain words; consent; screens pain, sensory impairment and education before testing (Abdulhakeem NB).

Q: Parietal lobe examination: what is the critical fail in this station? = Not establishing handedness before interpreting dominant versus non-dominant signs. | Diagnosing a focal frontal lesion from one bedside sign without considering confounders or completing the neurological examination. | Testing fields incorrectly (no eye covering) or not checking sensory confounders. | Missing lithium or alcohol toxicity as the likely cause in a psychiatric patient. | Omitting a nerve or confusing the side of uvula or tongue deviation. | Missing signs of Wernicke’s encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia), which needs urgent parenteral thiamine.
> Not establishing handedness before interpreting dominant versus non-dominant signs.

## Courtyard Block | Neurology II

### Pain basics
> - IASP: a sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage.
> - Nociceptors: A-delta and C fibres. Transduction ＝ stimulus activates nerve endings; transmission ＝ relay to brain.
> - Two main pain transmitters: glutamate and substance P.
> - WDR neurons in the dorsal horn; lateral spinothalamic → VPL thalamus. PAG ＝ pain modulation centre; met/leu-enkephalins.
> - Steroids inhibit phospholipase A2; THC ＝ psychoactive part of cannabis.
Q: The IASP defines pain as: = A sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage | A purely physical sensation from tissue damage | Any unpleasant emotion | Activation of C fibres | A reflex withdrawal response
> 'Pain is also defined as sensory and emotional experience associated with or resembling that associated with actual or potential tissue damage.'
Q: Acute pain follows activation of which peripheral nociceptors? = A-delta and C fibres | A-alpha and A-beta fibres | B fibres only | Muscle spindles | Golgi tendon organs
> '...activation of peripheral pain receptors — A delta and C sensory nerve fibres [Nociceptors].'
Q: The process by which tissue-damaging stimuli activate nerve endings is: = Transduction | Transmission | Modulation | Perception | Sensitisation
> 'Transduction of pain is the processes by which tissue damaging stimuli activate nerve endings.'
Q: The two main neurotransmitters of pain named in the lecture are: = Glutamate and substance P | Dopamine and serotonin | GABA and glycine | Acetylcholine and histamine | Noradrenaline and adrenaline
> 'Two main Neurotransmitters of PAIN: Glutamate, Substance P.'
Q: Visceral pain due to injury to internal organs, according to the lecture: = May be sharp and localised | Is never felt | Is always referred | Is purely emotional | Travels only in A-beta fibres
> 'Visceral pain due to injury to internal organs may be sharp and localised.'
Q: Wide dynamic range (WDR) neurons involved in pain transmission are located in the: = Dorsal horn of the spinal cord | Ventral horn | Cerebellum | Basal ganglia | Dorsal root ganglion only
> Lecturer's note: 'Wide Dynamic Range located in the Dorsal Horn of the spinal Cord.'
Q: The lateral spinothalamic tract terminates in the thalamic: = Ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus | Lateral geniculate nucleus | Anterior nucleus | Pulvinar | Dorsomedial nucleus

Q: The pain control/modulation centre involved in stress-induced analgesia is the: = Periaqueductal grey | Substantia nigra | Hippocampus | Nucleus accumbens | Cerebellar vermis
> 'Periaqueductal Grey — pain control/modulation center ... stress and analgesia.'
Q: Met- and leu-enkephalins are: = Endogenous opioid peptides involved in pain modulation | Excitatory amino acids | Inflammatory cytokines | Synthetic opioids | Calcium channel blockers
> Note: 'MET and LEU enkephalins are endogenous opioid peptides' involved in modulation of pain.

### Chronic pain
> - Peripheral and central sensitisation — a malfunction of the nervous system, different from the original insult; ↑ pain and sympathetic signalling, ↓ inhibition.
> - Symptoms: hyperalgesia, allodynia, poor sleep, fatigue, depression, anxiety, memory/attention problems.
> - Non-modifiable risks: old age, trauma/abuse, genetics, SES, female sex, ACEs.
> - Neuropathic pain ＝ nervous system injury, different from nociceptive.
> - MDT ＝ gold standard (better outcomes, function, lower cost). TENS releases endorphins.
Q: Chronification of pain is described as: = A malfunction of the nervous system, different from the original insult | The same process as the original injury | Purely psychological | Always due to ongoing tissue damage | A normal healing response
> 'Its a malfunction of the nervous system, different from the original insult. Needs to be addressed differently.'
Q: Peripheral and central sensitisation lead to: = Increased pain signalling and decreased inhibitory signalling | Decreased pain signalling and increased inhibition | Loss of all sensation | Reduced sympathetic activity | Increased endorphins only
> 'Leads to increased pain signaling and decreased inhibitory signaling.'
Q: Which is listed as a symptom of pain sensitisation? = Depression and anxiety | Improved memory | Increased energy | Bradycardia | Weight loss only
> Symptoms: pain, hyperalgesia, allodynia, poor sleep, fatigue, weakness, depression, anxiety, memory and attention problems.
Q: Which is a NON-modifiable risk factor for chronic pain? = Adverse childhood experiences | Substance abuse | Nutrition | Employment | Sleep problems
> Non-modifiable: old age, trauma/abuse, genetics, SES, female sex, adverse childhood experiences.
Q: Neuropathic pain is best described as: = Pain from nervous system injury, different from nociceptive pain | Identical to nociceptive pain | Pain only from visceral organs | Always psychogenic | Pain without any sensitisation
> 'Neuropathic Pain — injury to the CNS, diff from nociceptive pain; inappropriate response of the brain to the injury.'
Q: The gold-standard care for chronic pain is: = A multidisciplinary approach | Opioid monotherapy | Surgery | Bed rest | Acupuncture alone
> 'Multidisciplinary Approach — Gold Standard Care for Chronic Pain': better outcomes, function, decreased cost.
Q: TENS is thought to relieve pain by: = Promoting release of endorphins | Blocking COX enzymes | Destroying nerve fibres | Increasing substance P | Inducing sleep
> 'TENS — promoting the release of endorphins, the body's natural painkillers.'
Q: A specific reason to refer to pain experts named in the lecture is: = Fibromyalgia or CRPS | Simple ankle sprain | Mild tension headache once | Common cold | Routine paracetamol use
> Specific questions: fibromyalgia, CRPS, opioids, post-viral issues, complex regimens.
Q: Hypnosis, as a complementary pain therapy, is described as: = A state of relaxed and focused attention | Deep sleep | Sedation with drugs | Electrical stimulation | A form of massage
> 'Hypnosis is a state of relaxed and focused attention...'

### Headache
> - ~90% of people; 50% severe, 25% recurrent disabling, 4% chronic daily.
> - Trigeminovascular neurons (ophthalmic division) → pain referred to eye/temple; trigeminal nucleus caudalis gets upper cervical input; superior salivatory nucleus → lacrimation, nasal congestion.
> - Primary: migraine, TTH, trigeminal neuralgia, TACs (cluster). Secondary: tumour, GCA, SAH.
Q: Headache is experienced by approximately what proportion of the global population? = 90% | 10% | 25% | 50% | 100%
> 'Very common malady experienced by close to 90% of the global population.'
Q: What proportion of people have chronic daily headache? = 4% | 1% | 25% | 50% | 15%
> 50% severe, 25% recurrent disabling, 4% chronic daily headaches.
Q: Headache pain is often referred to the eye or temple because pain-sensitive intracranial structures are innervated mainly by: = The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve | The facial nerve | The vagus nerve | C5 roots | The optic nerve
> Trigeminovascular neurons, mainly of the ophthalmic division — 'main reason they're often referred to the eye or temple.'
Q: Nasal congestion and lacrimation with headache are explained by connections of which nucleus with the trigeminal nucleus caudalis? = Superior salivatory nucleus | Nucleus ambiguus | Red nucleus | Edinger-Westphal nucleus only | Hypoglossal nucleus
> 'Superior salivatory nucleus, a parasympathetic nucleus ... accounting for the autonomic symptom of nasal congestion and lacrimation.'
Q: Which is a SECONDARY headache? = Giant cell arteritis | Migraine | Cluster headache | Tension-type headache | Trigeminal neuralgia
> Secondary: tumour-associated, giant cell (temporal) arteritis, SAH.

### Migraine
> - Without aura (~80%): 4–72 h, unilateral, pulsating, mod–severe, worse with activity, nausea, photo/phonophobia.
> - With aura (15–20%): fully reversible, minutes, visual/sensory/speech/motor/brainstem/retinal.
> - Chronic: ≥15 days/month for >3 months, migraine features ≥8 days.
> - CGRP (trigeminal ganglion, NO, sensitisation) and PACAP (rises in attacks; infusion triggers) — a brain disorder, not a vessel disease.
> - Phases: prodrome (77%, 24–48 h, hypothalamus/dopamine, yawning 34%) → aura (~25%, <60 min) → headache → postdrome.
> - Scintillating scotoma ＝ commonest positive visual aura; field defect ＝ commonest negative; motor auras rare.
Q: An attack of migraine without aura lasts: = 4–72 hours | 5–60 minutes | 30 minutes to 7 days | 15 minutes to 3 hours | More than 7 days
> 'recurrent headache attack of 4 to 72 hours.'
Q: Chronic migraine is headache on at least how many days a month for more than 3 months? = 15 | 5 | 8 | 10 | 20
> '15 or more days in a month for more than three months and has migraine features on at least eight.'
Q: In chronic migraine, migraine features must be present on at least how many days a month? = 8 | 4 | 10 | 15 | 20
> '...migraine features on at least eight or more days in a month.'
Q: Migraine with aura accounts for roughly what proportion of migraine? = 15–20% | 5% | 50% | 80% | 95%
> 'migraine with aura ＝ 15-20%'; without aura ≈ 80%.
Q: The word 'migraine' derives from the Greek: = Hemikrania | Kephalos | Algos | Neuron | Aisthesis
> Greek 'hemikrania' → Latin 'hemigranea' → French 'migraine'.
Q: CGRP is abundant in: = Trigeminal ganglion neurons | Cerebellar Purkinje cells | Motor neurons | Retinal cells | Adrenal medulla only
> 'CGRP is abundant in trigeminal ganglion neurons.'

> '...its concentration is elevated during the attacks, and its infusion may trigger migraine.'
Q: The lecture's take-away is that migraine is: = A brain-system disorder, not primarily a vessel disease | Primarily a cerebral blood vessel disease | A psychological disorder | An infection | A muscle disorder
> 'Migraine is a brain system disorder ... NOT PRIMARILY CEREBRAL BLOOD VESSEL DISEASE.'
Q: The correct order of the four phases of migraine is: = Prodrome, aura, headache, postdrome | Aura, prodrome, headache, postdrome | Headache, aura, prodrome, postdrome | Prodrome, headache, aura, postdrome | Aura, headache, prodrome, postdrome

### Diagnosing migraine
> - Clinical, from history; investigations and exam normal. ICHD-3 (2018).
> - ≥5 attacks; 4–72 h; ≥2 of unilateral/pulsating/mod–severe/aggravated by activity; plus nausea/vomiting or photo+phonophobia; not another disorder.
> - Exclude secondary: inflammation, mass, CSF pressure, ictal epileptic headache, CADASIL.
> - Misdiagnosed as TTH, cluster, sinusitis — refer if in doubt.
Q: The diagnosis of migraine is based mainly on: = The history | MRI brain | EEG | CSF analysis | Serum CGRP
> 'Clinical diagnosis — based almost on the history. Investigations normal.'
Q: The IHS criteria for migraine require at least how many attacks? = 5 | 2 | 3 | 10 | 15
> A. At least 5 attacks.
Q: Which is NOT one of the IHS 'C' pain characteristics of migraine? = Bilateral pressing quality | Unilateral | Pulsating | Moderate or severe intensity | Aggravation by routine activity
> C: unilateral, pulsating, moderate/severe, aggravated by activity. Bilateral pressing ＝ tension-type.
Q: Current diagnostic criteria for headache are the: = ICHD-3 (Cephalalgia 2018) | DSM-5-TR | ICD-9 | NINCDS-ADRDA | McDonald criteria

### Migraine treatment
> - Triggers: stress, menses, OCP, glare, exertion, sleep loss, hunger, nitrite/glutamate/tyramine.
> - Acute: triptans first line (mod/severe); NSAIDs (mild/mod); gepants (ubrogepant, rimegepant); lasmiditan (5-HT1F); DHE; antiemetics. Limit to <8–10 days/month.
> - Preventive: beta-blockers first line; topiramate, valproate; amitriptyline, venlafaxine; verapamil; CGRP mAbs; Botox for chronic migraine (every 12 weeks); Mg, riboflavin, CoQ10.
> - Erenumab 70/140 mg SC monthly; fremanezumab 225 monthly or 675 quarterly; galcanezumab 240 load → 120 monthly; eptinezumab 100/300 IV quarterly.
> - ~50% overuse medication. Migraine ＝ most disabling neurological condition.

### Other primary headaches
> - TTH: 30 min–7 days, bilateral, pressing, mild–moderate, not worse with activity, no nausea.
> - Hypnic: only during sleep, same time nightly.
> - Trigeminal neuralgia: electric shocks, triggers, V2/V3 ≫ V1, no deficit → carbamazepine; microvascular decompression.
> - TACs: cluster, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT; pain + lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, miosis.
> - Cluster: men 20–50, periorbital, circadian, alcohol-triggered, clusters → 100% O₂ 5–10 L/min ×15–20 min, SC sumatriptan 6 mg; verapamil prophylaxis; lithium; prednisone.

### Secondary headache
> - Red flags: first/worst/abrupt; onset > 50; major illness; worse AM/Valsalva; wakes from sleep; trauma; progressive; seizure, LOC; fever, stiff neck; abnormal exam.
> - Tumour: dull, slowly increasing, worse with exertion/posture, disturbs sleep, nausea.
> - GCA: F>M, avg 70; headache 85%, tenderness 70%, jaw claudication 65%, PMR 40%, ESR > 50 in 95% → steroids.
> - SAH: explosive headache, neck stiffness; CT negative → LP.
> - Raised ICP: intubate/hyperventilate, osmotics, head up, limit fluids, call consultant.
Q: Which is a 'worrisome' (red flag) headache feature? = Onset after age 50 | Lifelong stable pattern | Relieved by paracetamol | Bilateral pressing pain for years | Family history of migraine

### Epilepsy definition and context
> - ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 h apart; or 1 + ≥60% recurrence risk over 10 years; or an epilepsy syndrome.
> - History: Babylonian text >3,000 years ("miqtu"); Greeks "disease of the gods"; Hippocrates → brain; "falling/sacred disease"; bromides → phenobarbital 1912 → phenytoin 1938; Hans Berger first human EEG 1924.
> - Nigeria: 8–13/1,000 (pockets 37/1,000); ~70% treatment gap. Myths: evil spirits, contagious via saliva. Senegal: revered as holy.
Q: By the ILAE operational definition, epilepsy can be diagnosed after: = Two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart | One provoked seizure | Two seizures on the same day | A single febrile seizure | Any abnormal EEG
> 'At least two unprovoked [or reflex] seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart.'
Q: After ONE unprovoked seizure, epilepsy can be diagnosed if the recurrence risk over the next 10 years is at least: = 60% | 20% | 40% | 80% | 100%
> '...probability of further seizures similar to the general recurrence risk [at least 60%] ... over the next 10 years.'
Q: The earliest detailed account of epilepsy is: = A Babylonian medical text over 3,000 years old | A Greek text by Hippocrates | An Egyptian papyrus from 500 AD | The Bible | A Chinese text from 1000 AD
> '...a Babylonian text on medicine written over 3000 years ago' (British Museum).
Q: Who first held that epilepsy was caused by abnormalities of the brain? = Hippocrates | Galen | Hughlings Jackson | Hans Berger | Penfield
> 'In 450 B.C., Hippocrates disputed this thinking and felt that epilepsy was caused by abnormalities of the brain.'
Q: Phenobarbital and phenytoin were introduced in: = 1912 and 1938 | 1812 and 1838 | 1950 and 1960 | 1890 and 1900 | 1980 and 1990
> 'Phenobarbital (1912) and Phenytoin (1938)', after bromides in the 19th century.
Q: Hans Berger, who recorded the first human EEG in 1924, was a: = German psychiatrist | British neurologist | French physiologist | American neurosurgeon | Austrian psychoanalyst
> Note: 'German psychiatrist and neuroscientist, 1924 recorded first human EEG using a galvanometer.'
