Q: The epilepsy treatment gap in Nigeria quoted in the lecture is about: = 70% | 10% | 30% | 50% | 90%
> 'treatment gap — 70% dont have access to care.'
Q: Which is a reason for the epilepsy treatment gap in developing regions? = Stigma, poverty and cultural beliefs | Excess neurologists | Overuse of EEG | Too many free drugs | Over-diagnosis
> Lack of access/knowledge of drugs, poverty, cultural beliefs, stigma, poor infrastructure, shortage of professionals.

### Classification wording
> - Simple partial → focal aware / focal conscious; complex partial → focal impaired awareness / impaired consciousness; secondarily generalised → focal to bilateral tonic-clonic; psychic → cognitive; dyscognitive dropped; arrest → behaviour arrest.
> - 2025: "motor" no longer used (e.g. "focal conscious tonic").
> - Unwitnessed, normal tests → unknown (onset) tonic-clonic. Focal lesion on MRI/EEG → focal to bilateral.
> - JME → myoclonic-tonic-clonic; Doose → myoclonic-atonic; LGS → atypical absence.
Q: The old term 'complex partial seizure' is now: = Focal impaired awareness (impaired consciousness) seizure | Focal aware seizure | Generalised seizure | Absence seizure | Unknown onset seizure
> Complex partial → focal impaired awareness (2025: focal with impaired consciousness).
Q: 'Secondarily generalised tonic-clonic seizure' is now called: = Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic | Generalised tonic-clonic | Unknown onset tonic-clonic | Myoclonic-tonic-clonic | Atonic seizure
> Secondarily generalised → focal to bilateral tonic-clonic.
Q: The descriptor 'psychic' seizure has been replaced by: = Cognitive | Dyscognitive | Emotional | Autonomic | Behaviour arrest
> Psychic → cognitive. 'Dyscognitive' was discontinued.
Q: A man has an unwitnessed-onset seizure with bilateral stiffening then shaking; EEG and MRI are normal. In 2025 this is: = Unknown tonic-clonic | Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic | Generalised absence | Unclassifiable | Myoclonic-atonic
> Old: unclassified; 2017: unknown-onset tonic-clonic; 2025: unknown tonic-clonic.
Q: Same patient, but EEG shows a right parietal focus and MRI shows cortical dysplasia. The seizure is now: = Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic | Unknown tonic-clonic | Generalised tonic-clonic | Atypical absence | Unclassified
> A focal aetiology makes focal onset overwhelmingly likely → focal to bilateral tonic-clonic.
Q: A 25-year-old woman hears 'familiar music playing', cannot make out speech, then is mildly confused. This is: = Focal seizure with impaired consciousness | Focal conscious sensory seizure | Generalised absence | PNES | Migraine aura
> She cannot interpret her environment and is confused → focal with impaired consciousness (old: complex partial).
Q: A fully aware man with 'hair standing on edge' and flushing has: = Focal conscious autonomic seizures | Panic attacks only | Focal impaired awareness seizures | Generalised tonic seizures | Absence seizures
> Focal conscious autonomic (old: simple partial autonomic).
Q: In juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, jerks followed by stiffening then rhythmic jerking of all limbs is classified as: = Generalised myoclonic-tonic-clonic | Myoclonic-atonic | Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic | Atypical absence | Epileptic spasms
> Generalised myoclonic-tonic-clonic seizure.
Q: In the 2025 terminology for focal seizures, which word is no longer used/assumed? = Motor | Focal | Tonic | Conscious | Autonomic
> 'This seizure is a focal tonic seizure (the word "motor" is no longer used/assumed).'
Q: Absence seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome with slow spike-wave are classified as: = Atypical absence | Typical absence | Focal impaired awareness | Myoclonic | Unknown
> '...the absence seizures are classified as atypical absence.'

### First seizure
> - First aid: calm, safe place, soft under head, ABCs, roll on side, nothing in the mouth, look for alert tags. Call emergency: first seizure, > 4–5 min, other acute problem.
> - Causes: neonates hypoxia-ischaemia; children febrile; adolescents drugs; adults alcohol withdrawal, tumour; > 45 stroke, degeneration.
> - Work-up: FBC, electrolytes, Ca, glucose, LFT, renal, ESR, tox, pregnancy; CT/MRI; EEG.
> - Treat if: no reversible cause, abnormal exam, abnormal EEG/MRI, serious consequences (driving).
Q: During a seizure, first aid includes: = Rolling the patient onto their side and placing nothing in the mouth | Placing a spoon in the mouth | Restraining the limbs | Giving water | Leaving them on their back
> Roll to the side; 'Do not attempt to place anything (e.g., tongue blade, spoon) into the patient's mouth.'
Q: Outside hospital, emergency care should be called if a seizure lasts more than: = 4–5 minutes | 30 seconds | 1 minute | 30 minutes | 1 hour
> 'the seizure lasts for more than 4-5 minutes' — also for first seizure or other acute problems.
Q: A characteristic cause of seizures in infants and children (1 month–12 years) is: = Febrile seizures | Alzheimer's disease | Alcohol withdrawal | Cerebrovascular disease | Illicit drug use
> Children: febrile seizures, genetic, infection, developmental, trauma.
Q: In older adults (> 45 years), a leading cause of new seizures is: = Cerebrovascular disease | Perinatal hypoxia | Febrile seizures | Genetic syndromes | Drug withdrawal in neonates
> Older adults: cerebrovascular disease, tumour, Alzheimer's and other degenerative diseases.
Q: Which is NOT part of the routine blood work-up of a first adult seizure? = Serum CGRP | Electrolytes and calcium | Glucose | Liver and renal function | Consider pregnancy test
> Bloods: FBC, electrolytes, calcium, glucose, LFT, RFT, ESR, ± toxicology, ± pregnancy test. Then CT/MRI and EEG.
Q: Which factor FAVOURS starting treatment after a single seizure? = Abnormal EEG or MRI | An immediately reversible precipitant | Normal work-up | Patient is a child | Provoked by hypoglycaemia
> Favouring treatment: no reversible precipitant, abnormal exam, abnormal EEG or MRI, serious consequences of recurrence (driving).

### Antiseizure medication
> - Goals: control, few adverse effects, cost-effective, quality of life.
> - Mechanisms: Na⁺ channels, Ca²⁺ channels, ↑GABA, ↓glutamate, ↓vesicle release.
> - Focal: lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine. Absence: ethosuximide (best), valproate. Myoclonic: clonazepam, valproate, levetiracetam.
> - Comorbidity: migraine → TPM/VPA; mood → LTG/CBZ; pain/RLS → GBP/PGB; liver failure → LEV/OXC, avoid VPA; cardiac → LEV.
> - Behavioural harm: phenobarbital, levetiracetam. Leucopenia: CBZ, PHT. Weight gain: VPA.
Q: Which is NOT a listed goal of epilepsy therapy? = Eliminate all EEG abnormalities | Control seizures | Minimise adverse events | Cost-effective therapy | Improve quality of life
> Goals: control seizures, minimise adverse events, cost-effective therapy, improve quality of life.
Q: The BEST drug for absence seizures, per the lecture, is: = Ethosuximide | Carbamazepine | Phenytoin | Gabapentin | Oxcarbazepine
> 'Absence Seizures: Valproate, Ethosuximide — best.'
Q: Which is a FIRST-CHOICE drug for focal onset seizures? = Lamotrigine | Ethosuximide | Acetazolamide | Piracetam | Clonazepam
> Focal first choice: lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine.
Q: First-line drugs for myoclonic seizures are: = Clonazepam, valproate, levetiracetam | Carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine | Gabapentin and pregabalin | Ethosuximide alone | Vigabatrin and tiagabine
> Myoclonic: clonazepam, valproate, levetiracetam. (Na-channel drugs can worsen myoclonus.)
Q: In liver failure, the preferred antiseizure drugs are: = Levetiracetam and oxcarbazepine (avoid valproate) | Valproate | Phenobarbital | Carbamazepine and phenytoin | Topiramate only
> 'Liver Failure — LEV, OXC, avoid VPA.'
Q: For a patient with epilepsy and migraine, the lecture suggests: = Topiramate or valproate | Levetiracetam | Phenytoin | Gabapentin | Lacosamide
> 'Migraine prophylaxis — TPM, VPA.'
Q: Antiseizure drugs with an antidepressant/mood benefit listed are: = Lamotrigine and carbamazepine | Levetiracetam and phenobarbital | Topiramate and vigabatrin | Phenytoin and ethosuximide | Gabapentin and lacosamide
> 'Antidepressant — LTG, CBZ.'
Q: Which antiseizure drugs are linked with ADVERSE cognitive or behavioural effects? = Phenobarbital and levetiracetam | Lamotrigine and valproate | Carbamazepine and lamotrigine | Gabapentin and pregabalin | Ethosuximide and clobazam
> 'Adverse Cognitive or behavioural: Phenobarbital, levetiracetam.'
Q: Leucopenia is an adverse effect particularly of: = Carbamazepine and phenytoin | Levetiracetam | Lamotrigine | Gabapentin | Ethosuximide
> 'Leucopenia: Carbamazepine, Phenytoin.'
Q: The antiseizure drug classically associated with weight gain is: = Valproate | Topiramate | Zonisamide | Levetiracetam | Lacosamide
> 'Weight gain: Valproate.'
Q: Which is a listed mechanism of antiseizure drugs? = Blocking voltage-dependent sodium channels | Increasing glutamate release | Blocking GABA receptors | Increasing synaptic vesicle release | Opening calcium channels
> Mechanisms: Na⁺-channel blockade, ↓ Ca²⁺ channels, ↑ GABA, ↓ glutamate, ↓ vesicle release.
Q: In cardiac disease, the preferred antiseizure drug per the lecture is: = Levetiracetam | Phenytoin | Carbamazepine | Lacosamide | Valproate
> 'Cardiac Disease — LEV.'
Q: Post-ictal psychosis typically follows a cluster of seizures after: = A lucid interval of 1–3 days | Exactly 1 hour | 2 weeks | No interval — during the seizure | Years
> Post-ictal psychosis: lucid interval of about 1–3 days after a cluster; brief; responds to low-dose antipsychotic/benzodiazepine.
Q: 'Forced normalisation' (Landolt) describes: = Psychosis emerging as seizures stop and the EEG normalises | Normal EEG during absences | Normal prolactin in PNES | Normal MRI in JME | Normal cognition after surgery
> Forced normalisation: alternative psychosis when seizure control is achieved and the EEG normalises.
Q: Which psychotropic most strongly lowers the seizure threshold in a dose-dependent way? = Clozapine | Aripiprazole | Sertraline | Haloperidol at low dose | Lorazepam
> Clozapine (dose-dependent; >600 mg high risk); also bupropion, clomipramine, chlorpromazine.
Q: Valproate in pregnancy is associated with: = Neural tube defects and reduced IQ/autism in offspring | No risk | Only cleft lip | Improved neurodevelopment | Only neonatal jaundice
> Valproate: neural tube defects, lower IQ, autism — avoid in women of childbearing potential unless no alternative.
Q: Interictal personality changes of Geschwind syndrome include: = Hypergraphia, hyperreligiosity, altered sexuality, viscosity | Euphoria and disinhibition only | Catatonia | Pseudobulbar affect | Grandiosity
> Geschwind syndrome (temporal lobe epilepsy): hypergraphia, hyperreligiosity, hyposexuality, viscosity.

### Special situations
> - Refractory: lesionectomy, lobectomy, hemispherectomy; stimulation; stereotactic radiosurgery.
> - Autoimmune epilepsy: new onset < 2 years + drug resistance, psychosis/hallucinations, movement disorder, headache, cognitive decline; autoimmune stigmata, cancer; take serum and CSF before immunotherapy.
> - NCSE → do EEG. Catamenial epilepsy; ictal epileptic headache.
> - PNES: eyes firmly closed, rarely injured, no incontinence, > 5–10 min, no post-event confusion, recall, crying, side-to-side rocking → psychotherapy.
> - Gut–brain axis: ~90% of serotonin made in gut; dysbiosis → anxiety, depression; FMT under study.
Q: Which is a RESECTIVE surgery for refractory epilepsy? = Hemispherectomy | Vagus nerve stimulation | Deep brain stimulation | Stereotactic radiosurgery | Ketogenic diet
> Resective: lesionectomy, lobectomy, hemispherectomy. Non-resective: electrical stimulation.
Q: Autoimmune epilepsy should be considered in new-onset epilepsy of duration under: = 2 years | 2 weeks | 2 months | 10 years | 20 years
> 'New onset epilepsy with incomplete seizure control and of duration less than 2 years.'
Q: Which accompaniment of new-onset epilepsy should prompt consideration of autoimmune epilepsy? = Psychosis and hallucinations | Good response to first drug | Family history of febrile seizures | Normal cognition | Childhood onset absence
> Plus: ASM resistance, psychiatric accompaniments (psychosis, hallucinations), movement disorder, headache, cognitive impairment.
Q: Before starting immunotherapy for suspected autoimmune epilepsy, you should: = Obtain serum and CSF samples | Stop all antiseizure drugs | Perform surgery | Wait 2 years | Start valproate
> 'Obtaining serum and CSF before starting immunotherapy.'
Q: Non-convulsive status epilepticus requires a high index of suspicion and: = An EEG | A CT only | Immediate surgery | Observation alone | Serum prolactin only
> 'NCSE — high index of suspicion, therefore do EEG.'
Q: Epilepsy linked to the menstrual cycle is called: = Catamenial epilepsy | Reflex epilepsy | Gelastic epilepsy | Rolandic epilepsy | Ictal headache
> Catamenial epilepsy — listed under 'Many faces of epilepsy' and 'Women and epilepsy'.
Q: Which feature favours a functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizure? = Eyes firmly closed and resisting opening | Occurrence during sleep | Post-ictal confusion | Tongue bitten laterally with incontinence | Stertorous breathing
> PNES: eyes firmly closed, resistant to opening; rarely injured; no incontinence; prompt recovery; recall of event.
Q: Duration typical of functional seizures, per the lecture: = More than 5–10 minutes | Under 30 seconds | 1–2 minutes | Exactly 3 minutes | Only seconds at night
> 'Events lasts more than 5-10minutes and more.'
Q: Which feature favours an EPILEPTIC seizure over PNES? = Post-event confusion | Crying | Side-to-side rocking | Detailed recall of the event | Eyes firmly closed
> Epileptic: occurrence in sleep, confusion, stertorous breathing, prolactin rise. PNES: no post-event confusion and recalls event.
Q: Treatment of functional seizures recommended is: = Psychotherapy with adjunct medication for anxiety/depression | High-dose antiseizure drugs | Epilepsy surgery | Restraint | Steroids
> 'Rx Psychotherapy + adjunct medication for anxiety and or depression.'
Q: Roughly what proportion of the body's serotonin is produced in the gut? = 90% | 10% | 30% | 50% | 70%
> '...with roughly 90% of serotonin produced in the gut.'
Q: The gut–brain axis is best described as: = A bidirectional network linking enteric and central nervous systems via neural, hormonal and immune pathways | A one-way signal from brain to gut | Only the vagus nerve | A purely hormonal loop | Irrelevant to mental health
> 'a bidirectional communication network ... via neural, hormonal, and immune pathways.'
Q: Faecal microbiota transplantation in gut–brain research aims to: = Correct dysbiosis and modulate neuroinflammation | Increase gut bacteria load indiscriminately | Treat only diarrhoea | Replace antidepressants entirely | Remove the microbiome
> FMT 'acts as a therapeutic tool to correct gut dysbiosis, thereby modulating neuroinflammation.'

### From Lunacy to the Act
> - Lunacy Ordinance 1916 → Lunacy Laws 1948 → amended 1958; in force until 5 January 2023.
> - Bill 2003 (Martyns-Yellowe & Tafida; Senate adopted 2004) → 2013 (Adejare & Adeola) → 7th/8th Assemblies stalled → 9th Assembly (Sen. Oloriegbe) → to President Nov 2022 → assented 5 Jan 2023 as the National Mental Health Act 2021.
> - WHO/OHCHR 2023: human-rights-based approach to mental health law.
Q: Until 5 January 2023, Nigeria's mental health legislation was the: = Lunacy Law of 1958 | Mental Health Act 1983 | Criminal Code Act 1916 | National Health Act 2014 | Lunacy Ordinance 1890
> 'Until the 5th of January, 2023, The mental health legislation in Nigeria was the Lunacy Law of 1958.'
Q: The Lunacy legislation originated as the Lunacy Ordinance of: = 1916 | 1866 | 1948 | 1958 | 1960
> 'It originated as Lunacy ordinance in 1916 and later transformed to Lunacy laws in 1948 and amended in 1958.'
Q: The 2023 joint publication 'Mental health, human rights and legislation' was produced by WHO and: = The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights | UNICEF | The World Bank | The African Union | The World Psychiatric Association
> 'The WHO and office of the high commissioner for human right 2023 joint publication...'
Q: Nigeria's quest for a modern mental health law began in: = 2003 | 1958 | 1990 | 2013 | 2021
> 'Nigeria's quest for a modern mental health law began in 2003.'
Q: The 2003 mental health bill was proposed by: = Sen. Ibiabuye Martyns-Yellowe and Sen. Dalhatu Tafida | Sen. Oloriegbe | Hon. Adejare and Hon. Adeola | The Minister of Health | Prof. Lambo
> Sen. Ibiabuye Martyns-Yellowe and Sen. Dalhatu Tafida — adopted by the Senate in 2004 but lapsed.
Q: The bill that finally passed was sponsored in the 9th National Assembly by: = Sen. Oloriegbe Yahaya Ibrahim (Kwara Central) | Sen. Dalhatu Tafida | Hon. Samuel Adejare | Hon. Solomon Adeola | Sen. Martyns-Yellowe
> 'Sponsored by Sen. Oloriegbe, Yahaya Ibrahim (Kwara Central).'
Q: The National Mental Health Act was assented to by the President on: = 5 January 2023 | 1 October 2021 | November 2022 | 31 May 2012 | 20 February 2026
> '...assented to by the president on the 5th January, 2023.'
Q: The re-introduction of the bill in 2013 was by: = Hon. Samuel Babatunde Adejare and Hon. Solomon Olamilekan Adeola | Sen. Oloriegbe | Sen. Tafida alone | The Lagos State House | The Federal Executive Council
> 're-introduced in 2013 ... by Hon. Samuel Babatunde Adejare and Hon. Solomon Olamilekan Adeola.'

### WHO Checklist on Mental Health Legislation (2005)
> - Companion to the WHO Resource Book; to review existing law and draft new law.
> - Committee: lawyer, government focal point, service users/families, professionals, NGOs — led by an independent human rights/legal expert.
> - Three questions: adequately covered / covered but not fully / not covered.
> - Items A–Z plus AZ (offences and penalties); G — voluntary preferred; H — non-protesting patients; K — proxy consent, advance directives; T — mentally ill offenders (diversion, unfit to stand trial, hospital orders, transfer, secure units).
Q: The WHO Checklist on Mental Health Legislation was published in: = 2005 | 1991 | 1996 | 2013 | 2023
> WHO Checklist on Mental Health Legislation (2005) — companion to the WHO Resource Book.
Q: The WHO checklist is a companion to the: = WHO Resource Book on Mental Health, Human Rights and Legislation | ICD-11 | mhGAP Intervention Guide | Mental Health Atlas | UN Principles 1991
> 'This checklist is a companion to the WHO Resource Book on Mental Health, Human Rights and Legislation.'
Q: The checklist review process should be led by: = An independent human rights and/or legal expert | The Minister of Health | A consultant psychiatrist | The police | A service user
> 'the process be led by an independent human rights and/or legal expert.'
Q: For each component of the checklist, how many questions are addressed? = Three | Two | Four | Five | Ten
> Three: adequately covered? covered but not fully? not covered at all?
Q: Which is NOT among the recommended members of the checklist committee? = Representatives of pharmaceutical companies | A legal practitioner | The government mental health focal point | Service user and family groups | NGOs
> Committee: legal practitioner, focal point, user/family groups, professionals, NGOs, government departments.
Q: In the WHO checklist, legislative issues are grouped alphabetically A–Z, with the last category designated: = AZ | ZZ | Z1 | Omega | X
> 'grouped in alphabetical order A–Z with the last category designated as AZ' — offences and penalties.
Q: Checklist item H, 'non-protesting patients', refers to patients who: = Are incapable of informed decisions but do not refuse admission or treatment | Refuse admission strongly | Are prisoners | Are minors | Have capacity and agree
> '...incapable of making informed decisions about admission or treatment, but who do not refuse.'
Q: Which checklist item covers advance directives? = K. Proxy consent for treatment | G. Voluntary admission | P. Seclusion and restraint | T. Mentally ill offenders | U. Discrimination
> K. Proxy consent — 'Does the law provide for use of "advance directives"...?'
Q: Item G of the checklist asks whether the law promotes: = Voluntary admission and treatment as a preferred alternative to involuntary | Involuntary admission as first choice | Seclusion | Long-term asylum care | Police custody
> 'Does the law promote voluntary admission and treatment as a preferred alternative to involuntary...?'
Q: Under item T (mentally ill offenders), the checklist asks whether the law allows: = Diversion of alleged offenders to the mental health system instead of prosecution | Automatic prison for all offenders | Sterilisation of offenders | Indefinite detention without review | Trial in absentia
> '...diverting an alleged offender with a mental disorder to the mental health system in lieu of prosecuting...'
Q: Checklist item X (social security) asks about: = Disability grants and pensions for people with mental disabilities | Police powers | Research ethics | Housing only | ECT
> 'Does legislation provide for disability grants and pensions...?'
Q: Item Z, protection of vulnerable groups, lists: = Minors, women and minorities | Prisoners only | Elderly only | Doctors | Refugees only
> Z. Protection of vulnerable groups: minors, women, minorities.

### The Act (2021)
> - Long title: establish a Mental Health Department; protect people with intellectual, psychosocial or cognitive disabilities; regulate services.
> - 5 parts: I administration; II rights; III facility-based care; IV criminal proceedings; V property/affairs and interpretation.
> - Department of Mental Health Services in the Federal Ministry of Health; care in the least restrictive environment.
> - Mental Health Fund: voluntary contributions, National Assembly, bilateral/multilateral grants, other approved sources.
Q: The official title of Nigeria's new mental health law is the: = National Mental Health Act 2021 | Mental Health Act 2023 | Lunacy (Amendment) Act 2023 | Mental Health Bill 2003 | Mental Health and Substance Abuse Act 2022
> It became an Act with a new title: National Mental Health Act 2021.
Q: How many parts does the National Mental Health Act 2021 have? = 5 | 3 | 4 | 7 | 10
> 5 parts: objective/administration; rights; facility care; criminal proceedings; property/affairs and interpretation.
Q: Part IV of the Act deals with: = Persons with mental health conditions and criminal proceedings | Rights of persons with mental health conditions | Facility-based care | Property and affairs | Administration
> Part IV — Persons with mental health conditions and criminal proceedings.
Q: The Act's long title refers to protecting the rights of persons with: = Intellectual, psychosocial or cognitive disabilities | Psychosis only | Substance use only | Epilepsy | Physical disabilities
> '...promote and protect the rights of persons with intellectual, psychosocial or cognitive disabilities.'
Q: Which is an objective of the Act? = Facilitate a community-based approach to mental health care | Promote institutional care | Reintroduce the Lunacy Law | Restrict psychotropic drugs | Privatise mental health services
> Objectives include facilitating a community-based approach and promoting recovery and community integration.
Q: The Department of Mental Health Services is established in the: = Federal Ministry of Health | Federal Ministry of Justice | Presidency | NAFDAC | National Assembly
> 'Department of Mental Health Services in the Federal Ministry of Health.'
Q: Which is a source of the Mental Health Fund? = Money approved by the National Assembly | Fines paid by patients | Hospital admission fees only | Pharmaceutical levies only | Court fees
> Sources: voluntary contributions, moneys approved by National Assembly, bilateral/multilateral grants, others approved by Finance.

### Mental Health Assessment Committee (set up by the Minister)
> - Chair: lawyer ≥ 10 years with medical-law knowledge; consultant psychiatrist; medical social worker ≥ 10 years; CSO rep; community gatekeeper (religious/traditional leader).
> - Hears appeals, investigates complaints, reviews involuntary/long-term cases, decides restraint/seclusion extensions, can order discharge.
> - Dissatisfied with the Committee → High Court (general); involuntary admission appeal → Court of Appeal.
Q: The Chairman of the Mental Health Assessment Committee must be: = A legal practitioner qualified for at least 10 years with knowledge of medical law | A consultant psychiatrist | A traditional ruler | A medical social worker | The Minister of Health
> 'A Chairman who shall be a legal practitioner ... qualified ... for at least 10 years ... medical law.'
Q: Which is a member of the Mental Health Assessment Committee? = A community gatekeeper (religious or traditional leader) | A police commissioner | A pharmacist | A judge of the High Court | A prison officer
> Members: legal chair, consultant psychiatrist, social worker ≥10 yrs, CSO rep, community gatekeeper.
Q: The Mental Health Assessment Committee is constituted by: = The Minister | The President | The Chief Judge | The NPMCN | The Medical and Dental Council
> 'The Committee shall be constituted by the Minister.'
Q: The medical social worker on the Committee must have at least how many years' experience? = 10 | 2 | 5 | 15 | 20
> 'a medical social worker with not less than 10 years of experience.'
Q: Which is a function of the Mental Health Assessment Committee? = Hearing applications to extend restraint or seclusion | Prescribing medication | Licensing psychiatrists | Prosecuting offenders | Setting fees
> Functions: appeals, complaints, periodic review, and applications to extend restraint or seclusion.
Q: A person dissatisfied with a decision of the Committee (in general) may seek redress in the: = High Court | Magistrates' Court | Supreme Court directly | Customary Court | Ministry of Health
> 'Where a person is not satisfied with the decision of the Committee, that person may seek redress in the High Court.'

### Part II rights
> - Same rights as other citizens; no discrimination; protection from abuse including chaining; witnesses of abuse must report to police.
> - No dismissal or eviction solely for a mental health condition.
> - Same standard of care as physical illness; least restrictive; access to psychotropics/essential medicines; join the MDT treatment plan; spend personal money.
> - Legal representative decides if capacity lacking; private visits and examination.
> - Information and confidentiality per National Health Act No. 8 of 2014, with a harm exception.
> - State provides legal aid if unaffordable. Staff who strike or neglect patients commit an offence.
Q: Under the Act, a person who witnesses abuse of a person with a mental health condition must report it to: = The police | The Committee | The family | The Minister | The media
> '...shall report the incident immediately to the police.'
Q: The Act explicitly names which practice among forms of cruel treatment prohibited? = Chaining | Psychotherapy | Day hospital care | Home visits | Group therapy
> '...cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, including but not limited to chaining.'
Q: Under the employment rights provisions, an employer: = Shall not terminate employment merely on grounds of present or past mental health condition | May dismiss a worker during psychiatric treatment | Must pay reduced wages | Must report the worker to police | Can withhold benefits
> 'An employer shall not terminate the employment ... merely on the grounds of present or past mental health condition.'
Q: Under the housing right, a tenant who develops a mental health condition: = Shall not be evicted solely on the grounds of the condition | May be evicted after 30 days | Must move to a facility | Loses tenancy rights | Needs a guardian to stay
> '...shall not be evicted from his place of residence solely on the grounds of his mental health condition.'
Q: The right to a quality standard of treatment includes: = The same standard of care as a person with physical health problems | Care only in asylums | Treatment chosen by family alone | Mandatory long-term admission | Lower standards in rural areas
> 'the same standard of care as a person with physical health problems and shall be treated on an equitable basis.'
Q: Treatment under the Act must be delivered in the: = Least restrictive environment and manner | Most secure setting | Nearest prison | Patient's home only | Teaching hospitals only
> 'receive treatment in the least restrictive environment and manner.'
Q: A patient in a facility has the right to access and spend personal money: = Unless their mental capacity does not allow it | Never | Only with family consent | Only after discharge | Only for food
> '...right to have access to and spend personal money ... unless the mental capacity of the person does not allow that.'
Q: Confidentiality and access to information under the Act are as provided in the: = National Health Act No. 8 of 2014 | Lunacy Law 1958 | Child Rights Act 2003 | Criminal Code | Evidence Act 2011
> '...as provided in the National Health Act No. 8 of 2014.'
Q: Confidentiality does NOT prevent health professionals from: = Taking reasonable steps to prevent serious harm to the person or others | Selling information | Publishing case details | Informing employers routinely | Telling neighbours
> 'Nothing shall preclude health professionals from taking reasonable steps to prevent the likelihood of serious harm.'
Q: If a patient cannot afford a lawyer, the Act provides that: = The State shall provide legal assistance | They go unrepresented | The hospital pays | The Committee represents them | The family must pay
> '...the State shall provide legal assistance to the patient.'
Q: Supervised visits may be required when: = There are reasonable grounds to believe the person may be violent or dangerous | The patient is a minor | Always for involuntary patients | The visitor is a lawyer | Never
> 'Where there are reasonable grounds to believe that a person will be violent or may otherwise pose a danger...'
Q: A legal representative appointed by a patient can make care decisions: = Where the person lacks the capacity to make decisions | At all times | Only about money | Only after court approval | Never
> '...power to make decisions ... where the person lacks the capacity to make decisions.'
Q: A health professional who strikes or neglects a person with a mental health condition: = Commits an offence | Receives a warning only | Is protected if acting in good faith always | Must only apologise | Is referred for training
> 'Any health professional ... who strikes, ill-treats or neglects ... commits an offence.'
Q: The functional test of capacity requires the person to be able to: = Understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision | Agree with the doctor | Read and write | Have no diagnosis | Be over 21
> Capacity: understand, retain, use/weigh, communicate — decision-specific and time-specific.

### Consent and voluntary care
> - No treatment without prior written consent; information in the person's language and literacy level; supported decision-making at no cost.
> - Every public facility integrates mental health care; Minister designates facilities; FMoH sets minimum standards and publishes licensed centres.
> - Voluntary patient told of right to discharge at any time; discharge against advice granted within 24 hours unless they meet involuntary criteria.
Q: Under the Act, treatment may not be administered without: = The prior written consent of the person | Verbal family consent | Police approval | Court order | Payment
> 'No treatment shall be administered without the prior written consent of the person.'
Q: Where a person cannot understand the information relevant to a decision, the Act requires: = Supported decision-making at no cost | Treatment without consent | Automatic involuntary admission | Family to decide alone | Postponement indefinitely
> '...provisions shall be made ... for supported decision making at no cost to the person.'
Q: A voluntary patient's request for discharge against medical advice must be granted within: = 24 hours | 6 hours | 72 hours | 7 days | 28 days
> '...the facility shall grant the request within twenty-four hours unless the person meets the conditions for involuntary admission.'
Q: Who may designate a hospital as a mental health facility? = The Minister | The Committee | Any consultant psychiatrist | The State Governor only | The NPMCN
> 'The Minister may designate any hospital with requisite facilities as mental health facilities.'
Q: Information for consent must be given: = In the language the person understands, accounting for literacy | Only in English | Only in writing | Only to the family | Only by a lawyer
> '...given in the language the person understands and ... the literacy level of the person.'

### Involuntary admission
> - Criteria: imminent serious harm to self/others, or illness so severe that not admitting → serious deterioration or blocks treatment only possible in a facility.
> - Applicants in order: parent/guardian → spouse → other legal rep → anyone (doctor, police, government agent).
> - Two independent practitioners complete Form A → Committee decides within 24 hours.
> - Treatment ≤ 28 days; extension ≤ 14 days each; no more than 6 weeks without Committee review. Appeal → Court of Appeal.
> - Minors: last resort. Only accredited facilities.
> - Penalties: fail to discharge ≤ 5 yrs or ≥ ₦1m (corporate ≥ ₦5m); unaccredited ≥ ₦2m, facility ≥ ₦10m.
Q: Which is a ground for involuntary admission under the Act? = Serious likelihood of imminent harm to self or others due to a mental health condition | Family request alone | Non-payment of fees | Homelessness | Refusal of medication alone
> '...because of this, there is a serious likelihood of imminent harm to that person or to other persons.'
Q: Who comes FIRST in the order of persons who may apply for involuntary admission? = Parent or guardian | Spouse | Medical officer | Police officer | Any other person
> Order: parent or guardian → spouse → other legal representative → any other person.
Q: Involuntary admission requires examination by how many independent qualified medical practitioners completing Form A? = Two | One | Three | Four | None if urgent
> 'two independent qualified medical practitioners must have examined the person, and completed Form A.'
Q: The Committee must approve or deny continued involuntary admission within: = 24 hours of receipt of documents | 72 hours | 7 days | 14 days | 28 days
> '...inform the facility of its decision ... within twenty-four hours of receipt of the documents.'
Q: An appeal against a decision of involuntary admission lies directly to the: = Court of Appeal | High Court | Supreme Court | Magistrates' Court | Minister
> 'an appeal ... shall lie directly to the Court of Appeal.'
Q: The initial period of involuntary evaluation and treatment must not exceed: = 28 days | 72 hours | 14 days | 6 weeks | 6 months
> '...for a period not exceeding 28 days beginning from the day of admission.'
Q: Each extension of involuntary admission granted by the Committee may not exceed: = 14 days | 7 days | 28 days | 3 months | 6 months
> '...extend the period of admission for a period not exceeding fourteen days.'
Q: A person may not be held involuntarily for a continuous period exceeding how long without Committee review? = 6 weeks | 2 weeks | 4 weeks | 3 months | 1 year
> '...shall not be admitted ... for a continuous period exceeding six weeks without review by the Committee.'
Q: Involuntary admission of a minor is: = A matter of last resort when community alternatives are unavailable, unlikely to work, or have failed | Routine | Prohibited entirely | Decided by the school | Allowed only after age 16
> '...shall be a matter of last resort and shall only be applicable where community based alternatives are unavailable...'
Q: A natural person who fails to discharge someone who no longer meets involuntary criteria is liable to: = Up to 5 years' imprisonment or a fine of at least ₦1,000,000, or both | A warning | Life imprisonment | A ₦10,000 fine | Suspension only
> ≤ 5 years or ≥ ₦1,000,000 or both; a corporate person ≥ ₦5,000,000.
Q: A FACILITY that admits involuntarily without accreditation is liable to a fine of not less than: = ₦10,000,000 | ₦1,000,000 | ₦2,000,000 | ₦5,000,000 | ₦50,000,000
> Worker/head: ≤ 5 yrs or ≥ ₦2m; facility: ≥ ₦10,000,000.
Q: Applications to extend involuntary admission must be made: = Before the expiry of 28 days from admission | After discharge | Within 24 hours of admission | Only by the family | After 6 weeks
> 'Application for extension ... shall be made before the expiration of the period of 28 days.'

### Restraint and seclusion
> - Only after ≥ 48 hours of care by a medical officer; two MOs certify it's the only way; head authorises in writing; accredited facility.
> - Never punishment or convenience; continuous contact by a medical officer.
> - Report to Committee within 72 h; lasts as long as necessary or 72 h, whichever is earlier; extension ≤ 48 h (second MO).
> - Chains, shackles, ropes illegal for anyone incl. faith-based institutions → ≤ 5 yrs or ≥ ₦2m.
> - Register of all restraint/seclusion.
Q: Before restraint or seclusion, the person must first have received adequate care by a medical officer for at least: = 48 hours | 6 hours | 24 hours | 72 hours | 7 days
> '...received adequate care by a Medical Officer for at least forty-eight hours.'
Q: How many medical officers must certify in writing that restraint/seclusion is the only means to prevent harm? = Two | One | Three | None | Five
> 'two Medical Officers examine the person and certify in writing...'
Q: Restraint or seclusion may last only as long as medically necessary or: = 72 hours, whichever is earlier | 24 hours | 48 hours | 7 days | Until the family agrees
> '...only last for as long as medically necessary or seventy-two hours, whichever is earlier.'
Q: The head of facility must report reasons and duration of restraint/seclusion to the Committee within: = 72 hours | 24 hours | 48 hours | 7 days | 1 month
> '...the head of the facility shall within seventy-two hours provide the Committee with the reasons and the duration.'
Q: An extension of restraint/seclusion granted by the Committee may not exceed: = 48 hours | 12 hours | 24 hours | 72 hours | 7 days
> '...it shall not be for a period exceeding forty-eight hours.'
Q: Use of chains, shackles or ropes on a person with a mental health condition by a faith-based institution is: = Unlawful — up to 5 years or a fine of at least ₦2,000,000, or both | Allowed in private places | Allowed with family consent | Allowed for 72 hours | Only a civil wrong
> 'It shall be unlawful for any individual, group of persons or faith-based institution to employ ... chains...'
Q: Restraint or seclusion may NEVER be used: = As punishment or for the convenience of staff | To prevent imminent harm | In accredited facilities | With two MOs' certification | With written authorisation
> 'No person ... shall be subjected to any form of restraint or seclusion as a means of punishment or for the convenience of staff.'
Q: During seclusion or restraint, the head of facility must ensure: = At least one medical officer maintains continuous, active, personal contact | The patient is left alone | Only nurses check hourly | Family supervise | CCTV only
> '...at least one Medical Officer ... maintains continuous, active and personal contact.'
Q: Under the Act, 'restraint' includes: = Physical, mechanical or chemical immobilisation | Physical holding only | Verbal de-escalation | Locked wards only | Sedation for sleep only
> 'Restraint means the immobilisation ... using physical, mechanical or chemical means...'

### Special provisions
> - Sterilisation as treatment prohibited → ≥ 7 years, no option of fine.
> - ECT, psychosurgery, irreversible treatments: only with licence + informed consent + clinical guidelines, in best interest.
> - Research only per the National Health Act and National Code on Health Research Ethics.
> - Minors: separate living area from adults, inspected and certified; parent/guardian represents; court can appoint an independent legal representative; Child Rights Act.
Q: Sterilisation as a treatment for mental health conditions under the Act is: = Prohibited — punishable by not less than 7 years without option of fine | Allowed with consent | Allowed by court order | Allowed in severe intellectual disability | Allowed with two opinions
> '...imprisonment of not less than 7 years, without an option of fine.'
Q: ECT and psychosurgery are lawful only with: = A valid licence, the person's informed consent, and prescribed clinical guidelines | Family consent alone | Police permission | Committee approval only | A court order only
> Except with a valid license; with the informed consent of the person; in accordance with prescribed clinical guidelines.
Q: Research involving persons with mental health conditions must follow the National Health Act and: = The National Code on Health Research Ethics | The Lunacy Law | The Criminal Code | WHO checklist | Mental Health Fund rules
> '...in accordance with the National Health Act and the National Code on Health Research Ethics.'
Q: A facility may admit a minor only where: = The living area is separate from adult patients and the facility has been inspected and certified | A parent stays overnight | The minor is over 16 | The court orders it | Beds are available
> 'the living area is separate from that of adult patients; and the FMoH or State agency has inspected the facility and certified...'
Q: If a parent's decisions are not in a minor's best interest, the health worker may: = Apply to court for an independent legal representative | Override them alone | Call the police | Discharge the minor | Ignore it
> '...may apply to the court for the appointment of an independent legal representative.'
Q: The rights of minors receiving mental health care must be in line with the: = Child Rights Act | Lunacy Law | Penal Code | Labour Act | Evidence Act
> 'The rights of the minors ... shall be in line with their rights in the Child Rights Act.'

### Part IV: offenders
> - Hospital order after conviction (High or Magistrates' Court) for observation.
> - Two practitioners' written evidence within 7 days (one specialist): mental disorder, severe mental impairment or dissocial disorder; warrants detention; likely to benefit.
> - Discharge within 3 days of the improvement report; no progress in 6 months → further 6-month orders; right to appeal to the Mental Health Review Tribunal.
> - Prisoner transfer by Minister (federal offences) or Governor (state offences); same force as a hospital order; also for remand prisoners.
Q: For a hospital order, the court needs written evidence from two medical practitioners made within: = 7 days of admission | 24 hours of admission | 28 days | 3 months | 6 months
> '...written evidence made within seven days of admission of two medical practitioners, one of whom is recognized to have special experience.'
Q: For a hospital order, the offender must suffer from: = Mental disorder, severe mental impairment or dissocial disorder | Any personality trait | Substance use only | Mild anxiety | Epilepsy only
> '...suffering from mental disorder, severe mental impairment or dissocial disorder.'
Q: On receiving a report that the patient has improved sufficiently, the court shall order discharge within: = 3 days | 24 hours | 7 days | 28 days | 6 months
> '...the Court shall order the discharge of the patient from hospital within three days of receiving the report.'
Q: If no satisfactory progress is made within 6 months of a hospital order, the court may: = Issue a compulsory order for further 6-month periods, with right of appeal to the Mental Health Review Tribunal | Release the patient | Transfer to prison | Close the case | Impose a death sentence
> ...another period of six months and multiple periods thereafter, with the right to appeal to the Mental Health Review Tribunal.
Q: Transfer of a prisoner convicted under a STATE enactment to hospital is directed by the: = Governor | Minister | Chief Judge | Committee | Prison controller
> 'the Governor shall exercise the power ... in respect of a person convicted for an offence committed under an enactment made by the Government of a State.'
Q: A transfer directive for a prisoner has the same force as: = A hospital order | A death warrant | Bail | An acquittal | A fine
> 'The transfer directive shall have the like force as a hospital order.'
Q: The transfer provisions also apply to: = People in custody pending trial | Hospital staff | Voluntary patients | Minors in school | Tenants
> '...shall apply for the purpose of the transfer of any person in custody pending trial.'
Q: Under the Nigerian Criminal Code, every person is presumed to be of sound mind until the contrary is proved by: = Section 27 | Section 28 | Section 36 | Section 225 | Section 316
> s.27 presumption of sanity; s.28 is the insanity defence.
Q: The M'Naghten Rules (1843) require that, owing to a disease of the mind, the accused: = Did not know the nature and quality of the act, or did not know it was wrong | Was intoxicated | Had a low IQ | Was provoked | Had an irresistible impulse only
> M'Naghten: defect of reason from disease of the mind → did not know the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong.
Q: Which is NOT one of the Pritchard criteria for fitness to plead? = Have no mental illness | Understand the charge | Instruct counsel | Challenge a juror | Follow the proceedings
> Pritchard: plead, understand charge, challenge jurors, instruct counsel, follow proceedings, give evidence. Having a mental illness doesn't itself make one unfit.

### Definitions
> - Mental health condition ＝ impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions from diagnosable disorders (thinking, emotion, behaviour); includes intellectual, psychosocial, cognitive disabilities.
> - Mental health professional ＝ trained and certified to practise psychiatry. Mental health workers ＝ trained volunteers/advocates under supervision.
> - Allied professionals ＝ non-medical (psychologists, social workers, psychiatric nurses, OTs, counsellors).
> - Restraint ＝ physical, mechanical or chemical immobilisation. Voluntary admission ＝ own accord, with or without referral.
> - Part V: property, sexual relationship with a patient, forgery, assisting unlawful leave.
Q: Under the Act, a 'mental health professional' is defined as: = A person trained and certified to practise psychiatry | Any nurse | Any counsellor | A trained volunteer | A clinical psychologist
> '"Mental health professionals" means a person trained and certified to practice psychiatry.'
Q: 'Mental health workers' under the Act are: = Trained volunteers and advocates under supervision of mental health professionals | Psychiatrists | Pharmacists | Police officers | Judges
> '"Mental health workers" means trained volunteers and advocates ... under the supervision of the mental health professionals.'
Q: Which is listed in Part V of the Act? = Sexual relationship with a patient | Seclusion procedures | Committee composition | Voluntary admission | Form A
> Part V issues include property, emergency powers, forgery, assisting unlawful leave, sexual relationship with a patient.
Q: 'Voluntary admission' under the Act means a person who goes to a facility: = On their own accord, with or without referral | Only with a referral letter | Brought by police | On a court order | With two doctors' certificates
> '...goes to a facility for treatment and admission on his or her own accord, with or without referral.'
Q: Psychiatric nurses and clinical psychologists are classed in the Act as: = Allied mental health professionals | Mental health professionals | Mental health workers | Committee members | Gatekeepers
> Allied mental health professionals — formally trained non-medical health professionals.

### Constitution, CPA and treaties
> - Right to liberty excludes persons of unsound mind detained for care/treatment or community protection.
> - s.36(1): fair hearing within reasonable time; criminal suspects within 1 day if court within 40 km.
> - CPA s.225: Governor may order indefinite detention in an asylum for non-bailable offences (e.g. homicide); asylum includes hospital, prison. ss.225 & 230 after acquittal on grounds of insanity.
> - UDHR Art. 1 free and equal. ICESCR: highest attainable standard of health. Banjul Charter Art. 4 (life/integrity), Art. 5 (dignity, no torture), Art. 16 (best attainable health).
> - Ghana MH Bill 31 May 2012 — free care. Lagos State MH Bill — Lagos State Mental Health Service.
Q: Section 36(1) of the Nigerian Constitution gives any detained person the right to: = A fair hearing within a reasonable time | Free treatment | Bail always | Release after 24 hours | Choose a hospital
> 'Section 36(1) ... gives any person detained the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time.'
Q: For criminal suspects, the Constitution requires a hearing within one day if a court is within: = 40 km | 10 km | 20 km | 100 km | 200 km
> '...a hearing within one day (if a court is within a radius of forty kilometers).'
Q: Section 225 of the Criminal Procedure Ordinance allows the Governor to: = Order indefinite detention of a mentally ill accused in an asylum for non-bailable offences | Pardon all mentally ill offenders | Abolish asylums | Appoint psychiatrists | Set up the Committee
> '...allows the governor to order the detention of a mentally ill accused person indefinitely in an asylum where the offence is not bailable (e.g homicide).'
Q: For CPA section 225, an 'asylum' includes: = A mental or other hospital, a prison, or any suitable place of safe custody | Only psychiatric hospitals | Only prisons | Churches | The patient's home
> 'An asylum ... includes a mental or other hospital, a prison and any other suitable place of safe custody.'

### Drug law timeline
> - 1966 Indian Hemp Decree: death or 21 yrs (cultivation), export 10 yrs, ≥ 10 yrs smoking/possession.
> - 1975: death abolished; smoking 6 months and/or fine.
> - 1984: Indian Hemp (Amendment) + Special Tribunal Decree — firing squad for cocaine.
> - 1986: life imprisonment replaces death; forfeiture of assets and passport.
> - 1989: NDLEA Decree No. 48 (UN 1988 Convention): trafficking life; possession 15–25 yrs.
> - 1990: offence to be convicted abroad / bring Nigeria into disrepute — double punishment; not applied since democracy.
> - 1995 Money Laundering Decree: bank surveillance, phone tapping.
Q: The 1966 Indian Hemp Decree prescribed for cultivation of cannabis: = Death penalty or 21 years in jail | 6 months or a fine | Life imprisonment only | 15–25 years | No penalty
> '...prescribed death penalty or 21 years in jail for cultivation of cannabis.'
Q: The 1975 amendment reduced the penalty for cannabis smoking to: = Six months and/or a fine | 10 years | Death | Life imprisonment | 21 years
> 'The death penalty was abolished and the punishment for cannabis smoking was reduced to six months and/or a fine.'
Q: The 1984 Special Tribunal (Miscellaneous Offences) Decree prescribed for dealing in cocaine: = Death by firing squad | Life imprisonment | 10 years | A fine | Deportation
> 'This law decreed the death penalty by firing squad for dealing in ... cocaine.'
Q: The 1986 amendment substituted the death penalty with: = Life imprisonment | 21 years | Six months | Community service | 15 years
> Life imprisonment was substituted; it also introduced forfeiture of assets and passport.
Q: The NDLEA was created by Decree No. 48 of: = 1989 | 1966 | 1984 | 1986 | 1995
> 1989 — NDLEA Decree No. 48, in response to the UN Convention of 1988.
Q: Under the 1989 NDLEA Decree, possession or use of cocaine, LSD or heroin attracts: = 15 years but not exceeding 25 years | 6 months | Life imprisonment | Death | A fine only
> Trafficking: life; possession or use: '15 years but not exceeding 25 years'.
Q: The 1990 amendment to the NDLEA Decree was criticised because it: = Punished Nigerians already convicted abroad, bringing 'Nigeria into disrepute' — double punishment | Legalised cannabis | Abolished NDLEA | Introduced rehabilitation | Reduced all penalties
> '...widely seen to be without justification and an abuse of human rights of people who had already paid a price for their crimes.'
Q: The 1995 Money Laundering Decree empowered the NDLEA to: = Monitor bank accounts and tap telephone lines | Run treatment centres | License pharmacies | Abolish cash | Grant amnesty
> '...mount surveillance on the bank accounts of suspects ... and gave powers to the NDLEA to tap any telephone line.'

> '...in response to the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988.'

### OSCE: Testamentary capacity | fps
> History taking station. Task: This patient with mild Alzheimer’s disease wants to write a will. Assess testamentary capacity.
> - Testator’s details (name, age, address); executors; beneficiaries; distribution of assets; guardianship of minor children; signature and at least two competent adult witnesses.
> - Legal test (Banks v Goodfellow, 1870): understands the nature of making a will and its effects; knows the extent of the property; comprehends and appreciates the claims of others; no disorder of mind poisons his affections or perverts his judgement.
> Critical fail: Equating a dementia diagnosis with lack of capacity, or not checking for undue influence.

### Bonus drill: OSCE: examination, capacity & communication | fps
> Practical stations mix examination, legal reasoning and communication. Say what you are doing as you do it, so the examiner can tick it.
L: OSCE: examining for extrapyramidal side effects = Introduce, consent, explain the examination | Observe at rest: tremor, abnormal movements, posture, facial expression | Tone at wrist and elbow: cogwheel or lead-pipe rigidity (use an activation manoeuvre) | Bradykinesia: finger tapping, hand opening | Gait: arm swing, shuffling, turning | Akathisia: watch for restlessness, ask about inner restlessness | Tardive dyskinesia: orofacial movements, tongue, limbs, trunk (AIMS style) | Summarise findings, offer temperature and observations if NMS is suspected ~~ Skip asking about inner restlessness :: Akathisia is partly subjective; you must ask | Test reflexes only :: Reflexes do not assess EPS | Forget to observe the tongue :: Tongue and orofacial movements are the commonest signs of tardive dyskinesia
> Name each sign as you find it. Rating scales: Simpson-Angus (parkinsonism), Barnes (akathisia), AIMS (tardive dyskinesia).
L: OSCE: assessing capacity to refuse treatment = Introduce and explain the purpose | Confirm the specific decision and give the relevant information | Can they understand the information? | Can they retain it long enough to decide? | Can they use or weigh it, including consequences of refusing? | Can they communicate a decision? | Conclude: has or lacks capacity for THIS decision, now | Document and plan (best interests if capacity is lacking) ~~ Assume no capacity because of a mental illness :: Capacity is presumed; diagnosis alone does not remove it | Decide based on whether you agree with the choice :: An unwise decision does not mean lack of capacity | Assess capacity for all decisions at once :: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific
> The four-part functional test (taught from the UK Mental Capacity Act 2005; similar common-law principles apply elsewhere): understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate. Failing any one means lacking capacity for that decision.
> Key principles: presume capacity, support decision-making, an unwise decision is not incapacity, and assess decision by decision.
L: OSCE: dealing with an angry relative = Acknowledge the anger and introduce yourself calmly | Move to a private place and sit down | Listen without interrupting | Empathise and name the emotion | Clarify the specific concerns | Apologise for their experience without blaming colleagues | Explain what you can, within confidentiality | Agree a plan and timeline | Offer the complaints route and follow-up ~~ Match their tone :: Escalation loses marks; stay calm | Blame a colleague :: Never criticise colleagues; take ownership | Refuse to discuss anything :: Listen and share what consent allows
> Examiners score de-escalation, empathy statements ("I can see how upsetting this has been"), honesty, and a concrete plan.
Q: An unwise decision by a patient means = Nothing on its own about capacity | Strong evidence that they lack capacity :: An unwise decision is not, by itself, evidence of incapacity | They must be assessed under mental health law :: Not automatically; mental health law has its own criteria | Their next of kin decides for them :: Relatives cannot simply override a capacitous adult
> Capacity is about the decision-making process, not the outcome you would choose.
Q: The four abilities in a capacity assessment = Understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate | Understand, remember, agree, communicate :: Agreeing is not part of the test; it is retain and use or weigh | Understand, retain, use or weigh, consent :: The fourth is COMMUNICATE the decision | Understand, retain, use or weigh, comply :: The fourth is COMMUNICATE the decision
> Think "URWC" (Understand, Retain, Weigh, Communicate).

### Biological theories of crime
> - MZ > DZ concordance; Scandinavian adoption — genes matter only in severe criminality; ~50% of persistent antisocial behaviour genetic, more in males.
> - XYY; low IQ (Rutter & Giller — not just being caught); most delinquency is in groups.
> - Hodgins 1992 (n=15,117 Swedes): ID → convictions OR 3.1 men, 3.7 women.
> - Frontal lobe injury; amygdala/orbitofrontal dysfunction in ASPD; EEG abnormality; serotonin; endogenous opiates → crime as reward.
> - Violence falls with age: ↑serotonin, ↓NA/DA/ACh.
Q: Scandinavian adoption studies suggest genes are significant: = Only in severe criminality | In all crime | Only in property crime | Only in women | Not at all
> 'Adoption studies (Scandinavia) — genes only significant in severe criminality.'
Q: What proportion of persistent antisocial behaviour is attributed to genetic factors? = 50% | 10% | 25% | 75% | 90%
> '50% of persistent antisocial behavior due to genetic factors — heritability > males than females.'
Q: In Hodgins' (1992) Swedish cohort, people with intellectual disability had criminal conviction odds ratios of: = 3.1 men, 3.7 women | 1.1 men, 1.2 women | 5 men, 2 women | 10 for both | 0.5 for both
> '...odds ratio of 3.1 for men and 3.7 for females.' (cohort 15,117; 192 with ID)
Q: Rutter and Giller concluded that the association between low IQ and delinquency is: = Not due to the likelihood of duller offenders being caught | Due only to duller offenders being caught | Non-existent | Only in girls | Due to schooling only
> 'Association between Low I.Q and delinquency — Rutter & Giller — not due to likelihood of duller offenders being caught.'
Q: The chromosomal pattern historically linked to tall, aggressive, violent men is: = XYY | XXY | XO | Trisomy 21 | XXX
> XYY — tall, aggressive, violent (may also reflect bodily abnormality).
Q: Most delinquent acts are committed: = With others | Alone | By girls | By the elderly | Under psychosis
> 'Most delinquent acts are committed with others.'
Q: Increased violent behaviour after brain injury is particularly linked to injury of the: = Frontal lobes | Occipital lobes | Cerebellum | Spinal cord | Pituitary
> '...violent behaviours among the brain damaged particularly among those with injuries to the frontal lobes.'
