> 'Neuro-imaging studies show amygdala & orbitocortical dysfunction in antisocial personality disorder.'
Q: The endogenous opiate theory proposes that crime is: = Rewarding through opiate release from the thrill (positive reinforcement) | Painful and avoided | Caused by opiate withdrawal | Unrelated to mood | Negative reinforcement only
> '...thrills involved in crime cause release of opiates ... crime seen as exciting/rewarding (positive reinforcement).'
Q: The reduction in violent offending with age is associated with: = Increasing serotonin and decreasing noradrenaline and dopamine | Increasing dopamine | Decreasing serotonin | Rising testosterone | Increasing acetylcholine
> 'increasing serotonin, decreasing noradrenaline, dopamine, acetylcholine.'

### Psychosocial theories
> - Frustration–aggression (Dollard 1939). Freud: id, superego lacunae.
> - Durkheim — anomie (normlessness after rapid social change).
> - Merton 1938 — strain: gap between promised success and available means.
> - Control theory — "why don't we?" Hirschi 1969 bonds: attachment, commitment, involvement, belief.
> - Gottfredson & Hirschi 1990 — low self-control.
> - Harriet Wilson 1980 — parental "chaperonage". Social learning; labelling.
> - Violent (against person) vs property (larceny, car theft, vandalism) crime.
Q: The frustration–aggression hypothesis was proposed by: = Dollard et al. (1939) | Merton | Durkheim | Hirschi | Bandura
> 'Frustration-aggression hypothesis: Dollard et al. (1939) suggested that frustration is the most potent means of inciting aggression.'
Q: Durkheim's 'anomie' refers to: = A state of normlessness after rapid social change or disorder | Genetic predisposition | Parental chaperonage | Low self-control | Learned aggression
> Anomie from rapid change or major disorder in society → normlessness → in severe forms suicide and homicide.
Q: Merton's (1938) strain theory emphasises: = A disconnect between the success society promises and access to the means of achieving it | Brain damage | Parental supervision | Labelling | Endogenous opiates
> '...a disconnect between the opportunities for achieving success that the society promised and the access ... made available.'
Q: In Freudian theory of crime, the term 'superego lacunae' implies: = Gaps in conscience | Excess guilt | Strong ego | Low IQ | Frontal lobe damage
> Freudian: id-dominated, superego lacunae (gaps in conscience), ego fractures, deprivation.
Q: Control theories of crime ask: = Why don't we do it? | Why do they do it? | Who labels them? | What genes cause it? | Which drug caused it?
> 'These theories try to answer the question Why don't we do it rather than why do they do it.'
Q: Hirschi's (1969) four elements of the social bond are: = Attachment, commitment, involvement and belief | Id, ego, superego, libido | Strain, anomie, labelling, learning | Genes, IQ, EEG, serotonin | Opportunity, motive, means, intent
> Attachment, commitment, involvement and belief.
Q: Gottfredson and Hirschi (1990) attributed crime mainly to: = Low self-control | XYY | Anomie | Poverty alone | Mental illness
> '...crime flow from low self control' — impulsive, insensitive, risk-taking, short-sighted.
Q: Harriet Wilson (1980) found that what distinguished deprived families with non-delinquent children was: = Parental 'chaperonage' | Higher income | Religion | Larger homes | Fewer siblings
> '...exercise of "chaperonage". Parents who acted as chaperons effectively prevented their children from offending.'
Q: Which is an example of a non-violent (property) crime? = Larceny | Armed robbery | Rape | Murder | Assault
> Property crimes: larceny, car theft, vandalism. Larceny ＝ unlawfully taking something from someone.
Q: The theory that examines how society ascribes deviance to a person is: = Labelling theory | Social learning theory | Strain theory | Control theory | Frustration–aggression
> Labelling theory examines the ascribing of a deviant behaviour to another person by society.

### Mental illness and offending
> - Most offending by the mentally ill is minor; modest increase in violence (esp. schizophrenia).
> - ASPD and substance use associate with offending more than other major disorders.
> - Much is explained by socio-economic disadvantage and higher apprehension.
> - Schizophrenia → violence with command hallucinations, threat/control-override, drugs, non-compliance, social stress.
> - Mania: fraud, impersonation, disinhibition. Depression: suicide, altruistic homicide then suicide, false confession.
> - ASPD: high recidivism; paranoid PD: stalking/threats; poor treatability.
Q: Most offending by the mentally ill is: = Minor in degree | Homicide | Sexual | Organised crime | Terrorism
> 'Most offending by mentally ill minor in degree.'
Q: Which disorders have a GREATER association with offending than other major mental disorders? = Antisocial personality disorder and substance use disorders | Depression and anxiety | OCD and phobias | Dementia and delirium | Autism and ADHD
> 'Antisocial personality disorder and substance use disorders have greater association with offending.'
Q: Much of the association between severe mental disorder and crime may be explained by: = Secondary socio-economic disadvantage and higher risk of apprehension | Genetic factors | Antipsychotic side effects | Better police training | Chance
> '...explained by secondary socio economic disadvantage ... and the increased risk of apprehension.'
Q: In schizophrenia, symptoms are said to result in violence particularly when: = Feelings of personal threat emerge | Negative symptoms dominate | The patient is on depot | The patient is elderly | Insight is good
> 'Symptoms result in violence if feelings of personal threat emerge.'
Q: Offences typical of mania include: = Grandiose fraud and impersonation | Infanticide | Shoplifting from guilt | Arson for profit | Neonaticide
> Mania: grandiose fraud, public disorder, impersonation, disinhibition, irritability, violence.
Q: In depression, an 'altruistic homicide' typically involves: = Killing family members, then attempting suicide | Killing a stranger for money | Killing in self-defence | Killing a rival dealer | Killing under command hallucinations only
> 'Altruistic homicide — kills family members (rare), infanticide/neonaticide, then attempts suicide.'
Q: Which personality disorder is associated with stalking and threats in the lecture? = Paranoid | Schizoid | Dependent | Avoidant | Anankastic
> 'Paranoid PD — stalker, threats.'
Q: Antisocial (psychopathic) personality disorder is associated with: = Higher recidivism than other mentally abnormal offenders | Low recidivism | Excellent treatability | Mostly property crime by women | Altruistic homicide
> 'Aggressive, socially irresponsible, higher rate of recidivists compared with other M.A.O's.'
Q: Victimology is the study of: = Victims of crime and the psychological effects of their experience | Offenders' genes | Prison design | Court procedure | Police methods
> '...study of the victim of crime and the psychological effect of their experience...'
Q: Litigious paranoid patients: = Use the legal system to act out delusional preoccupations | Avoid the courts | Have no grievances | Are always correct | Are usually children
> 'Litigious paranoids often utilize the legal system as a means of acting out their delusional preoccupations.'
Q: Common psychological consequences for victims of crime include: = Fear, shame, self-blame, sleep difficulty and PTSD | Mania | Kleptomania | Pyromania | Dementia
> 'Consequences are fear, anxiety, shame, self blame, sleep difficulty resulting in PTSD.'
Q: On the Hare PCL-R, the conventional UK cut-off for psychopathy is: = 25 | 15 | 20 | 30 | 40
> ≥25 in the UK, ≥30 in North America; maximum 40.
Q: Ganser syndrome, classically seen in prisoners awaiting trial, features: = Approximate answers (vorbeireden) | Pressure of speech | Flight of ideas | Perseveration only | Mutism only
> Approximate answers, clouding of consciousness, pseudohallucinations, somatic conversion.

### Specific disorders (ICD-11)
> - Kleptomania: stealing without intelligible motive; tension before, relief/pleasure during and after.
> - Pyromania: fire-setting without motive (not money, revenge, politics); fascination with fire.
> - Gambling: may offend for money/debts.
> - Paraphilic disorder: arousal focused on those unable/unwilling to consent, acted on or distressing.
> - Stalkers (Mullen): rejected, intimacy seeker (erotomania), incompetent suitor (LD/ASD), resentful, predatory.
Q: In ICD-11 kleptomania, objects are stolen: = Without an intelligible motive | For monetary gain | For personal use | Under command hallucinations | To fund drugs
> '...strong impulses to steal objects in the absence of an intelligible motive (e.g., not for personal use or monetary gain).'
Q: A feature of both kleptomania and pyromania in ICD-11 is: = Rising tension before and pleasure or relief during/after the act | Guilt before the act | Command hallucinations | Amnesia for the act | Profit motive
> Both: increasing tension/arousal before and pleasure, excitement, relief or gratification during and after.
Q: Fire-setting for revenge or insurance money is: = Not pyromania — there is an intelligible motive | Pyromania | Kleptomania | Paraphilia | Gambling disorder
> Pyromania requires the absence of intelligible motive (monetary gain, revenge, sabotage, political statement, attention).
Q: ICD-11 paraphilic disorder involves atypical arousal focused on others who cannot consent, AND: = The person has acted on it or is markedly distressed by it | It must be legal | It must occur only once | It must begin after 40 | No distress is required ever
> '...on which the person has acted or by which he or she is markedly distressed.'
Q: An angry, dependent man pursuing his ex-partner who can't accept the breakup is which stalker type? = Rejected | Intimacy seeker | Incompetent suitor | Resentful | Predatory
> Rejected stalker — angry, dependent, pursuing an ex-partner.
Q: Delusional erotomania is a subgroup of which stalker type? = Intimacy seekers | Predatory | Resentful | Rejected | Incompetent suitor
> 'Intimacy seekers ... Delusional erotomania is a sub group of this.'
Q: Stalking that is preparatory to sexual assault is the: = Predatory type | Resentful type | Rejected type | Incompetent suitor | Intimacy seeker
> 'Predatory — Stalking is preparatory to sexual assault.'
Q: Gambling disorder may lead to offending in order to: = Obtain money or evade debts | Satisfy delusions | Relieve tension by fire | Punish others | Obtain sexual gratification
> 'May offend in order to obtain money or evade debts.'
Q: The ICD-11 code block for pyromania and kleptomania is: = Impulse control disorders (6C7x) | Disruptive behaviour disorders | Personality disorders | Dissociative disorders | Paraphilic disorders
> ICD-11 impulse control disorders: pyromania 6C70, kleptomania 6C71, compulsive sexual behaviour 6C72, IED 6C73.

### Other disorders
> - LD: exploited, more often caught; sexual offences, theft, arson; violence less common.
> - Organic: disinhibition → dishonesty, sexual offences; elderly men with dementia may abuse children.
> - Epilepsy: now a rare contributory factor; automatisms rarely cause crime.
> - Morbid jealousy → spouse homicide. Erotomania (de Clérambault) — loved by an unattainable distinguished person.
> - Alcohol: disinhibition, amnesia, jealousy; victims often intoxicated too.
Q: Offending by people with learning disability is particularly associated with: = Sexual offences, theft and arson | Violent crime | Fraud | Drug trafficking | Cybercrime
> Associated with sexual offences, theft and arson; violent crime less common.
Q: Epilepsy is now regarded as: = A rare contributory factor to offending | A major cause of violent crime | Always an insanity defence | Overrepresented in prisons even after social matching | The commonest cause of homicide
> 'Now regarded rare contributory factor to offending ... Automatisms are rare causes of crime.'
Q: Erotomania (de Clérambault's syndrome) involves a delusion of being loved by: = A distinguished person, unattainable by social class | A spouse | A child | A neighbour of the same status | God
> '...delusion of love by distinguished person, unattainable by reason of social class.'
Q: The forensic importance of pathological jealousy is mainly: = Spouse homicide | Shoplifting | Arson | Fraud | Stalking celebrities
> 'Forensic importance — spouse homicide.'
Q: Organic brain disease with disinhibition may lead to: = Crimes of dishonesty and sexual offences | Organised crime | Elaborate fraud | Planned terrorism | Drug trafficking
> 'Impaired judgment / disinhibition ... may lead to crimes of dishonesty/sexual offences.'
Q: Regarding alcohol and violence, the lecture notes that: = Alcohol may contribute to homicide in both victim and offender | Victims are never intoxicated | Alcohol reduces violence | Only spirits matter | Alcohol causes kleptomania
> 'May contribute to homicide in victim/offender.'
Q: Morbid (Othello) jealousy is most strongly associated with which substance? = Alcohol | Cannabis | Heroin | Caffeine | Benzodiazepines
> Alcohol — and the management may include geographical separation because of homicide risk.

### Homicide
> - Male, low social class, inverse to suicide, alcohol. Normal (majority, young) vs abnormal (insane, homicide-suicide, infanticide, DR — older).
> - Women: kill less, more psychiatric, more often close relations.
> - Filicide (parent kills child; often with suicide); infanticide < 12 months (women 20–40, single, depressed, poor); neonaticide < 24 h.
> - Motives: altruistic, unwanted, accidental (abuse), spousal revenge, mental illness.
> - Infanticide Act: child < 12 months, mind disturbed by birth or lactation; not for men or another's child; charged as murder, disposed as manslaughter.
Q: Homicide rates are described as: = Inversely related to suicide | Directly related to suicide rates | Higher in women | Highest in upper social class | Unrelated to alcohol
> Homicide: predominantly male, low social class, inversely related to suicides, alcohol.
Q: 'Abnormal' homicides (insane murder, infanticide, diminished responsibility) are mostly committed by: = Older offenders | Young offenders | Children | Gangs | Women only
> Normal homicide — majority, mostly young; abnormal — mostly older.
Q: Infanticide refers to killing a child under: = 12 months | 24 hours | 28 days | 5 years | 12 years
> 'Infanticide — killing of child under 12 months.' Neonaticide ＝ within 24 hours.
Q: Neonaticide is killing a child: = Within 24 hours of birth | Within 28 days | Under 1 year | Under 5 years | In utero
> 'Neonaticide — killing of child within 24 hours of birth.'
Q: Women who commit infanticide are typically: = 20–40, single, depressed, poor | Over 50, married, wealthy | Teenagers with psychopathy | Professionals | Elderly with dementia
> '...such women usually 20-40 years, single, depressed, associated poverty.'
Q: The infanticide defence is NOT available to: = A man, or a woman killing another woman's child | A mother killing her own 6-month-old with postpartum depression | A lactating mother | A woman not fully recovered from childbirth | A mother of a 3-month-old
> 'Not defence open to a man, woman killing another woman's child, or if 12 months or older.'
Q: Under the Infanticide Act, disposal is: = As for manslaughter | As for murder | Automatic acquittal | Death penalty | Fine only
> 'Initial charge is usually murder. Disposal as for manslaughter.'
Q: Killing a child to relieve its suffering, or so as not to abandon it when the parent commits suicide, is which filicide motive? = Altruistic/mercy | Unwanted child | Accidental | Spousal revenge | Economic
> Altruistic/mercy killing — relieve suffering or 'not abandon' the child in suicide.
Q: Compared with men, female homicide perpetrators are more likely to: = Kill someone in a close relationship | Kill strangers | Have no psychiatric factors | Use firearms | Kill for money
> 'Female perpetrators more likely to kill someone in close relationship.'

### Goldstein (1985) tripartite model + drug-law model
> - Psychopharmacological: drug/withdrawal → violence. Alcohol most strongly linked; PCP, cocaine, amphetamines, barbiturates; heroin and cannabis less.
> - Economic-compulsive: crime to fund expensive dependence → acquisitive, non-violent (theft, fraud, sex work, dealing).
> - Systemic: violence within drug markets (no legal recourse) — turf, informers, debts.
> - Drug-law offences: possession, trafficking, laundering, drug driving — by legal definition.
> - Categories overlap. Direct causation weak, but correlated at heavy use.
Q: Goldstein's (1985) tripartite framework for drugs and violence comprises: = Psychopharmacological, economic-compulsive and systemic | Biological, psychological, social | Use, abuse, dependence | Supply, demand, harm | Possession, trafficking, laundering
> Psychopharmacological, economic-compulsive and systemic; plus a legal (drug-law offence) model for policy.
Q: In the psychopharmacological model, the substance most strongly associated with violent crime is: = Alcohol | Heroin | Cannabis | Caffeine | Nicotine
> 'Alcohol intoxication is strongly associated especially with violence crime.'
Q: Which drugs are generally LESS associated with violence? = Heroin and cannabis | PCP and cocaine | Amphetamines and barbiturates | Alcohol and PCP | Cocaine and alcohol
> 'Heroin and cannabis are generally less associated with violence.'
Q: Crimes in the economic-compulsive model are generally: = Acquisitive and non-violent | Violent and planned | Sexual | Political | Driving offences only
> 'The type of crime committed here are generally acquisitive and non-violent.'
Q: Systemic drug-related violence exists mainly because: = The illicit drug market affords no legal way of obtaining justice | Drugs make people violent | Users need money | Laws define it | Withdrawal causes irritability
> 'It exists mainly because the drug market affords no legal way of obtaining justice when rules are violated.'
Q: Drug driving and money laundering fall under which model? = Drug-law offences | Psychopharmacological | Economic-compulsive | Systemic | None
> Drug-law offences — linked by definition in law; includes precursors, money laundering, drug driving.
Q: Regarding direct cause-and-effect between drugs and crime, the lecture says: = Evidence is limited, but at the most intense levels of use drugs and crime are highly correlated | It is proven for all drugs | There is no correlation | Only cannabis causes crime | Crime causes drug use only
> 'Limited evidence exist for a direct cause-and-effect relationship. However, at the most intense levels of drug use, drugs and crime are highly correlated.'
Q: The four categories of drug-related crime are: = Not mutually exclusive — they overlap | Mutually exclusive | Applicable only to cocaine | Hierarchical | Purely theoretical
> 'These four categories ... are not mutually exclusive.'

### Courts and trial
> - Police → DPP → trial → sentence. NGRI → "Governor's pleasure" (prison or secure hospital).
> - Contact points: police diversion, fitness to plead, trial, pre-sentence disposal, post-disposal.
> - Beyond reasonable doubt (criminal); balance of probabilities (civil). No jury trials in Nigeria.
> - Federal: Supreme, Appeal, FHC, FCT. State: High, Sharia, Magistrates', Customary, Juvenile.
> - Fitness to plead (s.223(1) CPA): understand charge, plead, challenge juror, follow proceedings, instruct counsel.
> - Actus reus (physical) + mens rea (mental), concurrent in time.
Q: In Nigeria, a verdict of 'not guilty by reason of insanity' leads to: = Indefinite committal 'during the pleasure of the Governor' | Immediate release | Fixed 6-month detention | A fine | Retrial
> 'Indefinite committal "during the pleasure of the Governor"' — in an asylum, which may be prison or secure hospital.
Q: Which statement about Nigerian courts is correct? = There are no jury trials in Nigeria | Jury trials are used for murder | Civil cases need proof beyond reasonable doubt | Sharia courts are federal | Magistrates' courts are federal
> 'No jury trials in Nigeria.' Criminal: beyond reasonable doubt; civil: balance of probability.
Q: Which is a STATE court in Nigeria? = Customary Court | Supreme Court | Court of Appeal | Federal High Court | High Court of the FCT
> State: High, Sharia, Magistrates', Customary, Juvenile courts.
Q: The standard of proof in civil cases is: = Balance of probabilities | Beyond reasonable doubt | Absolute certainty | Prima facie | Reasonable suspicion
> 'Onus on prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt (criminal), or balance of probability (civil).'
Q: At the police stage, the psychiatrist's role with mentally disordered offenders is to advise on: = Possible diversion to care | Sentencing | Jury selection | Appeals | Bail amount
> 'With the police at the detention and or charge stage advise on possible diversion to care.'
Q: Who stands for the State in prosecution? = The Director of Public Prosecutions | The police | The judge | The psychiatrist | The Governor
> 'Public Prosecution Office (Director of Public Prosecution) stands for the State.'
Q: Fitness to plead relates to the accused's mental state: = At the time of trial | At the time of the offence | In childhood | After sentencing | At arrest only
> 'Fitness To Plead — relates to mental state at time of trial (pre-trial) — sectn 223(1) of c.p.a.'
Q: Fitness to plead in Nigeria is governed by: = Section 223(1) Criminal Procedure Act | Section 28 Criminal Code | Section 51 Penal Code | Section 36 Constitution | Section 117 Criminal Code
> Section 223(1) CPA.
Q: Which is NOT a criterion of fitness to plead? = Remember committing the offence | Understand the charge | Instruct counsel | Follow court proceedings | Challenge a juror
> Criteria: understand charge, plead, challenge juror, follow proceedings, instruct counsel. Amnesia for the offence does not itself make one unfit.
Q: 'Mens rea' refers to: = The guilty mind — the mental element/intent | The physical act | The victim | The sentence | The weapon
> Mens rea — the guilty mind; actus reus — the physical act.
Q: For conviction, actus reus and mens rea must: = Concur in time | Be separated in time | Only one is needed | Be proven on the balance of probabilities | Be admitted by the accused
> 'There must be a concurrence in time between both.'

### Insanity
> - s.24 CC: not responsible for acts independent of will or accident.
> - M'Naghten 1843: shot Edward Drummond (Peel's secretary); persecutory delusions → defect of reason from disease of mind → not know nature/quality or that it was wrong.
> - Irresistible impulse (1922) — "policeman at the elbow".
> - s.28 CC: mental disease/natural infirmity → incapacity to understand, control, or know he ought not.
> - s.51 Penal Code: unsoundness of mind → can't know nature or that it's wrong/contrary to law.
> - s.50 PC: child < 7 no offence; 7–12 only if mature.
Q: Daniel M'Naghten shot: = Edward Drummond, secretary to Robert Peel | Robert Peel | Queen Victoria | A police officer | His father
> 'M'Naghten was indicted for having shot Edward Drummond, Secretary to Robert Peel.'
Q: The M'Naghten Rules require a defect of reason from disease of the mind such that the accused: = Did not know the nature and quality of the act, or did not know it was wrong | Could not resist the impulse | Was intoxicated | Had a personality disorder | Was under 12
> '...not to know the nature and quality of the act he was doing: or ... that he did not know he was doing what was wrong.'
Q: The irresistible impulse test is also called the: = Policeman-at-the-elbow test | Durham rule | Product test | Bolam test | Pritchard test
> 'Referred to as Policeman-at-the-elbow law.' (1922 English committee of jurists)
Q: Section 28 of the Nigerian Criminal Code differs from M'Naghten by including incapacity to: = Control his actions | Remember the act | Plead | Instruct counsel | Read
> s.28: incapacity to understand, to control his actions, or to know he ought not to do it.
Q: The insanity provision of the Penal Code (Northern Nigeria) is section: = 51 | 24 | 28 | 50 | 223
> s.51 Penal Code — unsoundness of mind; incapable of knowing nature of act or that it is wrong/contrary to law.
Q: Under section 50 of the Penal Code, no act is an offence when done by a child under: = 7 years | 5 years | 10 years | 12 years | 14 years
> 'No act is an offence which is done by a child under 7 years of age, or ... 7–12 years ... not attained sufficient maturity.'
Q: Section 24 of the Criminal Code provides that a person is not criminally responsible for: = An act occurring independently of the exercise of his will, or an accident | Any act while drunk | Acts done after age 70 | Acts done abroad | Property crime
> '...an act or omission which occurs independently of the exercise of his will or for an event which occurs by accident.'

### Other defences
> - DR: balance of probabilities, murder only; abnormality of mental functioning substantially impairing understanding/judgement/self-control; causal link.
> - Age (s.30 CC): < 7 doli incapax; 7–12 if capacity proved; 12+ responsible. CYPA: child < 14, young person 14–17.
> - Intoxication not a defence, unless involuntary (→ discharged) or caused insanity (→ ss.229/230 CPA); may negate specific intent.
> - Automatism: sane/external (drugs, insulin hypo, hypnosis, concussion; sleepwalking) → acquittal; insane/internal (epilepsy, tumour, CVD, diabetes) → NGRI. Not if aware and failed to prevent.
Q: Diminished responsibility: = Applies only to murder and is proved on the balance of probabilities | Applies to all offences | Requires proof beyond reasonable doubt by the defence | Leads to acquittal | Applies only to theft
> 'Must be proved on balance of probability; Applicable only to murder.'
Q: Under section 30 of the Criminal Code, a child under 7 is: = Doli incapax — incapable of committing any crime | Fully responsible | Responsible if capacity is proved | Tried as an adult | Responsible for property crime only
> 'exempts children under 7 — doli incapax — incapable of committing any crime.'
Q: A child between 7 and 12 years is criminally culpable: = If the prosecution proves he had capacity | Never | Always | Only for murder | Only with parental consent
> 'Between 7 – 12, culpable if prosecution proved he has capacity.'
Q: Under the Children and Young Persons Act, a 'young person' is aged: = 14–17 | Under 7 | 7–12 | Under 14 | 18–21
> Child < 14; young person 14–17.
Q: Under section 29 CC, if intoxication was caused without consent by another's malicious act and the accused didn't know what he was doing, he is: = Discharged | Adjudged a lunatic under ss.229/230 | Convicted | Fined | Retried
> 'If a, the accused person shall be discharged; if b (insane through intoxication), sections 229 & 230 of CPA apply.'
Q: Voluntary intoxication is generally: = Not in itself a defence | A complete defence | Grounds for acquittal in murder | Grounds for infanticide | Treated as automatism
> 'Intoxication not in itself a defense.' It may negate specific intent.
Q: Hypoglycaemia from insulin causing an offence is classed as: = Sane (non-insane) automatism — leads to acquittal | Insane automatism | Diminished responsibility | Voluntary intoxication | Not a defence
> Sane automatism — external factors (drugs, hypoglycaemia, hypnosis, concussion) → acquittal.
Q: An offence during an epileptic seizure is classed as: = Insane automatism — leading to NGRI and committal | Sane automatism | Intoxication | Doli incapax | Infanticide
> Insane automatism — internal factors (epilepsy, tumour, CVD, diabetes) → not guilty by reason of insanity → committal.
Q: Sleepwalking is treated in the lecture as: = Non-insane automatism even though internal | Insane automatism | No defence | Intoxication | Diminished responsibility
> 'Sleep walking however non insane even though internal.'
Q: Automatism is NOT available as a defence when the person: = Knew of the condition beforehand but failed to take reasonable steps to prevent harm | Was concussed | Had a first-ever seizure | Was hypnotised | Was sleepwalking
> '...not available if the person is aware of the condition prior to offence but failed to take reasonable steps.'

### Expert witness
> - Honest, objective, impartial; decline matters outside expertise; tell the subject it's not treatment, not fully confidential, they may refuse.
> - Subpoena s.186(1) CPA (breach → 2 months); oath s.181(1); refresh memory s.215(1); hearsay barred s.76.
> - Evidence in chief → cross-examination → re-examination. Explain in lay terms; watch the judge's pen; avoid never/always; don't argue.
> - Perjury s.117 CC: 14 years (life if capital/life offence).
> - Only your own findings are facts; the rest are assumed facts; medical records are admissible hearsay.
> - Report: introduction, body, summary/conclusions — neutral, jargon-free.
Q: An expert witness must make clear to the person examined that: = They are only providing an opinion to the court and are not there to treat | The report is fully confidential | Cooperation is compulsory | They will be released | The expert works for the defence
> Only providing an opinion; subject may refuse; report not absolutely confidential; not there to provide treatment except in emergency.
Q: Breach of a subpoena under section 186(1) CPA may attract imprisonment of: = 2 months | 1 week | 1 year | 14 years | Life
> 'subpoena ... (breach of this may attract 2 month imprisonment).'
Q: Perjury under section 117 of the Criminal Code carries: = 14 years, or life if related to an offence punishable by death or life | 2 months | 2 years | A fine only | 7 years
> 'perjury (sectn. 117 ...) 14 years in prison or life if in relation to offence punishable with death or life sentence.'
Q: The order of examination of a witness in court is: = Evidence in chief, cross-examination, re-examination | Cross-examination, evidence in chief, re-examination | Re-examination, cross, chief | Chief, re-examination, cross | Cross only
> Direct (evidence in chief) → cross-examination → re-examination.
Q: During cross-examination, the expert should: = Remain calm, keep answers to the point, and avoid 'never/always' | Argue with counsel | Use 'never' and 'always' for emphasis | Refuse to answer | Praise his own expertise
> Remain calm; don't be drawn into argument; keep answers to the point; avoid use of never / always.
Q: The hearsay rule (s.76 Evidence law) bars: = Out-of-court statements not subject to cross-examination | All expert opinion | Medical records always | Oral evidence | Written reports
> 'Hearsay Rule ... bars out of court statements not subject to cross-examination.' Medical records are an admissible exception.
Q: Re-examination is: = Your counsel's opportunity to clarify and repair damage from cross-examination | The opposing counsel's attack | The judge's summing up | A second trial | Compulsory
> 'Your counsel's opportunity to regain lost ground or repair damage done in cross examination.'
Q: The only facts about which a psychiatric expert can usually testify directly are: = His own findings (mental state and physical examination) | What the family said | Police statements | Newspaper reports | The patient's account
> 'Usually only facts ... are your own findings... All rest ... are assumed facts.'
Q: The appropriate form of address for a High Court judge is: = My Lord / Your Lordship | Sir | Doctor | Chief | Mr President
> Forms of address: My Lord, Your Lordship, Your Worship (magistrate).

### Risk
> - Dangerousness ＝ potential for serious physical or lasting psychological harm.
> - Unstructured clinical (biased) → actuarial (VRAG, Static-99, ICT — more accurate but rigid, static) → structured professional judgement (HCR-20, OASys — flexible, treatment-relevant).
> - HCR-20 ＝ 10 Historical + 5 Clinical + 5 Risk management.
> - Tarasoff: Poddar killed Tatiana Tarasoff; "protective privilege ends where public peril begins" (Tobriner); I ＝ warn, II ＝ protect.
> - Nigeria: NHA 2014 ss.26–27, MDCN rule 44 — discretionary breach for public safety.
> - Prisons: clinics + weekly visiting forensic teams; constraints: staff, out-of-pocket funding, weak law.
Q: In Nigerian custodial centres, mentally disordered offenders are mostly managed by: = Prison clinics run by Correctional Service practitioners, sometimes with visiting forensic teams | High secure hospitals | Private psychiatrists | NGOs only | Nobody
> Clinics manned by Correctional Service practitioners, supported in some cases by weekly forensic team visits.
Q: Which is a constraint of Nigerian prison psychiatric services? = Out-of-pocket funding | Too many psychiatrists | Excessive legal frameworks | Too many beds | Overuse of psychotherapy
> Constraints: lack of manpower, funding (out-of-pocket), limited legal frameworks.
Q: Dangerousness is defined as the potential to cause: = Serious physical or lasting psychological harm | Any harm | Property damage only | Self-harm only | Embarrassment
> 'Potential to cause serious physical/lasting psychological harm.'
Q: Which mental-state feature is a risk factor for dangerousness? = Command hallucinations | Good insight | Euthymia | Compliance | Stable employment
> Mental state: command hallucinations, passivity, hostility, suspiciousness, lack of insight.
Q: 'The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins' was stated by: = Justice Tobriner | Lord Denning | M'Naghten | Hirschi | Justice Bolam
> Justice Tobriner, California Supreme Court, Tarasoff.
Q: Tarasoff II broadened the duty to warn into a duty to: = Protect | Detain | Treat | Report to police only | Prosecute
> Tarasoff II — duty to protect; 'duty to warn' now subsumed in it.
Q: In Nigeria, discretionary breach of confidentiality for public safety is allowed by: = Sections 26 and 27 of the National Health Act 2014 and MDCN Code rule 44 | Section 28 Criminal Code | Lunacy Law | Section 223 CPA | Penal Code s.50
> 'sections 26 and 27 of the National Health Act (2014) and MDCN Code of ethics rule 44.'
Q: In the Tarasoff case, the patient who killed Tatiana Tarasoff was: = Prosenjit Poddar | Daniel M'Naghten | Edward Drummond | John Hinckley | Ted Bundy
> Prosenjit Poddar, a student outpatient obsessed with her.
Q: The unstructured clinical judgement approach to risk is criticised because: = It is plagued with bias and error, with questionable reliability and validity | It is too rigid | It uses statistics | It ignores interviews | It is too expensive
> '...plagued with bias and error ... predictive reliability and validity is questionable.'
Q: The VRAG and Static-99 are examples of: = Actuarial risk instruments | Unstructured clinical tools | Structured professional judgement tools | Personality tests | Capacity tests
> Actuarial: VRAG (Quinsey 1999), Iterative Classification Tree (Monahan 2000), Static-99 (Hanson & Thornton 1999).
Q: A weakness of actuarial approaches is: = Focus on historical unmodifiable factors that may lack relevance to treatment | Less accurate than clinical judgement | Too flexible | No structure | Not replicable
> Weaknesses: generalisability, case-specific omissions, historical unmodifiable factors, rigidity.
Q: The HCR-20 is an example of: = Structured professional (clinical) judgement | An actuarial tool | Unstructured interview | A personality inventory | A cognitive test
> Structured clinical approach — HCR-20 (Webster 1997), OASys.
Q: The HCR-20 contains: = 10 historical, 5 clinical and 5 risk management items | 20 historical items | 5 historical, 10 clinical, 5 risk | 10 clinical, 10 risk | 15 historical, 5 clinical
> 10 Historical + 5 Clinical + 5 Risk management.
Q: Which is a CLINICAL item of the HCR-20? = Lack of insight | Previous violence | Young age at first violence | Lack of support | Access to weapons
> Clinical: lack of insight, negative attitudes, active psychosis, impulsivity, unresponsive to treatment.
Q: Which is a RISK MANAGEMENT item of the HCR-20? = Access to victims/weapons | Psychopathy | Early maladjustment | Substance misuse history | Relationship instability
> Risk management: destabilisers, weapons/access to victim, lack of support, stress, non-compliance.
Q: The main strength of structured professional judgement tools is: = Flexibility and relevance to treatment | Pure statistical prediction | No need for clinical expertise | Speed only | Legal acceptance only
> 'Strength — flexibility and relevance to treatment.'

### Civil issues
> - Presume capacity; illness ≠ incapacity; decision- and time-specific.
> - MCA 2005: assume capacity; help them decide; unwise ≠ incapable; best interests; least restrictive. Test: understand, retain, use/weigh, communicate.
> - Testamentary: know property, potential beneficiaries, claims; eccentric wills ≠ incapacity.
> - Contracts: binding unless the other party knew of the incapacity.
> - Lasting POA (advance proxy), guardianship (court; "ward"), advance directive (written care preferences).
> - Malpractice — 4 Ds: duty, dereliction, damage, direct causation; Bolam standard; respondeat superior.
> - Privilege belongs to the patient; waived when they raise a mental-condition defence. Subpoena duces tecum ＝ produce records.
Q: In law, a person is assumed to be: = Competent unless proven otherwise | Incompetent until proven competent | Incompetent if mentally ill | Competent only if over 21 | Incompetent if detained
> 'It is assumed in law that a person is competent to make decisions unless proven otherwise.'
Q: Capacity is best described as: = Issue-specific and time-specific | All or none | Fixed for life | Determined by diagnosis | Lost permanently in any psychosis
> '...competency not all or none concept but tied to specific decision — issue specific and time specific.'
Q: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, making an unwise decision: = Does not invariably mean lack of capacity | Proves incapacity | Requires guardianship | Requires detention | Invalidates consent automatically
> 'Making an unwise decision does not invariably mean lack of capacity.'
Q: Section 3(1) MCA 2005: a person is unable to decide if unable to: = Understand, retain, use/weigh the information, or communicate the decision | Agree with doctors | Read | Recall childhood | Pass the MMSE
> Understand, retain, use (weigh), communicate.
Q: Testamentary capacity requires the testator to know: = The nature/extent of property, who might expect to benefit, and the claims he ought to consider | The exact value of every item | The beneficiaries' addresses | The law of succession | The date of death
> Know property, know potential beneficiaries (even if excluded), comprehend claims.
Q: A capricious or malevolent will is: = Not always a sign of incapacity | Always proof of incapacity | Invalid automatically | Proof of dementia | Proof of undue influence
> 'Capricious, frivolous or malevolent disposition not always sign of incapacity.'
Q: A mentally incapable person is bound by a contract unless: = He can show the other party knew of his incapacity when the contract was made | He was detained at the time | He has a diagnosis | It was over ₦1m | His family objects
> '...bound by his contract, unless he can show the other party knew of his incapacity.'
Q: In assessing fitness to use firearms, the tool used for violence risk is: = HCR-20 | MMPI | MMSE | AIMS | PANSS
> MMPI (personality), MMSE (cognitive), AIMS (motor), HCR-20 (violence risk), urine toxicology.
Q: Which is listed among 'newer areas' of capacity? = Capacity to be executed | Capacity to drive a bicycle | Capacity to vote in school | Capacity to cook | Capacity to read
> Newer: marry, consent to sex, contraception, litigate, make a gift, be executed.
Q: A durable (lasting) power of attorney: = Lets a person choose in advance a proxy decision-maker for anticipated loss of capacity | Is made after capacity is lost | Is a court order | Applies only to minors | Ends when capacity is lost
> 'Durable power of attorney — Permits persons to make provision for anticipated loss of decision making capacity & advance selection of decision maker.'
Q: The subject of a guardianship is called the: = Ward | Agent | Attorney | Testator | Respondent
> 'After adjudication, the subject of the guardianship is termed a "ward."'
Q: An advance health directive is: = Written legal instructions specifying preferences for medical care if one loses capacity | A court order for treatment | A will for property | A power of attorney for money | An involuntary admission form
> '...a written legal instructions in which a person specifies his preferences for medical care if he is no longer able to make decisions.'
Q: The '4 Ds' of malpractice are: = Duty, dereliction (deviation), damage, direct causation | Diagnosis, drugs, dose, duration | Danger, delay, death, disability | Doctor, disease, decision, defence | Detention, discharge, documentation, disclosure
> Duty of care, deviation from standard, damage, direct causation — each must be present.
Q: Malpractice is: = A tort or civil wrong (non-criminal) | A criminal offence | Always perjury | A breach of contract only | A disciplinary matter only
> 'A tort or civil wrong from doctor's negligence, non criminal.'
Q: 'Respondeat superior' refers to: = Vicarious liability — the master answers for the servant | Duty to warn | Privilege | Capacity | Hearsay
> Vicarious liability — 'Let the master answer for the deeds of the servant'.
Q: Testimonial privilege between doctor and patient: = Belongs to the patient and is waived when the patient raises a mental-condition defence | Belongs to the doctor | Cannot be waived | Applies in all proceedings | Belongs to the court
> 'Right belongs to patient, so can waive it. Waived automatically when patient imports mental condition defense.'
Q: A 'subpoena duces tecum' obliges you to: = Produce relevant records and documents | Attend court only | Detain the patient | Break confidentiality to the press | Pay a fine
> 'Subpoena duces tecum — obliges you to produce the relevant records & documents.'
Q: A doctor's defence to negligence is that he acted in accordance with practice accepted as proper by: = A responsible body of medical practitioners skilled in that field | The patient | The hospital board | The family | The media
> '...in accordance with practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical practitioners skilled in that field.' (Bolam)

### OSCE: Violence risk assessment | fps

### OSCE: Fitness to plead | fps
> History taking station. Task: This man is in police custody facing a charge. Assess his fitness to plead.
> - The criteria derive from R v Pritchard (1836): understand the charge, decide on a plea, challenge a juror, instruct counsel, follow the evidence and proceedings.
> Critical fail: Assessing guilt instead of fitness, or missing a psychotic or cognitive cause.
L: Fitness to plead: the phases of the station, in order = Open | Understands the charge | Understands the plea | Can instruct counsel | Can follow the proceedings and challenge a juror | Mental state
Q: Fitness to plead. Which phase is this line from? Rapport; level of education. “Can you tell me more about what happened? Tell me why you were in police custody. How did the misunderstanding happen, and what was your… = Open | Understands the charge | Understands the plea | Can instruct counsel | Can follow the proceedings and challenge a juror | Mental state
> What to say: Rapport; level of education. “Can you tell me more about what happened? Tell me why you were in police custody. How did the misunderstanding happen, and what was your role?”
> Examiner checks: Non-judgemental; establishes his account.
Q: Fitness to plead, Open: what is the examiner looking for? = Non-judgemental; establishes his account. | Comprehends the nature of the charge. | Understands the difference between the pleas. | Able to give instructions and evidence to the defence. | Follows the proceedings; can challenge a juror; knows about appeal. | Links any impairment to a mental disorder.
> Say: Rapport; level of education. “Can you tell me more about what happened? Tell me why you were in police custody. How did the misunderstanding happen, and what was your role?”
Q: Fitness to plead. Which phase is this line from? “Do you know what you have been charged with? Do you know why you were arrested and charged to court? Do you think you have done anything wrong? Are you sorry?” = Understands the charge | Open | Understands the plea | Can instruct counsel | Can follow the proceedings and challenge a juror | Mental state
> What to say: “Do you know what you have been charged with? Do you know why you were arrested and charged to court? Do you think you have done anything wrong? Are you sorry?”
> Examiner checks: Comprehends the nature of the charge.

## OPD Clinic | Community & social psychiatry
> Community & social psychiatry. Source: Community Psychiatry lecture- 2026.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Community psychiatry: definition and principles
> - Farooq and Minhas (2001): development and provision of a coordinated and comprehensive programme of mental health care for residents of specified catchment areas.
> - Simply: services beyond hospital settings, integrated into primary care and community structures.
> - Thornicroft (2017): a whole system in which the community, not a facility, is the provider of care; accessible, acceptable, strengths-based, evidence-based and recovery-oriented.
> - Caplan and Caplan (1967) principles: accessibility, integration into PHC, continuity of care, multidisciplinary approach, human rights focus, consumer participation.
Q: Farooq and Minhas (2001) defined community psychiatry as care for residents of: = Specified catchment areas | Psychiatric hospitals only | Prisons | Urban centres only | Teaching hospitals
> '...a coordinated and comprehensive programme of mental health care for residents of specified catchment areas in a country.'
Q: In Thornicroft's (2017) description of community mental health care, who is the provider of care? = The patient's community | The psychiatric hospital | The general practitioner | The family alone | The Ministry of Health
> 'A whole system of care in which the patient's community, not a specific facility such as a hospital, is the provider of care.'
Q: Which is not one of Caplan and Caplan's (1967) principles of community psychiatry? = Centralisation of care in the asylum | Accessibility | Continuity of care | Consumer participation | Multidisciplinary approach
> The principles are accessibility, integration, continuity of care, multidisciplinary approach, human rights focus and consumer participation.
Q: 'Embedding mental health into primary health care' describes which principle? = Integration | Accessibility | Continuity of care | Human rights focus | Consumer participation
> Integration: embedding mental health into primary health care. Accessibility ＝ services close to where people live.

### Why community care, and how LMICs do it
> - Leading causes of disability: depression, anxiety, psychosis, substance use.
> - <1 psychiatrist per 100,000 in many LMICs; treatment gap up to 75–90%; mental health often <2% of health budgets.
> - Cultural factors: explanatory models, traditional and faith healing, stigma, total reliance on families.
> - Delivery: mhGAP integration into primary care, task-shifting to non-specialists, community-based rehabilitation (CBR), NGOs and faith groups, mobile outreach.
> - Case studies: Nigeria (PHC integration, sustainability problems), India (District Mental Health Programme, uneven), Ethiopia (task-shifting works).
Q: The lecture states that many LMICs have fewer than: = 1 psychiatrist per 100,000 | 1 psychiatrist per 10,000 | 10 psychiatrists per 100,000 | 1 nurse per 100,000 | 1 hospital per state
> 'Limited specialists (e.g., <1 psychiatrist per 100,000 population in many LMICs).'
Q: Training non-specialist health workers to deliver basic mental health care is called: = Task-shifting | Deinstitutionalisation | Trans-institutionalisation | Assertive outreach | Liaison
> Task-shifting — used successfully in Ethiopia with community health workers.
Q: Mental health often receives what share of LMIC health budgets? = Less than 2% | About 10% | About 15% | About 25% | Over 30%
> 'Funding limitations: mental health often receives <2% of health budgets.'
Q: Which country's District Mental Health Programme had mixed success from uneven implementation? = India | Nigeria | Ethiopia | Pakistan | Ghana
> India: District Mental Health Programme — mixed success. Nigeria: PHC integration with sustainability problems. Ethiopia: task-shifting.
Q: Which cultural factor does the lecture list as a reason for community care? = Entire reliance on families for care-giving | High literacy | Abundant specialists | Low stigma | Universal insurance
> 'Cultural factors: explanatory models of illness; traditional & faith healing; stigma; entire reliance on families for care giving.'

### Models of community care
> - Hive (hub-and-spoke): hospital at the centre. For: easy administration, expertise and beds together. Against: poor accessibility, delayed referral, poor knowledge of the community, resources concentrated in hospital.
> - Network: the hospital is one of many community resources; the core is a community-based multidisciplinary team.
Q: A disadvantage of the hive (hub-and-spoke) model is: = Poor accessibility and delayed referral | Difficult administration | Too little expertise | Too few beds | No role for the hospital
> Disadvantages: poor accessibility, delayed referral, poor knowledge of the community, resources concentrated in the hospital.
Q: In the network model, the core of the service is: = A community-based multidisciplinary team | The psychiatric hospital | The general practitioner | The family | The traditional healer
> 'The hospital is only one of them. The core of the service is a community-based multidisciplinary team.'
Q: An advantage of the hub-and-spoke model is: = Easier administration and a good range of expertise and beds | Better accessibility | Faster referral | Knowledge of community structure | Spreading resources widely
> 'Advantage of easier administrative system and good range of professional expertise and beds.'

### Rise, fall and balance of mental health services (Thornicroft and Tansella, 1999)
> - Asylums began as a humanitarian response and "sanctuary", with moral treatment (non-restraint).
> - Rise of the asylum (1880–1950): remote, custodial, containment over treatment, family sidelined.
> - Problems (Leff, 1997): isolation, poor training, poor management, maltreatment, and institutionalism — disability caused by isolation and institutional care.
> - Fall (1950 onwards): physical (1940s), drug (1950s) and psychological treatments; Goffman's Asylums (1968), Wing and Brown (1970).
> - Deinstitutionalisation (Reid et al., 2001) — 3 parts: prevent inappropriate admissions; discharge adequately prepared long-stay patients; build community support systems.
> - Balanced care (1990s onwards): smaller units, family as care-giver, multidisciplinary teams, control vs independence; mental health laws 1983/2005 (UK), 2021 (Nigeria).
Q: Thornicroft and Tansella (1999) describe how many periods in the history of mental health services? = Three | Two | Four | Five | Six
> Three: the rise of the asylum, the decline of the asylum, and balancing (fine-tuning) services.
Q: Large asylums were initially built as: = A humanitarian response to conditions in madhouses, prisons and workhouses | Prisons | Research centres | Military hospitals | Profit-making enterprises
> A humanitarian response — the asylum was first a place of 'sanctuary', with moral treatment.
Q: During the rise of the asylum (1880–1950), the dominant emphasis was: = Primacy of containment over treatment | Rehabilitation | Family therapy | Community outreach | Multidisciplinary care
> Remote, mainly custodial, staff of doctors and nurses only, a reduced family role, containment over treatment.
Q: Institutionalism is best defined as: = Disabilities that develop as a consequence of social isolation and institutional care | Overcrowding of asylums | Moving patients from hospital to prison | Hospital-based administration | A type of psychosis
> 'The development of disabilities as a consequence of social isolation and institutional care in remote asylums' (Leff, 1997).
Q: Which is not one of Reid et al.'s (2001) three components of deinstitutionalisation? = Building larger remote hospitals | Preventing inappropriate admissions | Discharging adequately prepared long-term patients | Strengthening community support systems | All of the above are components
> The three: prevent inappropriate admissions, discharge prepared long-stay patients, build community support.
Q: Whose works on institutionalisation fuelled the closure of Victorian asylums? = Goffman (1968) and Wing and Brown (1970) | Freud and Jung | Kraepelin and Bleuler | Beck and Ellis | Lambo and Asuni
> Goffman's Asylums and Wing and Brown's Institutionalism and Schizophrenia.
Q: Effective pharmacological treatments emerged in the: = 1950s | 1920s | 1940s | 1970s | 1990s
> 'Emergence of effective physical (1940s), pharmacological (1950s) and psychological therapies.'
Q: In the era of balanced care, the lecture lists Nigeria's mental health law as dating from: = 2021 | 1958 | 1983 | 2005 | 2013
> 'The mental health & capacity acts — 1983, 2005 (UK), 2021 (Nigeria).'
Q: The UK's Care Programme Approach (1991) was introduced mainly to: = Ensure coordinated care and follow-up of people with severe mental illness in the community | Close all hospitals | Fund private care | Replace the Mental Health Act | Train GPs
> The CPA provides an assessment, a care plan, a named care coordinator and regular review.

### Criticisms of community psychiatry
> - Torrey (1995): US deinstitutionalisation was "a failed social experiment"; prisons became the new asylums.
> - Trans-institutionalisation ("the virtual asylum"); "bring back the asylum" (Sisti, 2015).
> - Public protection measures: care programme approach, supervised discharge.
> - Christopher Clunis killed Jonathan Zito (Finsbury Park, London): transient patients lose contact with services.
> - Not universally applicable across countries (Goldberg, 1987, 1992); cost and socio-cultural factors.
Q: Who described US deinstitutionalisation as 'a failed social experiment of the 20th century'? = Torrey (1995) | Goffman | Thornicroft | Leff | Sisti
> Torrey (1995) — jails and prisons became 'America's new mental hospitals'.
Q: 'The virtual asylum' refers to fears of: = Trans-institutionalisation | Telepsychiatry | Hospital overcrowding | Moral treatment | Online therapy
> Trans-institutionalisation — and calls to 'bring back the asylum' (Sisti, 2015).
Q: The Christopher Clunis case highlighted the risk that community patients with a transient lifestyle may: = Lose contact with mental health services | Over-use services | Refuse medication only | Become institutionalised | Need more beds
> Clunis, with schizophrenia, killed Jonathan Zito at Finsbury Park — showing patients can lose contact with services.
Q: Goldberg (1987, 1992) argued that community psychiatric principles: = Cannot be universally applied in different countries | Work everywhere unchanged | Should replace primary care | Are only for children | Are cheaper than all alternatives
> 'Community psychiatric principles can not be universally applied in different countries.'

### Balanced care (Thornicroft and Tansella)
> - Aims: users' and carers' priorities; both hospital and community; care close to home; mobile services; treat symptoms and disabilities; individualised treatment.
> - Six components (2004): primary care and general hospital consultation, outpatients, day hospitals, home visits; day centres; acute inpatient care; community residential services; user and carer participation; a seamless interface with social, judicial and NGO agencies.
Q: Which is an aim of balanced care (Thornicroft and Tansella)? = Meet both hospital and community service needs | Hospital care only | Treat symptoms but not disability | Remove mobile services | Standard treatment for everyone
> Aims include both hospital and community needs, care close to home, mobile services, symptoms and disabilities, individual treatment.
Q: A 'seamless service interface' in a modern service links health with: = Social, judicial and non-governmental agencies | Only psychiatry | Only private hospitals | Only the family | Only pharmacies
> 'Seamless service interface (e.g. health, social, judiciary and non-governmental agencies).'
Q: Recreational, vocational or educational support with peer support belongs to: = Day centre services | Acute inpatient services | Residential services | Liaison services | Forensic services
> 'Day centre services (recreational, vocational or educational, professional/peer support).'

### Services by level of resources
> - Step A (low): primary care with specialist back-up; screening by primary care staff, structured guidelines, counselling, medicines; admissions to general hospital ward beds.
> - Step B (medium): mainstream care — outpatient clinics, community mental health teams, acute inpatient care, hostels and care homes, OT and employment.
> - Step C (high): specialised services — eating disorder, dual diagnosis, treatment-resistant affective and adolescent clinics; early intervention and assertive community treatment teams; crisis resolution / home treatment, crisis houses, acute day hospitals; group homes; sheltered work, clubhouse, transitional employment.
Q: In a low-resource setting (Step A), inpatient care for cases primary care cannot manage is provided in: = General hospital ward beds | Specialised eating disorder units | Crisis houses | Group homes | Forensic units
> Step A: limited specialist back-up, with admission to general hospital ward beds.
Q: Community mental health teams and acute inpatient care are characteristic of: = Step B — mainstream mental health care | Step A | Step C | Pre-asylum care | Traditional care
> Step B (medium resources): outpatient clinics, CMHTs, acute inpatient care, hostels and care homes, OT.
Q: Assertive community treatment and early intervention teams belong to: = Step C — specialised services | Step A | Step B | Primary care only | The asylum era
> Step C (high resources): specialised CMHTs — early intervention, assertive community treatment.
Q: Which is listed as an alternative to acute hospital admission? = Home treatment / crisis resolution teams | Clubhouse | Sheltered work | Group homes | Adult learning
> Alternatives to admission: home treatment/crisis resolution teams, crisis or respite houses, acute day hospital.
Q: The clubhouse is an example of: = Alternative occupation and vocational rehabilitation | Acute inpatient care | Liaison psychiatry | Primary care screening | Forensic care
> Vocational options: sheltered work, supported placements, cooperative schemes, self-help groups, clubhouse, transitional employment.
Q: Assertive community treatment (ACT) is designed mainly for: = People with severe mental illness who disengage from services | Mild anxiety in primary care | Children with ADHD | Post-natal depression only | Dementia
> ACT gives intensive, team-based outreach with small caseloads to people with severe mental illness who engage poorly.

### WHO network of community-based services: three circles
> - Mental health in general health care: general hospitals (inpatient, outpatient, liaison, crisis), primary care (counselling, community health work), specific programmes (maternal and child health, NCD, NTD, HIV/AIDS and TB).
> - Community mental health services: community mental health centres and teams, psychosocial rehabilitation (day care, vocational, adult learning), peer support, supported living.
> - Beyond the health sector: school, workplace and prison health; social services (child protection, housing, employment, benefits).
Q: In the WHO network diagram, HIV/AIDS and TB services sit under: = Specific health programmes (mental health in general health care) | Social services | Peer support | Supported living | Non-health settings
> Specific health programmes: maternal and child health, NCD, NTD, HIV/AIDS and TB services.
Q: School, workplace and prison health services are part of mental health: = Beyond the health sector | In general hospitals | In primary care | In psychosocial rehabilitation | In crisis services
> Mental health beyond the health sector — non-health settings (school, workplace, prison) and social services.
Q: Vocational assistance, day care and adult learning fall under: = Psychosocial rehabilitation | General hospitals | Social housing | Primary care | Liaison care
> Psychosocial rehabilitation (within community mental health services).

### Psychiatry in Nigeria and the Aro Village
> - Phases: traditional (pre-colonial); transitional 1903–1954 (Calabar 1903, Yaba 1907, Lantoro 1944); therapeutic 1954 to date.
> - Aro Village system — Lambo, 1956: patients lodged in nearby villages with a relative; nurses gave daytime care; villagers involved.
> - Borrofka and Olatawura (1977): 512 patients over 50 months; 94.1% psychotic; 57.8% discharged by 3 months, 88.9% by 5 months; 70.3% fit to return to work. Threat: urbanisation loosening family ties.
> - Now: 9 regional psychiatric hospitals, 12 federal teaching hospitals; poorly coordinated, institution-based; <10% of people with disorders use services (Gureje, 2006); about 0.4 beds per 10,000 (WHO, 2001).
Q: The first asylum in Nigeria was: = Calabar, 1903 | Yaba, 1907 | Lantoro, 1944 | Aro, 1954 | Enugu, 1960
> Transitional phase: Calabar 1903, Yaba 1907, Lantoro 1944.
Q: The Aro Village system was introduced by Lambo in: = 1956 | 1944 | 1954 | 1977 | 2006
> 'Dr. Lambo introduced the innovatory village system ... in 1956.'
Q: In the Aro Village system, patients were admitted: = To nearby villages with an accompanying relative | Alone to hospital wards | To prisons | To churches | To boarding schools
> Patients lived in nearby villages with relatives; nurses gave daytime care in rented homes.
Q: Borrofka and Olatawura (1977) reported what proportion of Aro Village patients fit to return to work? = 70.3% | 57.8% | 88.9% | 94.1% | 50%
> 70.3% fit to return to work. 94.1% had psychosis; 57.8% discharged by 3 months, 88.9% by 5 months.
Q: What threat to the village system did the authors foresee? = Loosening of traditional family ties with urbanisation | Drug shortages | Too many nurses | Legal bans | Rising literacy
> '...in view of the loosening of traditional family ties resulting from rapid urbanization.'
Q: Gureje (2006) found service use among community samples with disorders to be: = Less than 10% | Over 50% | About 30% | About 20% | Exactly 15%
> '...service utilisation by community samples of people with disorders less than 10% (Gureje 2006).'
Q: Nigeria's psychiatric bed ratio (WHO 2001) is about: = 0.4 per 10,000 | 4 per 10,000 | 0.4 per 1,000 | 10 per 10,000 | 1 per 1,000
> '...the ratio of psychiatric beds being about 0.4 to 10 000 persons (WHO 2001).'

### Primary care psychiatry, pathways and the treatment gap
> - India and Pakistan models (Goldberg, 1987, 1992): train primary health care workers to manage epilepsy, psychoses, neuroses and drug problems, with psychiatrist back-up — possibly the only viable option for many developing countries.
> - But no statutory catchment responsibility or continuity of care, so it is primary care psychiatry, not community psychiatry.
> - Goldberg and Huxley (1980) pathways to care: 5 levels, 3 filters — illness behaviour, recognition by the primary care clinician, referral to specialist care. Lecture figures: 250/1000 in the community down to 6 inpatients.
> - Treatment gap (WHO surveys): developed 35.5–50.3%, developing 76.3–85.4%; about 1 psychiatrist per million; resources uneven urban/rural, north/south.
Q: Why does the lecture call the India–Pakistan model 'primary care psychiatry' rather than community psychiatry? = Statutory catchment-area responsibility and continuity of care may not be possible | It uses only psychiatrists | It is hospital-based | It excludes epilepsy | It is too expensive
> 'Statutory responsibility to a catchment area, continuity of care may not be possible. This can best be seen as primary care psychiatry.'
Q: High-priority conditions targeted in primary care psychiatry include: = Epilepsy, psychoses, neuroses and drug-induced problems | Dementia and autism | Personality disorders only | Eating disorders | Gender incongruence
> '...high priority conditions like epilepsy, psychoses, neuroses and drug-induced problems.'
Q: In Goldberg and Huxley's pathway, Filter 2 is: = Recognition by the primary care clinician | Illness behaviour | Referral to specialist care | Admission to hospital | Discharge
> Filter 1: illness behaviour; Filter 2: recognition by the primary care clinician; Filter 3: referral to specialist care.
Q: Level 3 in the pathways to care model is: = Conspicuous psychiatric morbidity | General population | Psychiatric disorder in primary care | Specialist outpatient care | Inpatient care
> Level 3 ＝ conspicuous psychiatric morbidity — disorder recognised by the primary care clinician.
Q: The WHO World Mental Health Surveys put the treatment gap in developing countries at: = 76.3–85.4% | 10–20% | 35.5–50.3% | 50–60% | 95–99%
> Developed 35.5–50.3%; developing 76.3–85.4%.
Q: The lecture notes that within Nigeria, resources are unevenly spread by: = Urban/rural and north/south | Age and sex | Religion | Language | Season
> 'Within Nigeria ... resources are also unevenly spread (urban/rural; north/south).'
Q: In Goldberg and Huxley's model, the filter that most reduces numbers between levels 2 and 3 is: = Recognition by the primary care clinician | Illness behaviour | Referral to specialist care | Admission | Discharge
> Many disorders seen in primary care go unrecognised — the GP's detection (filter 2) is the classic bottleneck.

### mhGAP (WHO, 2008) and integration into primary care
> - Scale-up model: needs and resources assessment + political commitment + supportive policy → scaling-up strategy → deliver the intervention package (with human resources, M&E plan, financing) → reduced treatment gap.
> - Rationale for integration: burden, comorbidity, treatment gap, access, less stigma and human rights abuse, better outcomes, community integration, workforce development.
> - Recommendations: situational analysis; build on existing structures; funding; clear delineation of disorders; training; medicines; supervision and support; referral system; intersectoral links; recording systems.
Q: WHO's Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) was launched in: = 2008 | 1975 | 2001 | 2013 | 2023
> mhGAP, 2008.
Q: In the mhGAP scale-up model, the three inputs to the scaling-up strategy are: = Assessment of needs and resources, political commitment, supportive policy environment | Beds, drugs, staff | Research, teaching, audit | Diagnosis, treatment, follow-up | Prevention, cure, rehabilitation
> Needs and resources assessment, political commitment, supportive policy → strategy → intervention package → reduced treatment gap.
Q: Which is not listed as a rationale for integrating mental health into primary care? = Concentrates expertise in the asylum | Comorbidity | Reduces stigma and human rights abuse | Promotes access | The treatment gap
> Rationale: burden, comorbidity, treatment gap, access, less stigma and abuse, outcomes, community integration, manpower.
Q: The first WHO recommendation for integration is: = A preliminary situational analysis | Funding | Recruiting new staff | Building hospitals | Buying medicines
> Start with a preliminary situational analysis, then build on existing networks and resources.
Q: The mhGAP Intervention Guide is aimed primarily at: = Non-specialist health care providers | Psychiatrists in tertiary centres | Researchers | Lawyers | Teachers
> mhGAP-IG supports non-specialists in non-specialised health settings to manage priority mental, neurological and substance use conditions.

### Nigerian policy and law
> - National policy (1991, 2013, 2023): equity; same rights as physical illness, care close to the community; non-discrimination; integration with general health at all levels.
> - Policy 2023: vision — optimal mental health and wellbeing of all persons guaranteed; goal — strengthen the system especially at primary care level, community-based and recovery-based; coordinated by the Department of Mental Health Services, FMOH; framed by the National Health Act 2014 and Mental Health Act 2021.
> - Mental Health Act 2021: integrated services; recovery, rehabilitation and community integration; a community-based approach; the FMOH department supports community programmes.
Q: Nigeria's national mental health policies date from: = 1991, 2013, 2023 | 1958, 1991, 2021 | 2001, 2008, 2014 | 1903, 1954, 1956 | 2006, 2010, 2011
> 'National mental health policy emphasis! (1991 & 2013, 2023).'
Q: The vision of the National Mental Health Policy 2023 is: = A nation where optimal mental health and wellbeing of all persons is guaranteed | A hospital in every state | Zero suicides by 2030 | One psychiatrist per LGA | Free medicines for all
> Vision: 'A nation where optimal mental health and wellbeing of all persons is guaranteed.'
Q: The 2023 policy's overarching goal focuses on strengthening the system particularly at: = Primary health care level | Tertiary hospital level | Federal ministry level | Private sector level | University level
> '...particularly at the primary health care level ... particularly community-based mental health services.'
Q: Under the Mental Health Act 2021, which body supports community-based programmes for care and rehabilitation? = The Department of Mental Health Services, FMOH | The courts | State police | Local churches | Teaching hospitals alone
> 'The Department of Mental Health services at the FMOH shall support the development of community based programmes.'

### The Aro programmes
> - Community programme (2006 onwards): outreach (media education, shifted clinics, home treatment); residential rehabilitation (Hope Villa transitional home); partnerships (vocational placements such as barbing, hairdressing, vulcanising; sheltered work); a day centre and relatives' support.
> - Ogun primary care programme: pilot Abeokuta North, Feb 2010, 5 priority conditions; state-wide Oct 2011: 20 LGAs, 40 PHCs, 80 health workers (nurses, CHEWs), 8 supervisors (community psychiatric nurses), 4 consultants; fortnightly supervision, monthly monitoring; school services 2015/2019.
> - Success factors: institutional leadership; political will; leadership across boundaries; professional commitment; support and supervision; tackle attrition with retraining; M&E.
> - Challenges (Thornicroft, 2008): opposition to change and from neighbours, finance, rigidity, morale; build locally relevant services rather than import "the right answer".
Q: 'Hope Villa' in the Aro Community Mental Health Programme is a: = Transitional supported home for discharged patients | Day hospital | Forensic unit | Drug rehabilitation farm | Training school
> 'Establishment of a transitional community supported accommodation for discharged patients (Hope Villa).'
Q: The Aro Primary Care Mental Health Programme pilot began in: = Abeokuta North LGA, February 2010 | Lagos Island, 2006 | Ibadan, 1956 | Abuja, 2013 | Ogun State-wide, 2015
> Pilot Abeokuta North LGA, Feb 2010; state-wide extension Oct 2011.
Q: The state-wide extension trained how many health workers (nurses and CHEWs)? = 80 | 20 | 40 | 8 | 4
> 20 LGAs, 40 PHC centres, 80 trained health workers, 8 zonal supervisors, 4 zonal consultants.
Q: How often were support and supervision visits made in the Aro primary care programme? = Fortnightly | Weekly | Monthly | Quarterly | Yearly
> Fortnightly support and supervision; monthly programme monitoring meetings.
Q: Thornicroft et al. (2008) advise creating locally relevant services rather than: = Seeking 'the right answer' from elsewhere | Training staff | Involving families | Monitoring outcomes | Using primary care
> '...creating locally relevant services rather than seeking "the right answer" from elsewhere.'
Q: Which is a critical success factor from the Aro programme? = Political will and support from local and state government | Avoiding government involvement | One-off training only | Minimal supervision | Hospital-only care
> Political will is 'vital'; also leadership, cross-boundary leadership, commitment, supervision, retraining against attrition, M&E.

### Social treatment
> - Targets social and environmental factors: family, community, socioeconomic status.
> - WHO social determinants: socioeconomic status, housing, education, employment, social support, food security, health care access, environment.
> - History: moral treatment → deinstitutionalisation and social rehabilitation → social learning theory, CBT, family therapy → recovery-oriented and trauma-informed care, digital tools.
> - 7 principles: social support; social skills training (role-play, behavioural rehearsal); environmental modification (workplace accommodations); family therapy; community integration (supported housing); cultural competence; empowerment.
> - 7 strategies: case management (assess, plan, coordinate, monitor); group therapy (psychoeducational); community programmes (supported employment); family therapy; CBT (behavioural activation); peer support; interagency collaboration.
Q: Social treatment in psychiatry focuses on: = Social and environmental factors that contribute to mental health | Brain imaging | Genetic testing | Drug doses | Neurosurgery
> 'Focuses on addressing the social and environmental factors that contribute to an individual's mental health.'
Q: Which is one of the WHO's key social determinants of health? = Social support networks | Blood group | Handedness | Eye colour | Birth order
> SES, housing, education, employment, social support networks, food security, health care access, environment.
Q: Role-playing and behavioural rehearsal are methods of: = Social skills training | Environmental modification | Case management | Universal prevention | Advocacy
> Social skills training: role-play, behavioural rehearsal, social skills groups, CBT.
Q: The four steps of case management are: = Assessment, planning, coordination, monitoring | Screen, diagnose, treat, discharge | Engage, educate, empower, exit | Refer, admit, review, close | Plan, do, study, act
> Case management: assessment, planning, coordination, monitoring.
Q: Which approach dates from the 18th–19th centuries and stressed a supportive environment, social interaction and occupation? = Moral treatment | Trauma-informed care | Assertive community treatment | Digital therapy | Social learning theory
> Moral treatment — the early phase of social treatment.
Q: Supported housing is a means of promoting which principle? = Community integration | Cultural competence | Social skills training | Empowerment | Family therapy
> Community integration: case management, community programmes, supported housing.
Q: The clubhouse model of rehabilitation is based on: = Members (people with mental illness) running the club alongside staff, with work-ordered days | Locked wards | Medication alone | Family therapy | Inpatient ECT
> Clubhouse (Fountain House model): members share the running of the club in a work-ordered day, leading to transitional employment.

### Population treatment
> - A public health approach to promote mental health, prevent illness and reduce disparities at population level.
> - Prevention levels: primary (prevent onset), secondary (early detection and treatment), tertiary (reduce impact).
> - Prevention types (by target): universal — everyone regardless of risk; selective — high-risk groups (e.g. family history); indicated — early signs, not yet full criteria. Then treatment and recovery.
> - Screening follows the same pattern: universal, selective, indicated.
> - Evaluation: outcome, process, continuous quality improvement.
> - Benefits: outcomes, equity, cost-effectiveness (less absenteeism and presenteeism).
> - Challenges: resources; social, structural and self-stigma; language and culture; comorbidity.
Q: Population treatment in psychiatry is best described as: = A public health approach to promote mental health, prevent illness and reduce disparities | Individual psychotherapy | Hospital-based care | Pharmacogenomics | Forensic assessment
> 'A public health approach that aims to promote mental health, prevent mental illness, and reduce health disparities at the population level.'
Q: Interventions for people with early signs who do not yet meet full diagnostic criteria are: = Indicated prevention | Universal prevention | Selective prevention | Tertiary prevention | Recovery
> Indicated prevention. Universal ＝ everyone; selective ＝ high-risk groups.
Q: A support group for people with a family history of mental illness is an example of: = Selective prevention | Universal prevention | Indicated prevention | Treatment | Recovery
> Selective prevention targets high-risk groups, e.g. those with a family history.
Q: Reducing the impact of mental health problems on individuals and communities is: = Tertiary prevention | Primary prevention | Secondary prevention | Universal screening | Selective screening
> Primary: prevent onset. Secondary: early detection and treatment. Tertiary: reduce impact.
Q: 'Being present at work but not fully productive' is called: = Presenteeism | Absenteeism | Institutionalism | Malingering | Burnout
> Presenteeism — cost-effectiveness of population treatment includes less absenteeism and presenteeism.
Q: Which three types of stigma are listed as challenges? = Social, structural, self-stigma | Public, private, family | Primary, secondary, tertiary | Overt, covert, latent | Cultural, religious, legal
> Social stigma, structural stigma and self-stigma.
Q: Large mental health surveys and risk-factor research shaped population treatment mainly in the: = 1970s–80s | 1880s | 1950s–60s | 1990s–2000s | 2010s
> 1970s–1980s: epidemiological research — mental health surveys and risk factor identification.
Q: Rose's 'prevention paradox' states that: = A large number of people at small risk may give rise to more cases than a small number at high risk | High-risk strategies prevent most cases | Prevention never works | Screening increases disease | Only treatment reduces prevalence
> Rose: shifting the whole population's risk (universal prevention) can prevent more cases than targeting the high-risk few.

## Pharmacy | Telepsychiatry
> Telepsychiatry. Source: Telepsychiatry & Framework - 26.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Telepsychiatry
> - Distant delivery of mental health care via technology (from telemedicine/telehealth) — phone, chat, video.
> - Services: assessment, therapies, education, medication management.
> - Digital tools: mHealth, EHR, decision support, telemedicine, supply chain, SMART guidelines.
> - WHO DMHIs — scalable, close the treatment gap (esp. depression and anxiety); supplement, not replace.
Q: Telepsychiatry is best defined as: = The distant delivery of mental health care via technology | Psychiatry on television | Psychiatric care by telephone operators | Emergency psychiatry | Self-help books
> '...refers to the distant delivery of mental health care via technology.'
