> '...scalable solutions to bridge the global treatment gap, particularly for depression and anxiety.'

> 'These tools are designed to supplement, rather than replace, traditional health systems.'
Q: Which is NOT listed among digital tools for healthcare? = Electroconvulsive therapy | mHealth tools | EHR and databases | Decision support systems | SMART guidelines
> Listed: mHealth, EHR/databases, decision support, telemedicine, supply chain management, SMART guidelines.

> - mHealth "Targeted Client Communication" — reminders, adherence, psychoeducation.
> - mhGAP-IG App — decision support for non-specialists. SMART guidelines — digital guidelines.

### Implementation (WHO)
> - Human-centred design — culture, language, literacy.
> - Human support — guided > fully self-guided.
> - Data privacy and informed consent mandatory.
> - Feasibility and fidelity.

Q: Regarding data privacy and informed consent in digital interventions, WHO states they are: = Mandatory | Optional | Only for research | Unnecessary for apps | The patient's problem
> 'High standards for securing sensitive mental health data and ensuring informed consent are mandatory.'

### Benefits and evidence
> - Access (rural), care at the patient's location, fewer delays, continuity, less stigma (safety, privacy), integration with primary care.
> - High satisfaction; equivalent to in-person in diagnostic accuracy, effectiveness, quality, satisfaction; privacy equivalent.
Q: Which is a listed benefit of telepsychiatry? = Improves access to specialist care in rural areas | Increases stigma | Increases delays | Reduces continuity | Requires the patient to travel
> Benefits: improve access (e.g. rural), bring care to patient, reduce delays, improve continuity.
Q: How does telepsychiatry affect the stigma barrier? = Reduces it by enhancing feelings of safety, security and privacy | Increases it | Has no effect | Only affects doctors | Makes it worse in rural areas

Q: Telepsychiatry helps integrate behavioural health care with: = Primary care | Surgery | Prisons only | Pharmacies only | Schools only
> 'Help integrate behavioral health care and primary care, leading to better outcomes.'

### Social and transcultural psychiatry
> - Social psychiatry: interpersonal context; society's construction of and response to disorder; social impact on onset, course, outcome; complex social interventions.
> - Transcultural: cultural perception and expression of distress, coping; culture-bound syndromes — Koro (SE Asia), Susto (Latin America); adapt treatment; cultural competence.
Q: Social psychiatry focuses on the: = Interpersonal context of mental disorder and wellbeing | Molecular basis of disorder | Pharmacology of drugs | Neuroimaging | Genetics only

### Pathways to care (Nigeria)
> - First use of alternative care (Erinoso 1977, Gureje 1995, Odejide 1999...).
> - Burns & Tomita 2014: first contact traditional 7–33%, religious 14–61%.
> - Aro 2002: only 6.3% direct to Aro; 7.7% other psychiatric; traditional 26.6%; religious 26.0%; private/general hospitals 30%.
> - Recursive use of healers, driven by belief in supernatural causation (Adebowale & Ogunlesi 1999).
> - Competencies: know customs, indigenous/religious care (divination, sacrifice, herbs), interact and partner with them.
Q: Among new attenders at Aro Hospital in 2002, what percentage came directly to the Aro psychiatric service? = 6.3% | 26.6% | 26.0% | 30% | 50%
> 6.3% direct to Aro; 7.7% to other psychiatric facilities.
Q: In the Aro 2002 cohort, the proportion who first consulted traditional healers was: = 26.6% | 6.3% | 7.7% | 30% | 61%

> 30% first consulted private medical facilities and government general hospitals.

> Traditional healers 7–33%; religious healers 14–61%.
Q: The pattern of recursive use of traditional and religious healers is driven by: = Widespread belief in supernatural causation of mental illness | Cost of drugs alone | Distance only | Doctors' strikes | Government policy
> '...driven by the widespread belief in supernatural causation of mental illness (Adebowale & Ogunlesi 1999).'
Q: After first contact, a large proportion of patients: = Engaged in recursive traditional and religious service use in search of a cure | Never returned to any healer | Went straight to Aro | Were admitted | Recovered without care
> 'Large proportion of patients engaged in recursive traditional and religious service use ... in search of a cure.'
Q: Burns and Tomita's 2014 review included how many Nigerian studies? = 7 | 3 | 5 | 12 | 20
> '...by 7 Nigerian studies from different parts of the country.'
Q: Which indigenous practices should a culturally competent psychiatrist know about? = Divination, sacrifices and herbal medicine | Only Western psychotherapy | Only pharmacology | Only neuroimaging | Only court law
> '...including divination, sacrifices and herbal medicine.'
Q: A required competency for culturally informed practice is: = Interacting with indigenous and religious mental health systems in patient care | Avoiding traditional healers entirely | Reporting healers to police | Ignoring culture | Using only English
> 'Interacting with indigenous & religious mental health systems in the care of patients.'
Q: Culturally informed practice includes working in partnership with: = Community support systems and agencies | Pharmaceutical marketers | Only private hospitals | Only courts | Nobody

### Extras (editor)
> - Synchronous vs asynchronous (store-and-forward); verify identity and location, consent, emergency plan.

## Library | History of psychiatry
> History of psychiatry. Source: No lecture — Shorter Oxford / Kaplan. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Ancient to Renaissance
> - Hippocrates: natural causes; brain; epilepsy not sacred; black bile → melancholia; mania, phrenitis, hysteria.
> - Aretaeus: mania and melancholia in the same patient. Galen — humours for 1,500 years.
> - Islamic hospitals (Baghdad, Cairo); Avicenna.
> - Bethlem 1247. Malleus Maleficarum 1487 (witch-hunting).
> - Johann Weyer 1563 — "witches" were mentally ill; father of modern psychiatry. Burton 1621 — Anatomy of Melancholy.
Q: Hippocrates argued in 'On the Sacred Disease' that epilepsy: = Was a disease of the brain | Was caused by the gods | Was contagious | Was caused by the moon only | Was caused by witches
> Hippocrates: epilepsy is not sacred but a brain disease — natural causes for madness.
Q: In humoral theory, melancholia was attributed to an excess of: = Black bile | Blood | Phlegm | Yellow bile | Water
> Black bile — Greek melaina chole.
Q: Who first described mania and melancholia occurring in the same patient? = Aretaeus of Cappadocia | Galen | Soranus | Plato | Avicenna
> Aretaeus of Cappadocia — an early description of bipolar illness.
Q: Which physician systematised humoral medicine so that it dominated for about 1,500 years? = Galen | Hippocrates | Pinel | Paracelsus | Vesalius
> Galen (2nd century AD).
Q: The term 'hysteria' derives from the ancient Greek idea of: = A wandering womb | Black bile | Possession | Brain inflammation | Moon phases
> Hystera ＝ womb — the 'wandering womb' theory.
Q: Bethlem (Bedlam) in London was founded as a priory in: = 1247 | 1066 | 1487 | 1793 | 1845
> 1247; it housed the insane by the late 14th century.
Q: The 1487 text used to identify and persecute witches was: = Malleus Maleficarum | The Anatomy of Melancholy | De praestigiis daemonum | Canon of Medicine | On the Sacred Disease
> Malleus Maleficarum (The Hammer of Witches).
Q: Johann Weyer (1563) argued that many people accused of witchcraft were: = Mentally ill | Truly possessed | Criminals | Heretics | Malingering
> De praestigiis daemonum — they were mentally ill; Weyer is sometimes called the father of modern psychiatry.
Q: 'The Anatomy of Melancholy' (1621) was written by: = Robert Burton | Thomas Willis | William Harvey | Thomas Sydenham | John Locke
> Robert Burton, 1621.
Q: Early hospitals with wards for the mentally ill in the medieval period were found in: = Baghdad and Cairo | London only | New York | Lagos | Tokyo
> The Islamic world — Baghdad, Cairo, Damascus — built early hospitals (bimaristans).

### Moral treatment
> - Pinel unchained patients at Bicêtre (1793), with Pussin; then Salpêtrière; "traitement moral".
> - Tuke — York Retreat 1796 (Quaker). Chiarugi (Florence).
> - Esquirol: defined hallucination ("perception without an object"); monomania.
> - Benjamin Rush — father of American psychiatry. Dorothea Dix — US asylums. Conolly — non-restraint (Hanwell 1839).
Q: Philippe Pinel is famous for: = Unchaining patients at the Bicêtre (1793) | Inventing ECT | Discovering lithium | Coining 'schizophrenia' | Founding psychoanalysis
> Pinel unchained patients at the Bicêtre in 1793 (with Pussin) — moral treatment.
Q: The York Retreat (1796) was founded by: = William Tuke | Pinel | Esquirol | Conolly | Rush
> William Tuke, a Quaker.
Q: Who defined a hallucination as 'a perception without an object'? = Esquirol | Jaspers | Bleuler | Kraepelin | Schneider
> Jean-Étienne Esquirol — also distinguished hallucination from illusion and described monomania.
Q: The 'father of American psychiatry' is: = Benjamin Rush | Adolf Meyer | Dorothea Dix | William James | Karl Menninger
> Benjamin Rush — first American psychiatry textbook (1812).
Q: John Conolly at Hanwell asylum (1839) is known for: = Non-restraint | Insulin coma | Lobotomy | Hypnosis | Psychoanalysis
> Non-restraint policy in England.
Q: Dorothea Dix campaigned for: = State asylums in the USA | Psychoanalysis | ECT | Deinstitutionalisation | Witch trials
> State asylums for the mentally ill in the USA (mid-19th century).
Q: Which pairing is INCORRECT? = Korsakoff — folie à deux | Pinel — Bicêtre | Tuke — York Retreat | Esquirol — definition of hallucination | Alzheimer — Auguste Deter
> Folie à deux — Lasègue & Falret; Korsakoff described the alcoholic amnestic syndrome (1887).

### 19th-century description
> - Griesinger: "mental diseases are brain diseases".
> - Morel: démence précoce; degeneration.
> - Hecker 1871 hebephrenia; Kahlbaum 1874 catatonia.
> - Falret folie circulaire; Baillarger folie à double forme (1854).
> - Lasègue & Falret 1877 folie à deux. Wernicke 1881; Korsakoff 1887.
> - Charcot — hysteria, hypnosis; Janet — dissociation.
Q: 'Mental diseases are brain diseases' was stated by: = Griesinger | Freud | Pinel | Laing | Jaspers
> Wilhelm Griesinger (1845).
Q: Catatonia was described in 1874 by: = Kahlbaum | Hecker | Kraepelin | Bleuler | Morel
> Karl Kahlbaum (1874); Hecker described hebephrenia (1871).
Q: Hebephrenia was described by: = Hecker | Kahlbaum | Morel | Falret | Schneider
> Ewald Hecker (1871).
Q: The term 'démence précoce' was first used by: = Bénédict Morel | Kraepelin | Bleuler | Pinel | Esquirol
> Morel — démence précoce; also the degeneration theory.
Q: Folie à deux was described in 1877 by: = Lasègue and Falret | Charcot and Janet | Kraepelin and Bleuler | Pinel and Pussin | Cade and Schou
> Lasègue and Falret (1877).
Q: 'Folie circulaire' and 'folie à double forme' (1854) are early descriptions of: = Manic-depressive (bipolar) illness | Schizophrenia | Epilepsy | Dementia | Hysteria
> Falret (folie circulaire) and Baillarger (folie à double forme) — bipolar illness.
Q: Charcot at the Salpêtrière is best known for studying: = Hysteria and hypnosis | Lithium | Lobotomy | Schizophrenia genetics | Alcohol amnesia
> Charcot — hysteria and hypnosis; Freud studied with him.

### The founders of modern psychopathology
> - Kraepelin 1899 (6th ed.): dementia praecox vs manic-depressive insanity — by course/outcome.
> - Bleuler 1908/1911: "schizophrenia"; 4 As — Association, Affect, Ambivalence, Autism (fundamental); hallucinations/delusions accessory.
> - Jaspers 1913 General Psychopathology — phenomenology; understanding vs explaining; primary delusions.
> - Schneider — first-rank symptoms.
> - Alzheimer 1906 — Auguste Deter, plaques and tangles.
Q: Kraepelin separated dementia praecox from manic-depressive insanity mainly on the basis of: = Course and outcome | Brain imaging | Response to lithium | Genetics | Psychoanalytic theory
> Course and outcome — deterioration vs episodic recovery (6th edition, 1899).
Q: The term 'schizophrenia' was coined by: = Bleuler | Kraepelin | Schneider | Jaspers | Morel
> Eugen Bleuler (1908; monograph 1911).
Q: Bleuler's fundamental symptoms (the '4 As') are: = Association, Affect, Ambivalence, Autism | Apathy, Alogia, Anhedonia, Avolition | Agnosia, Aphasia, Apraxia, Amnesia | Anxiety, Agitation, Aggression, Arousal | Attention, Arousal, Awareness, Alertness
> Loosening of Associations, blunted Affect, Ambivalence, Autism. Hallucinations and delusions were accessory.
Q: Karl Jaspers' 'General Psychopathology' was published in: = 1913 | 1899 | 1938 | 1952 | 1980
> 1913 — founded descriptive phenomenology.
Q: Jaspers distinguished 'understanding' (verstehen) from: = Explaining (erklären) | Feeling | Diagnosing | Interpreting dreams | Classifying
> Understanding (meaningful connections) vs explaining (causal); primary delusions are not understandable.
Q: First-rank symptoms of schizophrenia were described by: = Kurt Schneider | Bleuler | Kraepelin | Jaspers | Langfeldt
> Kurt Schneider.
Q: Alois Alzheimer's 1906 patient with plaques and tangles was: = Auguste Deter | Anna O | Little Hans | Phineas Gage | HM
> Auguste Deter. Kraepelin named the disease after Alzheimer.
Q: Which is one of Schneider's first-rank symptoms? = Thought insertion | Loosening of associations | Ambivalence | Blunted affect | Catatonia
> FRS: audible thoughts, third-person/running commentary voices, thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcast, passivity, delusional perception.
Q: The Aro Village System, Bleuler's 4 As, and Kahlbaum are linked respectively to: = Lambo, schizophrenia, catatonia | Asuni, mania, hebephrenia | Prince, dementia, catatonia | Lambo, depression, hebephrenia | Leighton, schizophrenia, folie à deux
> Lambo — Aro Village System; Bleuler's 4 As — schizophrenia; Kahlbaum — catatonia (1874).

### Psychotherapies
> - Freud & Breuer 1895 Studies on Hysteria (Anna O); Interpretation of Dreams 1900; id/ego/superego.
> - Jung collective unconscious; Adler inferiority complex; Anna Freud defences (1936); Klein positions; Winnicott good-enough mother; Bowlby attachment.
> - Pavlov, Watson (Little Albert), Skinner (operant), Wolpe (systematic desensitisation 1958).
> - Beck — CBT; Ellis — REBT; Rogers — client-centred.
Q: 'Studies on Hysteria' (1895), describing Anna O, was written by: = Freud and Breuer | Jung and Adler | Charcot and Janet | Klein and Winnicott | Pavlov and Watson
> Freud and Breuer — Anna O's 'talking cure'.
Q: 'The Interpretation of Dreams' was published in: = 1900 | 1895 | 1913 | 1923 | 1936
> 1900, Freud.
Q: The 'collective unconscious' and archetypes are concepts of: = Jung | Freud | Adler | Klein | Rogers
> Carl Jung — analytical psychology.
Q: The paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions were described by: = Melanie Klein | Anna Freud | Winnicott | Bowlby | Kohut
> Melanie Klein — object relations.
Q: The 'good-enough mother' and 'transitional object' are concepts of: = Winnicott | Bowlby | Klein | Freud | Erikson
> Donald Winnicott.
Q: Systematic desensitisation was developed by: = Wolpe | Skinner | Beck | Pavlov | Ellis
> Joseph Wolpe (1958) — reciprocal inhibition.
Q: The cognitive triad of depression is associated with: = Aaron Beck | Albert Ellis | Carl Rogers | B. F. Skinner | Freud
> Aaron Beck — negative views of self, world and future.
Q: The 'inferiority complex' is associated with: = Adler | Jung | Freud | Klein | Bowlby
> Alfred Adler — individual psychology.
Q: Anna Freud's major work (1936) was: = The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence | The Interpretation of Dreams | Totem and Taboo | Civilisation and its Discontents | The Divided Self
> The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence (1936).

### Early physical treatments
> - Wagner-Jauregg 1917 malaria therapy for GPI — Nobel 1927.
> - Sakel 1933 insulin coma.
> - Meduna 1934 — camphor/cardiazol convulsions.

Q: ECT was introduced in 1938 by: = Cerletti and Bini | Meduna | Sakel | Moniz | Kalinowsky

### Psychopharmacology
> - Lithium — Cade 1949; Schou prophylaxis.

Q: The antipsychotic effect of chlorpromazine was shown in 1952 by: = Delay and Deniker | Cade | Kuhn | Janssen | Sternbach

Q: Haloperidol was developed in 1958 by: = Paul Janssen | Leo Sternbach | Roland Kuhn | Delay | Carlsson
> Paul Janssen.
Q: Clozapine was reintroduced after which landmark study showed its superiority in treatment-resistant schizophrenia? = Kane et al. (1988) | CATIE (2005) | IPSS (1973) | Rosenhan (1973) | Feighner (1972)
> Kane et al., 1988. Withdrawn in the 1970s after agranulocytosis deaths.

> Kuhn — imipramine. Cade — lithium; Delay & Deniker — chlorpromazine; Janssen — haloperidol; Sternbach — benzodiazepines.
Q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia is particularly associated with: = Arvid Carlsson | John Cade | Roland Kuhn | Henri Laborit | Paul Janssen
> Arvid Carlsson (Nobel 2000 for dopamine work).

### Deinstitutionalisation and critics
> - Goffman Asylums 1961 — total institution. Barton 1959 — institutional neurosis. Wing & Brown 1970 — Institutionalism and Schizophrenia.

Q: The concept of the 'total institution' comes from: = Goffman's Asylums (1961) | Szasz | Foucault | Basaglia | Rosenhan

Q: 'The Myth of Mental Illness' (1961) was written by: = Thomas Szasz | R. D. Laing | Michel Foucault | David Cooper | Goffman

## Records Office | Basic statistics
> Basic statistics. Source: Basic statistics 1 & 2_NPMCNFac Psych_Revision Course 2026_OGUNWALE.pptx. Each run plays one concept: read its summary in the briefing, then answer all of its questions.

### Basics
> - Ghaemi: "medicine without statistics is quackery; statistics without medicine is numerology".
> - Research: descriptive (case series, audit, surveys) → analytical (case-control, cohort) → experimental (RCT, cluster, cross-over).
> - Descriptive ＝ summarise; inferential ＝ test hypotheses.
> - Primary (surveys, experiments) vs secondary (records) data.
> - Quantitative (measured) vs qualitative (categorised). Discrete (whole numbers) vs continuous (fractions).
> - Statistic ＝ from sample; parameter ＝ from population.
Q: Who said 'Medicine without statistics is quackery; statistics without medicine is numerology'? = S. N. Ghaemi | William Osler | Laplace | Bradford Hill | Gauss
> S. N. Ghaemi (2009), A Clinician's Guide to Statistics and Epidemiology in Mental Health.
Q: Biostatistics is: = Statistics applied to biological and medical research | Biology of statistics | Only clinical trials | Bioinformatics | Genetics
> 'Biostatistics — the employment of statistics in the field of biological and medical research.'
Q: In the architecture of biomedical research, a case-control study is classed as: = Analytical | Descriptive | Experimental | Qualitative | Audit
> Analytical studies: case-control and cohort.
Q: Clinical audit falls under which category of research? = Descriptive (observational) | Analytical | Experimental | Meta-analysis | Cross-over trial
> Descriptive: case reports/series, clinical audit, qualitative studies, surveys.
Q: Which is an EXPERIMENTAL study design? = Cross-over trial | Cohort | Case-control | Survey | Case series
> Experimental: controlled trials, RCTs, cluster trials, cross-over trials.
Q: Testing hypotheses about research questions is the domain of: = Inferential statistics | Descriptive statistics | Graphs | Data entry | Sampling only
> 'Inferential statistics: involves testing hypotheses.'
Q: Routine hospital records used for research are a source of: = Secondary data | Primary data | Experimental data | Qualitative data only | Random data
> 'Secondary ("routine" records, external sources e.g. published reports, databanks).'
Q: Diagnosis, social class and marital status are examples of: = Qualitative variables | Quantitative variables | Continuous variables | Ratio variables | Discrete numerical variables
> Qualitative — cannot be measured numerically but may be categorised.
Q: Blood pressure is a: = Quantitative variable | Qualitative variable | Nominal variable | Ordinal variable | Constant
> Quantitative — measured in the usual numerical sense (BP, height, weight).
Q: The number of beds in a hospital is a: = Discrete random variable | Continuous random variable | Ratio of proportions | Qualitative variable | Parameter
> Discrete — gaps between values; whole numbers only (number of beds, patients).
Q: Height is a: = Continuous random variable | Discrete random variable | Nominal variable | Ordinal variable | Dummy variable
> Continuous — no gaps; fractions possible.
Q: A population, in statistics, is: = The largest collection of values of a random variable of interest; finite or infinite | Always a country's people | Any group of 100 | Only patients | A sample
> 'Population: the largest collection of values of a random variable in which one is interested ... may be finite or infinite.'
Q: Measurement is defined as: = Assignment of numbers to objects or events according to a set of rules | Counting patients | Weighing | Asking questions | Recording diagnoses
> 'Measurement: assignment of numbers to objects or events according to a set of rules.'
Q: Prevalence is approximately equal to: = Incidence × duration | Incidence ÷ duration | Mortality × incidence | Incidence + mortality | 1/incidence
> Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration (in a steady state).

### Scales (NOIR)
> - Nominal — lowest; names; mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories (gender, diagnosis).
> - Ordinal — ranked (severity, SES).
> - Interval — equal distances, arbitrary zero (°C).
> - Ratio — highest; true zero (height, weight).
Q: The LOWEST type of measurement scale is: = Nominal | Ordinal | Interval | Ratio | Continuous
> 'Nominal scale: Lowest type of measurement scale.'
Q: Clinical severity rated mild–moderate–severe is measured on a: = Ordinal scale | Nominal scale | Interval scale | Ratio scale | Binary scale
> Ordinal — ranking (mild → severe, poor → good).
Q: A scale with a true zero point is: = Ratio | Nominal | Ordinal | Interval | Likert
> 'Ratio Scale: Highest level ... It has a true zero point.'
Q: On an interval scale, the zero point is: = Arbitrary | True | Absent | Negative | Always 100
> Interval: 'Unit distance and "zero point" are arbitrary.'
Q: Nominal categories must be: = Mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive | Ordered | Equally spaced | Numerical | Continuous
> '...classifying them into mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive categories.'

### Describing data
> - Mean — affected by extremes. Median — middle, resists extremes. Mode — most frequent; works for qualitative data ("modal diagnosis").
> - Range ＝ L − S; variance ＝ Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1); SD ＝ √variance (original units).
> - Median ＝ 50th percentile; Q1 ＝ 25th; Q3 ＝ 75th; IQR ＝ Q3 − Q1 (middle 50%).
> - Box plot shows median, quartiles, outliers. Bar/pie for nominal data; scatter for relationships.
> - Class intervals: non-overlapping; 6–15; Sturges k ＝ 1 + 3.322 log n; width R/k.
Q: A descriptive measure computed from a SAMPLE is called a: = Statistic | Parameter | Constant | Variable | Population value
> Statistic ＝ from sample; parameter ＝ from population.
Q: Which measure of central tendency is affected by every value, including extreme ones? = Mean | Median | Mode | IQR | Range
> Mean: uniqueness, simplicity, affected by each value including extreme ones.
Q: The measure of central tendency LEAST affected by extreme values is the: = Median | Mean | Range | Variance | SD
> Median — not drastically affected by extreme values.
Q: Which measure of central tendency is useful for qualitative data, e.g. the commonest diagnosis in a hospital? = Mode | Mean | Median | Standard deviation | Geometric mean
> Mode — e.g. 'modal diagnosis' in a psychiatric hospital could be schizophrenia.
Q: For an odd number of ordered values n, the median is the: = (n + 1)/2th value | n/2th value | Mean of all values | Most frequent value | (n − 1)th value
> Median of an odd set ＝ the (n + 1)/2th value of the ordered array.
Q: Standard deviation is: = The square root of the variance, in original units | The square of the variance | The range divided by 2 | The mean deviation | Q3 − Q1
> SD ＝ √variance, expressed in the original unit of measurement.
Q: The interquartile range is: = Q3 − Q1 | Max − min | Q2 − Q1 | Mean ± SD | 75th percentile only
> IQR ＝ Q3 − Q1 — variability of the middle 50%.
Q: The 50th percentile is the: = Median | Mean | Mode | Q1 | Q3
> '50th percentile is the median; 25th ＝ Q1; 75th ＝ Q3.'
Q: Sample variance is calculated by dividing the sum of squared deviations by: = n − 1 | n | n + 1 | 2n | √n
> s² ＝ Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1).
Q: In the SPSS age example (n ＝ 47, values 28–46), the range was: = 18 | 14 | 28 | 32 | 46
> Range ＝ 46 − 28 ＝ 18. Mean 32.79, median 32, mode 33.
Q: A box-and-whisker plot displays: = Median, quartiles, range and outliers | Only the mean | Proportions of categories | Correlation | Frequencies of nominal data only
> Box plot: median, Q1, Q3, min/max and outliers.
Q: Which graph is suited to nominal (qualitative) data? = Pie chart | Scatter plot | Box plot | Histogram | Stem-and-leaf
> Bar and pie charts for qualitative/nominal data.
Q: The stem-and-leaf plot is described in the lecture as: = Mainly of theoretical interest, not commonly used | The most used display today | Only for nominal data | A test of significance | A measure of reliability
> 'Mainly of theoretical interest. Not commonly utilised these days.'
Q: Sturges' rule is used to determine: = The number of class intervals when grouping data | Sample size | Power | Reliability | Effect size
> Sturges (1926): k ＝ 1 + 3.322 log₁₀ n — number of class intervals (a guide).
Q: The rule-of-thumb number of class intervals for grouping data is: = 6–15 | 2–4 | 20–30 | 50 | Equal to n
> '"Rule of the Thumb": 6 ≤ no. of intervals ≤ 15.'
Q: Class intervals when grouping data should be: = Contiguous and mutually exclusive (non-overlapping) | Overlapping | Random | Unequal always | Based on the mode
> 'Principle 1: select a set of contiguous, exclusive (non-overlapping) intervals.'
Q: The standard error of the mean equals: = SD ÷ √n | SD × n | Variance ÷ 2 | Range ÷ 4 | Mean ÷ SD
> SE ＝ SD/√n — precision of the mean, not spread of the data.

### Normal distribution (Gauss)
> - Symmetrical; area ＝ 1; mean ＝ median ＝ mode; defined by μ and σ.
> - 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD (1.96), 99.7% within 3 SD.
> - Central Limit Theorem — large samples approximate normality.
> - Positive skew: mean > median > mode; negative skew: mean < median < mode.
Q: In a normal distribution: = Mean ＝ median ＝ mode | Mean > median > mode | Mean < median | The mode is undefined | The median is zero
> 'The mean, median and mode are all equal.'
Q: What proportion of observations lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean in a normal distribution? = 95% | 50% | 68% | 99.7% | 100%
> 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD.
Q: The total area under the normal curve is: = 1 | 0.5 | 100 | Infinite | Equal to the mean
> 'Total area under the curve is one square unit i.e. 1.'
Q: A normal distribution is completely determined by: = The mean and standard deviation | The median and mode | The range | Sample size only | The IQR
> 'Distribution completely determined by the values of μ and σ.'
Q: The principle that estimates approximate the normal distribution when samples are large is the: = Central Limit Theorem | Law of small numbers | Sturges rule | Bayes' theorem | Hardy-Weinberg
> Central Limit Theorem.
Q: In a positively (right) skewed distribution: = Mean > median > mode | Mean < median < mode | Mean ＝ median ＝ mode | Median > mean | Mode > mean
> Positive skew: tail to the right pulls the mean above the median (mean > median > mode).
Q: The normal distribution is also called Gaussian after: = C. F. Gauss (1777–1855) | Laplace | Gosset | Pearson | Fisher
> C. F. Gauss (1777–1855).

### Estimation
> - Point (single value) vs interval estimate (range at a confidence level).
> - Sampled (drawn from) vs target (want to infer about) population — generalise to the sampled population.
> - 95% CI ＝ estimate ± 1.96 × SE; SE ＝ √(variance/n).
> - CI for a difference including 0 → not significant; for a ratio, including 1 → not significant.
> - Meaning: 95% of such intervals in repeated sampling contain the true value.
Q: An interval estimate is: = A range of values that includes the parameter at a specified confidence level | A single value | The sample size | The p-value | The variance
> Interval estimate: two values representing a range, at a specified confidence level.
Q: A researcher samples schizophrenia patients from Yaba NPH to study relapse. Yaba patients are the: = Sampled population | Target population | Parameter | Control group | Census
> Yaba patients ＝ sampled population; all schizophrenia patients ＝ target population.
Q: Statistical generalisation should be made to the: = Sampled population, unless the two are shown not to differ | Target population always | Whole world | Only the sample | Nobody
> '...generalize estimate to sampled population and not to target population except it can be shown that the two are not different.'
Q: Statistical inference is: = Reaching a conclusion about a population from a sample | Describing a sample only | Collecting data | Drawing graphs | Calculating the mode
> '...procedure by which we reach a conclusion about a population on the basis of ... a sample.'
Q: The reliability coefficient (z) for a 95% confidence interval is: = 1.96 | 1.64 | 2.58 | 3.0 | 0.05
> 'z ... it is 1.96 at 0.05.'
Q: The standard error of the mean is: = √(variance/n) | Variance × n | SD × n | Range/4 | Mean/SD
> 'standard error is the square root of variance/n' (= SD/√n).
Q: A 95% CI for the difference between two means is 0.22 to 2.18. The conclusion is: = The means differ, because the interval does not include 0 | No difference | The test is invalid | Increase the sample | The means are equal
> 'Check if the interval includes zero; if it does not, we conclude that the two population means are different.'
Q: The correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval is: = In repeated sampling, 95% of such intervals will contain the population mean | There is a 95% chance the sample mean is correct | 95% of patients improve | p ＝ 0.95 | The data are 95% normal
> '...100(1 − α) percent of all intervals will in the long run contain the population mean.'
Q: A 95% CI for a difference in means of −0.5 to 1.4 indicates: = No significant difference (it includes 0) | A significant difference | A large effect | Type I error | Perfect correlation
> The interval includes 0 → no significant difference.

### Hypothesis testing
> - H₀ ＝ no difference; set up to be rejected. H_A ＝ research hypothesis.
> - α ＝ probability of rejecting a true H₀ (usually 0.05 or 0.01).
> - Type I (α) ＝ false positive (reject true H₀). Type II (β) ＝ false negative (fail to reject false H₀). Power ＝ 1 − β.
> - "Accept" H₀ ＝ H₀ may be true.
Q: The null hypothesis is: = The hypothesis of no difference, set up to be rejected | The hypothesis of a difference | The researcher's belief | Always true | The alternative hypothesis
> 'Null hypothesis: the hypothesis of no difference ... set up for the purpose of being rejected.'
Q: The alternative hypothesis is the same as the: = Research hypothesis | Null hypothesis | Statistical decision | Significance level | Power
> 'The alternative hypothesis and research hypothesis are the same.'
Q: If we fail to reject ('accept') H₀, we conclude that H₀: = May be true | Is definitely true | Is false | Was badly stated | Equals H_A
> 'Accept Ho ＝ conclude that Ho "may" be true.'
Q: Which steps of hypothesis testing are usually done by statistical software? = Determining the distribution, stating the decision rule region and calculating the statistic | Stating hypotheses | Evaluating data | Reviewing assumptions | Making the clinical conclusion
> Steps 5–7 (distribution, decision rule, calculation) are performed by software (SPSS, Epi Info).
Q: A hypothesis stated in a form that permits evaluation by statistical techniques is a: = Statistical hypothesis | Research hypothesis | Theory | Conjecture | Null result
> Statistical hypothesis — stated to permit evaluation by statistical techniques.
Q: α (the significance level) is the probability of: = Rejecting a true null hypothesis | Accepting a false null hypothesis | Finding a true difference | Power | Having a large sample
> 'α is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis.'
Q: A Type II error is: = Failing to reject a false null hypothesis | Rejecting a true null hypothesis | A data entry error | Using the wrong test | A false positive
> Type II (β) — fail to reject a false H₀ (false negative).
Q: A study concludes a drug works when it actually doesn't. This is a: = Type I error | Type II error | Correct decision | Power | Sampling frame
> Type I (α) error — false positive: rejecting a true H₀.
Q: Power is: = 1 − β | α | β | 1 − α | α + β
> Power ＝ 1 − β.
Q: The significance level is usually set at: = 0.05 or 0.01 | 0.5 or 0.1 | 0.95 | 0.80 | 1.96
> 'Usually is set at 0.01, 0.05.'

### Which test
> - t-test ↔ Mann–Whitney U; paired t ↔ Wilcoxon signed-rank; ANOVA ↔ Kruskal–Wallis; repeated ANOVA ↔ Friedman; Pearson ↔ Spearman/Kendall; paired χ² ＝ McNemar.
> - Parametric assumptions: normal, equal variance, interval data, independence.
> - t-test (Gosset): 2 means; one-sample, independent, paired; report t, df, p.
> - ANOVA: 3+ groups; F ＝ between ÷ within variance; factorial (several factors + interactions); repeated measures.
> - χ²: proportions; Σ(O − E)²/E; E ＝ row × column ÷ total. Yates (2×2); Fisher's exact if n < 20, or 20–40 with expected cell < 5.
Q: The non-parametric equivalent of the independent-samples t-test is: = Mann–Whitney U | Wilcoxon signed-rank | Kruskal–Wallis | Friedman | McNemar
> Independent t-test ↔ Mann–Whitney U.
Q: The non-parametric equivalent of the paired t-test is: = Wilcoxon signed-rank | Mann–Whitney U | Chi-square | Kruskal–Wallis | Spearman
> Paired t-test ↔ Wilcoxon signed-rank.
Q: The non-parametric equivalent of one-way ANOVA is: = Kruskal–Wallis | Friedman | McNemar | Fisher's exact | Kendall's tau
> One-way ANOVA ↔ Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks.
Q: For paired nominal data (before/after in the same patients), the test is: = McNemar's chi-square | Chi-square | Fisher's exact | Mann–Whitney | Pearson
> Paired: McNemar's χ².
Q: Which is NOT an assumption of parametric tests? = Ordinal data | Normally distributed data | Homogeneity of variance | At least interval data | Independence
> Parametric needs interval data at least — nominal and ordinal do not meet it.
Q: The non-parametric equivalent of two-way/repeated ANOVA is: = Friedman's test | Kruskal–Wallis | Mann–Whitney | Wilcoxon | Chi-square
> Two-way ANOVA ↔ Friedman's test.
Q: Comparing ordinal scores between THREE independent groups calls for: = Kruskal–Wallis | ANOVA | Mann–Whitney | Paired t-test | Pearson
> Ordinal, 3 groups → Kruskal–Wallis.
Q: The t-test was first computed by: = William Sealy Gosset | Karl Pearson | Ronald Fisher | Bradford Hill | Gauss
> 'First computed by the British statistician, William Sealy Gosset.'
Q: Which is NOT one of the three types of t-test? = Three-sample | One-sample | Independent-samples | Paired-samples | All are types
> Three types: one-sample, independent-sample, paired-sample.
Q: When reporting a t-test you should always state: = t, degrees of freedom and p | Only p | Only the means | U and mean ranks | F only
> '...value of t and the degrees of freedom should always be stated e.g. t ＝ 1.175, df ＝ 45, p ＝ 0.246.'
Q: Comparing mean age of onset in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and OCD uses: = One-way ANOVA | t-test | Chi-square | Pearson correlation | McNemar
> ANOVA — three or more group means.
Q: The F statistic in ANOVA is the ratio of: = Between-group to within-group variance | Within-group to between-group variance | Mean to SD | Observed to expected | Sensitivity to specificity
> F ＝ between-group variance ÷ within-group variance.
Q: Measurements on the same sample at 1, 3 and 6 months should be analysed with: = Repeated-measures ANOVA | One-way ANOVA | Independent t-test | Chi-square | Mann–Whitney
> 'For paired data (... 1mth, 3mths, 6mths), Repeated Measures ANOVA.'
Q: An ANOVA showing the effect of diagnosis AND family history, and their interaction, is a: = Factorial ANOVA | One-way ANOVA | Kruskal–Wallis | t-test | MANOVA always
> Factorial ANOVA — several factors and their interactions.
Q: The Mann–Whitney U test is based on: = Ranking of values | Means | Variances | Proportions | Correlation
> 'Based on ranking of values in two different groups.'
Q: For Mann–Whitney, you should report: = Mean ranks, U and p | t and df | F and two df | χ² only | r only
> 'Always state ... mean ranks, U and the p value.'
Q: The chi-squared test is used to compare: = Proportions between groups | Means | Medians | Variances | Correlations
> χ² tests differences in proportions of groups with a characteristic.
Q: In a chi-square test, the expected frequency of a cell is: = Row total × column total ÷ grand total | Observed − expected | Row total ÷ column total | Grand total ÷ cells | Observed²
> E ＝ (row total × column total) ÷ total sample size.
Q: Fisher's exact test is preferred when: = n < 20, or n is 20–40 with an expected cell frequency < 5 | n > 1000 | Data are continuous | There are 3 groups of means | Data are paired
> 'Fisher's Exact test: useful when n < 20 or if n is between 20 and 40 + one expected cell < 5.'
Q: Yates' continuity correction is applied to: = 2 × 2 chi-square tables | ANOVA | Correlation | t-tests | Regression
> 'Yates' continuity correction: used for 2 × 2 tables generally.'
Q: If two groups for a rank-based comparison are paired rather than independent, use: = Wilcoxon signed-rank | Mann–Whitney | Kruskal–Wallis | Chi-square | ANOVA
> '...where paired, Wilcoxon sign rank test should be used.'

### Correlation and regression
> - Correlation ＝ linear relationship; −1 to +1; 0 ＝ none.
> - Pearson (parametric); Spearman, Kendall (non-parametric, less power); Kendall's tau better with ties and small n.
> - Regression y ＝ a + bx (a intercept, b slope); B / β coefficients; dummy variables for categories.
> - Many one-way ANOVAs → inflated Type I error. ANCOVA controls a covariate; MANOVA 2+ dependent variables; MANCOVA both.
> - Logistic regression: categorical outcome (binary or multinomial); OR ＝ exp(B), adjusted for other predictors.
Q: A correlation coefficient of −1 indicates: = Perfect negative correlation | No relationship | Perfect positive correlation | Weak correlation | Causation
> −1 ＝ perfect negative; +1 ＝ perfect positive; 0 ＝ no relationship.
Q: The parametric correlation coefficient is: = Pearson's r | Spearman's rho | Kendall's tau | Kappa | Cronbach's alpha
> Pearson's r (parametric); Spearman and Kendall (non-parametric).
Q: With many tied values and a small sample, the better correlation coefficient is: = Kendall's tau | Pearson's r | Spearman's rho | ICC | Phi
> 'Spearman's coefficient tends to exaggerate the association when there are many tied values (Kendall's tau is better ... esp. when n is also small).'
Q: Compared with parametric tests, non-parametric correlation coefficients have: = Less power to detect associations | More power | Equal power always | No assumptions about ranks | Greater precision
> 'Non-parametric correlation coefficients like Spearman's ... have less power.'
Q: Correlation measures: = Linear relationship between variables | Causation | Difference in means | Agreement | Prevalence
> 'Is a measure of linear relationship between variables.'
Q: In the regression equation y ＝ a + bx, b is the: = Slope | Intercept | Error | Dependent variable | Correlation
> a ＝ intercept, b ＝ slope.
Q: Categorical predictors such as gender enter a multiple regression as: = Dummy variables (e.g. 0/1) | Continuous values | They cannot be included | Ranks | Squares
> 'Such variables must be coded as "dummy variables" (e.g. male ＝ 0, female ＝ 1).'
Q: Running a series of one-way ANOVAs for many dependent variables risks: = Inflated Type I error | Type II error | Reduced sample size | Perfect power | No interactions
> 'Conducting a series of one-way ANOVA ... leads to increased possibility of Type I error.'
Q: Comparing quality of life across diagnoses while controlling for internalised stigma uses: = ANCOVA | Chi-square | t-test | Kappa | Spearman
> ANCOVA — compares means while controlling for a covariate (confounder).
Q: MANOVA is used when there are: = Two or more dependent variables | Only one dependent variable | Only nominal data | Two groups only | Paired proportions
> 'MANOVA: used for analyses with two or more dependent variables.'
Q: When the outcome is binary (yes/no), the appropriate model is: = Binary logistic regression | Linear regression | ANOVA | Pearson correlation | MANOVA
> Binary logistic regression; multinomial if the outcome has 3+ levels.
Q: In logistic regression, the odds ratio equals: = exp(B) | B² | √B | 1/B | B × SE
> '...the odds ratio is exp (B)' — adjusted for all other predictors in the model.
Q: The logistic regression odds ratio differs from a simple odds ratio because it: = Holds all other predictors in the model constant (adjusted) | Ignores other variables | Is always larger | Uses means | Requires paired data
> '...determined while holding all other predictor variables in the model constant.'

### RR and OR
> - RR ＝ [a/(a+b)] ÷ [c/(c+d)] — cohort (prospective).
> - OR ＝ ad/bc — case-control (retrospective).
> - Range 0 to ∞; 1 ＝ no difference; < 1 less likely; > 1 more likely.
> - OR ≈ RR when the disease is rare.
Q: Relative risk is used mainly in: = Prospective (cohort) studies | Case-control studies | Cross-sectional surveys only | Meta-analysis only | Qualitative studies
> 'RR ... Used for prospective studies.'
Q: The odds ratio is used mainly in: = Retrospective case-control studies | RCTs only | Cohort studies only | Audits | Surveys of means
> 'Odds ratio ... Used for retrospective case-control studies.'
Q: From a 2 × 2 table (a, b / c, d), the odds ratio is: = ad/bc | a/(a+b) ÷ c/(c+d) | a/c | (a+d)/n | bc/ad
> OR ＝ (a/b)/(c/d) ＝ ad/bc.
Q: Relative risk is calculated as: = [a/(a+b)] ÷ [c/(c+d)] | ad/bc | a/b | (a+b)/(c+d) | a − c
> RR ＝ [a/(a + b)] ÷ [c/(c + d)].
Q: An OR or RR of 1 indicates: = The event is equally likely in both groups | The event is more likely in the exposed | A protective effect | Statistical significance | An error
> 'The value of 1 indicates that the event is equally likely in the two groups.'
Q: The odds ratio is a good approximation of relative risk when: = The disease is rare | The disease is common | The sample is small | The study is an RCT | Never
> 'OR is a good approximation of the population RR in the case of a rare disease.'
Q: An RR of 0.6 for an exposure means the outcome is: = Less likely in the exposed | More likely in the exposed | Equally likely | Impossible | Certain
> < 1 → less likely in the group of interest.
Q: If the control event rate is 40% and the treatment event rate is 30%, the NNT is: = 10 | 3 | 30 | 40 | 100
> ARR ＝ 0.40 − 0.30 ＝ 0.10; NNT ＝ 1/ARR ＝ 10.

### Reliability ＝ consistency, free from error
> - Coefficient 0–1: poor < 0.5, moderate 0.5–0.75, good > 0.75; Cronbach's α 0.7–0.8 satisfactory.
> - Test–retest; rater (intra-, inter-); alternate forms; internal consistency.
> - Correlation ≠ agreement → use ICC (continuous) or kappa (categorical): κ ＝ (Pₒ − Pₑ)/(1 − Pₑ), corrects for chance.
> - Cronbach's α ＝ average of all split-half reliabilities; fewer items → lower α; very high ＝ redundancy.
Q: Reliability refers to: = Consistency — freedom from error in repeated measurement | Measuring what it claims to measure | Sensitivity | Sample size | Effect size
> 'The extent to which a measurement is consistent and free from error.'
Q: A reliability coefficient above 0.75 is considered: = Good | Poor | Moderate | Invalid | Perfect
> Poor < 0.5; moderate 0.5–0.75; good > 0.75.
Q: A satisfactory Cronbach's alpha is generally: = 0.7–0.8 | 0.2–0.3 | 0.4–0.5 | Exactly 1.0 | Below 0.5
> 'General rule: Cronbach's alpha of 0.7 – 0.8 is satisfactory (Bland & Altman, 1997).'
Q: Why is simple correlation unsuitable for test–retest reliability? = It measures association, not agreement | It is too complex | It only works for nominal data | It requires 3 time points | It ignores sample size
> 'Correlation is not suitable because it measures "correlation" and not "agreement".'
Q: For agreement on categorical (nominal) data, the statistic used is: = Kappa | Pearson's r | ICC | t | F
> Kappa (κ) ＝ (Pₒ − Pₑ)/(1 − Pₑ) — corrects for chance agreement.
Q: For continuous data, the preferred reliability statistic that separates measurement bias from random variation is: = Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) | Kappa | Chi-square | Spearman | Cronbach's alpha
> ICC distinguishes measurement bias from random variation.
Q: Two psychiatrists rate the same patients at the same time. This tests: = Inter-rater reliability | Intra-rater reliability | Test–retest reliability | Construct validity | Alternate forms reliability
> Inter-rater — two or more raters, same patients, same time.
Q: Cronbach's alpha may be regarded as: = The average of all possible split-half reliabilities | A measure of validity only | The correlation with a gold standard | Kappa for continuous data | The test–retest coefficient
> 'Cronbach's alpha may be regarded as the average of all possible split-half reliabilities.'
Q: Fewer items on a scale tend to give Cronbach's alpha values that are: = Lower | Higher | Unchanged | Negative | Exactly 0.7
> 'Responsive to the total number of items on the scale: fewer items tend to yield lower coefficients.'
Q: In test–retest reliability, the interval between tests should be: = Long enough to forget initial responses but not so long that the variable changes | As short as possible | At least a year | Exactly 24 hours | Irrelevant
> Far enough apart for responses to be forgotten, not so far that the variable changes (Bland & Altman 2002).
Q: Very highly correlated items on a scale may imply: = Redundancy | Excellent validity | Poor reliability | Low power | Bias
> 'NOTE: highly correlated items may imply redundancy!'

### Validity ＝ measures what it claims
> - Face (looks right; subjective) · content (covers all aspects) · construct (convergent — agrees with MMSE; discriminant — doesn't correlate with unrelated) · criterion (vs gold standard; concurrent/predictive).
> - Sensitivity ＝ TP/(TP+FN); specificity ＝ TN/(TN+FP); PPV ＝ TP/(TP+FP); NPV ＝ TN/(TN+FN).
> - PPV and NPV depend on prevalence.
Q: Validity is whether an instrument: = Measures what it purports to measure | Gives consistent results | Is cheap | Is quick | Has many items
> 'This is whether an instrument measures what it purports to measure.'
Q: The simplest and most subjective form of validity is: = Face validity | Construct validity | Criterion validity | Predictive validity | Content validity
> Face validity — does it 'look right'? Highly subjective.
Q: A quality-of-life scale lacking any section on activities of daily living lacks: = Content validity | Face validity | Reliability | Sensitivity | Power
> Content validity — do the items cover all aspects of the variable?
Q: A new cognitive screening scale correlating well with the MMSE demonstrates: = Convergent validity | Discriminant validity | Face validity | Inter-rater reliability | Specificity
> Convergent validity — agreement with an established scale of the same construct.
Q: A new suicidality scale correlating poorly with an anxiety scale shows: = Discriminant (divergent) validity | Convergent validity | Content validity | Low reliability | Face validity
> Discriminant/divergent validity — not correlating with an unrelated construct.
Q: Comparing a new test against a 'gold standard' assesses: = Criterion validity | Face validity | Internal consistency | Test–retest reliability | Power
> Criterion validity — new test vs reference/gold standard; concurrent or predictive.
Q: Sensitivity is: = TP/(TP + FN) | TN/(TN + FP) | TP/(TP + FP) | TN/(TN + FN) | FP/(FP + TN)
> Sensitivity ＝ TP/(TP + FN) — positive test given disease.
Q: Specificity is the probability of: = A negative test given no disease | A positive test given disease | Disease given a positive test | No disease given a negative test | A false positive
> Specificity ＝ TN/(TN + FP).
Q: The probability that a patient with a positive screening test actually has the disease is the: = Positive predictive value | Sensitivity | Specificity | Negative predictive value | Likelihood ratio
> PPV ＝ TP/(TP + FP).
Q: Which values are affected by the prevalence of the disease? = PPV and NPV | Sensitivity and specificity | Kappa and ICC | Alpha and beta | Range and IQR
> 'These two values (PPV, NPV) are affected by the prevalence rate.'
Q: As prevalence rises, the positive predictive value of a test: = Rises | Falls | Is unchanged | Becomes zero | Equals sensitivity
> Higher prevalence → higher PPV, lower NPV.
Q: The positive likelihood ratio is: = Sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity) | Specificity ÷ sensitivity | PPV ÷ NPV | (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity | TP ÷ TN
> LR+ ＝ sensitivity/(1 − specificity); LR− ＝ (1 − sensitivity)/specificity.

### Sample size
> - Depends on: effect size, variability (SD), power, α, one/two-tailed.
> - Smaller difference, bigger SD, higher power, smaller α → bigger sample.
> - Power usually 80% (90% in some RCTs); α 0.05.
> - Mean: n ＝ z²σ²/d². Proportion: n ＝ z²pq/d². Finite population correction when N is small.
> - Variability (SD) used for means, not proportions.
Q: Statistical power is the probability of: = Finding a significant difference when one truly exists | Rejecting a true null | A Type II error | Getting p < 0.05 always | Random error
> '...probability that a test will find a significant difference when there is truly one.'
Q: As the minimum expected difference (effect size) gets smaller, the required sample size: = Increases | Decreases | Stays the same | Becomes zero | Halves
> 'As difference becomes smaller, sample size increases.'
Q: Power is customarily set at: = 80% | 50% | 95% | 99% | 5%
> 'Customarily, power is set at 80% ... some RCTs seem to prefer 90%.'
Q: As the significance criterion (α) gets smaller, the sample size: = Increases | Decreases | Is unchanged | Becomes infinite | Is irrelevant
> 'The smaller the p-value, the larger the sample size.'
Q: Estimated measurement variability (SD) is used in sample size calculation for: = Means, not proportions | Proportions only | Both equally | Neither | Qualitative studies
> 'This variability is not computed for proportions but only for means.'
Q: Cochran's formula for estimating a proportion is: = n ＝ z²pq/d² | n ＝ z²σ²/d² | n ＝ ad/bc | n ＝ 1/ARR | n ＝ (Pₒ − Pₑ)/(1 − Pₑ)
> n ＝ z²pq/d² (q ＝ 1 − p, d ＝ margin of error); for means n ＝ z²σ²/d².
Q: Which is NOT one of the five parameters sample size depends on? = The journal's impact factor | Effect size | Measurement variability | Power | Significance criterion
> The five: effect size, variability, power, significance criterion, one- or two-tailed test.
Q: In Chan's (2003) RCT sample size formula, the power constant at 80% power is: = 7.9 | 1.96 | 10.5 | 0.8 | 2.58
> 'C ＝ power constant (7.9 at 80%, 10.5 at 90%).'

### Trials and meta-analysis
> - RCT — Bradford Hill; randomisation balances known and unknown confounders and prevents selection bias (allocation concealment).
> - Blocked, stratified, minimisation randomisation.
> - Superiority / equivalence / non-inferiority.
> - Cluster trials: randomise groups; unit of randomisation ＝ unit of analysis → need many clusters.
> - Meta-analysis coined by Glass 1976; PRISMA (systematic reviews/MA), MOOSE (observational). Forest plots.
> - Funnel plot asymmetry → publication bias; also time-lag, language, multiple publication, citation bias.
Q: The randomised controlled trial was developed by: = Bradford Hill | Gosset | Glass | Gauss | Cochran
> 'Developed by Bradford Hill.'
Q: Randomisation achieves even distribution of: = Known and unknown confounders | Known confounders only | Outcomes | Side effects only | Sample sizes only
> 'Even distribution of both known and unknown confounders.'
Q: Avoiding selection bias in randomisation depends on: = Allocation concealment | Blinding the statistician | Large samples only | Stratification only | Using a placebo
> 'Avoids potential selection bias (depends on allocation concealment).'
Q: A trial aiming to show that drug A is not worse than drug B is a: = Non-inferiority trial | Superiority trial | Equivalence trial | Cluster trial | Cross-over trial
> Non-inferiority — A is not inferior to B.
Q: According to the lecture, two-sided statistical tests are used for: = Equivalence trials | Superiority trials | Non-inferiority trials | All trials | No trials
> 'one-sided tests ... for superiority and non-inferiority trials while two-sided tests are performed for equivalence trials.'
Q: The main drawback of cluster randomised trials is that: = The unit of randomisation should be the unit of analysis, so many clusters are needed | They can't be blinded | They are always unethical | They need fewer participants | Confounders are ignored
> 'unit of randomisation should be the unit of data analysis ＝ large numbers of clusters are required.'
Q: Which is NOT a method to balance trial groups? = Alternate allocation by day of week | Blocked randomisation | Stratified randomisation | Minimisation | All are methods
> Balanced methods: blocked, stratified, minimisation. Alternate allocation is predictable — not proper randomisation.
Q: The term 'meta-analysis' was coined by: = Glass, a psychologist, in 1976 | Bradford Hill in 1948 | Cochrane in 1972 | Fisher in 1925 | Egger in 1997
> '"Meta-analysis" coined by Glass (Psychologist) in 1976.'
Q: The reporting guideline for systematic reviews and meta-analyses of trials is: = PRISMA | CONSORT | STROBE | MOOSE | STARD
> PRISMA — Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (Moher 2008).
Q: MOOSE guidelines apply to meta-analyses of: = Observational studies in epidemiology | RCTs | Diagnostic tests | Qualitative studies | Case reports
> MOOSE — Meta-analysis Of Observational Studies in Epidemiology.
Q: Publication bias can be detected with a: = Funnel plot | Forest plot | Box plot | Scatter plot | Kaplan-Meier curve
> 'Can be discovered using Funnel Plots ... Asymmetry → publication bias.'
Q: Positive results being published more quickly is called: = Time-lag bias | Language bias | Citation bias | Recall bias | Multiple publication bias
> Time-lag bias — positive results published more rapidly.
Q: The results of a meta-analysis are typically displayed as a: = Forest plot | Pie chart | Stem-and-leaf plot | Histogram | Bar chart
> Forest plots with effect sizes (weighted mean difference or odds ratio).
Q: Positive results being more likely to be published in English is: = Language bias | Citation bias | Time-lag bias | Selection bias | Attrition bias
> Language bias.
Q: Which Bradford Hill criterion is the only one essential for causation? = Temporality | Strength | Consistency | Biological gradient | Analogy
> Temporality — the cause must precede the effect.
Q: Analysing participants in the group they were randomised to, regardless of what they received, is: = Intention-to-treat analysis | Per-protocol analysis | Subgroup analysis | Interim analysis | Sensitivity analysis
> Intention-to-treat preserves the benefits of randomisation.
